# Ivo Mercado

Ivo is sixteen or seventeen, old enough to be useful, young enough to still feel trapped by usefulness.

He has grown up in the repair shop and knows too much about other people’s shoes. He can tell who drags their left foot when they’re tired, who buys expensive sneakers but walks like they expect puddles to apologize, who works on concrete, who stands all day, who is cheating on a spouse because they started taking care with polish again. He is often right, which has made him insufferable in small ways. He thinks this counts as insight. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it’s just judgment.

His background is narrow and dense: school, neighborhood, shop. He has not seen much of the world, which is partly why he is so hungry for the idea of elsewhere. He is embarrassed by the shop in the way only a child raised inside a thing can be embarrassed by it. The hand-painted sign. The ancient receipt spike. The smell of glue in his jacket. People his age lining up for new releases while he resoles old men’s work boots and reglues split midsoles for people who say “can you just do it cheap?”

He is good with his hands in a way that came before self-esteem. His grandmother taught him by making him watch, then making him do, then making him redo what he thought was good enough. He can stitch neatly, match thread by eye, clean suede without overworking it, and tell from the bend of a sole where a repair will fail again. He also has a habit of making little pronouncements he thinks sound sharp and worldly. For example:
- “You can tell a liar by toe box creases.”
- “Anybody who says they don’t care about shoes cares too much or not enough.”
- “People only want handmade if they can post it.”

Some of this is defensive intelligence. Some of it is adolescent nonsense.

His absent parent matters, but not in a melodramatic way. He has grown up around a gap and around his grandmother’s refusal to romanticize it. The parent left the trade and the neighborhood, maybe for good reasons, maybe not. Ivo tells himself he won’t end up stuck in the same little room, breathing in cement glue forever. But he also knows the work with embarrassing depth. He can’t help taking pride in a clean edge finish or a nearly invisible patch. He would die before admitting this early in the story.

Idiosyncrasies and grounding details:
- He cleans his fingernails with an awl without realizing he’s doing it.
- He sorts people automatically into “heel walkers,” “toe diggers,” “leaners,” “collectors,” “performers.”
- He has one pair of sneakers he babies and wipes with a soft cloth, while acting like hype culture is stupid.
- He hates when customers say “it’s just shoes.”
- He can smell wet leather, mildew, bargain glue, and expensive rubber compounds distinctly.
- He is terrible at texting back but remembers absurdly specific shoe models from three years ago.
- He is prone to silent, mean little observations he never says aloud—until stress makes him say one aloud and regret it.
- He is not especially brave. He is especially attentive.

His main flaw is that he confuses discernment with superiority. He thinks noticing more than other people exempts him from needing them. He is also embarrassed by tenderness, whether in himself or others. He’d rather sound bored than sincere. Under stress, he gets snappish and controlling, especially when someone handles tools wrong.

Physically, Ivo is all in-between stage: still growing into his limbs, narrow-shouldered, quick in the wrists. He has glue nicks on his fingers, a faint burn scar near one thumb knuckle, and the posture of someone always folding over a workbench. His clothes are practical but curated in small ways—shop apron over a carefully chosen hoodie, work pants with good pockets, one pair of shoes he keeps cleaner than the rest of his life. His face is expressive when he forgets himself: skepticism, annoyance, concentration, brief flashes of delight he tries to suppress. He carries himself with street-corner watchfulness and bench-worker precision. He touches objects before trusting them.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- He wants out, or thinks he does.
- He wants to be taken seriously, especially by people who do not understand how skilled his work is.
- He is loyal to his grandmother in practice more than in speech.
- He resents Hermes almost immediately but is drawn to his speed, ease, and obvious access to a larger world.
- He is vulnerable to Eris because she can articulate the humiliating truth in things he is already half-thinking.
- His real allegiance, whether he knows it or not, is to making things hold.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “If you wanted these dead, you could’ve just said so.”
- “That’s not wear and tear. That’s a decision.”
- “People always say ‘just glue it’ like glue is prayer.”

**Internal**
- Hermes looked like the kind of guy who said relax while setting your house on fire.
- The shoe wasn’t fake. Fake was easier. Fake had rules. This was worse: somebody had copied the wrong thing faithfully.

# Elena Mercado

Elena is Ivo’s grandmother, owner of the repair shop, and the real gravitational center of the story.

She did not set out to become keeper of a hidden trade. She inherited, endured, improved, and outlasted. Her authority comes less from mystique than from competence sharpened over decades. Gods, mortals, fools, athletes, widowers, strippers, nurses, cops, dancers, delivery guys—they all wear through soles in the end. Elena has handled them all, and she is not overawed by divinity. She thinks reverence is bad for business and bad for eyesight.

Her history should feel dense rather than fully explained. She has been doing this work a long time. Long enough to have seen styles cycle, neighborhoods turn, rents rise, and old powers change costume. Long enough to remember when the gods wore different things and still complained exactly the same way. She may have inherited divine clientele from her own elders, but what matters more is that she kept the shop alive through grief, departures, and bad years.

She is withholding, but not because she is a generic wise elder guarding lore. She withholds because explanation is labor, because she does not trust panic, because once you tell someone what world they’re in, they can’t untell it, and because a part of her resents always being the one who stays and keeps things going while others leave.

She is funny in a cutting, dry way. She does not banter. She skewers.
Examples:
- She calls Hermes “late again” before she calls him by name.
- She refers to gods collectively as “clients with delusions of grandeur.”
- If someone asks whether a repair is possible, she says, “Possible costs extra.”

Idiosyncrasies and grounding details:
- She keeps nails, eyelets, and lace tips in old mint tins sorted by year and metal.
- She talks to shoes under her breath while working, but not sentimentally—more like scolding.
- She writes down who owes what in a ledger she trusts more than any phone.
- She still sharpens certain tools by hand because “machines make people lazy.”
- She drinks coffee gone cold without noticing.
- She cuts thread with her teeth when irritated.
- She has a habit of tapping the counter twice when she’s made up her mind.
- She refuses to wear orthopedic shoes even though she should.
- She knows everyone’s feet hurt before they admit it.

Her flaws are substantial. She is controlling, secretive, and often unkind when afraid. She has let competence harden into authority. She has likely hurt both Ivo and Ivo’s parent with the logic of necessity: this has to be done, so stop making feelings about it. She can confuse endurance with virtue. She does not apologize well. When she is worried, she becomes harsher, not softer.

Physically, Elena is compact, strong through the forearms and back, moving with the economy of someone who hates wasting motion. She is not fragile, though age shows in the small accommodations she refuses to acknowledge: the hand pressed briefly to the workbench when standing, the slower turn of the neck. Her hair is practical, silver or steel-dark pulled back. Her clothes are utilitarian and permanent-looking: cardigan, apron, sturdy shoes she has repaired herself three times. Her face can seem severe until some tiny private amusement slips through. She handles tools like extensions of thought. She interacts with the world by testing it first.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- Her first allegiance is to the work itself: not to myth, not to glamour, to the fact of mending.
- She wants Ivo capable, not impressed.
- She may not want him in this life, but she absolutely does not want him helpless.
- She has a long, irritated history with Hermes; she likes him more than she thinks is prudent.
- She distrusts Eris not because Eris is chaotic in theory, but because she knows exactly what kind of damage she leaves behind for other people to clean up.
- She still carries unresolved anger at Ivo’s parent for leaving and unresolved guilt about why they left.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “He’s a god. That doesn’t make him special. It makes him expensive.”
- “Sit down if you’re bleeding. Stand up if you’re lying.”
- “New isn’t better. New is just not tested yet.”

**Internal-ish perspective line**
- The shoe would tell the truth if you held still long enough. People almost never did.

# Hermes

Hermes in this story should feel less like “the cool trickster archetype” and more like a man who has been getting by on speed and charm for so long that he has forgotten those are not the same as being reliable.

He is still funny, still quick, still impossible to ignore. But he is frayed. He has adapted well to the modern city because he understands movement, circulation, messages, transactions, shortcuts, and the psychology of people in transit. He belongs in train stations, delivery routes, curbs, alley mouths, bike lanes, late-night lights. Sneakers suit him because they let him belong anywhere people are moving fast and trying not to think too hard.

He is a bad client in concrete ways. He does not pay on time. He promises favors instead of money. He arrives bleeding and calls it “a scrape.” He treats urgency like weather. But he is not unserious. He is the first to feel when something is wrong in the city’s circulation, and this time he is genuinely scared—just unwilling to stand still long enough to show it plainly.

His idiosyncrasies:
- He steals sugar packets and leaves foreign coins as if this evens out.
- He always has too many things in his pockets: receipts, keys, a transit card from a city he’s not in, gum gone linty, notes meant for other people.
- He drinks whatever is nearest and then makes a face.
- He is impossible to keep seated while a repair sets.
- He says people’s names like he’s already halfway out the door.
- He cuts corners physically—vaults things, sidesteps lines, uses windows instead of doors if no one stops him.
- He notices exits before faces.

His flaws are central. He is unreliable, manipulative, evasive, and capable of making himself beloved in situations where he ought to be accountable. He lies by omission as a reflex. He recruits people into danger by sounding like danger is a favor. He hates owing anyone. He can mistake motion for care: if he is doing something, surely that counts as helping. Sometimes it doesn’t.

But he also has real tenderness, usually in flashes and sideways. He remembers tiny details about people. He knows who likes what pastry from which block. He knows which old man in the neighborhood should not be crossing alone. He carries messages others cannot bear. He does not sneer at mortal life; he is addicted to it.

Physically, Hermes is wiry, quick, and difficult to keep visually still. Even resting, he seems tilted toward his next movement. He dresses in the way of someone who could belong almost anywhere if you glanced fast enough: good jacket, worn hoodie, expensive-looking sneakers currently destroyed, a messenger bag or pockets that suggest constant transit. His smile comes easy; his fatigue shows in the split-second after it leaves. He touches counters, doorframes, the backs of chairs—testing paths. His face is more open than is wise, until it shuts all at once.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- He wants to keep traffic flowing—literal, social, divine.
- He is alarmed by the counterfeit movement because he recognizes unstable circulation when he sees it.
- He is allied with Elena out of long habit and earned trust, though he has strained it repeatedly.
- He likes Ivo quickly, partly because Ivo notices things, partly because irritation amuses him, partly because he sees talent.
- He is vulnerable to Eris because they are cousins in energy: both understand how quickly crowds tilt.
- His loyalty is real but undisciplined. He means well faster than he follows through.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “Tell me you can save them before you tell me what I did to them.”
- “I’m not late. Time and I have an understanding.”
- “That? That’s cosmetic catastrophe. The structural problem is different.”

**Internal-ish**
- The kid looked at shoes the way judges looked at evidence. Dangerous habit. Useful one.

# Eris

Eris should not enter as a grand villain draped in obvious chaos. She should feel like someone who knows exactly where to stand in a room to make everybody compare themselves to each other.

She is sharp, amused, socially gifted, and unsentimental. She understands status not as theory but as physics. She knows how people lean when they want to be seen wanting. She does not need to scream or smash to make trouble. She can do it by introducing one object, one rumor, one look, one tiny asymmetry. In a sneaker-drop context, she is in her element: scarcity, envy, aspiration, belonging, humiliation, performance. To her, this is not corruption of worship—it is worship in its most honest modern form.

What makes her more interesting than a pure antagonist is that she is partly right. People do pour devotion into objects. They do build identity around access and exclusion. They do long to win each other’s eyes. Eris is not inventing this. She is surfacing it, weaponizing it, enjoying it.

Her idiosyncrasies:
- She notices fakes immediately and is delighted by convincing ones.
- She compliments with surgical cruelty hidden inside.
- She rarely raises her voice; she leans closer instead.
- She adjusts other people’s collars, laces, hems without permission.
- She enjoys making people say what they want out loud.
- She is not precious about objects, but she understands exactly why others are.
- She laughs when people think they are immune to her.

She should not overexplain herself. Her perspective comes through in cuts and observations, not speeches. She sees hypocrisy very fast and presses on it. She is especially dangerous to someone like Ivo because she can make his private contempt feel like insight and his embarrassment feel like sophistication.

Her flaws:
- She is cruel.
- She confuses revelation with justification.
- She values truth when it destabilizes, not when it heals.
- She has a streak of boredom that makes her reckless with collateral damage.
- She likes being right more than she likes being loved.
- She underestimates labor because she prefers ignition to maintenance.

Physically, Eris is exact. Not necessarily glamorous in a maximal way—more devastatingly controlled. Her clothes are impeccably chosen but not loudly branded; she never needs a logo to win a room. Her sneakers should be uncanny not because they sparkle, but because they seem half a second ahead of trend, as if everyone else copied from a future she already got bored with. She moves with deliberate economy. She invades personal space gently. Her expressions are minute and therefore unnerving. She interacts with the world by tuning it, like an instrument she means to tighten until something snaps.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- She wants pressure. She wants exposure. She wants everyone to stop pretending wanting is noble only when it is quiet.
- She is loyal mainly to the principle of discord, but not in a cartoon sense; she believes systems become honest under strain.
- She likely has history with Hermes—mutual recognition, irritation, maybe even old fondness turned adversarial.
- She does not despise Elena; if anything, she respects her as someone who actually deals with consequences.
- She sees Ivo clearly and tries to recruit him not formally, but psychologically.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “No, keep the box. People love the box. It’s the waiting they’re really buying.”
- “You say ‘fake’ like desire stops counting when it’s embarrassing.”
- “Everybody wants to be chosen. I just save time.”

**Internal-ish**
- The boy had that useful age where humiliation still felt like revelation.

# Mateo Mercado

Mateo is Ivo’s absent parent—likely father, though you could shift this if needed. He does not need much page time, but he should exist as a real pressure in the story, not an abstract absence.

Mateo grew up in the same shop under Elena’s standards and left because he could not imagine surviving if every obligation became inheritance. He may now work in something adjacent but shinier—retail design, logistics, warehouse management, sales, or another trade entirely. What matters is not whether he “escaped,” but that his leaving created a script Elena and Ivo both live inside. Elena sees abandonment. Ivo sees possibility mixed with accusation. Mateo likely sees necessity and guilt.

He should not be idealized. He left work undone. He may send money irregularly, call inconsistently, or overcompensate with gifts he thinks are useful and Elena thinks are insulting. But neither should he be simplistically condemned. He may have left because the trade consumed too much, because secrecy bred silence, because he could not raise a child around constant emergency and obligation. His absence works best if it contains truth on all sides.

Idiosyncratic anchors:
- He buys expensive shoes but never breaks them in properly.
- He sends voice notes instead of calling because it lets him control the timing.
- He once relaced all his shoes in store-display style and Elena called him an idiot.
- He hates the shop smell because it clings.
- He says “Mom” and Elena says his full name when angry.

Physicality can remain lightly sketched in-story, mostly through remembered traits or photos. But as a person he is probably taller than Ivo, softer-handed now, carrying himself with the mild self-consciousness of someone who has spent years proving he belongs elsewhere. When he appears in memory, he is moving quickly, leaving.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- He wants less weight than Elena thinks a person should bear.
- He loves Ivo but is bad at the form that love requires.
- He and Elena are bound by resentment, competence, and resemblance.
- He is a warning and an invitation to Ivo at once.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “There’s staying, and then there’s disappearing into a place. Those aren’t the same.”
- “You act like leaving means I didn’t know how to do it.”
- “I know what the work is. That’s why I left.”

# Hephaestus

Hephaestus should appear briefly and memorably rather than becoming a lore machine.

He is a maker first, god second in terms of how he feels on the page. He respects use, hates posturing, and can tell in one look whether someone loves an object or merely wants to possess it. He has no patience for decorative reverence around craft. If he appears, it should be because the story needs one concentrated scene of another sensibility: large-scale divine making contrasted with Elena’s small-bench repair.

He is not warm exactly, but he is honest in a way the others are not. He understands failure in materials, in bodies, in plans. He is likely interested in Ivo because Ivo notices strain and compromise instead of just admiring finish.

Idiosyncrasies:
- He keeps broken prototypes.
- He talks to materials differently depending on whether they fought him.
- He dismisses “innovation” if it means bad construction with better marketing.
- He notices balance before beauty.
- He burns himself and does not react.

Physically, he should feel heavy, heat-marked, asymmetrical in some memorable way, with the calm of someone used to dangerous tools. He moves more slowly than Hermes but with complete confidence in space. He picks things up like he already knows their weak points.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- He cares that things function.
- He dislikes Eris’s counterfeit pressure because it mistakes volatility for liveliness.
- He respects Elena.
- He may offer Ivo not mentorship exactly, but recognition.

Flavour voice:

**Dialogue**
- “Anybody can make a thing shine. Make it last.”
- “Original is overrated. Useful is harder.”
- “If it fails where it always fails, that’s not fate. That’s design.”

## Chapter 1: Near Closing

By six-thirty the shop smelled like wet leather, old polish, and the glue Elena said was still better than anything legal now.

Ivo had the left sneaker in one hand and a bone folder in the other, working softened suede back into shape while rain ticked at the front window. The hand-painted sign on the glass—**MERCADO SHOE REPAIR**—had lost half its gold leaf years ago, so from outside it probably read **ERC D  SHOE EPAI**. Which, honestly, felt accurate.

On the stool beside him sat a paper cup of coffee gone cold and a box with somebody’s wedding shoes in it, tagged **RUSH** by a customer who had said rush in the tone people used when they meant my emergency should improve your character. Under the bench was a milk crate of pickups nobody had come back for: two loafers, one child’s boot, a pair of white sneakers yellowing into surrender.

His grandmother was in the back, where the old Landis machine sat like a cast-iron aunt nobody argued with. The machine clunked, paused, clunked again. Elena never hummed, never whistled, never talked to fill silence. When she worked, the whole shop took its pace from her hands.

Ivo turned the sneaker toward the light. Kids his age paid stupid money for this model, then walked like they were crossing a museum. This pair, at least, had lived a little. Mud dry in the grooves, heel drag on the right, toe-box crease honest and deep. College kid, probably. Too much standing around in them to be a runner. The suede nap had been brushed the wrong way with something desperate.

He called toward the back, “If he comes in and says he only wore them twice, I’m charging him for lying.”

From behind the machine, Elena said, “Add tax.”

That got a smile out of him despite himself.

The bell over the door gave a tired little ring. Ivo didn’t look up right away. “We’re closing in—”

He did look up then.

The man standing in the doorway had rain in his hair and blood soaking through one sock.

Not a lot of blood. Enough to make a point.

He was maybe thirty, maybe younger, maybe one of those people who looked expensive even when they were wrecked. Good jacket, dark hoodie, messenger bag hanging cross-body, face open in that dangerous way some people had when they expected the world to forgive them in advance. He was holding one sneaker by the laces.

The sneaker looked like it had been hit by a car and then struck by a better car.

Silver-gray high-top, sleek shape under all the damage. The sole had half-peeled away at the forefoot. The side panel was sliced open. Stitching had burst along the collar. At the ankle, threaded into the design, was a little wing worked in dull metallic embroidery.

Not a logo wing. Not decorative. Something about it made the back of Ivo’s neck tighten.

“Please,” the man said, and set the shoe on the counter with absurd care. “Tell me you can save these before you tell me what I did to them.”

Elena had gone still in the back.

Ivo set down the shoe he was holding. “If you wanted them dead, you could’ve just said so.”

The man smiled like that was encouraging. “So yes?”

Ivo picked up the ruined sneaker. It was wet and warmer than it ought to be. The upper smelled like rain, street heat, and something metallic underneath. Not blood exactly. Ozone, almost. The outsole was worn in a pattern that made no sense—heavy strike at toe and heel both, like the wearer had run uphill and fallen out of the sky in alternating steps.

He turned it over. There was grit embedded in the tread, gold-flecked and sharp. Not city grit. Too clean for that. The cut through the side panel wasn’t from scraping a curb or catching on exposed metal. It was smoother. As if something had passed through it without resistance, deciding late to become a blade.

“Where were you running,” Ivo said before he could stop himself, “through a blender?”

The man leaned both hands on the counter. Quick hands. Ringless fingers, scraped knuckles, little crescent scar at the base of one thumb. “Not running,” he said. “More of a strategic retreat.”

From the back, Elena said, “Late again.”

The man’s smile changed. Less performance in it. “Elena.”

She emerged wiping her hands on a rag, took one look at the shoe, then his sock, then his face. “Sit down if you’re bleeding.”

“It’s cosmetic catastrophe,” he said. “Structurally I remain excellent.”

“Sit.”

He sat.

Ivo looked from one of them to the other. “You know this guy?”

Elena gave him a look that meant stop being bright in public. To the man she said, “How bad?”

“Localized,” he said.

“How bad, not how fast.”

A flicker crossed his face then, there and gone. Real worry. It made him look younger and older at once.

“Bad enough I came here first.”

Elena held out her hand. “The other one.”

He hesitated, then unlaced the remaining sneaker and peeled it off carefully. His sock was indeed bloody, though the cut across the top of his foot had already crusted dark. Ivo stared before he could help it. The man’s foot was narrow, hard-used, the tendons standing sharp under the skin. Around the ankle bone, for just a second as the fabric caught, Ivo thought he saw the impression of another wing beneath the sock, as if something had pressed there for years.

Elena took the intact shoe and handed the ruined one back to Ivo. “Bench.”

“What?”

“Don’t stand there blinking. Put paper in the toe, open the side, tell me what failed.”

Ivo obeyed on reflex. He carried the shoe to the workbench under the front window, set it down, and reached for tissue, awl, spreader. The customer watched him with bright, restless attention, one knee jiggling.

Outside, rain silvered the street. Headlights dragged by. Across the block, the sneaker boutique with the blacked-out windows had a line barrier already stacked by the door for Saturday’s drop. Even closed, it looked smug.

Ivo slid tissue into the toe box, eased the torn panel apart, and hissed through his teeth.

“Well?”

Elena said.

He ran one finger lightly along the split seam. “This isn’t wear. Something cut through and the shoe kept moving after. Midsole delaminated from heat, not age. Stitching didn’t pop from stress first—the stress came after. And…” He pinched some of the grit from the outsole, rubbed it between finger and thumb. It glittered faintly against his skin. “What is this?”

The customer said, “Complicated.”

“Annoying,” Elena corrected.

Ivo looked up. “Seriously, who is this?”

The man opened his mouth.

Then, from somewhere outside, there came the sound of footfalls too fast to belong to a person.

Not a car, not a bike, not normal running. A rapid drumming approach that seemed to hit the pavement and the air both.

The customer was on his feet before the second beat.

The bell over the door rattled without opening. The glass shivered in its frame. Across the threshold, the shop mat—faded black, edges curling, **WELCOME** reduced to **WEL**—gave a tiny crackle like static.

Ivo looked down.

The little stitched wing at the sneaker’s ankle twitched under his hand.

Not like fabric in a draft.

Like muscle.

He dropped it.

The customer winced. “To answer your question,” he said.

The footfalls stopped directly outside.

Rain hissed.

Elena didn’t even turn her head. She only said, very tiredly, “Hermes. What did you bring to my door?”

## Chapter 2: Bad Client, Worse News

For a second nobody moved.

The thing outside did not knock. It paced once across the storefront, fast enough that Ivo only caught a blur through rain and gold lettering—something narrow, hooded maybe, with light skidding under its feet where light had no business skidding.

Hermes had gone still in a way he hadn’t while bleeding. That was worse.

Elena walked past both of them, flipped the deadbolt with one hand, and drew down the front shade halfway. The metal rattled. The blur outside passed again, and this time the glass whined softly, as if a fingertip had been dragged over it.

Ivo said, “Tell me that’s normal.”

“No,” said Hermes.

“Yes,” said Elena at the same time.

She shot Hermes a look. He raised both hands, surrendering the point.

The blur stopped. On the far side of the glass, at about shoulder height, something left three pale streaks like fingers in fog. Then it moved on. The too-fast footfalls receded down the block and were gone.

Only then did Hermes breathe out.

Ivo realized he had half-risen from his stool. He sat back down because standing there clutching an awl like an idiot would not improve anything.

Elena turned from the door. “Now,” she said. “Start again, this time use small words and don’t flatter yourself.”

Hermes dragged a hand through his wet hair. “I was trying to avoid involving you.”

“That’s how I knew it was serious.”

He gave her a quick, crooked grin that didn’t reach the rest of him. “You always did know me.”

“Unfortunately.”

Ivo looked between them. “Can somebody tell me why my floor just twitched?”

Hermes glanced at him, then at the shoe on the bench. “Because I stepped on it.”

“That clears everything right up.”

Elena pulled out the chair by the counter and sat, rag still in one hand. “You can panic later,” she told Ivo. “Pay attention first.”

Which was her version of kindness, so he did.

Hermes leaned back against the counter, favoring his uncut foot. “There’s a piece missing,” he said.

“A piece of what?” Ivo asked.

Elena said, “Work.”

That was somehow less helpful.

Hermes nodded toward the cellar door behind the counter. “Old work. Old enough most people forgot it was still moving around. It shouldn’t have been loose to begin with.”

“Nothing should be loose to begin with,” Elena said. “Things get loose because people don’t maintain them.”

“Thank you, yes, I can feel the moral lesson from here.”

She didn’t blink. “Good.”

Ivo folded his arms. “You’re both doing this on purpose.”

Hermes looked at him as if noticing, maybe for the first time, that Ivo was not furniture. “Your grandmother repairs for unusual clients.”

“Understatement of the century,” Ivo muttered.

“She also keeps certain things no one else should be trusted with.” Hermes tapped the counter once, then seemed to think better of fidgeting under Elena’s eye. “Patterns. Old forms. Work that gets copied into later work. Most of the time that’s harmless. Somebody borrows a stitch, a shape, an idea about balance. That’s what craft is. But one particular piece—”

“Don’t mythologize it,” Elena said.

“I wasn’t.”

“You were winding up.”

Hermes blew air through his nose. “Fine. There was an old sole fragment. A template, if you like. Been patched more times than either of us can count. A lot of later shoes were made from it, or corrected by it, or measured against it. Not because it was holy.” He looked at Ivo. “Because it worked.”

That, at least, sounded sane.

“Worked how?” Ivo asked.

Hermes spread a hand. “For movement. For holding shape under pressure. For crossing from one kind of place into another without coming apart.”

“Road shoe,” Elena said. “Not display.”

Hermes pointed at her. “Exactly.”

Ivo stared at the ruined sneaker on the bench. “And somebody stole it.”

Hermes made a face. “Borrowed. Split. Started copying.”

“Poorly,” Elena said.

“Very.”

Ivo looked at the jagged side panel, the half-peeled sole, the metallic dust still bright on his fingertips. “Those weren’t copies in a factory.”

“No,” said Hermes. “Those were test runs.”

A laugh tried to come out of Ivo and failed. “You’re saying there are fake magic sneakers in the neighborhood.”

Elena snapped, “Don’t say magic like you’re six.”

“Then what do I call—” He gestured at the door, the twitching wing, the blood, all of it. “This?”

“Work,” she said again. Then, after a beat: “And trouble.”

Hermes was watching him with that bright, measuring attention of his. “You already saw the damage pattern.”

“So?”

“So most people don’t. Most people see expensive ruined shoes and assume the story is money or stupidity.” His mouth twitched. “Usually they’re right. But not always.”

Ivo didn’t like how that felt, being noticed. “Congratulations,” he said. “I have eyes.”

“You have hands,” Elena said. “Better. If you used your head more, I could retire.”

“You say that like it’s my fault you won’t.”

“It is everyone’s fault I won’t.”

Hermes pushed himself upright from the counter. Restless again. “The point is, whoever’s doing the copying is building toward Saturday.”

Ivo glanced toward the blacked-out boutique across the street. They’d had a line around the corner last month for a collaboration drop that made three separate boys nearly cry. “The release.”

“Mm.”

“Why?”

Hermes gave him a look that suggested the answer should have been obvious. “Crowds. Wanting. Pace. Compression. Scarcity. All that lovely modern devotion packed heel to heel before sunrise.”

Elena said, “Eris.”

Not a question.

Hermes rubbed at the back of his neck. “That would be my guess.”

Ivo had heard the name before, in school maybe, in stories half-remembered. Golden apple, trouble, vanity contest. It sounded ridiculous in the fluorescent light of the shop.

“She does shoes now?” he said.

Hermes barked a laugh. “She does whatever people are foolish enough to make easy.”

Elena got up, crossed to the bench, and picked up the ruined sneaker by the tongue. The little wing lay still now, damp and stupid-looking, which somehow made it worse. “And you brought this here because?”

“Because I need them repaired.”

“Besides the obvious.”

Hermes’s face lost its joke entirely. “Because if she’s fragmenting that old pattern into release pairs, I need to know how far she’s gotten and where the copies are breaking.”

The silence after that had weight to it.

Ivo said, more quietly, “What happens if she does?”

Hermes looked toward the rain-dark window. “You ever watch a crowd decide there aren’t enough of something? Really watch it?”

Ivo thought of boys pressed to the boutique glass, phones up, pretending they weren’t shaking. Thought of a fight outside the bodega last summer over a raffle ticket. Thought of shoes dropped and trampled in the street.

“Yeah,” he said.

Hermes nodded. “Now imagine the shoes help.”

That sat in the room like a bad smell.

From outside came another sudden burst of motion—a body, a runner, human this time maybe, shooting past the half-drawn shade so fast Ivo only saw a stripe of white sole and a face stretched open in something between glee and terror. There was a woman on the sidewalk who yelped and jumped back, grocery bag swinging. The runner clipped the curb, caught himself impossibly, and kept going. For two steps after he’d gone, faint sparks spat from the wet pavement.

Ivo swore.

Elena was already moving. She stepped to the door, listened, then looked back at Ivo. “Lock up.”

“What?”

Ivo stared at her. “Downstairs?”

Hermes gave him an apologetic shrug that managed to be both sheepish and irritating. “Bad night to learn the family trade, I know.”

Ivo didn’t move.

Elena tapped the counter twice. Decision made.

“Lock up,” she said. “And bring the shoe.”

## Chapter 3: The Cellar and the Track Marks

The cellar steps were older than the building had any right to be.

That was Ivo’s first thought carrying Hermes’s ruined sneaker down behind Elena, one hand on the rail, the other curled around the shoe by its wet laces. The stairs should have led under a narrow neighborhood shop with a leaking back wall and two and a half generations of bad wiring. Instead they kept going another turn past where the foundation ought to have ended.

“Elena,” Hermes said behind him, a little out of breath now that nobody was watching. “If there’s one of those old bulbs swinging down there, I’m leaving.”

“There is,” Elena said.

“Cruel.”

“You survived empire. You can survive atmosphere.”

The cellar smelled cool and dry, not moldy like basements usually did. Dust, oil, cedar, leather gone sweet with age. Elena reached the bottom, pulled a chain, and one naked bulb did indeed come on overhead, yellow and mean.

Ivo stopped on the last step.

The room was not large, which somehow made it stranger. Shelves lined the walls. Wooden forms by the dozens, pairs and singletons. Boxes with old handwritten tags. Tin drawers. Wrapped bundles of fabric. A row of shoes set high on one long shelf, each one unlike anything sold in any store he’d ever entered and all of them worn in some intimate, undeniable way: cracked sandals with bronze-green buckles, mud-stiff boots with nails in the heels, a silk slipper gone gray at the toe, black trainers so plain they looked almost ashamed of themselves.

At the center stood a bench older than the one upstairs and cleaner. Not clean as in unused. Clean as in respected.

“This is inventory?” Ivo said.

“This is work,” Elena said.

Hermes limped past him and sat on an overturned crate without being told this time. He looked around with the expression of someone who had passed through a hundred places and still recognized a sanctuary when he saw one. “You kept the river pair.”

Elena didn’t look at him. “I keep what’s instructive.”

Ivo moved closer to the shelves. Nothing glowed. Nothing rang. That almost made it worse. They were just shoes. Shoes with cracked straps, replaced heels, visible repairs, old stains impossible to romanticize. A pair of running shoes with one sole rebuilt twice over. A work boot patched at the ankle with leather from a different boot entirely.

He pointed at the shelf. “Those are theirs?”

“Some of them,” said Elena. “Some are people who mattered to them. Same difference, often.”

Hermes let his head fall back against the wall. “That is not a reassuring sentence.”

Elena ignored him. She went to a set of shallow drawers under the bench and pulled one open. Inside lay lasts wrapped in cloth, sole patterns cut from thick board, envelopes, and one ledger swollen with paper slips. She lifted out a bundle tied in waxed string and set it on the bench.

Ivo put Hermes’s sneaker down more carefully than he meant to.

Elena untied the string. Inside was not a whole sole, not a relic polished into importance, just a warped fragment of old material the size of a hand. Leather? Rubber? Something between. Dark with age, edges scarred and reworked, stitch holes crossing stitch holes where it had been patched, cut down, patched again. Someone had written tiny notes along one edge in at least three different inks.

It was ugly.

It was also the most handled object in the room.

“That?” Ivo said.

Hermes opened one eye. “That.”

“It looks like trash.”

“It looks,” Elena said, “like something that kept being useful.”

He shut up.

She touched one scarred edge with a blunt finger. “No one worshipped this. That’s why it lasted. People used it, corrected from it, copied its balance, checked repairs against it. Then they put it away before they got sentimental.”

Hermes said, “Until somebody took it apart.”

Ivo leaned in. The fragment had the same kind of hand-done irregularity he’d found in the counterfeit damage: not machine-perfect, but stable because of the decisions inside it. Tiny asymmetries compensating for stress. A curve adjusted half a degree where weight must have landed badly. He could almost feel the logic through his fingertips.

“Where’s the rest?” he asked.

Elena looked at him. “If it were here, he wouldn’t be bleeding on my floor.”

Hermes lifted two fingers. “In fairness, I bled very neatly.”

“Quiet.”

She turned to another drawer, took out a wrapped object, and unrolled it. Inside was a piece of sole from something much newer—foam, rubber, tread pattern half-burned away. Hermes’s jaw tightened.

“Found near Canal three nights ago,” Elena said. “Before he came embarrassing himself at my counter. I was waiting to see if it was stupidity or pattern.”

“It’s pattern,” Hermes muttered.

Ivo picked up the newer fragment in one hand, the old one in the other. They were not identical. Not close. But the relationship between them was obvious in the way family resemblance is obvious: a line through the midfoot, the distribution of pressure points, the flex groove cut where it shouldn’t have mattered but did.

“Whoever copied this,” he said slowly, “didn’t understand why it works.”

Hermes sat forward. “Go on.”

Ivo hated being put on display and hated even more that he had something to say. “The old piece adjusts for uneven load. It expects impact from weird angles. This one—” he lifted the newer fragment “—just exaggerates the forward drive. It’s all push. No correction. No recovery.” He looked at the burn line across the edge. “That’s why it blows out.”

For the first time Elena’s face shifted by half a degree toward approval.

Hermes pointed at him. “That. That’s why I came.”

“Don’t point in my shop,” Elena said automatically.

“This is your cellar.”

“Then definitely don’t point.”

Ivo set the pieces down. “So what now? We wait for your chaos goddess to hand out exploding shoes?”

Hermes got up too fast and had to catch himself on the bench. “No. We find where the copies are being made.”

“With what address?” Ivo asked. “To the back room of bad ideas?”

“With the shoes,” Elena said.

She was already reaching for Hermes’s ruined sneaker. She opened the torn side panel wider, then handed it to Ivo. “Read it.”

He frowned. “I’m not a psychic.”

“No. You’re a cobbler. Better.”

So he looked.

Not at the glitter, not at the ridiculous little wing, not at Hermes trying not to hover. He looked at the strain marks, the angle of the split, the grit embedded in the rubber, the odd fine dust caught in the lace eyelets. One black hair trapped in the collar lining—not Hermes’s; too coarse. A smear near the heel where another sole had clipped it in passing. The counterfeit’s tread pattern had a shallow diamond nick missing at the edge.

He remembered the sound outside. The runner. The sparks on wet pavement.

“He got passed on the left,” Ivo said. “Close. Whoever hit this lands hard on the forefoot and twists out. Not a trained runner. Somebody juiced by the shoe.”

Hermes grinned despite himself. “Juiced.”

“Shut up. And…” Ivo bent closer. “There’s resin in the tread. Cheap customization kind. Heat-set. Smells sweet when it burns.”

Elena’s eyes sharpened. “From where?”

Ivo thought. There were three places within walking distance that did after-market work on hype pairs. Two were fronts for idiots with heat guns. One, in the alley behind the boutique, actually knew how to take a shoe apart and put it back together.

He looked up. “Val’s old print room behind Blacktop.”

Hermes was already reaching for his other shoe.

Elena slapped his hand away. “You are not going anywhere until I wrap that foot.”

“I can move.”

“You can limp.”

“I excel at limping.”

“Then limp in ten minutes.”

Ivo was still staring at the bench. At the old fragment, the blown-out copy, the mess of lineage between them. At all the years of hands that had repaired, adjusted, passed along. Work, his grandmother kept saying. Not magic. Work.

Upstairs, muffled through floorboards, a siren rose and fell somewhere toward the avenue.

Elena began bandaging Hermes’s foot with brutal efficiency. “Get your jacket,” she told Ivo.

He looked at her. “I’m going too?”

She gave him a flat stare. “If you’re going to make yourself useful, start now.”

Hermes flashed him a bright, tired smile. “Congratulations. Terrible night to leave the house.”

Ivo grabbed his jacket off the peg by the stairs.

On the way up, he took the counterfeit fragment with him. It was still faintly warm.

## Chapter 4: Counterfeit

Rain had thinned to a cold mist by the time they stepped into the alley behind Blacktop.

The alley always smelled faintly of cardboard and fryer oil from the Thai place on the corner, but tonight there was something sweeter under it: heated resin, singed rubber, solvent. Ivo would have recognized it blind. Customization smell. The kind that clung to little back rooms where men with ring lights and scalpels called themselves artists because they could distress a midsole on purpose.

Blacktop’s front shutters were down. The mural on the side wall—a giant sneaker dissolving into roses and flames—gleamed wetly under the security light. Behind the boutique, the old loading door stood open three inches.

Hermes rolled his injured foot once and hissed. Elena heard it and didn’t bother to hide her satisfaction.

“You see?” she said.

“I was stretching.”

“You were making regret noises.”

“I make beautiful noises.”

“Not in my hearing.”

Ivo raised a hand before they could keep going. “If Val’s in there, let me talk first.”

Hermes blinked at him. “You know him?”

“Everybody knows him. He used to print fake tour shirts, now he ‘ages’ sneakers for rich kids who want to look like they had a childhood.” Ivo adjusted his hood and wiped his palm on his jeans. “He likes me.”

Elena gave him a sidelong glance. “Does he pay on time?”

“No.”

“Then he doesn’t like you. He uses you.”

Hermes, unhelpfully, looked delighted.

They went in.

The room beyond the loading door had once been storage and now wanted badly to be a studio. Shelves stacked with boxes, rolls of vinyl, jars of pigment, spare laces hanging from nails, a heat press in the corner, worktables spotted with paint. Ring lights. A cheap speaker. A pegboard of tools arranged for social media. On one wall, six sneakers sat on floating shelves like museum pieces, each one customized to death.

Val himself was nowhere in sight.

Ivo moved first, weaving through the tables. He could hear Hermes behind him, not as quiet as he thought, and Elena behind both of them, walking like she had every right to search the place.

On the nearest table lay a half-disassembled pair of white leather low-tops, their uppers peeled open and masking tape striping the sides. Next to them sat a tray of soles in clear plastic sleeves. Too many soles.

Ivo touched one.

Warm.

He picked it up and turned it over. The tread pattern was fresh, but the rubber had been dusted with something dark and fine. Under the lamp he saw tiny gold flecks in it, like the grit from Hermes’s shoe but ground down and mixed through.

“Here,” he said.

Hermes came to his shoulder. His expression changed immediately. “Don’t put that on.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“Good. Because it would probably turn your bones into an opinion.”

“That sentence means nothing.”

“It means no.”

Elena took the sole from Ivo and sniffed it. “Cheap pour,” she said. “Fast mold. The fool who made this knows enough to be dangerous and not enough to be alive for long.”

Something clattered in the back room.

Hermes moved.

He was fast even injured, a blur around the edge of the table and through the hanging strip curtain. Ivo followed because standing still while gods went out of sight felt worse than moving.

Val was on the floor among cartons of laces and folded apparel blanks, hands up over his head.

“Don’t,” he said to no one and everyone. “I said I was done.”

He looked terrible. Eyes bloodshot, apron smeared black, one cheek blistered red as if he’d leaned too close to a heat gun. Beside him lay a pair of sneakers with their soles split cleanly down the middle.

Hermes crouched. “Who’s after you?”

Val squinted up at him. “You’re not the one from before.”

“No.”

“That’s… somehow not comforting.”

Ivo pushed past Hermes. “Val.”

Val focused on him with visible relief. “Mercado. Thank God.”

“Not him,” Hermes said.

“Who cares?” Val dragged himself backward until his shoulders hit a stack of boxes. “I told her I was out.”

Elena had arrived in the doorway, and Val flinched harder at her than he had at Hermes. “Mrs. Mercado.”

“Valentino.” She took in the room in one sweep. “You should be ashamed.”

“I am,” he said instantly. “Deeply. Productively. Can we make that enough?”

Ivo crouched and looked at the split shoes. The uppers were decent work, but the sole join was wrong. Too stiff through the arch, too eager at the toe. Overcorrected. He picked one up. The edges were scorched.

“How many?” he asked.

Val swallowed. “I didn’t know what it was.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Enough for a sample run. Not the whole release. I’m not stupid.”

Elena made a low sound in her throat that suggested she considered that debatable.

Hermes said, “Who brought you the pattern?”

Val laughed once, a terrible little sound. “Nobody brings a pattern anymore. They bring a file, a mood board, references, a panic attack. She brought me one sole and said copy the feeling.”

That got everyone’s attention.

“She?” Ivo said.

Val looked at him like maybe he was the only sane person in the room, which was insulting. “Tall. Beautiful. Mean in a classy way. Knew more about construction than she should. Didn’t blink enough.”

“Eris,” Hermes said.

“See, now, I didn’t ask her name on account of survival.”

Ivo turned the split shoe over in his hands. There it was again—that family resemblance to the old fragment downstairs, but mangled into pure aggression. Push and push and push. No give. No correction.

“Why’d you do it?” he asked.

Val looked at the room as if the answer were hanging from the walls. “Because Blacktop got the drop. Because if I touched the collab before release, I’d be set for six months. Because she paid cash and talked like she already knew the part where I said no.” He rubbed his face with both hands. “And because when she left that sole here, every idea I’d had for the last year suddenly felt slow.”

Hermes’s expression flattened. “That’s not inspiration.”

“No,” said Elena. “That’s bait.”

Val nodded miserably. “Figured that out around pair seven.”

“Where are they now?” Hermes asked.

Val pointed at the front room. “Some there. Some already gone to pre-release seeding. Influencer nonsense. Hype shots. Friends-and-family pairs.” He looked at Ivo. “I didn’t know they’d… do that.”

“Do what?” Ivo asked.

Val stared at him. “Move.”

No one spoke for a second.

Then from the street out front came a sudden shout, the scrape of sneakers on wet concrete, and the unmistakable sound of bodies colliding.

Hermes was upright in an instant.

They pushed through the workroom and out to the loading door. In the mouth of the alley, two boys were grappling over a shoebox while a third one hopped uselessly around them with one shoe on and one off, screaming at both. The boy missing the shoe moved wrong—too quick in stuttering bursts, his planted foot chewing sparks from the pavement when he twisted.

“Take it off!” Ivo shouted before he could stop himself.

The kid looked at him wild-eyed and did the opposite, bolting.

He made three impossible strides, hit a slick patch, and went down hard enough that the whole alley seemed to flinch. The shoe flew off, slammed into a dumpster, and split at the sole with a crack like a snapped branch.

The kid lay there gasping, not broken, just shocked.

Hermes was already over him. Elena was already picking up the shoe with a rag so she wouldn’t touch the inside directly. Ivo stared.

The sole fragment exposed in the split was dark, old-looking, and scarred—not ancient itself, but copied from something ancient by someone who had mistaken violence for speed.

Eris wasn’t here, but she was in the room anyway. In the speed of the kid’s stupid grin before he fell. In the way the other two boys were still glaring at each other over an empty box. In the sweetness of hot resin and panic.

Val said behind them, very softly, “She said people wanted to feel chosen.”

Elena turned the broken sneaker in her hands and looked at Ivo.

Not at Hermes. At Ivo.

“You see it now?” she said.

He did. Not the whole shape of it, not yet. But enough.

The wrong thing had been copied faithfully.

And Saturday was still two days away.

## Chapter 5: What Gets Worn

By midnight, Hermes was asleep in the chair by the polish wall with his head tipped back and his mouth slightly open like a man who would deny both under oath.

Elena had wrapped his foot again after they got back from Val’s. “Because I’m not wasting good repairs on bad healing,” she’d said, which Hermes, already sagging with exhaustion, had accepted like tenderness.

Now the front lights were off except for the lamp over the bench. Outside, the rain had stopped. The street shone empty and dark, the boutique across the way a black rectangle holding its breath for Saturday.

Ivo sat at the workbench with the broken counterfeit pair from the alley laid out on brown paper. Elena had given him one half and kept the other. Between them sat the old fragment from downstairs, wrapped and unwrapped now so many times it seemed to resent cloth.

There were easier ways to spend a Friday night than comparing severed soles under a task lamp while a bleeding god slept in the corner. He was aware of this. He was also aware that he hadn’t wanted to go upstairs, hadn’t wanted his bed, hadn’t wanted normal back.

Elena pared blackened foam from the broken edge with a blade so sharp it whispered. “Too much front load,” she said.

“I know.”

“Say it correctly anyway.”

He gritted his teeth. “Too much forward bias, no recovery through midfoot, correction line copied but not understood.”

She nodded once. “Better.”

On the radio, very low, a late-night host laughed at something in another room of the world.

Ivo held the counterfeit sole fragment up beside the old one. The resemblance was there, but not in the way copies usually worked. Not brand to knockoff, not direct theft. This was more intimate than that. Somebody had touched the old logic and pulled out only the part they found exciting.

“Why keep it?” he asked.

Elena didn’t look up. “Keep what?”

“The old piece. If it’s this much trouble.”

“Because throwing things away doesn’t stop fools from reinventing them badly.”

He snorted.

She scraped another curl of foam. “Also because it was earned.”

That made him look at her. “By who?”

Elena set the blade down. For a moment she only flexed her left hand, working out a stiffness she would have denied if asked. Then she reached behind her without turning and took a box from the shelf.

Inside were a pair of shoes Ivo had seen only once before, years ago, and been told not to touch. Not divine-looking. Just old. Black leather trainers, low and plain, the kind nobody would notice until they saw how beautifully they had been worn. The left heel had been rebuilt twice. The lining was patched with a scrap of dark blue fabric.

“Whose?” he asked.

“A courier,” Elena said. “Long dead.”

“That narrows it down.”

“One of his, once.” She nodded toward Hermes without affection. “Not him. One of the men before. Messages through war. Through plague. Through borders that changed names faster than maps could print them. He wore through six pairs in my grandfather’s care and this was the pair that lasted because he stopped asking for new ones and started mending the old.”

Ivo looked at the shoes again. They were not important-looking. That was what made them important.

Elena took one out and turned it over in her hands. “People think sacred means untouched. That is because they’ve never had to keep anything alive.”

The radio crackled. Hermes snored once, very softly, then stopped as if embarrassed in his sleep.

Ivo stared at the old sole fragment on the bench. Stitches over stitches. Cuts corrected by later cuts. A thing made durable not by perfection but by being worth another attempt.

“She wants the feeling,” he said.

Elena glanced at him.

“Val said Eris told him to copy the feeling.” He rubbed his thumb over the edge of the counterfeit. “That’s what this is. Not the sole. Not even the pattern. Just the push. The chosen part.”

“People are very good at wanting the effect without the structure.”

Ivo almost smiled. “You should paint that on the wall.”

“I don’t decorate.”

He hesitated, then said, “Why didn’t you tell me?”

Elena put the courier’s shoe back in its box. “Tell you what.”

“Any of it.”

She was quiet long enough that he thought she might not answer. Hermes shifted in the chair. Outside, a car rolled by slow enough to make the glass hum.

Finally she said, “Because children like secrets until the secret asks them to work.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is mine.”

He sat back, anger flickering up because it was easier than the other thing under it. “You could’ve at least told me I wasn’t crazy.”

“You weren’t seeing enough yet to be useful with the truth.”

“That’s a horrible way to talk to a person.”

“It kept you a child for a little longer.”

He laughed once, sharp. “Did it?”

Her face changed then, not softening, exactly. Just showing wear. “Your father thought leaving would do a better job.”

The room went still around the sentence.

Ivo set down the sole in his hand very carefully. Elena rarely brought him up directly. The absence had its own furniture in the shop; everyone knew where not to bump into it.

“He left because of this?” Ivo asked.

“He left because of many things.”

“That’s not an answer either.”

“No.” She picked up the blade again, then set it down. “He was good with uppers. Better than me at finishing edges when he was your age. Too vain, but precise. He hated repairs. Always wanted to make from scratch. New looked cleaner to him. Less compromise.”

Ivo didn’t say anything.

“He thought the work took too much,” she went on. “Not just time. Attention. Obligation. He said there was always another emergency, another pair at the door, another favor owed to people who never bled where anyone could see it.” She finally looked at him. “He wasn’t wrong.”

“So maybe he was smart.”

“Maybe.”

That was almost worse than a fight.

Hermes spoke from the chair without opening his eyes. “He was also bad at lasting.”

Both of them turned.

Hermes lifted one hand vaguely. “Sorry. Was asleep. Accidentally heard everything.”

Elena said, “Then apologize properly.”

“Absolutely not.” He cracked one eye. “For what it’s worth, leaving and lasting aren’t opposites. Plenty of people do both badly.”

Ivo should have told him to mind his own business. Instead he said, “Did he know you?”

Hermes looked at the ceiling. “Since he was small enough to untie other people’s laces for fun.”

“And?”

“And he wanted a life that ended at the edges of itself.” Hermes closed his eye again. “Can’t blame him. Terrible profession, this.”

Elena made a dismissive sound, but not a hard one.

Ivo looked back at the old fragment.

People did worship now, he thought. They just didn’t call it that. They lined up in the dark. They watched unboxings like devotionals. They cared about what touched the ground and what that said about who they got to be. It was ridiculous. It was real. Eris wasn’t wrong about that part.

The problem was what she did with it.

He picked up the broken counterfeit sole, then the old fragment, feeling the difference in balance between them. One wanted to be seen. One wanted to work.

“You can’t lock it back up,” he said.

Elena’s gaze sharpened. “No.”

“Because she’ll just keep copying the worst part.”

“Yes.”

Ivo looked toward the blacked-out boutique across the street. In a few hours people would start camping out. Coolers, folding chairs, phone chargers, little social hierarchies forming in the dark. Wanting with witnesses.

He took a breath.

“So we don’t go to stop a relic from being stolen,” he said. “We go to stop bad construction.”

Hermes smiled with his eyes still shut. “Now you’re speaking my language.”

“That’s unfortunate,” Ivo said.

Elena tapped the bench twice. Decision made.

“Get some sleep,” she said. “We go before dawn.”

## Chapter 6: The Drop Line

At four-thirty in the morning the line already curved around the corner.

Ivo saw it from half a block away: folding chairs, hoodies, blankets, puffer jackets, coffee cups balanced on milk crates, the little islands of forced intimacy that formed whenever strangers agreed to wait for the same thing. The boutique’s black windows reflected them back in long strips. **BLACKTOP** glowed above the door in narrow white letters, looking calm and superior.

Saturday had come cold and clear after the rain. The sidewalk still held last night in the cracks. Breath showed. A kid in a varsity jacket was asleep upright against a parking meter. Two girls near the front were taking turns filming each other with the line behind them, one making bored face, then excited face, then bored face again. Somewhere someone had brought a camping stove. Coffee and bacon drifted over everything in waves.

“This is deranged,” Hermes said, not without admiration.

Elena adjusted the strap on the canvas tool bag she’d brought and said, “People have always stood in line for nonsense. This is just more expensive nonsense.”

Ivo kept his hands in his pockets and scanned feet automatically. Good habit, today worse than usual. New releases from three years back. Beaters held together with hope. Work boots on security. One kid in house slippers. There were already fights hidden in the line if you knew how to read posture: shoulders too square, feet planted too wide, one guy bouncing on his toes because he had not slept and had mistaken adrenaline for destiny.

The counterfeit pattern was harder to spot until he stopped looking at shoes and started looking at how people moved in them.

Tiny surges. Little overeager recoveries. As if the crowd kept almost leaning into a run.

“They’re seeded already,” he said.

Hermes followed his gaze. “How many?”

“Enough.”

Across the street, a reseller van idled with two men inside pretending not to stare. At the end of the block, a police cruiser rolled by and kept going. Nobody wanted to own this kind of morning unless it got ugly enough to film.

Blacktop staff moved inside behind the glass, setting out stanchions and branded bags. Every motion looked rehearsed.

One of the staff cracked the door and called, “Wristbands in twenty!” and the line tightened like a muscle.

Ivo felt it physically. Not panic. Not yet. But pressure had found somewhere to go.

Hermes had put on his repaired sneaker and one borrowed boot from the shop’s pile of unclaimed practicals, which made him look insane in a way he was pretending not to notice. He rolled his shoulders, restless. “I can do a pass.”

“No,” Elena said.

“I can identify the hot pairs.”

“You can inflame a queue.”

“I can be subtle.”

Elena and Ivo both looked at him.

Hermes sighed. “Cruelly judged.”

Ivo’s eyes kept snagging on the line. A boy maybe thirteen wore a pair too big for him, pristine except for one sole edge dusted dark. A woman with immaculate eyeliner and a folding stool had a tote bag full of chargers and snacks and one foot tapping too fast. A broad-shouldered man near the barricade kept shifting his weight forward as though the pavement were pulling him by the knees.

Not all of them. Not enough to call obvious. Enough to spread.

A black car slid up to the curb and stopped without fanfare. No one in line paid it much attention, which was somehow the slickest thing about it. The door opened. A woman stepped out.

Eris did not look theatrical. That was the first thing. No dramatic coat, no blood-red anything, no visible effort. Dark wool, clean lines, hair pulled back, sneakers so understated they made every other pair nearby seem needy. If you looked too fast, you might not have remembered her face a second later. If you looked properly, you would remember it too long.

She closed the car door herself. No driver got out. She glanced once up and down the line and smiled, though not at anyone in particular.

Several people nearby immediately adjusted themselves. Straightened. Checked their phones. Looked at each other.

Hermes muttered, “Oh, don’t start.”

Eris crossed the street and stopped in front of Blacktop like she was waiting for a restaurant table. Her gaze passed over Hermes, Elena, then landed on Ivo.

Not surprise. Recognition.

“Mercado,” she said, as if they had met and he had forgotten. Her voice was soft enough to make listening feel like leaning in. “You came.”

Ivo hated the way his stomach moved. “You know me?”

“I know your type.” Her eyes dropped briefly to his hands, the little glue shine still trapped at the cuticles no matter how much he scrubbed. “Useful. Proud. Underpraised.”

Elena stepped between them by half an inch, which on Elena counted as a bodily threat. “Go play somewhere else.”

Eris looked delighted. “Mrs. Mercado. I hoped you’d be here. Nothing gets interesting in this city without eventually becoming your cleanup.”

“That’s because you leave filth.”

A boy in line nearby laughed too loud at something nobody had said. Two places up, a woman snapped, “Hey, watch your spot,” and the answer came back sharp enough to hook.

Eris tipped her head, listening to the line the way musicians listen backstage to a crowd finding its rhythm. “Listen to that. All this wanting before sunrise.” She looked at Ivo again. “And people say the old gods are dead.”

Ivo said, “You’re going to get somebody killed.”

She shrugged, almost regretful. “People do more dangerous things for less honest reasons every day.”

Hermes stepped forward. “You used a broken pull.”

“I used the part they actually came for.”

“That’s the problem.”

“No,” said Eris, still watching Ivo. “The problem is that everyone here will say they love the object when what they love is being near the win.”

Inside the boutique, staff began putting numbered wristbands on a table.

The line compressed.

It was slight. A collective, unconscious fold toward the door. But the seeded pairs answered it at once. Ivo saw it in ankles, knees, the angle of planted feet. The too-big pair on the kid near the corner flickered into an ugly little burst of speed. The broad-shouldered man surged one half-step without meaning to. Somebody behind him protested. Someone else shouted that they’d been there first.

Hermes said, “Take them out of the line.”

“How?” Ivo snapped.

“Convince them.”

“With what?”

Eris laughed. “There it is.”

The woman with the eyeliner suddenly stood so fast her stool tipped over. “Don’t shove me.”

“Nobody shoved you.”

“Bullshit.”

The broad-shouldered man turned. The thirteen-year-old bent to tighten one lace and came up moving too hard, shoulder clipping a knee. Coffee went down. A cup hit the sidewalk and burst.

The sound changed.

That was the thing. Not louder, exactly. Tighter. The line stopped being a line and started becoming a mechanism.

Hermes moved before Elena could stop him, cutting toward the center with one mismatched foot and both hands up. “Everybody relax—”

Three people shouted at once. One shoved him instinctively. Hermes, insulted by physics, shoved back harder than a mortal should have been able to.

Wrong choice.

The whole section of line buckled.

Elena swore in a language Ivo only heard when thread snapped or bills arrived.

Eris did not move. She only watched, eyes bright and still. “There,” she said softly. “That’s your copy. Not the sole. The urge.”

A barricade skidded sideways. Someone near the front screamed. One of the seeded pairs squealed against the concrete and kicked sparks.

Ivo saw it then—not in the crowd, but in the release stacks visible through the shop window behind the staff. Same outsole. Same bad bias. The whole drop was loaded with it.

Not one shoe to snatch. Not one person to tackle.

Construction.

He grabbed Elena’s arm. “The table.”

She looked at him once and understood immediately.

“We need a bench,” he said. “Now.”

## Chapter 7: Bench Work

The “bench” ended up being a folding table behind the reseller van.

It was the only flat surface not already full of branded water bottles or panicking employees, and by the time Ivo and Elena dragged it into the alley beside Blacktop, the morning had gone from tense to stupid. Not full riot. Worse, in a way—bursts of near-riot, enough to keep resetting everyone’s nerves. Shouting at the front. A barricade over. Someone crying from pure frustration. Security trying to sound authoritative while backing up.

Hermes had managed to redirect one ugly surge by climbing onto a newspaper box and yelling, “If you trample each other you still only get one pair,” which was not wisdom but had, briefly, confused people into stopping. He was buying time badly, exactly as predicted.

Eris drifted where she liked, untouched by elbows. Every few minutes the crowd seemed to tighten around wherever she’d just been, as if she left a wake in people’s want.

Elena dropped the tool bag onto the table and snapped it open. Awls, blades, thread, contact cement, clamps, bone folder, pliers, waxed cord. The ordinary holiness of the kit hit Ivo harder now than the cellar had.

“What do you need?” she asked.

He was already laying out what they had: Hermes’s ruined sneaker, the split counterfeit from the alley, the old fragment wrapped in cloth, one release pair snatched off a stock cart in the confusion while a Blacktop employee yelled at no one in particular.

The release pair looked beautiful in the dead, stupid way expensive things often did before they met use.

Ivo flipped it over. There. The same line through the forefoot. The same bad hunger in the cut.

“We don’t fix all of them,” he said, mostly to hear it. “Can’t.”

“No,” Elena said. “So stop wishing for miracles and make a repair.”

He slit the outsole carefully. His hands shook once. Elena saw and shoved the waxed cord at him.

“Use your fingers for work, not nerves.”

He took the cord.

The release sole peeled back with more ease than a well-made shoe should allow. Underneath, nested in fresh foam and glue, ran the counterfeit pattern: copied, smoothed, prettied up for production, but still wrong. All thrust. No settling. It turned weight into argument.

Ivo laid the old fragment beside it. Ugly against sleek. Scarred against pristine. He stared at the differences until they became instructions.

Not restore, he thought. Rebalance.

Hermes stumbled into the alley, grabbed the van’s side mirror to steady himself, and said, “How long?”

“How long until you stop making it worse?” Elena shot back.

Hermes grinned weakly. “Unclear.”

From the mouth of the alley came another flare of sound—someone shouting thief, someone else shouting liar, the crowd answering in all the old human ways.

Eris appeared there as if the noise had introduced her.

She leaned one shoulder against the brick, entirely unruffled. “This is charming,” she said. “A little field hospital for footwear.”

“Get out,” Elena said without looking up.

Eris ignored her. She watched Ivo’s hands. “You won’t save the line with one pair.”

“Good thing I’m not trying to impress you,” Ivo said.

“No?” She smiled. “That would make you unusual.”

He cut deeper into the sole. Clean. Don’t rush and call it speed. The trick was not removing the counterfeit line entirely. Too much of the release structure depended on it now. You had to interrupt it, redirect it, make room for recovery where the design insisted only on push.

Elena slid him the alley counterfeit fragment. “Use the failure.”

He looked at her.

“People trust what broke more than what preached,” she said.

Which was one of the most Elena things he had ever heard.

So he did. He pared down the alley fragment, keeping the stress line where it had blown. He trimmed a sliver from Hermes’s destroyed midsole, where the old pattern had resisted longest. He held both against the old fragment, not copying the shape but the logic: impact, correction, settle, release.

Eris watched all this with irritating calm. “You’re making compromise,” she said.

“That’s the job,” Elena answered.

“It’s so small,” Eris said, almost wonderingly. “That’s what I never like about repair. Everyone acts as if humility is a virtue because it’s all they can afford.”

Ivo pressed a thumb into the foam bed and felt the give. “You keep saying everyone wants to be chosen.”

“They do.”

“No. They want the feeling after. They want people to see it happened.”

Eris’s eyes sharpened. “And you think function is nobler?”

“I think function keeps your face off concrete.”

Hermes laughed despite the situation, then winced because laughing moved his ribs in ways the morning had punished.

The glue went down. Fast and even. Elena lit the little alcohol lamp from the kit. Heat bloomed under the alley smell. Ivo seated the corrected pieces into the sole channel one by one, fingers blackening with residue, then pressed the outsole back into place and stitched where the factory had never meant a stitch to show.

His first pass pulled too tight.

“Again,” Elena said.

“No time.”

“Again.”

He cut it out and redid it, angrier and cleaner.

Outside, the crowd hit another dangerous pitch. Metal banged. Someone was chanting something dumb. Hermes pushed off the van.

“Stay put,” Ivo snapped.

“I need to wear it.”

“I’m not done.”

“You’ll be done when it meets the street.”

That was infuriating because it was true.

Eris came off the wall and stepped close enough that Ivo could smell her perfume—something dry and cold, expensive without trying. “Make one pair,” she said quietly, just for him. “Make it undeniable. One pair no one else can have. That’s the truth, isn’t it? Not this little mercy project. One thing everyone wants.”

He kept stitching.

“Your father would have made something beautiful,” she added.

His hand stopped.

Elena looked up so sharply the awl flashed in her fist. “Careful.”

Eris smiled at her too. “Oh, I am.”

Ivo stared at the half-open sole in his hands. For one ugly second he could see it: perfect finish, hidden stitch, impossible balance, a shoe so singular it would turn every head on the block and prove he was not born only to mend other people’s damage.

Then he looked at Hermes’s wrecked sneaker beside him. The blown-out alley pair. Elena’s hands, nicked and steady. The line outside folding in on itself because everybody wanted to win a thing none of them had even worn yet.

He bent over the table and ran a visible stitch right through the sidewall.

Not pretty. Strong.

Eris’s mouth flattened by a millimeter. Real displeasure at last.

He tied off, cut the thread with his teeth, and shoved the shoe at Hermes. “Now.”

Hermes snatched it, dropped the borrowed boot, jammed his foot into the repaired release pair, and stood.

He looked down once. Rolled onto the ball of the foot. Shifted back. His expression changed.

“It settles,” he said.

“Go,” said Elena.

He went.

Not divine blur this time. Not at first. He ran like a man wearing a repair to test whether the repair deserved him. Out of the alley, into the pressure point by the barricade, straight across the line’s worst seam.

The corrected sole hit concrete and answered differently.

Not faster. Better.

The force in the crowd broke sideways instead of forward. A shove turned into a stumble instead of a pileup. The boy in the too-big pair missed his surge and had to catch himself laughing in embarrassment. The broad-shouldered man suddenly looked around as if waking from a stupid dream. One toppled barrier clanged down harmlessly instead of taking three people with it.

Confusion spread faster than frenzy.

It was not graceful. It was enough.

Eris watched Hermes cut through the unraveling knot of people, then looked back at Ivo.

“That won’t last,” she said.

“No,” Ivo said, breathing hard. “That’s why we repair things.”

Her expression did something almost like approval and then was gone.

“Terrible philosophy,” she said.

And walked away into the crowd before anyone could stop her.
