The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸

At 12:07, to be exact, which I know because I looked at it for a solid fifteen seconds without breathing properly, like time might change if I stared hard enough.

My room was dark except for the phone screen and the orange smear of the streetlamp coming through the gap in the curtain. There was rain needling at the window in that annoying, committed way it has here, like weather with a grievance. Jonah had gone to bed an hour earlier after yelling at someone through his headset about camping, which I gather is a military term now and not just what failed middle-class dads do in August. Mum was on late shift and not due back till half one.

So there was no one awake to witness me behaving exactly like the sort of girl I spent a lot of time insisting I wasn’t.

The message was from Cleo.

Not “Cleo” because I’d deleted her name in some bleak fit of principle in September. Just the number. But I knew it anyway. You don’t spend three years textually entangled with someone without learning the shape of their existence by heart. There are people I couldn’t pick out of a line-up if they were on fire, but I’d know Cleo Bell’s number in a coma.

🩸🩸🩸

No words. No “u up?” No “please answer.” No explanation. Just three blood drops sitting there in the thread like they owned the place.

My first thought, embarrassingly, was not fear. It was: for God’s sake.

That probably makes me sound evil. In my defence, Cleo and I had once used the blood-drop emoji to mean all sorts of things, most of them stupid. It started with periods, obviously. Not in a heartfelt feminist solidarity way. In the practical way fifteen-year-old girls do things, which is to text from a cubicle with all the urgency of a hostage negotiator because Year 10 taught us two important truths: biology waits for no one, and school toilet paper is decorative.

Then it became code.

One blood drop meant Bring pads.
Two meant Emergency but mainly embarrassing.
Three meant Come outside now or I’ll die / kill someone / set fire to my own life.

Which was a joke. Until, in the Cleo way, it stopped being entirely one.

There were other meanings too. Over time she used the same three drops for You are dead to me, and Did you see what she posted, and If you don’t answer I’m climbing in your window. With Cleo, symbols had a habit of multiplying like mould. She never saw why a thing should mean one thing if it could mean six and all of them make the recipient sweat.

I should have ignored it.

That sounds nobler than the truth, which is that I nearly replied immediately, but only to say what the hell now. My thumb actually hovered over the keyboard before pride kicked in. We hadn’t had a real conversation in months. We’d had one exchange in October about coursework where she wrote “have u done the bibliography” as if we were two women discussing rail replacement services. Then nothing.

Nothing direct, anyway. Which is the modern teenage equivalent of saying we’d fought a war.

I locked the phone, unlocked it again, then read the message a second time as if blood drops might reveal hidden text on a reread.

No typing bubble appeared. No follow-up. No dramatic “Maeve?” as punctuation. That was what got me, I think. Cleo without commentary was like finding a swan in Aldi. Something had gone wrong at the level of nature.

I put the phone face-down on the duvet and lay back, staring at the ceiling.

The sensible explanation was obvious. She was bored, drunk, spiralling, trying to drag me into one of her late-night symbolic episodes because everyone else had got wise or blocked her or gone to sleep. She had form for all three.

And yet.

There are some messages that arrive carrying the full weight of who sent them. If anyone else had texted me three blood drops after midnight, I’d have assumed gang initiation, period trouble or a deeply poor sense of humour. From Cleo, it came with a whole undertow of old meanings, some of them mine.

I checked her profile picture. Nothing. No weird update, no black screen, no dramatic lyric. Last seen hidden, because of course it was.

I opened our old messages, which is a grotesque thing to do after midnight if you’d like to preserve any remaining fragments of self-respect. Whole eras of us sat there in the dark.

Look alive x  
Can u see Ryan by the bikes  
I’m actually going to kill myself if she wears that hat tomorrow  
🩸🩸🩸  
bring supplies  
What supplies  
ALL SUPPLIES  
That means literally nothing

It should have been funny. Some of it was. We had been funny, which was part of the issue.

I told myself, quite firmly, that I was not doing this. I was not getting hauled back into Cleo Bell’s haunted little weather system because she’d sent me three wet cartoon organs in the night. I had school in the morning. I had a politics essay in disgraceful condition. I had, theoretically, matured.

So I put my phone on Do Not Disturb, turned over, and spent forty-five minutes not sleeping.

At 12:58 the front door went downstairs. Keys, a muffled swear, Mum dropping something in the kitchen. I nearly went down. Not because I wanted to tell her about the message — absolutely not, I’m not deranged — but because the idea of another human being in the house made my room feel less like the sort of place where old mistakes texted you after midnight.

I didn’t go. Instead I listened to cupboard doors and kettle sounds and Mum humming one line of something tuneless to herself, then eventually I slept in that thin, breakable way where your dreams know your phone is nearby.

In the morning, the message was still there.

That was somehow offensive.

I got ready in a foul mood. Grey sky, wet pavement, hair refusing any known arrangement. Jonah was in the kitchen eating dry cereal straight from the box and watching some video of a man restoring a knife for reasons too depressing to ask about.

“You look rancid,” he said.

“Morning to you too.”

“No, like medically. Did you sleep?”

“Obviously.”

He gave me the sort of look only a younger brother can give, one which says I know you’re lying and also your entire generation is emotionally unfit for service.

Mum was already gone again, having left toast under foil and a note saying Pharmacy audit. Back by six. x. Her handwriting always looked apologetic even when she was writing things like buy bin bags.

I checked my phone while the kettle boiled.

Still nothing from Cleo.

No second message. No explanation. Just the three blood drops and, above them, the time: 12:07.

And then something cold and neat slid into place in my stomach.

12:07.

There are timestamps your brain keeps against your will. I had not thought about that one in weeks, maybe months, in the disciplined way people say they’re not thinking about a thing while arranging their entire lives around not touching it.

But there it was all the same.

12:07 was the timestamp on the video.

Not the whole video. The bit at the top of the screenshot Tasha had shown me in September before I told her to delete it and she said, “Bit late for moral hygiene, babes.” Grainy corridor light. Someone laughing off-camera. Cleo turning towards the lens, already knowing.

12:07.

Jonah crunched cereal behind me. The kettle clicked off.

I opened the message again and for the first time it didn’t feel dramatic or pathetic or annoying.

It felt deliberate.

Then my phone buzzed in my hand, and I nearly threw it into the sink.
step_outputs.7:
The buzz was only my phone reminding me I had not done my politics reading, which felt petty even for technology.

I stared at the notification until it dissolved back into the lock screen. Jonah watched me over his cereal with open contempt.

“If you’re trying to act normal,” he said, “maybe don’t look like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like your phone’s just confessed.”

I told him to shut up, which in our house is effectively tenderness, and left five minutes later in a blazer that still smelled faintly of damp from last week. The rain had given up by then, but not with grace. Everything outside looked rubbed grey. The bus was late, naturally, and when it did come it was full of Year 9s behaving like a public inquiry had concluded adults no longer had authority.

Ordinarily I would have put my headphones in and ignored the world. Instead I sat there with Cleo’s message open in one hand and the bus fogging up around me, trying not to think in circles.

There were a dozen explanations and all of them were bad in specific ways.

By the time I got to school, I’d half-convinced myself the timestamp was coincidence. Human beings are excellent at this. We call it perspective when what we mean is selective cowardice.

School looked exactly as it always did after rain: the main building damp and mildly disappointed in us, the windows streaked, the fake-cheerful Sixth Form banner outside reception listing values no one had ever once displayed near the vending machines. Resilience. Community. Curiosity. There should have been one saying plausible deniability and left it at that.

I cut through the lower corridor toward form and nearly got taken out by two Year 11 boys fake-fighting with umbrellas.

“Language, please,” called Mr Firth from nowhere, with the odd priestly timing of pastoral staff.

Neither of them had actually said anything, but they nodded anyway because adults in school often seem to operate on frequencies inaccessible to the rest of us.

“Maeve,” he added, spotting me. “You all right?”

This is one of the reasons pastoral teachers are exhausting. They ask “you all right?” in a tone that makes any honest answer feel both melodramatic and administratively unhelpful.

“Thriving,” I said.

He gave me the look of a man deciding whether sarcasm counts as disclosure, then let it go. “Don’t forget personal statements by Friday.”

“Cruel.”

That got half a smile, which was probably what he wanted. Evidence of life. Tick.

Form was form: damp sleeves, low-level panic, everyone pretending UCAS was not a bloodsport. Tasha slid into the chair behind me three minutes late with a croissant in a paper bag and the expression of someone prepared to be reasonable only under protest.

“You’ve got that face,” she said quietly.

“What face?”

“The one where you’ve either committed a crime or remembered one.”

“Bit early.”

“Interesting non-denial.”

I ignored her and opened my planner to a page I had no intention of reading. Tasha let it sit for all of ten seconds, which for her is spiritual restraint.

“Was it Cleo?”

I turned round.

She shrugged, tearing off a piece of croissant. “You’ve only looked haunted by one person for this long.”

This is what I mean about Tasha. She says things in a tone suggesting she’s discussing weather patterns while actually inserting a knife between your ribs.

“I got a text,” I said.

“From?”

I looked at her.

“Oh my God.” She sat back. “That is so much better than coursework.”

“Your moral centre is a puddle.”

“It’s not immoral to prefer a live crisis to constitutional reform.”

I showed her the message under the desk. She read it, then raised her eyebrows.

“Right,” she said. “That’s either a cry for help or the most embarrassing attempt at menace I’ve ever seen.”

“It was sent at 12:07.”

That changed her face. Not massively. Just enough.

“Ah,” she said. “So not random, then.”

No, not random.

No one ever called it anything official, the blood-drop thing. That would have been too organised, too self-aware. It wasn’t one of those sinister school traditions in American films where everyone wears masks and swears oaths in Latin. It was just something that spread.

First it was Cleo and me, because of course it was. We were fifteen and bored and very pleased with ourselves. If one of us wanted the other out of a lesson, or in the toilets, or at the back gate with supplies or gossip or a fake emergency, we sent blood. Stupid and dramatic and ours.

Then other people started nicking it, because that is what happens to anything with enough style and not enough dignity. By Year 11, girls were sending one another blood drops before dares, humiliations, prank confessions, “you’ve been chosen” nonsense. If you got it, there’d usually be something waiting: your bag hidden, your crush texted from your phone, your name Sharpied onto a sanitary bin in the loos if someone was feeling particularly enlightened.

It was not a cult. It was not folklore. It was the kind of low-grade cruelty school specialises in because no one wants to be the person who says actually this is weird. Half the time it was funny. The other half it was only funny if it wasn’t happening to you.

And, because everyone involved was a coward in some arrangement, it always travelled under softer names. Banter. A joke. Drama.

By break, I’d heard “drama” twice and “Cleo being Cleo” once, and neither was even about my text. Her name still moved around school like mould in a ceiling corner: unsightly, persistent, easier to ignore if you didn’t look directly at it.

At the lockers, two girls from Year 12 were talking in that fake-casual whisper people use when they absolutely want to be overheard.

“I just think if she wanted people on her side,” one of them said, “she could have maybe not—”

She stopped when she saw me. Not because she cared. Because gossip has standards, apparently.

I smiled at her before I could help it, which made her flinch and me hate myself. Then I yanked my locker open harder than necessary.

Something small and red dropped out and hit the floor.

Not blood. Not even close. Three jelly sweets in the shape of little hearts, the cheap shiny sort dusted in sugar, rolled in a neat line toward my shoe.

For one stupid second I just stared. Around me, corridor noise kept going: locker doors, shouting, someone laughing too hard at something mediocre. No music swell, no dramatic hush. Real life is rude like that.

Taped to the inside of my locker door, half hidden by my timetable, was a scrap of lined paper.

It had only one thing on it.

🩸🩸🩸

Not the actual emoji, obviously. Someone had drawn them in red pen. Badly.

Behind me, Tasha said, “Well. That’s not ideal.”

I peeled the note off and folded it into my fist.

“This is stupid,” I said.

“Mm.”

“It’s literally jelly hearts. That is aggressively naff.”

“Also true.”

“This is someone being twelve.”

Tasha looked at me carefully. “You keep saying that like it’s making you calmer.”

I shut the locker and there, reflected faintly in the metal for half a second before the corridor swallowed him, was Ryan Lacey at the far end of the hall, talking to someone from rugby with his easy, patient little smile.

Then he glanced up.

Not at the sweets. Not at the note. Straight at me.
step_outputs.8:
Ryan didn’t do anything dramatic. That would have been useful.

He just looked at me for half a second too long, like he was checking whether I’d seen him seeing me, and then went back to whatever bland male alliance was happening by the science stairs. It was such a normal movement that I instantly hated myself for noticing it.

“Don’t,” said Tasha.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You did a whole internal documentary with your face.”

“It was one expression.”

“It was five, layered.”

I shoved the jelly hearts into my blazer pocket because leaving them on the floor felt deranged and throwing them away felt somehow weak. Then we went to lesson.

I retained nothing from double politics except that Mr Jansen has somehow made coalition theory sound like a minor digestive complaint and that Tasha wrote on the corner of my worksheet: if this turns out to be year 13 flirting I will kill you myself.

I wrote back: with jelly sweets?

She looked at it, nearly smiled, and underlined flirting twice as if to show she had standards.

By lunch I had reached that point where dread starts making you practical. Not calm, exactly. Efficient in odd little bursts.

“Tasha,” I said, catching up with her outside the canteen, “show me the screenshot.”

She stopped. “You told me to delete it.”

“I know.”

“And I did.”

“You absolutely did not.”

“Correct,” she said. “I’m not an idiot.”

We took our lunch — chips, because if your life is collapsing there should at least be chips — to the Sixth Form study room, which at lunchtime was mostly empty because everyone prefers to suffer publicly. Rain was starting again outside, silvering the windows. Tasha sat opposite me, dug through her camera roll with the concentration of a surgeon, and turned the phone around.

There it was.

A screenshot of a video no one was meant to have anymore. Grainy corridor lighting, the horrible yellow sort the school uses after hours when it wants to imply a duty of care but not spend money. The timestamp at the top: 12:07. Cleo half turned towards the camera. Mouth open as if speaking. One hand lifted. Someone just out of frame on the left.

It was nothing, really. If you didn’t know. That was the genius of it.

“Where did you get this?” I asked.

“Ria sent it to me in September because she thought I’d enjoy the social ecology.”

“You’re a ghoul.”

“Thank you. She deleted it after. I kept it because one day, I thought, this may become useful or ruinous.”

I looked at Cleo’s face again. Grainy, blurred, but recognisably her. She looked angry. Or frightened. Or both. The thing about screenshots is they trap a moment without helping you at all.

“Can you get the actual video?”

“Probably not. If I could, I would have sold it for influence by now.”

I ignored that. “Who else got sent the blood drops?”

Tasha reached for a chip. “Possibly no one. Possibly everyone. Depends how committed your little ghost is.”

“That’s not helping.”

“No, but this might. I heard Freya Lomax got something in her bag this morning.”

“Freya?” That surprised me enough to be useful. Freya was in Year 12 and had the skittish, expensive energy of someone whose parents describe holidays as investments. She and Cleo had never had anything to do with each other.

“Three red lollies tied with dental floss. Very serial-killer craft fair. She binned them because she’s allergic to atmosphere.”

“Why her?”

Tasha tipped one shoulder. “Maybe it means nothing. Maybe it means she saw something. Maybe your sender’s just gone broad.”

None of that helped. Which is to say, all of it did.

We spent the next twenty minutes doing what passes for investigation when you are seventeen and under-supervised: trawling old message threads, checking tagged photos from the summer, following who had suddenly unfollowed whom and when. It was ridiculous, except that this is actually where half of modern truth lives — not in confessions, but in petty digital weather.

Cleo’s Instagram was still private. Profile unchanged. One photo archived, though, because there was a gap where I knew a post used to be: her on someone’s shoulders at the party in a silver top, looking expensive and doomed. Ryan’s account was public in the smug male way, all rugby mud and pub lighting and one surprisingly tender picture with his dog that probably did more for him socially than all his GCSEs combined.

“What’s this?” Tasha said, tapping the screen.

It was an old close-friends story highlight on somebody else’s account, one I would never have looked at because the girl in question once called me “intense” in Year 11 and I’ve never fully recovered. A blurry clip from the same night. Music too loud, camera swinging. People in someone’s kitchen yelling lyrics no one knew. At the edge of the frame, barely there, Ryan leaning in close to someone by the back door.

Not Cleo. Freya.

“That’s odd,” I said.

“Mm.”

“Could be nothing.”

“Everything can be nothing if you’re committed enough,” Tasha said. “That’s practically the school motto.”

I zoomed. Useless. Pixels became theology.

“What’s the event this week?” I asked.

“Sixth Form open evening on Thursday. Why?”

Because suddenly I remembered a conversation half-overheard yesterday in the corridor, Ryan saying to someone, “No, Thursday’s better, everyone’ll be here.” At the time I’d assumed rugby or some jointly managed male disaster. Now it came back with too much shape.

“Nothing,” I said. “Maybe nothing.”

Tasha looked at me in a way that suggested she was once again tolerating my personality under severe strain.

“I hate mysteries run by people with A-levels,” she said. “At least proper criminals commit.”

After lunch I did something I absolutely hadn’t planned to do and went looking for Freya.

I found her outside the English block standing under the overhang with two friends and a coffee the colour of varnish. She looked at me the way girls like Freya look at girls like me, which is to say as if I were either about to ask for help with a printer or mention Marx.

“Did you get something in your bag this morning?” I said, because subtlety had, by then, been exhausted.

Her friends immediately became architecture.

Freya blinked. “What?”

“Three red sweets. Or something like that.”

There was a tiny pause. Very small. But enough.

“No?”

“You sure?”

She gave a little laugh, badly aimed. “Why would I not be sure what’s in my own bag?”

This was going so well. “Because maybe you threw it out without thinking.”

“Maeve,” she said, lowering her voice with the solemnity of someone discussing local tax policy, “if this is about Cleo, I’m honestly not interested.”

There it was. Not denial. Deflection.

“I didn’t say it was.”

“You didn’t have to.”

I might still have pushed if one of her friends hadn’t said, with awful brightness, “God, is Cleo back?” in exactly the tone people use for mildew.

Freya shot her a look. Too quick, too frightened. Then she said, “I’ve got class,” and left with both of them, coffee in hand, spine very straight.

Tasha, who had appeared at some point during this exchange like a witness summoned for sport, exhaled through her nose.

“Well,” she said. “That was subtle and terrible.”

“She was lying.”

“Probably.”

“And she’s scared.”

“Yes.”

I looked at the rain darkening the paving stones. My phone felt heavier in my pocket than a phone should.

“Thursday,” I said.

Tasha nodded once. “Thursday.”

At the end of the day, as we were leaving, she caught my sleeve.

“One more thing.”

She showed me her phone. A screenshot of Cleo’s number in her contacts. Under it, one unread message received at 1:14 a.m.

Not words.

Just 🩸🩸🩸.
step_outputs.9:
By Wednesday morning, I had managed to make myself look both guilty and unstable, which was efficient even for me.

The trouble with having a real problem at school is that you still have to do all the normal humiliating things as well. Hand in essays. Borrow a glue stick. Nod along while someone called Evan explains inflation as if he discovered it personally. The world does not suspend routine just because your old life has started texting.

Tasha got the blood-drop message at 1:14. Freya had almost certainly received something physical. I had the note in my blazer pocket and three jelly hearts now slowly furring themselves with lint. Cleo still hadn’t sent a single actual word.

I considered going to Mr Firth. Not because I thought he’d fix anything, but because there is a specific sort of panic where adults begin to seem useful by sheer force of not being seventeen. Then I pictured his face if I tried to explain that I was being haunted by an emoji I helped popularise three years ago and chose pride instead.

At break, I made the mistake of deciding to confront Ryan without a plan.

This was less a decision than a mood.

He was by the bike sheds with two of the rugby lot, eating something from the corner shop and doing that thing boys do where they stand around in a triangle pretending not to enjoy being observed. The rain had stopped but the ground was still wet, and the whole yard smelled faintly of leaves and deodorant.

“Can I talk to you?” I said.

One of his friends made a little ooh noise under his breath, because boys are born in a state of permanent spiritual Year 8. Ryan glanced at them, then at me, and did the mild, patient face that made adults think he was mature.

“Yeah, course.”

“Alone.”

That bought me thirty seconds of silence and one highly interested look from a girl nearby smoking in defiance of all visible futures. Ryan handed his half-eaten flapjack to one of the boys and walked a few steps away with me, not far enough to be private, just far enough to imply decency.

“What’s up?”

I hadn’t thought beyond this point, which became obvious to both of us at once.

“You know exactly what’s up.”

His expression shifted by a millimetre. “Do I?”

“The messages. The notes. Don’t do that.”

“Maeve, I genuinely have no idea what you’re talking about.”

There is a way some people say genuinely that should count as perjury.

“Really? Three blood drops? Ringing any bells?”

He gave a tiny laugh. Not because anything was funny. Because he wanted us both to know he wasn’t rattled.

“That old thing?”

“Old thing?”

“Come on. People have been doing that for ages.”

“You’re the one saying people.”

“Because it is people. Not me.”

There was movement at the edge of my vision. Other students pretending not to look. Of course. School can smell conflict at a quarter mile.

“You were there yesterday,” I said. “At the lockers.”

“I am at school most days, yes.”

“And Thursday. ‘Everyone’ll be here.’”

He blinked, still calm. “Sorry, have you been collecting my corridor dialogue now?”

The smile that came with it was almost kind. That was the worst thing about Ryan. He had a way of making your own urgency seem socially excessive. Not wrong, exactly. Just embarrassing.

“You think this is funny?” I said.

“No.” He lowered his voice, which somehow made me feel louder. “I think you’re winding yourself up over something stupid and using me because I’m convenient.”

I actually laughed then, once, a nasty little sound. “That is rich.”

“Is it?”

“Yes.”

His eyes sharpened at that. For a second the patient concern slipped, and underneath it was the old thing: not menace, exactly. Irritation. The annoyance of a boy who’d arranged events into a manageable version and didn’t enjoy seeing pieces move.

“Look,” he said, “if this is about what happened in summer—”

“It is.”

“—then I’m not doing this with an audience.”

He glanced past me as he said it. I turned.

Audience was generous. It was basically half of break. Not everyone. Just enough. Tasha near the wall with a look of pure disbelief. Freya by the doors, frozen. A cluster of Year 12s trying to seem accidental.

“You’ve got one anyway,” I said.

“Right.” Ryan stepped back. “Then I’m definitely not.”

And because school is a machine designed to convert private horror into public farce, that was exactly when Mr Firth appeared from around the corner carrying a stack of photocopies and the expression of a man whose tea has once again gone cold in service of children.

“What’s going on here?”

Nothing says dignity like being caught in a social detonation by pastoral staff.

“Nothing,” Ryan said immediately.

“Maeve?” Mr Firth asked.

This was the point at which a better person would have lied. Or a smarter one. Instead I said, “Someone’s been sending messages. About summer. And he knows.”

Mr Firth looked from me to Ryan and straight away I saw the problem: I was breathing too fast and Ryan looked like a charity volunteer wrongly accused of arson.

“What sort of messages?” he said carefully.

“Blood drops.”

There was a brief silence.

Not a dramatic silence. A bad one.

“Emoji,” I clarified, because of course I did, making it somehow worse.

One of the Year 12s gave a tiny involuntary snort, then pretended to cough himself inside out. Mr Firth shot him a look.

“Maeve,” he said, in the tone adults use when they are deciding whether a thing is serious or merely adolescent, “why don’t you come and talk to me properly?”

That should have helped. It didn’t. Because Ryan was already shaking his head a little, not theatrically, just enough to imply this was exactly the kind of thing he had been trying to avoid.

“I’ve got class,” he said. “I’m happy to come by later if needed.”

If needed. Like we were discussing a printer complaint.

By lunch, everyone knew some version of it, none of them correct. That I’d accused Ryan of threatening me. That Cleo was back. That there was a sex tape. That there had always been a sex tape. That I’d had some sort of breakdown over fruit pastilles. School gossip is what happens when boredom gets a knife.

I ended up in Mr Firth’s office, where he gave me tea in a mug that said IT’S OKAY TO NOT BE OKAY, which felt less comforting than a threat.

“I’m not dismissing this,” he said.

“You are a bit.”

“I’m trying to understand it.”

“No, you’re trying to phrase it.”

He rubbed his temple. “All right. Then help me understand. Why now? Why would someone send you this now?”

Because of 12:07, I thought. Because of Thursday. Because of the thing I did.

And then, because apparently humiliation had not yet reached its legal limit, I remembered.

The night of the party.

Cleo in the corridor, face white with fury, phone in her hand. “Maeve, look at this.”

Me already wanting to leave, already hating the way everything had tilted. Music too loud behind us. Someone shouting from the garden. Her trying to show me the video and me seeing enough — enough to know it wasn’t funny, enough to know she wasn’t joking, enough to know I was now being asked to choose.

And me smiling. God.

Not because it was funny.

Because people were there.

Because if I’d looked as shocked as I felt, I would have been in it with her.

So I’d smiled that awful nervous smile and said, “Cleo, maybe don’t,” like she was the embarrassing one.

In Mr Firth’s office, with the tea cooling untouched between us, I went suddenly hot all over.

“Maeve?” he said.

I looked at him.

Then I looked past him, through the office window into the corridor beyond.

Cleo was there.

Not fully. Not like an apparition. Just a flash as someone turned the corner: dark blonde hair, school coat, head down.

By the time I got to the door, she was gone.
step_outputs.10:
I left Mr Firth mid-sentence.

There may have been consequences to this in a technical sense. If so, they never fully ripened, because pastoral staff are like minor gods of process: slow to wrath and mostly powered by Outlook. I heard him call my name once behind me, but by then I was already out in the corridor, blazer half on, moving too fast.

The corridor beyond his office was empty.

Not empty in a haunting way. Empty in a school way: a dropped worksheet near the skirting board, one of those institutional display boards about resilience, the smell of floor cleaner failing to defeat feet. The stairwell door was still swinging slightly, though, which was enough to make my stomach kick.

I went down the stairs two at a time and nearly collided with a Year 8 carrying a papier-mâché volcano.

“Sorry,” I said.

He looked at me as if I was a badly supervised horse.

Outside, the lower yard was slick with rain. Students were drifting toward lunch in knots and singles. No Cleo. No dramatic silhouette at the gates. Nothing except cold air and my own pulse trying to become public.

This is the thing no one tells you about chasing someone you used to know completely: your body recognises them before your certainty does. I knew that glimpse was her in the same way I know my own front door key by touch. Not from logic. From years.

Tasha found me five minutes later by the bins behind the drama block, where I was pretending to be there for a reason.

“You look appalling,” she said.

“Thank you.”

“Did you sprint?”

“Maybe.”

“Why?”

“I saw Cleo.”

That landed.

“Where?”

“Outside Firth’s office.”

“And?”

“She vanished.”

Tasha stared at me for a second, then nodded once as if updating some internal chart. “Right. So she’s here.”

“Or I’ve finally lost it in a way that’ll make the school newsletter.”

“No, if you’d hallucinated her, she’d have made more of an entrance.”

That should not have been comforting and somehow was.

We spent the rest of lunch doing laps of the likely places Cleo would not go. This is harder than it sounds. If you haven’t spoken to someone in months, your map of them goes stale in odd patches. I knew where Cleo had hidden in Year 10 after crying over a maths test she absolutely did not need to cry over. I knew where she liked to stand before assemblies because the light hit her hair well from the left. I knew which toilet cubicle she used if she wanted privacy and which one if she wanted to be found.

But this version of her? The version who texted after midnight and moved through school like a rumour? Less clear.

We checked the old music block steps, the side path by the MFL wing, the gap behind the sports hall where sixth formers vape under the wild belief no one can smell mango death. Nothing.

At last Tasha said, “Could she be waiting for you to stop doing a perimeter sweep and think?”

“That sounds unkind.”

“That sounds like Cleo.”

She wasn’t wrong.

My phone buzzed at 2:13, halfway through history. Unknown number.

Library. Top floor. Don’t arrive looking rabid.

No signature. None needed.

I stared at it until Mr Patel asked whether I planned to contribute to the discussion on interwar appeasement or merely suffer through it silently. Tasha, two seats over, saw my face and mouthed well?

I held up the phone under the desk. She looked at the message, then back at me, and wrote on her notes in block capitals: SHE’S SO ANNOYING.

Also not wrong.

The library top floor is where our school keeps all the books no one wants and all the students staff would rather not supervise closely. It has that particular hush of institutional neglect: warm air, old paper, computers from a previous moral era. I got there straight after the bell and found no one at first except a Year 12 asleep behind a sociology textbook and Mrs Dyer at the desk entering something into a spreadsheet with priestly disappointment.

Then a voice, low and dry, from between the biographies and travel.

“You took your time.”

I turned.

Cleo was sitting on the floor in the gap between shelves, knees up, school coat over her uniform, looking both exactly like herself and completely altered by the fact of being there. Her hair was tied back badly. No makeup, or not enough to matter. She looked tired in a way she would once have considered a personal attack.

For one unhelpful second all I felt was relief, swift and humiliating.

Then I remembered I was angry.

“You texted me blood drops at midnight.”

“Yes.”

“That’s not normal.”

She looked up at me. “I’m touched you’ve become such a robust defender of normal.”

Even exhausted, she could still do this. Find the line and slide it in.

I sat opposite her on the carpet because standing felt like surrender. Between us was a shelf of failed travel writing and one very battered atlas.

“You sent them to Tasha too.”

“She has initiative.”

“And Freya?”

A tiny pause. “Possibly.”

“Why?”

“Because people only become honest when they think a story might start moving without them.”

It was such a Cleo answer I nearly laughed. Instead I said, “Are you back?”

“In school? No. In the spiritual sense, perhaps.”

“Can you not.”

“No, apparently I can’t.”

There she was. The old rhythm, intact enough to be dangerous.

Up close, though, she looked thinner. Not dramatically. Just less arranged. There was a healing scratch by her thumb where she’d clearly picked at the skin. Cleo had always been very still in a social way, all held lines and controlled angles. Now she seemed to be using that same control simply to remain in one piece.

“I saw you in September,” I said before I meant to. “The screenshot.”

“Of course you did.”

“You could’ve just told me.”

That got me a look so flat it should have taken wallpaper off.

“I did tell you,” she said. “In August. In the corridor. With my actual mouth.”

I swallowed.

There was no point denying it. Not with her. Not with the exact memory still sitting in me like glass.

“I know.”

“No, you know now. At the time you decided to become very interested in not making things worse.”

“You think I don’t know what I did?”

“I think you know now because it’s come back for you. Which is not quite the same.”

There are arguments where the air itself starts choosing sides. This was one.

I said, “Why text me at all?”

At that, something in her shifted. Not softened. Focused.

“Because he thinks it’s over,” she said. “And because he’s wrong.”

From inside her coat pocket she took out her phone. Cracked screen, old case, still the ridiculous green nail varnish stain in one corner from Year 12 mocks. She unlocked it and held it where I could see.

On the screen was a video.

Not the screenshot. The actual clip.

Grainy corridor. Music from the hall bleeding through the walls. A cluster of people just out of frame laughing in that sharp, anticipatory way groups do before someone gets hurt.

Cleo in the middle of it, clearly not in on the joke. Ryan’s voice, low and amused, saying, “No, wait, just let her see—”

Then the camera jerking as if whoever filmed it was trying not to be obvious. Cleo reaching for the phone. Her own face changing as she realises what’s already been sent, and to whom.

Not sexy. Not scandalous.

Worse.

Humiliating.

Designed to look consensual if you already wanted it to be.

I felt sick.

“He still has copies,” Cleo said. “Or had. And now, conveniently, he wants everything gone before open evening.”

“Why open evening?”

“Because his mum’s helping. Because staff will be distracted. Because if it leaks then, he can say someone’s being malicious for attention.” She looked at me steadily. “And because Freya was there. She saw more than she’s saying.”

I looked from the phone to her face.

“Why me?”

Cleo’s laugh was tiny and awful. “Because, Maeve, you remember things properly. And because if this comes out, your part comes with it.”

There it was. Not trust. Usefulness.

Fair enough.

She locked the screen. “I need somewhere to leave a copy.”

I said, “With me?”

“With someone I know won’t accidentally grow a conscience and hand it to a safeguarding form.”

“That’s an incredibly flattering way to phrase blackmail.”

“It’s not blackmail.” She stood up, brushing dust from her skirt. “It’s delegation.”

Then, after a beat:

“Thursday,” she said. “Don’t make me ask twice.”
step_outputs.11:
By Thursday morning, I was carrying Cleo’s backup copy of the video in the zipped coin pocket of my school bag like a Victorian child with a family secret.

It was on an ancient USB stick shaped like a lipstick, which was exactly the sort of detail Cleo would provide in order to remain irritatingly herself under pressure. She’d handed it over outside the library at the end of last lesson the day before, saying, “If you lose this, I’ll actually haunt you,” and walked off before I could answer.

I hadn’t slept much. Not because I spent the whole night nobly strategising. Mostly because every time I started to drift, my brain replayed the corridor clip and the exact tone of Ryan’s voice in it — casual, amused, already sure of the ending. There’s a special quality to remembered humiliation, even when it isn’t yours. It enters your body by sound.

Mum noticed something was off in the morning but, being my mother, approached it sideways.

“You’re early,” she said, coming into the kitchen in her coat with her badge still clipped on. “Either you’ve become responsible overnight or civilisation’s ended.”

“Bit of both.”

She looked at me for half a second longer than usual. “Everything all right at school?”

This was dangerous ground. Parents can smell distress best when you least want them to.

“Fine.”

“Mm.”

She put the kettle on. “You say ‘fine’ in three distinct ways, by the way. This is the one that means ‘absolutely not but don’t ruin my day by being attentive.’”

“Have you considered a hobby?”

“I had one. Then I had children.”

That should have ended it, but as I was leaving she added, not looking at me, “If anything has got bigger than you thought it would, tell somebody before it gets bigger than them too.”

Which was unhelpfully perceptive for eight in the morning.

At school, the open evening had already infected everything. Student ambassadors in blazers were being briefed on smiling. Display boards had appeared overnight bearing such phrases as Aspirational Learners and Future Ready, which sounded less like education than a minor threat. Teachers were carrying trays and extension leads. The whole place had the strained cleanliness of an estate agent’s viewing.

Tasha found me at my locker.

“You look like hell in a legalistic way,” she said.

“Good morning.”

“Do you have it?”

I put a hand on my bag.

She nodded. “Right. I hate this.”

“Why?”

“Because now it’s become real enough to inconvenience me.”

That was Tasha’s version of saying she was in.

We went over what little plan there was during free period in the Sixth Form study room. Cleo had texted at 7:42 with one sentence: Don’t hand anything to Ryan, staff, or anyone with a lanyard and a calming voice. Helpful if broad. The idea, if it deserved the name, was that she’d come in during the evening, meet me somewhere less visible than the hall, and we’d decide whether to send the video to Mr Firth, a governor, the local paper, or God.

This did not feel watertight.

“What if she doesn’t show?” Tasha said.

“She’ll show.”

“You say that like faith and not trauma.”

Before I could answer, my phone buzzed.

Unknown number again.

Wouldn’t do that if I were you. Funny thing about old videos. People forget who else is in them.

I read it twice.

Then a second message:

Open your email.

I did.

There was one new message from an address I didn’t recognise. No subject line. Attached: screenshot.jpg.

The image was from a different angle on the same night. Blurry, zoomed, but clear enough where it mattered. Cleo in the corridor, furious. Me opposite her. Mid-smile.

Not a real smile. My awful panic smile. The one that says this is fine when the room is visibly on fire.

In still form, stripped of context, it looked monstrous.

Tasha read over my shoulder and made a low sound through her teeth. “Oh, that’s nasty.”

“He’s threatening me.”

“Technically anonymous, but yes.”

“What does he mean, who else is in them?”

“That if he goes down, he’ll make sure you look like part of the joke.”

I sat down very abruptly.

This was the thing I had known all along and still managed not to prepare for: the truth did not divide neatly into victim and villain with everyone else lined up by moral usefulness. It had me in it. Not centrally. Not equally. But enough.

Tasha leaned against the table, arms folded. “So. Options.”

“Die.”

“Valid but logistically poor.”

Before we got further, Freya appeared in the doorway. She looked immaculate in the way girls do when they’re one panic level above vomiting. Hair glossy, nails pale pink, school makeup saying I woke up glowing and did not cry in a disabled loo before registration.

“Can I talk to you?” she said to me.

Tasha raised both eyebrows. “Excellent. More girls saying that like it’s a hostage situation.”

Freya ignored her. “Alone.”

“No,” I said.

That surprised all three of us.

Freya swallowed. “Fine.”

She came in and shut the door behind her. The room smelt faintly of printer toner and cold chips.

“I didn’t send those,” she said immediately.

“Didn’t say you did.”

“No, but you all keep looking at me like I’ve got a knife.”

“Have you?”

Tasha asked.

Freya shut her eyes for one second. “I was there that night, all right? Not at the start. After. I saw them with the phones.”

“Them?” I said.

She hesitated.

There it was: the moment where people become historians of their own cowardice.

“Ryan,” she said at last. “And Luca. Maybe Noah, I don’t know. They were laughing. Cleo was trying to get the phone back. I thought it was some weird flirting thing, then—” She shook her head. “Then I realised it wasn’t.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?” I asked, and heard how useless that sounded the instant it left my mouth.

Freya looked at me with sudden, vicious clarity. “You didn’t.”

Fair enough.

“I know,” I said.

She glanced at Tasha, then back at me. “He told me if anyone dragged it all up again, he’d say I helped send it around. I didn’t. I didn’t even have it. But my mum already thinks school is ‘too much socially’ and if there was a whole thing—”

She broke off. Not crying. Just choking slightly on the shape of her own life.

Tasha, very gently for once, said, “What do you want?”

Freya gave a tiny laugh. “I want to be the sort of person who didn’t need that as a question.”

Silence. Rain tapping the windows. Somewhere outside, a teacher cheerfully telling Year 11 volunteers where to stand for tours.

My phone buzzed again.

This time it was Cleo.

Change of plan. He knows. Reprographics corridor. 6:40. If I’m not there by 6:50, do it without me.

Below that, after a pause:

And Maeve — if you bottle it again, at least be original.

I stared at the message until the words stopped feeling like words.

Open evening would begin at six. By 6:40 the hall would be full of parents being sold aspiration in PowerPoint form. Ryan would be there. Staff would be everywhere and nowhere. The school would be at its most polished and least able to cope with anything untidy.

Tasha read the text over my shoulder.

“Well,” she said. “That’s bleakly encouraging.”

Freya looked between us. “What are you doing?”

I put the phone in my pocket and stood up.

“For once,” I said, though my voice didn’t entirely sound like mine, “I think I’m ruining everyone’s evening.”
step_outputs.12:
By six o’clock the school had become a version of itself no actual student recognised.

The hall was full of folding chairs and captive parents wearing the expressions adults reserve for institutional hope. Student ambassadors in perfect blazers stood by display boards explaining extracurricular opportunities as if anyone had ever joined debating for the love of discourse rather than because a teacher trapped them. Someone from catering had produced mini brownies on white platters. The headteacher’s slideshow was already glowing on the stage with stock photos of smiling children from about 2016.

Open evening is always faintly grotesque if you already go to the school. You spend years watching a building fail to contain ordinary misery and then, for one night, it gets dressed as possibility.

I was meant to be helping in History, which I had agreed to weeks ago when my biggest concern was whether I could convincingly discuss source evaluation with strangers. Instead I did one frantic tour of the corridor to establish where everyone was.

Mr Firth near reception with a clipboard and his best approachable face. Ryan by the hall doors in ambassador mode, tie straight, shaking hands with a father as if applying for local office. Freya in the English block handing out prospectuses and looking as if all her internal organs had become administrative. Tasha nowhere visible, which in her case usually meant somewhere useful.

Cleo, obviously, absent.

At 6:18, my phone buzzed.

Tasha: by reprographics. also your boy looks rattled.

He was not my boy.

I texted back: if i die tell people i had nuance

She replied: no

The reprographics corridor is one of the least atmospheric places in school. Narrow, overlit, lined with cupboards full of paper and toner and one machine that always sounds as if it is being harmed. That was probably why Cleo picked it. No one chooses it. No one lingers there unless they are a teacher or in trouble.

At 6:34, I slipped away from a conversation with a Year 11 girl’s mother about A-level politics and made for the corridor with my pulse doing deeply unhelpful things. The USB was in my blazer pocket now, because a bag felt too removable. Every person I passed seemed either too ordinary or too deliberate.

Tasha was waiting by the fire door, phone in hand.

“Where’s Freya?” I whispered.

“On lookout near English. Which is generous considering she’d rather professionally die.”

“And Cleo?”

Tasha looked at the time. “Not here yet.”

Of course not.

We waited.

From the hall came the muffled rise and fall of the headteacher beginning his speech about excellence, ambition, and community. Somewhere closer, a printer whirred with tragic determination. The lights in the corridor had that school-evening quality I’ve always hated, too bright and not bright enough, making every scuff mark look meaningful.

At 6:41, footsteps.

I turned too quickly.

Not Cleo. Ryan.

He stopped when he saw us, which was almost satisfying. He had not expected witnesses arranged this tidily. For a second all his ambassador smoothness deserted him and he just looked his age — tired, annoyed, trapped in a blazer.

Then it was back.

“Maeve,” he said quietly, with a glance at Tasha. “Can we not do this here?”

“Excellent start,” said Tasha.

He ignored her. “Where is she?”

“Who?”

His jaw tightened. There it was. The first crack.

“Don’t be stupid.”

“I’m trying not to be. It’s new.”

He stepped closer, lowering his voice further. “You’ve made your point.”

“What point’s that?”

“That you’re still obsessed with summer. Fine. Message received. But if you bring this out now—”

“Now?” I said. “That’s your issue? Timing?”

He exhaled through his nose, as if I were the difficult one in a customer service exchange. “You know what I mean.”

I did. He meant not in front of parents, not in front of staff, not in a way he couldn’t immediately manage.

“You sent the screenshot,” I said.

“No.”

“You threatened Freya.”

He actually flinched at that, tiny but real. “Freya needs to keep out of things she doesn’t understand.”

Behind him, at the far end of the corridor, the fire door opened.

Cleo came through in her school coat, hair tucked up, face pale and absolutely composed. She looked at Ryan first, then me, and smiled without humour.

“Oh, good,” she said. “The panel.”

Ryan turned. Any colour he had left went.

“Cleo—”

“No, don’t.” Her voice was calm enough to make mine feel juvenile by comparison. “If you start with my name in that tone I’ll actually be sick.”

Tasha, beside me, muttered, “Fair.”

Ryan put his hands up slightly, the old harmless gesture. “I’m not trying to start anything.”

Cleo gave a short laugh. “That is, unfortunately, your entire thing.”

From the hall came applause. Presumably the headteacher had finished congratulating us all on our futures.

I felt the USB sharp against my palm inside my pocket.

Ryan looked between us. “What do you want?”

There are questions that sound practical and are actually confessions. He knew what. He wanted terms.

Cleo said, “For once? Accuracy.”

“Come on.”

“No, really. Let’s be adults since the school’s so keen on that this evening.” Her voice sharpened. “You filmed something I didn’t agree to. Then you sent it around. Then when I kicked off, everyone said I was making a scene. Then you spent months pretending the problem was my reaction.”

“It was deleted.”

There it was. The scale of his morality. Not I’m sorry. Not I shouldn’t have. It was deleted.

Cleo looked at me. “You hear that?”

Ryan followed her gaze, and in that second I understood exactly what he’d feared all day. Not exposure. Corroboration.

“It was stupid,” he said, quicker now. “Obviously it was. But it wasn’t some planned attack. People were drunk, things got out of hand—”

“That video didn’t get sent by gravity,” Tasha said.

He rounded on her. “Why are you even involved?”

“Professional curiosity.”

Cleo took one step closer to him. Not dramatic. Precise. “You said, ‘let her see.’”

Ryan’s face changed. Not much. Enough.

“That doesn’t prove anything.”

“No,” she said. “But this does.”

I took out the USB.

For one surreal moment we all just looked at it. Tiny, tacky, lipstick-shaped. Years of shame housed in a novelty object from Claire’s Accessories.

Ryan stared at it as if hatred might erase plastic.

“You don’t want to do that,” he said to me.

And because this was the point everything had been walking toward, because there is only so long you can live in your own avoidance before it starts speaking, I said, “I know.”

He looked relieved.

Then I went on.

“I didn’t want to do it in August either.”

That landed harder than I expected. On him, yes. On Cleo too. Maybe on me most of all.

My voice sounded thin but stable. “You showed me enough and I knew it was bad. I knew. And I still stood there like if I acted normal enough it would become normal. So no, I don’t want to do this. I just don’t think wanting gets to be the main criterion anymore.”

Behind us, footsteps. Mr Firth’s voice somewhere near the hall doors. A parent asking where Science was. The evening carrying on, offensively intact.

Ryan looked at me as if I’d violated some private agreement. “Maeve—”

Cleo cut across him. “No. We’re done with tone.”

She reached past me, took the USB from my hand, and turned as Mr Firth appeared at the end of the corridor, clipboard gone, face shifting from public-smile mode to something harder.

“What’s happening?” he said.

For once, no one answered “nothing.”

Cleo held up the USB.

“This,” she said, “is what happened.”
step_outputs.13:
The school email went out at 8:13 the next morning.

Dear Parents and Carers,  
Following an incident at last night’s Sixth Form Open Evening, we are aware of concerns relating to student conduct and online behaviour. We take all matters of wellbeing and safeguarding extremely seriously and are following the appropriate procedures. We would ask that students and families refrain from speculation while we establish the facts.

Kind regards,  
Mr A. Merriweather  
Headteacher

It was a masterpiece of institutional laundering. If you read it without context, you’d think someone had perhaps posted an unwise meme. Not that a months-old humiliation had finally dragged itself into fluorescent light because a group of teenagers, having failed each other repeatedly in private, ran out of alternatives.

Jonah read it over my shoulder at breakfast and said, “That’s grim.”

“Insightful as ever.”

“No, but specifically. It sounds like somebody got caught vaping near a school trip.”

He wasn’t wrong.

After Mr Firth took the USB, events became both more dramatic and less satisfying than I’d imagined, which I suppose is realism for you. There was no single perfect reveal. No hall falling silent as the truth blazed onto a projector. Mr Firth did not, despite what would have improved my mood considerably, march Ryan onstage and denounce him between the welcome speech and the mini brownies.

What happened instead was messier.

Cleo, white-faced and shaking only once Mr Firth had actually taken the USB, insisted on staying while he found somewhere private to view it. Tasha refused to leave because she’d “already emotionally budgeted for this.” I stayed because there was no plausible version of my life in which I walked away at that point and remained inhabitable to myself.

Ryan asked to explain, which was so perfectly him that even Mr Firth looked tired.

Freya, summoned by text from Tasha, arrived and said just enough to make it impossible to reclassify the whole thing as misunderstanding. Not everything. Not heroically. But enough. That seemed to be the governing ethic of the evening: late honesty in workable quantities.

By 7:20, two more staff were involved, one of whom kept saying “right” in the tone of a person building a bridge while standing on it. Ryan’s mother appeared at some point in a camel coat and practical fury, and for a horrifying second I thought she was going to improve his legal positioning by sheer force of diction. Instead she took one look at his face, one look at Cleo’s, and went very still.

Interesting, that. The moment someone else’s mother understands.

No police. No immediate apocalypse. Just statements, tears from someone unexpected, Ryan saying “it wasn’t like that” until even he seemed to hear the flimsiness of it. Mr Firth, to his credit, did not once say “let’s all calm down,” which may be why I’m capable of remembering him without violence.

By the time Mum picked me up at quarter to nine, the school had emptied back into darkness and she had that terrifying parent quiet which means she’s saving her questions until they can hurt more.

She drove home in silence for nearly five minutes before saying, “Would you like to tell me why I’ve just collected you from a safeguarding incident?”

There are some sentences your mother should not have to say.

“I can explain,” I said.

“Excellent. Because at the moment I’ve got ‘emoji,’ ‘video,’ and Mr Firth looking like he aged eight years in one evening.”

So I did. Not elegantly. Not in a complete and noble arc of confession. Just in fragments: Cleo, the party, the message, what I knew, what I did not stop. Mum drove with both hands at ten and two and did not interrupt once.

When I finished, she said, very quietly, “You should have told me.”

“I know.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“I know.”

Then, after a beat, “You were scared.”

It was almost worse than anger, that. Accuracy delivered kindly.

“At the time,” she said, “you were scared. Last night you were less scared than ashamed. Those are not the same thing, but they are cousins.”

I looked out the window so I wouldn’t have to answer with my face.

At school on Friday, the atmosphere was that peculiar post-event fizz where everyone knows something happened and no one agrees on what. The official version had already started breeding unofficial ones. Ryan had been suspended, or not. Cleo had returned heroically, or hysterically. There was a video, but maybe not of what people said. Freya was in it. I was in it. Half the rugby team was in it. The headteacher was resigning. The school was banning phones. School gossip abhors a vacuum and fills it with compost.

People looked at me more than usual, but not in a coherent way. Sympathy from some. Curiosity from most. One or two bright, avid expressions from the sort of girls who collect scandal as a hobby and call it concern.

Tasha intercepted me by the stairs with a packet of cheese-and-onion crisps.

“Congratulations,” she said. “You’re now a cautionary tale and a feminist icon depending who’s telling it.”

“I’ve always wanted range.”

“You really haven’t.”

She handed me the crisps like a ceremonial object. “Freya’s gone home. Ryan’s in with deputy head and his mother. Cleo left after registration because apparently she enjoys entering and exiting institutions theatrically.”

That made something in me loosen, just slightly. “Is she all right?”

Tasha gave me a look. “Define.”

Fair.

I found Cleo at lunchtime anyway.

Not in school. Just outside the back gate, by the ugly little strip of grass where people wait to be collected or pretend to vape. She was sitting on the low brick wall in her coat, no bag, as if she had only partially committed to the day.

“Hi,” I said.

She looked up. “Bold of you.”

I stood there for a second, because all the speeches I’d half-written in my head on the walk over had gone swampy and useless.

“I’m sorry,” I said at last.

Cleo considered this. “Yes.”

That was so exactly her I nearly smiled.

“I don’t mean as closure,” I said. “Or because I think saying it now fixes anything. I just—”

“You don’t get points for discovering cause and effect late.”

“I know.”

She looked away toward the road. Cars hissed past on wet tarmac. Somewhere nearby a Year 11 laughed too loudly at something not worth it.

After a moment she said, “I wasn’t trying to get you back.”

“I know.”

“That text.”

“I know.”

“I was trying to see if you still understood me.”

That one landed lower.

I sat beside her on the wall. Not close enough to touch. We stayed like that for a bit, facing the road like two women waiting for a bus neither intended to catch.

Then Cleo said, “You have a truly appalling panic smile, by the way.”

I laughed before I could stop myself. “I’m aware.”

“It makes you look like a Victorian child trying to survive an operation.”

“That is so specific.”

“You’re welcome.”

And there it was, briefly: the shape of us, still there and no use to anyone.

My phone buzzed in my blazer pocket. We both looked at it.

For one absurd second my body still reacted the old way — the jump, the flash of cold.

I took it out.

Not blood drops. Just Mum.

Milk. Bin bags. And don’t make me hear about you via email again.

I showed Cleo.

She snorted. “Terrifying.”

“Generationally.”

I put the phone away. Across the road, a little girl was dragging her parent toward the open evening banner still tied to the fence, now damp and curling at the corners. Future Ready, it said.

Cleo followed my eye line and said, “Bleak.”

“Mm.”

After a minute she stood. “I’m going home.”

“All right.”

She adjusted her coat, then looked at me with that same sharp, assessing expression she’d had since we were fourteen and thought naming things gave us power over them.

“It still means emergency,” she said.

“What does?”

She just gave me a look.

Then she walked away, not turning back once.

I waited till she was almost at the corner before taking the three jelly hearts out of my pocket and dropping them in the bin.

chapter_raw_judge_text.8:
[Analysis]

This is a genuinely accomplished piece of YA fiction that executes its chapter plan with considerable skill and restraint. Let me work through the key elements.

VOICE AND CHARACTER: Maeve's voice is the chapter's greatest strength. The defensive intelligence, the compulsive categorisation, the smile that reads wrong — all of it is present and consistent with the profile. Lines like "accuracy delivered kindly" and the Victorian child operation joke land precisely because they're earned by the preceding characterisation. Cleo's brief appearance is equally well-handled: she is not softened into a victim, she remains exasperating and sharp ("You don't get points for discovering cause and effect late"), and the line "I was trying to see if you still understood me" is the emotional centre of the chapter, delivered without fanfare. Tasha's cameo is pitch-perfect — the cheese-and-onion crisps as ceremonial object, the "feminist icon and cautionary tale" line, the brisk "Define" in response to "is she all right?" — all consistent with her profile.

PLOT EXECUTION: The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The aftermath is deliberately anti-climactic, the school email is a masterpiece of institutional laundering (and the story knows it), Ryan's mother's moment of stillness is a small, precise detail that does real work. The plan called for "something true has surfaced, but everyone will go on being themselves" and that's exactly what's delivered. The resolution is messy and partial, not cinematically triumphant.

DIALOGUE: The dialogue is the chapter's strongest technical achievement. It sounds like actual teenagers — clipped, oblique, funny in the way people are funny when they're also in pain. "Bold of you." / "Yes." is a perfect exchange. The mother's dialogue is excellent: "You were scared. Last night you were less scared than ashamed. Those are not the same thing, but they are cousins." This is the one moment that risks being slightly too polished, but it earns its place because it's delivered in a car, quietly, and Maeve's response is appropriately deflated.

LIGHTNESS AND DARKNESS: The tonal balance is the chapter's most impressive quality. The dark comedy arises naturally from institutional blandness (the email, the "right" bridge-builder, the Future Ready banner), teenage overperformance, and the specific embarrassment of doing the right thing too late. The jelly hearts dropped in the bin at the end is a small, perfect gesture — not redemptive, not symbolic in an over-engineered way, just the right action at the right moment.

WEAKNESSES: A few moments approach over-polish. "Two women waiting for a bus neither intended to catch" is the most obvious — it's a nice image but slightly too composed for Maeve's voice, which tends toward the drier and more self-deprecating. The "Future Ready" banner is a touch on-the-nose as ironic commentary, though it's brief enough not to damage the chapter. The Jonah scene at breakfast is good but his "grim" line, while consistent with his profile, feels slightly like a character note being checked off. The chapter is also slightly long for what it needs to do — the middle section covering the aftermath could be tightened — but this is a minor complaint given the quality of the closing scene.

ENDING: The final exchange — "It still means emergency" / the look / walking away — is genuinely moving without being sentimental. The three jelly hearts dropped in the bin closes the symbolic thread without explaining it. This is exactly the kind of ending the plan called for: something true has surfaced, the friendship is not restored, but the symbols have been acknowledged and released.

OVERALL: This is a high-quality chapter that executes its plan faithfully, maintains consistent characterisation, earns its emotional moments, and resists the temptation to over-resolve. The voice is distinctive and sustained. The dark comedy works because it arises from specificity rather than performance.

The dark comedy is well-calibrated. The chapter doesn't tip into either pure comedy or pure dread; it holds both, which is the hardest thing to do. The rain silvering the windows is the one moment where the prose reaches for atmosphere in a slightly generic way, but it's brief.

[Analysis]

This is Chapter 6 of a darkly comic British YA story, and it's executing at a high level across most dimensions. Let me work through the key elements critically.

VOICE AND CHARACTER CONSISTENCY

Maeve's voice is sharply maintained throughout. The defensive intelligence, the compulsive noticing, the panic smile detail — all consistent with the profile. The line "Die. / Valid but logistically poor." is exactly the register the character profile calls for. Her mother's appearance is brief but excellent: the "three distinct ways of saying fine" exchange is one of the chapter's best moments, and the mother's parting observation ("tell somebody before it gets bigger than them too") lands with the right weight — perceptive without being cartoonishly wise.

Tasha functions well as the socially grounded, slightly opportunistic ally. "Because now it's become real enough to inconvenience me" is a perfect Tasha line. Her taxonomy of the situation is brisk and useful without being cold. The "Gothic yearning" energy from her voice samples is present in spirit.

Cleo's text messages are excellent — "if you bottle it again, at least be original" is precisely the kind of line that is simultaneously cruel, funny, and emotionally loaded. It carries the weight of their history without explaining it.

Ryan's threat via anonymous text is handled well — the screenshot of Maeve mid-panic-smile is a genuinely clever plot device that also deepens her guilt and implication. It's not over-engineered.

FREYA

Freya is a new character introduced here (not in the profiles), and she works. She's not a named character in the plan but the chapter plan does mention "someone who immediately turns it into gossip" and "allies not because they love him but because accepting the truth would implicate them too." Freya functions as a witness-turned-reluctant-ally, and her line "You didn't" in response to Maeve's "Why didn't you say anything?" is the chapter's sharpest moment of moral accountability. It's earned, not telegraphed.

PLOT MECHANICS

The chapter follows its plan closely: the threat escalates (anonymous screenshot), pressure is applied to Maeve, an adult tries inadequately (the mother, not Firth — though Firth is mentioned in the plan, his absence here is fine given the chapter's focus), Maeve and Cleo communicate more honestly, and the chapter ends with Maeve deciding to act at the open evening. The lipstick USB stick is a perfect Cleo detail. The "reprographics corridor, 6:40" setup is appropriately mundane and specific.

DIALOGUE

The dialogue is consistently strong. It avoids the over-polished trap the writing plan warns against. "I want to be the sort of person who didn't need that as a question" (Freya) is slightly on the nose — it's the most "written" line in the chapter, a touch too self-aware for a panicked teenager — but it's not egregious. Most exchanges feel like actual teenagers talking under pressure.

DARK COMEDY

The comedy is well-calibrated. The open evening backdrop ("Aspirational Learners and Future Ready, which sounded less like education than a minor threat") is exactly the institutional blandness the plan calls for. The "die / valid but logistically poor" exchange. The estate agent viewing simile. These land without feeling forced.

METAPHOR AND PROSE QUALITY

"There's a special quality to remembered humiliation, even when it isn't yours. It enters your body by sound." — This is the chapter's most overtly "literary" moment. It's slightly purple but it earns its place because it's tied to a specific, concrete detail (Ryan's voice in the corridor clip). It doesn't feel like decorative riffing.

"Victorian child with a family secret" — good, specific, funny.

"Historians of their own cowardice" — this is the chapter's most self-consciously literary phrase and it's slightly too neat, too aphoristic. It's the kind of line that sounds profound but is really just a clever formulation. It's the one moment where the prose tips toward performing insight rather than delivering it.

The "rain tapping the windows" is a minor cliché but it's brief and doesn't linger.

EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT

The chapter builds genuine tension through accumulation rather than melodrama. The screenshot threat is emotionally effective because it implicates Maeve in a way that's morally complex — she's not guilty of the original harm but she looks like she is, and she knows why she looks like she is. That's the chapter's emotional core and it's handled with restraint.

FOLLOWING THE PLAN

The plan calls for: threat escalation (yes — anonymous screenshot), pressure on protagonist (yes), adult trying inadequately (the mother does this, though Firth was specified — minor deviation), protagonist and ex-best-friend communicating more honestly (yes, via text), working out the culprit's plan for the open evening (yes), protagonist deciding to act (yes). The plan also mentions "a doctored screenshot" — the chapter delivers this. The plan mentions "exposure of an unrelated secret" — this is gestured at but not fully developed (the threat is more about implicating Maeve in the original incident than exposing something separate). Minor deviation.

WEAKNESSES

The chapter's main weakness is that it's almost too competent — it executes the plan cleanly without many surprises. The Freya scene, while well-written, is somewhat predictable in structure (reluctant witness confesses, gets threatened, asks what to do). The ending line — "I think I'm ruining everyone's evening" — is good but slightly too neat as a closing beat, a little too self-consciously quippy. The chapter plan warns against "dialogue that sounds too polished" and this final line edges toward that.

The "historians of their own cowardice" line is the clearest instance of the prose reaching for aphorism when it should stay in the moment.

Overall, this is strong, disciplined, voice-consistent YA writing that follows its plan faithfully and delivers genuine emotional and comedic texture without overreaching.

final_raw_judges_texts:
[Analysis]

This is a remarkably accomplished piece of darkly comic British YA fiction. Let me assess it across multiple dimensions.

VOICE AND STYLE: The first-person narrator's voice is the story's greatest strength. It's consistently rendered, genuinely funny, and never slips into parody or self-congratulation. Lines like "Jonah was in the kitchen eating dry cereal straight from the box and watching some video of a man restoring a knife for reasons too depressing to ask about" are exactly right — the comedy is embedded in observation, not performance. The British specificity is authentic rather than performed: the pastoral teacher's "you all right?" as institutional gesture, the UCAS bloodsport, the open evening as aspirational theatre. This is not a writer reaching for Britishness; it's a writer who knows it.

METAPHOR AND POETIC LANGUAGE: The prose is frequently excellent and the metaphors generally land. "School gossip is what happens when boredom gets a knife" is sharp. "Cleo without commentary was like finding a swan in Aldi" is genuinely funny and precise. "There are arguments where the air itself starts choosing sides" is a little more generic but still functional. Occasionally the narrator's voice becomes slightly too polished — "the truth did not divide neatly into victim and villain with everyone else lined up by moral usefulness" is good but feels slightly essayistic for a teenager, even a self-aware one. However, the story largely earns its register because Maeve is established as someone who processes experience through wit as a defence mechanism. The metaphors are mostly earned rather than decorative.

CHARACTER: Maeve is genuinely nuanced — her complicity is the story's moral engine, and the story doesn't let her off the hook while also not making her a villain. The moment where she remembers smiling at Cleo in the corridor is the story's best beat: "Not because it was funny. Because people were there." This is psychologically precise and devastating. Cleo is well-drawn — sharp, exhausted, using Maeve instrumentally while also genuinely needing her. The line "I wasn't trying to get you back... I was trying to see if you still understood me" is excellent character work. Ryan is perhaps the weakest character — he functions more as a mechanism than a person, though his "it was deleted" as the full extent of his moral accounting is a nice touch. Tasha is a strong supporting character, her sardonic commentary never feeling like mere comic relief.

PACING: The story moves well across eight chapters. The mystery of the blood drops is sustained without becoming tedious. The escalation from personal text to school-wide incident feels organic. The open evening as climax is well-chosen — the institutional performance of aspiration against the private reality of harm is thematically resonant. The final chapter's quieter register is appropriate and earned.

DIALOGUE: The dialogue is strong throughout. It's witty without being stagey, and characters are distinguishable by voice. Cleo's "It still means emergency" as the final spoken line is excellent — it closes the loop on the emoji's meaning while leaving the relationship genuinely ambiguous. The confrontation in the reprographics corridor is well-handled; Ryan's "it was deleted" is the right kind of damning understatement.

PLOT AND COHERENCE: The plot is coherent and well-constructed. The blood-drop emoji's multiple meanings are established early and paid off throughout. The timestamp 12:07 as a recurring detail is effective. The USB stick shaped like a lipstick is a perfect Cleo detail. The resolution is appropriately messy — no triumphant revelation, just "late honesty in workable quantities." This is exactly right for the genre and the story's moral seriousness.

UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: Maeve's shift from avoidance to action is the story's central arc, and it's handled carefully. The story doesn't pretend she becomes a hero — she acts, but the story is clear that this is "less scared than ashamed" rather than genuine courage. The final scene with Cleo is deliberately unresolved. This is mature storytelling.

WEAKNESSES: The story occasionally over-explains its own observations. "This is what I mean about Tasha" followed by an explanation of what Tasha does is slightly redundant when the dialogue has already shown it. Some of the narrator's more philosophical asides ("Human beings are excellent at this. We call it perspective when what we mean is selective cowardice") are very good but there are perhaps one or two too many of them, risking the sense that the narrator is performing self-awareness rather than experiencing events. The open evening climax, while well-constructed, is slightly less dramatically satisfying than the build-up promises — the confrontation is good but Ryan's capitulation comes quickly. The school email in Chapter 8 is a nice touch but the chapter overall is slightly longer than it needs to be.

FAITHFULNESS TO PROMPT: The prompt asked for darkly comic British YA fiction responding to the blood-drop emoji text. The story delivers all of this with considerable skill. The darkness is real (image-based abuse, complicity, institutional inadequacy) and the comedy is genuine rather than tonal decoration.

OVERALL: This is a high-quality piece of YA fiction that takes its genre seriously. The voice is distinctive and consistent, the moral complexity is handled with intelligence, and the comedy earns its place rather than deflecting from the darkness. Minor weaknesses in over-explanation and a slightly rushed climax prevent it from being a masterpiece, but it's genuinely impressive work.
