By morning the bed smelled ordinary again.

That was almost enough to make me ashamed of myself.

Sun through the blinds, dust in it, the radiator clanking like it always did when the pipes heated unevenly, Mara standing at the counter in one of my old T-shirts with her hair twisted up and clipped. If you squinted, there was a shape here that could pass for our life. She had a mug in both hands. Tea gone cold, from the look of it. She stared out the window over the sink while the kettle sat empty on the back burner.

“You want coffee?” I asked.

She glanced over, not startled. “Already made some.”

There was a cup by the machine. Black, untouched.

I poured it anyway. The coffee had gone from bitter to burnt on the hot plate, but I drank it. Mara set her mug down, picked up the dish towel by the sink, folded it once, then unfolded it and left it there crooked. That more than anything made me uneasy. She was not a neat person by instinct, but she had categories. Systems. Little private tyrannies of arrangement. Drawers alphabetized by medicine type. Pantry labels facing out. The bathroom cabinet had looked like a crime scene all week, cotton swabs and ointment tubes and gauze tabs left open where she used them.

“You sleep at all?” I asked.

“A little.”

I watched her profile as I drank. “You were up again.”

“So were you.”

There are marriages built on honesty. Ours had always been built more on accuracy. We corrected each other the way some couples flirt. It was close enough most days. That morning it made me tired.

“I wasn’t standing over somebody.”

She rubbed at a spot low on her wrist where the hospital tape had taken skin. “I wasn’t standing.”

“Fine. Sitting. Watching.”

Her jaw moved once. “Do you want toast?”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

She opened the breadbox anyway. The bread was stale; she touched the heel of it and put it back. I stood there with my coffee cooling in my hand and felt a quick stupid flare of anger that had less to do with the bread than anything. This was how the last three weeks had gone. Every practical thing in the house still happened, more or less, but with just enough drag in it to make each one feel staged.

I left for work and got as far as the school parking lot before I called in sick.

I told the secretary I’d been up all night with my wife and she made the sympathetic noise people make when they hear “wife” and “hospital” in the same sentence. I sat in my truck under a sky the color of dishwater, hand still on the steering wheel, and tried to think what I would have done with a day teaching ninth graders how not to lose fingers to a band saw. Gone through motions. Corrected grip. Checked goggles. Smelled sawdust and lacquer and thought about my wife in the dark watching me breathe.

I went home.

Mara was upstairs. I could hear the bathwater running, though she almost never took baths. She said sitting in cooling water felt like marinating. I stood in the kitchen listening to the pipes knock and looking at the dish towel she had folded and abandoned. There were two damp footprints on the floorboards by the back door, small and pale where the water had darkened the wood. Bare feet. Hers, probably. The odd thing was the back door was still chained.

I crouched and touched one. Cold. Real enough. I wiped it with my thumb and got only water.

The bath ran for a long time.

I busied myself because that’s what I do when I don’t know what to do. Stripped the bed. Started laundry. Opened windows to let out the stale warm smell of the house, though the day outside was raw and smelled like rain on pavement. When I pulled the fitted sheet free, there it was again under the detergent and sleep-sweat and us: that thin mineral damp, not rot exactly, not algae, just the smell of water that has sat over stone a long time. The lake in late season. Cold enough to hurt your ankles.

I stood with the sheet bunched in my fists until the machine beeped for me to choose a cycle.

You can keep a lot of thoughts from becoming words if you keep your hands full.

By noon Mara had come downstairs and changed into jeans and a gray sweater she wore at home when she meant to work. Her laptop was open on the table, but the screen had gone to sleep. She sat in front of it with one hand around another reheated cup of tea.

“You called out?” she asked without looking up.

“Yeah.”

“You shouldn’t keep doing that.”

“It’s been one day.”

“You called out Friday too.”

I leaned against the doorway. “You keeping track now?”

Her mouth did a tired, humorless almost-smile. “Somebody should.”

That was the first thing all day that sounded enough like her to get under my skin.

I went to the table and sat opposite her. The laptop reflected part of my face, warped in the black screen. “Mara.”

She looked up.

In daylight her face was too familiar to be frightening for long. Fine lines at the corners of her eyes that deepened when she was amused. A pale healing scrape near her hairline. Mouth too expressive to hide much for very long. She looked exhausted. Human. There was a part of me that hated the version of events in which I was the kind of man who turned his half-recovered wife into a problem because she’d been strange at night.

“Why are you doing it?” I asked, quieter.

“Doing what.”

I nearly laughed again. “Come on.”

Her gaze dropped to the laptop, then to the tea. “I wake up.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“I know.”

We sat with that.

Outside, a truck shifted gears on the hill. Upstairs, one of the old windows gave a soft tick in its frame. Mara reached for the tea, missed the handle by half an inch, then corrected. It was such a tiny off movement I might not have noticed before the lake. Now I noticed everything.

“Are you scared?” I asked.

She let out a breath through her nose. “Of what?”

“That you’ll stop breathing again. That I’ll—” I stopped.

That I’ll miss it. That I won’t be fast enough. That I already wasn’t.

Mara looked at me then with an expression I couldn’t sort. Not pity. Not anger either. Something flatter and more tired.

“Daniel,” she said, “if I was scared of sleeping, do you think I’d choose your face to stare at?”

Despite myself, I barked out a laugh. It felt rusty. “That’s mean.”

“It’s accurate.”

“There you are.”

“For ten seconds, maybe.”

She pushed back from the table and took her tea to the sink. Didn’t drink it. Just poured the whole thing out. Steam barely rose. Cold already.

The rest of the day passed with the ugly pace of a day two people are trapped inside on purpose. I fixed the loose leg on the kitchen chair she always used. She moved from room to room and seemed to leave dampness behind without ever being wet. Not puddles. Just a used, chilled feel to spaces she’d just been in. The bathroom mirror clouded after she stood before it with no hot water running. In the living room she sat through half an old nature documentary without, as far as I could tell, seeing any of it.

By night I knew two things. One: if I asked her again, she’d lie or refuse. Two: I was not going to sleep without knowing more.

So when she came to bed, I waited until her breathing evened a little—not sleep, exactly, but the approximation of it—and let my own body go loose the way it does when you’re trying to impersonate yourself. Arm over my face at first, then down. Mouth slack. Slow, regular breaths. I lay facing away from her this time, toward the window.

Minutes passed.

The old house made its small sounds. Pipes settling. Wind nudging the siding. A dog barking twice somewhere down the block. I was starting to think maybe she’d sensed it somehow, maybe she’d stay still all night out of spite, when the mattress gave a slow careful shift behind me.

Her weight moved closer.

I felt, more than heard, her lean in. The air touched the back of my neck, cooler than it should have been. Her breath stirred the short hair there.

Then, very softly, almost with affection, she said, “Not when you’re listening.”

Every muscle in my body went hard.

I kept my eyes shut.

I could feel her waiting to see if that had made me move.
step_outputs.8:
The next day I ordered weather stripping I didn’t need and a new mattress protector I did not believe would help.

It gave me something to do with my hands.

I also spent forty minutes online reading about post-traumatic sleep disturbance, parasomnias, hypervigilance, sensory distortion after near-death experiences, and the ways grief and interrupted sleep can make sane people behave like idiots. Every article was either written in a tone of bright patient authority that made me want to throw my phone, or so vague it might as well have said sometimes bad things happen and the body is weird.

Nothing in any of them covered your wife leaning close to your neck in the dark and speaking like she was sharing a joke with someone else in the room.

Mara stayed upstairs most of the morning. I could hear drawers opening and closing, then silence, then one drawer opening again. Around eleven she came down in leggings and one of my old flannels and asked if we had any more of the gauze pads. I told her top shelf of the hall closet. She nodded and went there without looking. On her way back she paused in the doorway to the living room.

“You didn’t go in today.”

“No.”

She gave one small shrug. “You should.”

“You say that like I’m skipping school.”

“You kind of are.”

I looked up from my phone. “You want me out of the house?”

“No.”

She said it quickly enough that I believed her. Then, just as quickly, I couldn’t tell what believing it got me.

At lunch she made herself half a sandwich and ate the crusts, which she never did. Mara had always eaten around edges—pizza, toast, pie crust, all of it—with the explanation that the best parts were in the middle and she had no interest in proving moral character through bread. I watched her chew the crusts standing at the counter, eyes somewhere over my shoulder, and had the stupid intrusive thought that maybe she simply didn’t know the rule anymore. Maybe whatever came back with her knew enough to use her body and not enough to understand her preferences.

I hated myself for the thought as soon as I had it.

“You’re staring,” she said.

I looked away. “Sorry.”

That got a real reaction, faint but unmistakable. Her mouth twitched.

“See?” she said. “Creepy.”

I almost smiled back. Almost. Then she set the plate down and asked, without any lead-up at all, “Did you dream about the dock again?”

The floor seemed to slope under me.

“What?”

She licked a crumb from her thumb and frowned at the plate like the sandwich had disappointed her. “You were grinding your teeth.”

“That doesn’t answer—”

“It wasn’t a complicated question.”

“I didn’t tell you I dreamed about the dock.”

“You dream about it most nights.”

The shame of that hit first. Then the colder part. I kept my voice level with effort. “How would you know?”

She looked up. “You talk.”

“I don’t.”

“You do now.”

The answer was so flat, so matter-of-fact, that I had nothing ready for it. Mara had always talked in complete thoughts. Even angry, even tired. This recent habit of saying things that sounded finished but weren’t had begun to wear at me worse than the staring.

That afternoon I found myself listening to the house every time she left the room. Not because I thought she’d do something dramatic. Because I’d begun to dread the ordinary evidence that she had been somewhere: the damp handprint on the bathroom counter, the smell that was and wasn’t there, the feeling of walking into a room too soon after somebody had whispered in it.

By six I was as wrung out as if I’d done something harder than boil pasta.

We ate in front of the TV with the volume too low, both of us pretending to watch a quiz show while contestants smiled and failed to name rivers. Mara sat tucked into the corner of the couch with a blanket over her legs. Halfway through, she reached out and turned the volume down another click without taking her eyes off the screen.

“What?” I said.

“Nothing.”

“Mara.”

She listened a second longer. “I thought I heard water.”

The radiators hissed softly in the walls. Rain ticked against the back windows. I wanted to tell her that was all. Instead I muted the television. We sat there in the sudden house-noise silence, hearing only the rain and the low mechanical throat-clearing of old pipes.

“Happy?” I asked.

“No.”

By bedtime my nerves felt peeled.

I brushed my teeth longer than I needed to. Watched myself in the mirror over Mara’s shoulder while she stood at the sink moisturizing the tape-burned skin on her wrists. We looked like a couple from far away. Tired, strained, surviving a bad month. Her hair clipped up, my T-shirt inside out, one of us asking if we were out of aspirin. If anybody had looked through the doorway, they’d have seen exactly what I wanted them to see.

Then Mara rinsed her hands and said to my reflection, “If you’re going to fake it again tonight, at least commit.”

I turned too fast and spat toothpaste foam into the sink. “You knew.”

Her eyes met mine in the mirror, cool and unsurprised. “Daniel.”

“Well, excuse me for not sleeping great.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“Then what do you mean?”

She capped the lotion. “You breathe differently when you’re pretending.”

I laughed once. It had no humor in it. “Good to know.”

“For me, yes.”

She left me there with the sink running.

I told myself I wouldn’t do it again.

Then we got into bed and all I could think was that whatever this was had become worse once she knew I knew, and I could not bear turning my back and hoping for the best.

So I lay on my back and let my breathing slow. Not immediately. Gradually, the way she would expect. If she was measuring, let her measure. The room was almost dark except for a pale strip of streetlight on the ceiling. Mara lay on her side facing me. I could feel her eyes closed for the first few minutes, or maybe that was wishful thinking. I counted breaths to keep from thinking. At fifty I lost track. At some point her breathing changed.

I waited.

The mattress gave a shallow pull as she shifted closer. Not enough to touch. Just enough that I could smell her shampoo, the cedar one she’d used for years. Then colder beneath it, that faint stone-water smell again.

A long pause.

I felt rather than saw her hand lift. Air moved over the skin of my throat, my collarbone, stopping there as if she were gauging heat from a fire.

My whole body wanted to jerk.

Instead I kept still and listened.

At first I thought the sound was the radiator. A wet little knock somewhere behind me. Then I realized it was lower, closer, and regular. Mara’s mouth barely moving.

Not words, not exactly. Breath shaped almost into them.

I opened my eyes.

Her face was inches above mine. Her hand hovered over my chest. Her sleeve, pushed back to the elbow, was dark with moisture.

“Mara.”

She stopped.

For one impossible second I heard a second breath under hers—ragged, submerged, as if another set of lungs had tried to use the same air too late.

Then she blinked and sat back so fast the bed shook.

“What are you doing?” I said.

Her expression changed after the fact, as though anger had to travel to her from a distance. “You were supposed to be asleep.”

The cold that went through me then had nothing to do with the room.

“Supposed to?”

She looked at my throat, not my face. “You keep interrupting it.”

“Interrupting what?”

But she was already pulling the blanket over herself, turning away, every inch of her body saying the conversation was over.

I sat up in bed and stared at the damp mark her sleeve had left on the sheet between us until it cooled and vanished.
step_outputs.9:
The next morning I drove to the lake house without telling her.

I left a note on the counter that said Hardware store, back later, because it was easier than deciding whether I was lying. Mara was still asleep—or looked asleep—on her side of the bed when I got dressed. I stood in the doorway longer than I should have, watching the shape of her under the blanket. She hadn’t slept with the blanket tucked under her chin in ten years, not unless she had a fever.

Outside, the air had that raw washed-clean smell after rain. The drive north took just under an hour, long enough for coffee to go from too hot to useless in the travel mug and for me to rehearse half a dozen versions of what I thought I might learn when I got there. None of them made much sense even to me. I wasn’t going for proof. I was going because I couldn’t bear another day in the house with only my own thoughts to push against.

The lake house had belonged to Mara’s aunt Ruth, then to Mara, then to both of us in the soft legal way things become both of yours after enough years. It was a square cedar-sided place with green trim gone chalky and a screened porch that listed half an inch toward the water. Ruth had bought it because she loved birds and privacy and old wood. Mara loved it because no one else did enough to claim it hard. I had loved it too, once, in the uncomplicated way you can love a place that belongs more naturally to somebody else.

That had changed before the accident. Not all at once. In bills and repairs and weekends spoken for six weeks ahead. In the low-grade argument of what counted as keeping something and what counted as being trapped by it.

I parked on the gravel and sat a moment with the engine off, listening to it tick as it cooled.

The dock was visible through the trees, gray boards wet-dark from the previous night’s rain. The lake beyond it looked flat and patient. From a distance it gave nothing back.

Inside, the house smelled closed up and faintly tannic, the way old cabins do when they’ve been empty too long. I opened the porch door, then the kitchen windows. The curtains stirred. Nothing dramatic happened. No chill, no whisper, no sudden revelation that I had brought my fear to the right address. Just dust in the slant of light and the ordinary embarrassment of being a grown man standing in a room because he half suspected a lake of keeping secrets.

I went to the mudroom and picked up the shoes Mara had left there that weekend. One sneaker on its side, one upright, laces dark from where they’d been soaked and dried badly. She had come back from the hospital in borrowed flip-flops and never asked about the shoes. I’d meant to throw them away. Instead they sat there exactly where I’d put them after the paramedics were gone and the police questions were over and the dock was empty again.

I should have taken them then and gone home.

Instead I walked down to the water.

The boards of the dock gave a little under my weight in the same places they always had. Third board from shore soft at the edge. Nail head proud halfway down. At the end, the lake smell came up cold and mineral and faintly weedy. The sky was low and white. Somewhere across the water a motor coughed to life.

I stood where I’d stood that day and tried not to make memory into theater.

We had argued in the kitchen first. Quietly, which is sometimes worse. Mara had wanted to stay through the fall and do the porch herself. I had said that was not doing the porch, that was pretending a structure problem was a personality trait. She had laughed at me in that clipped way that meant I’d become ridiculous in her eyes. I had said something about Ruth leaving her a house and a martyr complex in the same will. She had gone still. Then she had walked out to the dock in her socks.

Not running. Not dramatic. Just done with me.

I had waited ten, maybe fifteen seconds before following. That was the part my mind had polished into a blade these last weeks: the waiting. Not because I thought she’d drown. Because I was angry and wanted her to know I could let her walk away. Then the sound—the skid of a foot on wet wood, a crack that might have been knee or board, the splash.

I had reached the dock in time to see only circles widening.

I stared at the water now and felt my chest tighten in the same place.

“She took a while to come up.”

I turned so hard the dock rocked.

Neil Hammett stood at the shore end with a tackle bucket in one hand. He lived two properties down, retired electrician, good at lending tools and talking too long about weather. He was in a waxed jacket and a cap darkened by mist.

“Jesus,” I said.

He gave me a careful look. “Didn’t mean to sneak up.”

“I didn’t hear you.”

“Mm.”

He came down the dock a little, not all the way. Left decent distance. “You back to close up?”

“Something like that.”

His eyes went to the water, then to me. “How’s she doing?”

There are times when “fine” is a lie so obvious it becomes an insult. I said, “Not great.”

He nodded like that was sensible. “That’ll take.”

I almost left it there. Then I heard myself ask, “When you pulled her out—”

Neil shifted the bucket to his other hand. “I didn’t. You did. I just came running.”

“You were there.”

He looked at me longer this time. Not unkind. “I was there.”

I swallowed. “Was she conscious?”

“Not at first.”

“After?”

He scraped a thumb over the handle of the bucket. “Why?”

“Because I’m asking.”

“Yeah.” He squinted past me toward the end of the dock, where the water darkened. “She coughed. Threw up half the lake. Then she opened her eyes.”

Something in me braced.

“And?”

Neil shrugged once, uneasy now. “And she looked around.”

“At me?”

He didn’t answer right away. “Past you, I thought.”

The lake gave a small slap against the posts below us.

“Like she was confused,” he added. “Wouldn’t make too much of that. People come to strange after oxygen goes out.”

I nodded, because what else was there to do with that.

Neil looked at me once more, then, as if against his better judgment, said, “Only odd thing was she’d gone real still again before the ambulance came. Eyes open. Looking at the water. Like she was listening.”

I wanted to ask, Listening to what. I didn’t. The question would have made us both stupid.

By the time I got back to the house, rain had started again. Thin, cold, needling rain that slicked the windshield and made every road look newly made. I drove too fast on the way home and had to brake hard at the light by the pharmacy. My hands hurt on the steering wheel from gripping it.

Mara was in the kitchen when I came in. Not at the table this time. Standing by the sink with both palms flat on the counter, shoulders rigid under one of her thin sweaters.

“You went back there,” she said.

Not asked. Said.

I closed the door behind me. “I needed—”

“What?”

I had no answer that didn’t sound pathetic.

She turned then. Her face was drawn and colorless, but her eyes were sharp in a way they hadn’t been for days. “Don’t do that again.”

“What, go to the lake?”

“Pretend I’m not here and go looking around me like a crime scene.”

The words hit because they were fair.

“Mara,” I said, “tell me what’s happening.”

For a second I thought she would. I saw the effort of it in her mouth, in the small pulse at her throat. She took one step toward me.

“Don’t pretend to sleep anymore,” she said. “If you feel yourself going, get up. Wake me. I don’t care. Just don’t—”

Her voice cut off.

I watched it happen. Not dramatically. Her face emptied by degrees, as if whatever had pushed to the surface had stepped back and taken the heat with it. The set of her shoulders changed. Her gaze dropped to my chest, then rose slowly to my face.

“Did you ever let yourself fully sleep beside me again?” she asked.

The calm in her voice was worse than anger.

I stood dripping rainwater onto the kitchen mat and understood, finally, that whatever answer I gave would not reach the same person who had asked the first question.
step_outputs.10:
That night I took a pillow and blanket to the spare room without discussing it.

Mara watched me from the hallway with one hand on the doorframe, not trying to stop me. The spare room had once been an office and was now where unused things went to become categories later: winter coats in dry-cleaning bags, a broken lamp, two boxes of books we’d packed when we thought we might move and never unpacked when we didn’t. The bed in there was narrow and hard, the mattress bowed in the middle. I spread the blanket anyway.

“This isn’t permanent,” I said, because the silence from her was somehow harder to bear than argument.

“Alright.”

That should have relieved me. It didn’t. “You don’t care?”

She folded her arms. “Would it help if I pretended to?”

I looked past her into the hall. There was a damp crescent on the runner rug where she’d just been standing with wet hair from the shower. Or maybe it had been there already. I couldn’t tell anymore.

“I’m trying to make this safer,” I said.

“For who?”

I let out a breath through my teeth. “You tell me.”

She nodded once, sharp and humorless, and went back to our bedroom.

I lay awake in the spare room listening to the house settle around me and feeling like an idiot. Anger is easier to maintain when the person you’re angry at stays in front of you. Alone with the old smell of cardboard and wool coats, all I had was the truth that I was frightened of my wife and ashamed of being frightened of her, and that these were not mutually canceling feelings.

At some point I slept.

I knew that because I woke with my neck bent wrong and one foot bare, the sock missing. The room was cold. Not night-cold. A deeper stale chill that seemed to have been waiting under the house all along. My mouth tasted metallic. I sat up too fast and had to steady myself on the edge of the mattress.

Mud gritted under my heel.

Not much. Just a smear of dark damp where my foot had dragged across the fitted sheet.

I stared at it until my vision sharpened. Then I looked around the room. My missing sock was half under the dresser. The window was still latched. The door stood three inches open. Beyond it the hall was dim with first light.

I touched the mud. Fine grit, wet enough to mark my thumb.

For a crazy second I thought of taking a picture like that would make any of this more bearable to look at later. Instead I wiped my hand on the blanket and stood.

Mara was in the kitchen making tea.

“You sleep?” she asked without turning.

I looked at her bare feet on the floorboards. Dry. Clean.

“I was in the spare room.”

“So?”

There was no accusation in it. That made it worse. “So how the hell do I wake up with mud on my foot?”

She went very still.

The kettle gave its thin, rising whistle. Neither of us moved to stop it for a second too long. Then Mara reached over and turned off the burner.

“I don’t know,” she said.

“You don’t know.”

“No.”

“You expect me to believe that?”

She turned then, cup in one hand, steam between us. “I expect you to believe I’m not doing this on purpose.”

That landed somewhere below anger. “Doing what, exactly?”

Her eyes flicked toward the hallway, toward the stairs, toward anywhere but me. “I don’t know what to call it.”

“Try.”

“You want a name so badly? Fine. Something is wrong at night.”

“Something.”

She laughed once under her breath and set the cup down too hard. Tea slopped over her fingers and she didn’t flinch. “You think if I say it cleanly enough it becomes manageable. It doesn’t.”

“What am I supposed to do, Mara?”

She looked at me then, really looked, and for one clear second I saw how exhausted she was. Not vague exhaustion. The bodily kind. Skin too fine over the bones of her face, shoulders carried half an inch too high, the stare of somebody who has spent too many nights refusing their own body basic things.

“Stop asking me to make it sound reasonable,” she said.

The words shut me up because they were true.

I changed the sheets from the spare bed. I scrubbed the smear from my heel at the bathroom sink. I put the muddy sock in the utility basin and watched the water cloud brown around it. Then I stood there with my hands braced on porcelain and admitted, if only to the mirror, that the spare room had not fixed anything. Either I was getting up in my sleep or something in this house no longer respected walls, distance, or common sense.

Late morning I found Mara in the hall closet, kneeling in front of the top shelf with the first-aid bin open beside her.

“What are you looking for?”

“Flashlight.”

“We have three in the junk drawer.”

“Those are dead.”

“How do you know?”

She sat back on her heels. “I checked.”

“Why?”

No answer. She dug past old batteries and a package of gauze, found the heavy yellow flashlight we kept for outages, and set it aside. Then she reached for the duct tape.

“Mara.”

She held the tape in both hands without looking at me. “Did you ever sleepwalk as a kid?”

“No.”

“Talk?”

“I don’t know. Maybe.”

“You do now.”

I stared at her. “What does that mean?”

She stood, flashlight under one arm, tape in the other hand like she was gathering supplies for a leak. “It means I hear you.”

“Hear me say what?”

She hesitated. It was small, but I knew her well enough to see it cost something.

“Not words always,” she said. “Sometimes just… like you’re answering something.”

“There’s no one there to answer.”

At that, her mouth pulled tight. “That’s exactly the problem.”

I followed her into the bedroom. The curtains were still half-drawn from the morning. Light lay pale across the unmade bed. She put the flashlight on the dresser and the duct tape beside it.

“What are those for?”

“I don’t know yet.”

It should have been absurd. Instead I found myself lowering my voice. “Mara, if you know something—”

“I know what I see.”

“Which is?”

She turned on me hard enough that I took a step back before I could stop myself. “You want the version I can say without sounding insane? Fine. When you drop too far asleep, the room changes.”

I opened my mouth, shut it.

She went on, angry now, which made her sound more like herself than she had in days. “It gets colder. Not all at once. Like a door’s open somewhere you can’t find. And you—” She swallowed. “Your face changes.”

“My face.”

“You don’t move. That’s not what I mean.” She pressed the heel of her hand to her eye and laughed once, sharp and miserable. “I know your sleeping face, Daniel. I’ve had ten years of it. This is different. It’s like watching somebody practice being you.”

Neither of us said anything for a moment.

Then she added, quieter, “Sometimes if I keep looking, it stops.”

The room felt suddenly too small.

“That’s why you watch me?”

“Sometimes.”

The word hung there.

“Sometimes?” I said.

Mara looked at the bed, not me. “Sometimes I’m making sure it isn’t getting closer.”

“And the other times?”

Her voice was almost flat. “The other times I don’t know who started it.”

That night, for the first time, I did not try to avoid the dark. I waited for it, and when it came I sat in the chair by our bedroom window with the flashlight on my knee and watched my wife lie down as if we were both pretending not to understand what that meant.
step_outputs.11:
Mara fell asleep before she meant to.

Not deeply. Not all at once. I watched it happen in small betrayals of the body: the way her jaw unclenched, then tightened again; the way her fingers, laced over her stomach, loosened one by one; the little hitch in her breath each time she tipped toward sleep and dragged herself back. We had agreed—without using the word agreed, because saying this out loud made it uglier—that one of us would stay awake and keep watch. She had insisted she could do it. I had insisted harder.

So I sat in the chair by the window with the flashlight and a mug of coffee gone oily and cold, and watched my wife lose a fight with her own body.

It was after midnight. The streetlight outside striped the room through the blinds, pale bars across the wall and bed. Our bedroom looked offensively normal. Laundry basket by the dresser. The paperback Mara had abandoned three weeks ago face-down on the nightstand. One of her socks under the radiator. The ordinary details did not comfort me anymore. They had started to feel complicit, as if the room had decided to keep behaving like a bedroom no matter what was using it.

Mara’s eyes opened once, found me in the chair, and shut again.

“Don’t drift,” she murmured.

“Then stop setting the example.”

The corner of her mouth moved. It might have been almost a smile. Then she was gone under again.

I checked my phone. 12:17.

The first hour passed in stretches and skips. The house made itself known in old-house ways. Pipes clicked. A truck went by on the hill outside. Somewhere a dog barked and was barked quiet. I stood twice to walk the room because sitting too long made my thoughts start to tilt. The coffee helped less than it should have. My eyes felt packed with grit. Every time I blinked I saw the afterimage of Mara’s face where she lay.

At 12:46 I thought I heard water in the wall behind the headboard.

Not a pipe noise. Not the familiar clank and run of heat. A softer sound. A held, interior trickling. Like somebody pouring from one glass to another in the next room.

I stood up fast enough to slosh coffee on my hand.

“Mara,” I said.

Her eyes opened immediately. Too quickly for someone asleep. “I hear it.”

That should have steadied me. It didn’t. She pushed herself upright, blanket falling to her waist, and turned her head toward the wall with the concentration of someone listening through a door.

“It’s not the pipes,” I said, hearing how stupidly hopeful it sounded.

“No.”

The sound stopped.

We stayed like that, both listening into silence. My hand was sticky with old coffee. Mara’s hair had come half loose from its tie. In the dark her face looked sharper, the planes of it cut clean by the blinds’ shadow. Familiar and not. Wife and witness and something else besides.

“You should lie back down,” I said finally.

Her laugh was only breath. “Why. So one of us can be horizontal when it starts?”

“You’re tired.”

“So are you.”

We looked at each other long enough that I had to look away first.

At some point after one, I must have blinked longer than a blink. I know that because when I next registered the room, Mara was no longer propped against the headboard. She was standing.

I did not see her get out of bed.

She stood between the bed and the mirror on the closet door, facing me. Barefoot. Arms loose at her sides. The blanket pooled by her ankles. For one nauseating second the mirror behind her showed only the bed and the chair and the slatted white bars of window-light. Empty space where she should have been.

Then she moved, and the mirror caught up.

I was on my feet before I understood I’d risen.

“Mara.”

Her expression did not change. Not blank, exactly. Attentive. The same patient attention from the bed, from the nights before, now held upright in the middle of the room.

“Get back in bed,” I said.

She tilted her head.

The pressure in my ears changed. That’s the only way I can describe it. As if we’d driven down a mountain too fast, or gone underwater and not quite equalized. The room seemed to pull farther away while staying the same size. I heard my own breath loud and close. Mara took one step toward me.

I clicked on the flashlight and the beam shook over her chest, throat, face. Her pupils had gone huge. The light should have made her squint. It didn’t.

“Mara.”

Her lips parted. For an instant I was certain she was going to say my name in her own voice and put an end to all of this by sounding ordinary. Instead she said, very softly, “You keep waking at the wrong part.”

I felt, absurdly, offended before I felt afraid. “What the hell does that mean?”

No answer.

She took another step.

Behind her, in the mirror, the bed was still occupied.

I saw the shape under the blanket where she should have been lying and my body reacted before my mind did. I dropped the flashlight. It hit the rug and rolled, beam wheeling crazily up the wall and across the ceiling. The room pitched. Mara’s standing body turned with impossible smoothness to follow the light, while in the mirror the shape on the bed remained still.

Then both images jerked into one.

I stumbled backward into the chair hard enough to crack my shin. “Mara!”

This time the body in front of me flinched. Hard. Like I had reached her from a distance.

She folded suddenly at the waist, one hand clapped over her mouth. A choking sound came through her fingers. I lunged without thinking and caught her shoulders. Her skin was ice-cold through the thin cotton of her shirt. She sagged against me, shaking.

“Don’t,” she said, and the voice was hers. “Don’t let me—”

Her whole body went rigid.

Not seizure-rigid. Deliberate. Every muscle tightening at once under my hands as if she had chosen stillness down to the bone. Her head turned toward me by degrees. Her mouth was still covered, but her eyes had fixed somewhere over my shoulder.

I could hear water again.

Not in the walls now. Closer. Behind me. A small patient dripping, as if from a coat left on a hook.

My own name came from my throat before I knew I meant to say anything.

“Mara.”

Something answered.

Not in words. In the feeling of an answer. In the unmistakable sense that a second attention had entered the room and was listening from inside my skin.

I let go of her as if burned.

The flashlight had rolled under the bed. Its beam cut a bright wedge through dust and the underside slats. Wet footprints crossed through the light from one side of the bed to the other.

Bare feet. Mine.

I looked down. My soles were damp against the rug.

I do not remember what happened for the next few seconds. I remember Mara grabbing my wrist hard enough to bruise. I remember both of us backing toward the door. I remember the bedroom seeming to breathe once, in and out, all the curtains lifting though the windows were shut.

Then I was in the hallway, gasping.

Mara slammed the bedroom door and leaned against it with both hands, white-faced. The flashlight beam still glowed under the gap at the bottom.

Neither of us spoke.

My heartbeat knocked against my ribs so hard it hurt. I looked down at my feet. Wet. Clean, except for the crescent of dirt packed under one toenail.

Mara followed my gaze and shut her eyes.

“You can’t sleep in here,” she said.

There was terror in her voice now. No ambiguity, no anger left to hide in.

I touched the door behind her. The wood was cold enough to feel damp.

“Because of you?” I asked.

She opened her eyes.

“No,” she said. “Because of you.”

We spent the rest of the night in the kitchen with every light on.

Not because light helped. By then I didn’t know what helped. But brightness at least insulted the thing that had happened upstairs. Brightness made it harder to slip accidentally into dream logic. Mara sat at the table in one of the straight-backed chairs, a blanket around her shoulders and both hands wrapped around a mug she never drank from. I stood more than I sat. Every time I tried the chair opposite her, I felt the pull of sleep behind my eyes and got up again.

At four in the morning, our life looked like a police interview after the real questions were over.

The bedroom door stayed shut. Once, around two, I thought I heard a soft knock from the other side. Not a fist. Something lighter. Maybe the flashlight settling where it had rolled. Maybe wood cooling. Neither of us went to check.

“You should call somebody,” I said finally.

Mara gave a tired, disbelieving sound. “Who.”

“I don’t know. A doctor. Your mother.”

“My mother thinks chamomile tea is a treatment plan.”

“A priest, then.”

At that she actually looked up. “You don’t believe in God.”

“I’m willing to outsource.”

That got the ghost of her old expression, the one that meant I had said something she would have liked under different circumstances. It vanished almost immediately.

“We don’t need a priest,” she said.

“How do you know?”

“I don’t. I know I don’t want a stranger in the house asking me if I’ve invited darkness into my heart.”

“That sounds specific.”

She rubbed her thumb over the mug handle. “My mother had one come when I was fourteen because I bit another girl at camp.”

Despite everything, I stared. “You what?”

“She deserved it.”

I barked out a laugh before the room could stop me. It lasted one second and left me feeling almost sick with relief. Mara’s mouth twitched. Then we were back where we were.

The clock over the stove clicked to 4:12.

“I don’t know what this is,” I said.

“No.”

“I thought it was you.”

“I know.”

The plainness of that hurt more than if she’d snapped at me.

I leaned against the counter, arms folded hard across my middle. “And now?”

“Now I think it started with me.”

“Started.”

She nodded once.

“Not helpful, Mara.”

“It’s what I have.”

I wanted to demand better. Instead I said, “Tell me what you think you know.”

For a while she only looked at the table. I could see her deciding whether saying it aloud would make it truer. Finally she said, “The first night home, you fell asleep before I did.”

I remembered. I had been awake for almost forty hours between the accident, the hospital, the drive back, the phone calls, the casseroles, the stunned practical debris of survival. I’d sat on the edge of our bed to take off my shoes and next thing it was after midnight and Mara was still upright against the headboard.

“You were talking,” she said. “Not much. Just little bits.”

“What kind of bits?”

She winced, frustrated. “Nothing useful. Sounds. Like you were answering questions too quietly for me to hear them.”

A damp chill went through me.

“I thought it was the TV at first. Then I realized the TV was off. I looked at you and…” She stopped.

“And what?”

Her eyes flicked up to mine. “You looked wrong.”

I almost said that again, as if repetition might force detail out of it. Mara cut me off before I could.

“Not dramatic-wrong. That’s the problem. It’s always almost you. But there’s a point where your face goes slack in a way I’ve never seen, and the room…” She pressed her lips together. “The room feels occupied.”

The radiator gave a small hiss in the wall behind me. I flinched anyway.

“I woke you,” she said. “It stopped.”

She looked down at the mug again. “Then the next night I waited. To see if it happened again.”

“Jesus.”

“I know.”

“You couldn’t have told me?”

Her laugh this time was bitter enough to taste. “You? Three days after pulling me out of the lake while I was still coughing up water? You would have looked at me exactly the way you’re looking now.”

I opened my mouth, shut it.

“I thought maybe it was the hospital drugs,” she said. “Or lack of sleep. Or maybe I was losing my mind and at least if I watched long enough I could figure out the pattern before I told anyone. Then I fell asleep one night before you did. And when I woke up you were standing in the hallway outside the bathroom.”

I thought of the mud on my foot. The wetness. My own footprints under the bed.

“What was I doing?”

“You were just standing there.” Her fingers tightened around the mug. “Head down. Barely breathing. I said your name twice. You didn’t answer until I touched you.”

A rush of anger came up so fast it felt clean. “And you let this go on?”

She stood so abruptly the chair legs screeched.

“Don’t,” she said. “Do not do that. I am not the only one who kept waiting for a reasonable version.”

We stared at each other across the kitchen. Her blanket had slipped; one shoulder was bare and goose-pimpled in the bright light. I wanted to apologize. I wanted to be right. I wanted to sit down on the floor and put my head against the cabinet door until morning found us and solved this by ordinary means.

Instead I said, “So what happens if I leave?”

Mara’s face changed.

Not possession-changed. Something more naked than that.

“Leave where?”

“A hotel. My brother’s. Anywhere but here.”

“You can try.”

“Try?”

“I left once,” she said.

“When?”

“The afternoon you went back to the lake.”

I stared.

“I got as far as Maple and Third.” She rubbed her arms as if she’d just remembered being cold. “I lost five minutes. Came to in the car outside the pharmacy with the engine running and my hands around the wheel so hard they were cramping. I don’t remember turning around.”

We stood with that.

“So maybe it follows the house,” I said.

“Or us.”

Neither option improved things.

Gray began to thin the kitchen windows. Dawn without warmth. I suddenly understood how far into exhaustion we had gone. Mara looked breakable. I probably looked worse.

“What if we go back there together,” I said. “The lake.”

“Why.”

“Because whatever started, started there.”

“That’s not knowledge. That’s symbolism.”

“It’s more than we have now.”

She sat again, heavily this time. “You always do this.”

“What.”

“Turn terror into a project.”

I almost argued. Then didn’t. Because that, too, was true.

Mara watched her hands a long moment. Then she said, quieter, “When I look at you at night, sometimes I’m trying to keep it from leaning closer. Sometimes I’m checking if you’re still all there. And sometimes—”

She stopped.

“And sometimes?”

Her voice was very small. “Sometimes I can feel it wanting to, and I don’t know if the wanting is mine.”

The fluorescent hum over the stove seemed suddenly louder than the room.

I took the chair opposite her and sat, finally. My knees cracked.

“So what do we do?”

Mara looked toward the ceiling, toward the bedroom above us, then back at me.

“No more pretending,” she said. “No more sleeping near each other. No answering voices unless we can see each other’s mouths. And if one of us says wake me, the other one does it. Hard, if necessary.”

I nodded.

It was a plan in the way a handful of towels is a flood plan. Human, inadequate, all we had.

By evening we were back at the lake house anyway.

Not because it was wise. Because once the idea had been spoken it lodged in me like a splinter, and because Mara, after resisting for hours, had gone quiet in the particular way that meant she’d decided I might be wrong but not absurd. We packed without saying much. Flashlights, coffee, phone chargers, duct tape for reasons neither of us would explain. I drove with both windows cracked though the air was cold.

The lake was iron-gray by the time we arrived. The house waited under the trees exactly as it had before, and exactly as if it had been expecting us.

At the foot of the dock, Mara touched my sleeve.

“If I ask you to wake me,” she said, “don’t be gentle.”

I looked at her face, pale in the failing light, and thought how little confidence either of us had in who might be doing the asking by midnight.

Then we went inside.
step_outputs.13:
The lake house sounded different at night.

At home there had always been the muffled reassurance of neighbors—cars on wet pavement, a dog, somebody’s late television through a wall. Here there was only the house settling on its old posts and the lake moving in the dark beyond the windows. Water has a way of making silence feel occupied.

We set up in the front room because neither of us wanted the bedroom. Ruth’s old sofa sagged in the middle. The lamp by it cast a yellow cone over the braided rug and left the corners of the room to themselves. Mara sat in the armchair with a blanket over her knees and the heavy flashlight in her lap. I took the sofa. We had both sworn we wouldn’t lie down. Ten minutes after saying it, we were each pretending the furniture did not count.

The drive had used up what little determination we had left. Exhaustion sat in my bones like a second weather. Mara’s face looked transparent with it. She had gone almost white around the mouth. Every few minutes her gaze snapped to me as if checking whether I was still where she’d left me.

“You don’t have to keep doing that,” I said.

“Yes I do.”

I looked at the window. Beyond it the dark was complete except for the path of weak light from the porch bulb over the yard and the first silver suggestion of the dock beyond the trees. “I’m awake.”

“For now.”

There was no malice in it. Just arithmetic.

Around ten we tried to eat crackers and failed. Around eleven the lamp began to buzz faintly and Mara unplugged it and plugged it back in, jaw set, furious with ordinary electricity for choosing tonight to become noticeable. At some point she laughed once, very quietly, at nothing I could see.

“What?”

She shook her head. “I was thinking how much Ruth would hate this.”

“Us?”

“This.” She gestured at the room, the blankets, the flashlight, us. “She believed every problem could be solved by replacing a window latch.”

“That’s not the worst philosophy.”

“No.” Mara looked down at the flashlight in her lap. “Just incomplete.”

Midnight passed. One o’clock. The room thinned around the edges.

I got up twice to splash water on my face in the kitchen sink. The water was so cold it made my teeth ache. The second time I came back, Mara was no longer in the armchair.

For a second my body simply stopped.

Then I saw her through the porch screen, already halfway down the yard toward the dock. Barefoot. Blanket trailing from one hand like a shed skin.

“Mara!”

She didn’t turn.

I was through the porch door and after her before I remembered to grab the flashlight. The yard sloped slick under my shoes. Dead leaves pasted themselves to the soles. Mara moved with that same awful smoothness I’d begun to dread, not fast, not stumbling, simply continuing. The dock boards shone dimly with moisture ahead of her.

When I caught her arm at the shore end, she whipped around so suddenly I nearly lost my footing.

Her face was hers. That was the cruelest part. No blankness, no obvious vacancy. Her eyes were wide and wet in the weak porch light and full of terror.

“Wake me,” she said.

Then her expression emptied.

I jerked back as if the words had burned.

She smiled. Not broadly. Not in any way another person would have seen and run from. Just enough to be wrong on her face at that moment.

“Mara,” I said, and heard the plea in it.

She tilted her head toward the end of the dock. Toward the water beyond. “You took too long.”

The sentence hit me in the chest like a blow because it belonged to no single moment. The argument. The fall. The waiting I had replayed until it polished itself raw. I stepped back without meaning to. The boards gave under my heel.

“Mara,” I said again, but this time it came out smaller.

She moved toward me and I saw the conflict in it before I understood it. A hitch in one shoulder. The jaw tightening against the smile. Her hand rising not quite under her control, fingers curled as if reaching for my face and my throat at once.

“No more pretending,” I said aloud, to her or myself or whatever was listening.

I slapped her.

Not hard enough to knock her down. Hard enough to crack in the dark and jolt up my arm. The sound startled both of us. Mara reeled, blinking, one hand to her cheek. The smile vanished.

For one clean second she looked absolutely herself.

“Good,” she gasped. “Again if I—”

Her body bowed sharply, as if something had hooked under her ribs from inside. She made a sound I had heard once before and never forgotten: that half-choked, drowning-not-drowning pull for breath.

I reached for her. She shoved me away so hard I stumbled onto one knee.

“Don’t let it have you because it sounds like me,” she said.

The lake slapped softly against the dock posts below us.

Then she stepped backward toward the end of the dock.

I got up too fast and the world grayed at the edges. Lack of sleep, cold, panic—all of it narrowing. Mara kept going, one bare foot behind the other on the wet boards, eyes never leaving my face. Whether she was watching me or whatever in me she feared, I couldn’t tell.

At the last safe board she stopped.

“If I ask you to lie down,” she said in her own voice, strained through clenched teeth, “you don’t.”

“I’m not leaving you out there.”

“You have to wake up, Daniel.”

“I am awake.”

Her laugh broke in the middle. “No. That’s the problem.”

Something moved at the edge of my sight. Not on the water. In me. That same loosening sensation from the bedroom, the sense of a second attention waiting just behind my own thoughts for me to tire enough, grieve enough, love enough to make room.

Mara saw it happen in my face. I know she did.

Her expression changed. Not fear now. Decision.

Before I could move, she stepped off the end of the dock.

The splash was small.

I think I shouted. I know I ran. The dock slick under me, cold air tearing my throat, every part of me choosing the old motion before thought: after her, after her, after—

At the edge I stopped.

Not because I didn’t want to go in. Because at the exact lip of the dark water I understood what she had done. Not a suicide. Not even, fully, a sacrifice. An interruption. The oldest one between us. She had put the lake where I would have to choose waking over reflex.

Below, I could just make out her face breaking the surface once, pale and brief in the dark.

“Daniel,” she called.

My body leaned.

Then I saw that her mouth had not moved.

I staggered back so hard I fell onto the boards. Cold shot up my hands. Below me the water lapped and shifted and showed nothing. No face. No hand. No Mara.

I do not know how long I stayed there. Seconds. Hours. Long enough for the porch light to go off on its timer and leave the dock in total dark. Long enough for dawn to begin thinning the eastern edge of the trees.

They found me at first light, Neil and one of the year-round neighbors, after I failed to answer my phone and someone saw the car. There was no sign of Mara in the water that morning. Not until later. They asked questions in the practical tones people use when they are trying not to look directly at catastrophe. I answered some of them.

Afterward there were statements, searches, casseroles again. A second set of flowers. The bed at home felt too large and then, somehow, too small. I did not sleep much. When I did, it was in bursts, sitting up, lights on, my own pulse for company.

Sometimes I woke with the sure, humiliating certainty that someone had been standing over me. Watching to see what woke up.

Weeks later, in the dark before morning, I rolled toward the empty side of the bed because I smelled lake water.

There was no one there.

Still, I lay very still, eyes almost shut, and waited.

For a moment—just one—I had the calm, patient feeling that if I kept watching long enough, something might finally surface.

She thought I’d been sleeping.

The opening chapter establishes dread through accumulation of small wrongnesses rather than dramatic revelation — the cold mattress, the non-blinking, the smell of lake water — and this restraint is maintained impressively throughout. The dialogue is one of the piece's strongest elements. The exchange rhythms feel authentic to a long marriage under strain: "You weren't asleep." / "That's not an answer." / "No. It isn't." This kind of clipped, layered communication rings true and does real character work simultaneously. The banter about the priest and the girl Mara bit at camp is a genuine tonal achievement — lightness that earns its place by making the darkness around it more credible.

Character work is strong. Daniel's self-deception, his tendency to "turn terror into a project," his guilt about the dock — these are rendered with psychological specificity. Mara is more than a vessel for the supernatural; she has a distinct personality that persists even as it's being eroded, and the story is careful to show her fighting back rather than simply being a passive victim.

The central conceit — that the possession works through sleep, through the threshold between consciousness and unconsciousness, and that watching is both symptom and defense — is genuinely inventive and thematically coherent. The mirroring of the opening line at the close is earned.

The pacing across eight chapters is largely well-managed. The escalation from domestic unease to the dock confrontation follows a believable arc. Chapter 6's mirror scene is the horror set-piece, and it delivers genuine dread.

WEAKNESSES:

The prose occasionally tips into overworking its effects. Sentences like "Exhaustion sat in my bones like a second weather" and "The ordinary details did not comfort me anymore. They had started to feel complicit, as if the room had decided to keep behaving like a bedroom no matter what was using it" are reaching for profundity and landing somewhere between evocative and strained. There are enough of these moments to constitute a pattern without being pervasive.

Some metaphors don't quite land: "as if normal were a casserole someone could pull out of the oven if you gave it another ten minutes" is clever but slightly too clever, calling attention to itself. "The shame of that hit first. Then the colder part" — "the colder part" is vague in a way that feels like it's gesturing at depth rather than achieving it.

The ending, while structurally satisfying in its circularity, is somewhat ambiguous in a way that feels slightly evasive rather than genuinely mysterious. What happened to Mara? The story seems to want to have it both ways — she sacrificed herself AND the possession continues — but the mechanics are murky. The final image is strong, but the chapter 8 resolution feels rushed compared to the careful build of earlier chapters.

Neil Hammett's appearance at the lake in chapter 4 is a little convenient, and his revelation ("past you, I thought") is the one moment where the story tells us something it should trust us to feel.

The "second breath" moment in chapter 3 is the story's most overtly supernatural moment and it's handled well, but the mirror scene in chapter 6 (the shape still in bed while Mara stands) is slightly unclear in its mechanics — is this a hallucination, a bilocation, or something else? The ambiguity here feels unintentional rather than deliberate.

The piece is long and occasionally repeats its own effects — the lake smell, the cold, the watching — to diminishing returns in the middle chapters. Chapters 4 and 5 could be tightened.

OVERALL: This is a genuinely strong piece of horror fiction with real literary ambition that it mostly fulfills. The craft is evident, the characters are human, and the central horror is original. Its flaws are the flaws of overreach rather than incompetence.
