The rain hit like thrown gravel and then like hands.

Rita slid first, boots skidding on the slick pitch of the side roof, one palm braced, the other gripping the gutter. Ava came after her on all fours with the orange radio bumping against her ribs. Below them, side-yard lanterns cut white cones through the downpour. Men moved in and out of them like actors in a terrible play.

“Don’t look down,” Rita said.

“I wasn’t,” Ava lied.

The unfinished house next door stood twenty feet away across a strip of mud and stacked pavers, wrapped in torn housewrap that snapped and slithered in the wind. The side gate between properties had never been latched properly; Rita had noticed that too.

She dropped first, hanging from the gutter and letting herself fall into wet hibiscus mulch with a jolt all the way up her bad knee. Pain flared mean and bright. She breathed through it.

“Jump.”

Ava did. Rita caught her awkwardly around the waist and almost went over backward. For a second they were both in the flowerbed, mud and leaves and rainwater in their mouths.

From inside the Mercer house a man shouted, “Back side! Go!”

Rita hauled Ava up and shoved her toward the gate. It stuck halfway. Rita kicked it open. Metal screamed.

They ran bent low through a side yard of fresh sod and construction trash, into the skeletal dark of the model home next door. No windows yet on the second floor. No drywall. Just studs, wiring, damp plywood, and the smell of wet lumber.

They climbed because height bought seconds.

On the raw subfloor upstairs, rain hissing through open cutouts, Rita took Denny’s phone from her pocket and the memory card from the radio. Her fingers were slick. She swore under her breath, wiped them on her shirt, and shoved the card into the phone.

“Can you—”

“Maybe.”

Ava stood beside her, soaked hair plastered to her face, trying not to shake. Down below, flashlights skimmed through the framed first floor next door. Voices scattered. Kearse’s came once, calm and carrying: “She’s got the girl. Watch the lot line.”

The phone recognized the card after a second that felt rude. A list of files appeared. Videos. PDFs. Images. Dates. One thumbnail loaded automatically before Rita could stop it: a body half-buried in churned earth at a construction site, one arm visible, a work glove still on.

Ava inhaled sharply.

Rita clicked away before more came up. Enough. More than enough.

“What is it?” Ava asked.

“Proof.”

“Of what?”

“That your father was keeping insurance.”

Ava looked down into the rain-dark studs below them as if her father might materialize there and explain himself. “Is he dead?”

“I don’t know.”

“You keep saying that.”

“Because I don’t know.”

That seemed to offend her more than a lie would have.

A siren sounded somewhere in the distance. Not close. Not for them. Just weather or highway or somebody else’s bad night.

Rita checked the files again, scanning names. Doran Holdings. Parish fill permits. Shell invoices. Video clips. One audio file labeled K 6/11. Another PDF with Leon Kearse’s name in a reimbursement chain too dumb to be real.

Bought and paid for. Fine.

A flashlight beam knifed across the open lower floor. Someone had come into the model home.

Rita pocketed the phone and card. “We’re moving.”

“To where?”

“That depends how many friends your deputy has.”

They went down the back side of the frame and out through plastic sheeting into the drainage ditch behind the lots. Water was already running there shin-deep, warm and fast, carrying grass clippings, Styrofoam cups, somebody’s escaped sandal. Ava made a sound of disgust and stepped in anyway.

Bell Street was all wrong in storm-light. The pretty houses sat with their uplighting and shutters while runoff swallowed the curbs. Rita cut behind them, through utility easements and strips of ornamental grass, keeping to the dark between pools of motion light. Ava stayed close without needing to be told now.

At the end of the block Rita stopped behind a transformer box and looked back. White headlights turned slow at the Mercers’ house. Another vehicle cruised the cross street too deliberately.

No easy exits.

“You got anybody local who’d come get you if your mother called crying?” Rita asked.

Ava gave her a look. “No.”

“Good.”

“That’s not good.”

“It is tonight.”

They made it to Rita’s car by luck and geography. She’d parked two streets over under a live oak because rich developments hated curb clutter. The old Civic looked indecent among the wet Mercedes and tall trucks.

Rita got them in, locked the doors, and sat for one beat with both hands on the wheel, rain drumming the roof.

“You’re bleeding,” Ava said.

Rita looked down. Shallow slice along her forearm, probably from the broken glass. “Still inside the body. Fine.”

“Where are we going?”

Rita started the car. “I’m deciding.”

The obvious choices lined up and died one by one. Police station: Kearse. Emergency room: cameras, forms, cops. Motel: names and receipts. Any friend from her current life: too close, too soft. If Doran had local reach, which he did, then every respectable door was a slow trap.

She drove toward town anyway, wipers slapping. Bell Street gave way to the county road, then to a strip of chain stores and gas stations shining ugly in rain.

At the first red light she called the sheriff’s non-emergency line from Denny’s phone and said, “I need to report a home invasion at the Mercer property on Bell Street. Armed men. One identifies himself as Deputy Kearse.”

The dispatcher paused exactly one beat too long. “Ma’am, units are already on scene.”

“Are they?”

“Yes, ma’am. The situation is under control.”

Rita hung up.

Ava had heard enough. “So no one’s coming.”

“No one useful.”

They drove past the emergency room entrance anyway. Fluorescent awning, people smoking in scrubs, an ambulance backing in with no lights. Safe enough for ordinary miseries. Not for this.

At a gas station Rita bought two bottles of water, chips, and a prepaid phone with cash. She left Ava locked in the car and watched her in the reflection the whole time. Inside the station, the television behind the counter played radar over cheerful music. Outside, everything smelled like wet asphalt and diesel.

Back in the car she handed Ava the chips.

“I’m not hungry.”

“Eat anyway.”

Ava obeyed after a second, taking tiny furious bites.

Rita drove toward the older part of town where streets had names instead of branding and live oaks bent over cinderblock churches. Her phone buzzed once. Unknown number. Then again. Then a text from Celia Mercer at last.

IS AVA WITH YOU

No hello. No apology. No where are you. Rich people saved panic for when it might cost them.

Rita typed back: Yes.

Three dots. Then: KEEP HER HIDDEN. DON’T TRUST ANYONE FROM COUNTY.

A laugh escaped Rita before she could stop it.

Ava looked over. “What?”

“Your mother finally got brave enough to be useful by text.”

Another light. Another hiss of tires through standing water. Rita thought of all the hard, official places in this county she could be funneled if she chose wrong.

There was one place not hard, not official, and exactly why men like Doran would overlook it.

“You religious?” she asked.

Ava frowned. “No.”

“Good. Makes the pitch easier.”

“Where are we going?”

Rita turned onto a narrow street lined with old houses, a bait shop gone dark, and the low brick shape of Saint Bartholomew’s annex hall with its storm shutters folded open.

“To a church,” she said. “Try not to look thrilled.”
step_outputs.10:
Saint Bartholomew’s annex hall sat two blocks from the bayou behind a chain-link fence and a row of crape myrtles that had survived more storms than most marriages. In daylight it looked tired but serviceable. In the storm, with the parking lot half-flooded and the sodium lights buzzing, it looked like the sort of place people remembered only when everything else had failed.

Eunice Bell opened the side door before Rita knocked twice.

She wore church slacks, compression stockings, and a gray cardigan over a T-shirt that said JESUS LOVES YOU, EVERYBODY ELSE THINKS YOU’RE A PROBLEM. Reading glasses hung on a chain at her chest. Her hair was wrapped in a silk scarf the color of plums.

“Well,” she said, taking in Rita’s wet clothes, the blood on her sleeve, and Ava at her side. “If you brought trouble in here, at least wipe its feet.”

“No time,” Rita said. “Need the shelter room for a few hours.”

Eunice’s eyes flicked to Ava, then back. “Child yours?”

“No.”

“Mm. Better chance she lives, then. Come on.”

The annex smelled like old coffee, floor wax, and canned green beans from the pantry closet. Eunice led them past a bulletin board of curling flyers and into the interior room they used during hurricane season, a cinderblock rectangle with folding cots, battery lanterns, and a mural of Noah’s ark that looked less reassuring the older you got.

“Sit,” Eunice said to Ava. “You need dry socks?”

Ava, too tired now for suspicion to do all the work, nodded once.

Eunice handed her a church-lost-and-found sweatshirt with a retreat logo and disappeared toward the office. Rita checked the room on instinct: one door, one tiny reinforced window, heavy cabinet, no second exit. Bad if found. Decent if not.

Ava sat on a cot and peeled off wet sneakers. “Is she always like that?”

“Yes.”

“I like her.”

“Your standards are improving.”

Ava changed into dry socks and the huge sweatshirt, swallowing herself in it. She looked suddenly younger. Rita hated that. Childhood looked worst when it returned at the wrong time.

Eunice came back with towels, a first-aid kit, and a mug of coffee she handed to Rita without asking. “Office line’s been ringing twice and stopping,” she said. “That means somebody thinks they know where to look and isn’t sure who’s home.”

Rita nodded. “County dirty.”

“County was dirty when I still had knees worth bragging on.” Eunice glanced at Ava. “You got names?”

“Mick Doran. Deputy Leon Kearse.”

Eunice made a face like she’d bitten foil. “Mm. That kind of dirt.”

Rita cleaned the cut on her forearm at the sink in the corner while Ava ate saltines from the storm supplies and watched everything. The water in the basin ran pink and then clear.

“What did your father do?” Rita asked without turning.

Ava crunched, swallowed. “Business.”

“Not a real answer.”

“It’s the one he used.”

Rita looked at her in the mirror over the sink. “Try again.”

Ava picked at a thread on the sweatshirt cuff. “He was scared all week. He yelled at my mom in the pantry because he thought I couldn’t hear through the vent. He said Mick would bury all of them if the files got out. She said he should have thought of that before he got greedy.”

Children in rich houses, Rita thought, always heard through vents.

“You saw him hide the card?”

“He had his jacket on the mud bench. The pocket was ripped. I took it after he left. I thought maybe if I had something, somebody would tell me what was happening.”

Rita believed that. Not because it was noble. Because it was child logic sharpened by neglect.

She dried her arm, taped a pad over the cut, and went into Eunice’s tiny office. A desktop computer the church should have retired ten years ago hummed under a saint calendar and a jar of peppermints. Rita slid the memory card into an adapter and opened the files.

The still image from the construction site came up larger this time. Not just a body. A man in county utility coveralls, face turned partly to mud. Next file: ledger sheets hidden as change orders. Next: a video clip shot from inside a truck, grainy but clear enough to catch Doran at a night dig site, Kearse’s deputy cruiser in the background, Mercer arguing with someone off-camera. Then the audio file.

A woman’s voice: agitated, likely Celia. A man: Mercer, drunk or scared. Then Doran, unmistakable even tinny through bad speakers.

You think because it was an accident that makes him less dead?

Mercer: I’m not saying that.

Doran: Then stop acting like your conscience is premium material.

Another voice, smooth and bored. Kearse. We move him, we fix the permit timeline, and we all keep paying our taxes.

Rita shut it off.

Enough.

She printed nothing. Too slow. Too fragile. Instead she transferred copies to the prepaid phone and another old church USB Eunice had in a drawer labeled RECEIPTS. Then she pocketed all of it.

When she came back into the shelter room, Ava was half-curled on the cot but still awake. Eunice sat beside her reading a devotional with the expression of a woman who had long ago ceased expecting the Lord to improve people substantially.

“What now?” Ava asked.

Rita leaned against the cinderblock wall. “Now I go ask one of Mick’s men where to find him before he asks harder where to find you.”

Ava sat up. “No.”

“That wasn’t a democracy briefing.”

“They’ll kill you.”

“They’ve been trying the amateur version.”

Ava looked furious enough to cry and too proud to do it. “You said not to trust anybody, and now you’re leaving me in a church.”

“With Eunice.”

“That’s still somebody.”

Good, Rita thought. The child was learning.

Eunice closed her devotional. “Baby, if men come through that door, they’re not taking you without making my paperwork complicated.”

Ava stared at her. “Do you have a gun?”

“I have opinions and a Louisville Slugger. Same effect up close.”

That got a short laugh out of the girl, shocked out of her.

Rita crouched in front of the cot, not softening her face because that never worked on children like this. “Listen. The only reason you’re breathing easier than your parents right now is because men like Doran still think they’re dealing with the kind of woman who waits to be told what to do. I need to keep that mistake expensive.”

Ava looked at her for a long second. “Will you come back?”

There it was. Not please. Not promise. Just the one question she could stand to ask.

“Yes,” Rita said.

That answer meant something because she said it plain.

She stood, took Denny’s phone and keys from her pocket, and handed the prepaid to Eunice. “If I don’t answer in one ring, you call this number and send the files to every reporter, preacher, and bored divorcee in the county.”

Eunice nodded. “I know some dangerous women.”

“I know.”

Outside, the storm had moved east into a steadier rain. The air felt scrubbed raw.

Rita drove Denny’s phone to the edge of the industrial strip and followed his map history, because stupid men let their phones tell on them. Construction yard. Supply trailer. Thirty minutes away at the edge of Doran’s newest development, where marsh became lot line under enough money.

The yard was lit by one security flood and the blue blink of a vending machine in a trailer office. A stack of PVC pipes gleamed wet as bones. Somewhere nearby a generator throbbed.

Rita parked in the dark behind a dozer, checked the small knife in her boot, and limped toward the trailer with the same old cold room opening inside her.

A shadow moved past the frosted window.

Good. Somebody was home.
step_outputs.11:
The trailer door was unlocked.

That told Rita one of two things: Denny was inside and hurting enough to forget basic fear, or the men around Mick Doran believed the world was still arranged in their favor. Either way, good.

She went in sideways.

A portable AC unit rattled in the corner, losing badly against the wet heat. The trailer smelled like antiseptic, diesel, and male panic. Denny sat shirtless on a vinyl bench with his broken wrist splinted in duct tape and a bag of melting ice on his face. A younger man in a tank top stood over him with a stapler kit and the expression of someone doing medicine as revenge.

Neither saw her until she kicked the door shut.

The younger man turned with the staple gun still in his hand. “Who the—”

Rita hit him in the throat with the flashlight and caught him by the collar as he folded, using his body to ram Denny backward into the bench and wall. The ice bag burst. Meltwater and blood went everywhere.

Denny made a noise like a sick dog. “Jesus Christ.”

“Still no,” Rita said.

The younger man clawed at her wrist. She drove her knee into his sternum and he went flat on the floor trying to remember lungs. Rita picked up the staple gun, aimed it at Denny’s cheek, and smiled without warmth.

“Let’s try this without your usual team spirit.”

Denny looked worse in fluorescent light: one eye sealed nearly shut, lips split, skin going waxy around the edges. Fear had thinned him.

“I told you what I knew.”

“You told me what got me out of your kitchen fastest.”

She pressed the staple gun hard enough to dimple skin. “Where’s Doran taking the girl?”

Denny blinked. “What girl?”

Rita fired one staple into the vinyl seat by his thigh.

He yelped and recoiled. “Fuck!”

“The one from Bell Street. You tell Mick she had the card?”

He hesitated. There it was.

Rita didn’t raise her voice. “You get one more lie before your face starts looking decorative.”

“He knows,” Denny said, words tripping now. “Okay? He knows the kid had it. Kearse said the old church was a good hold because nobody’d think to watch it twice.”

For one beat the trailer got very quiet except for the AC choking.

Rita felt the world tilt narrow.

“When?”

Denny swallowed. “Tonight.”

“How long ago?”

He looked at the wall clock automatically. Nine-eighteen.

Rita had left Saint Bartholomew’s at eight-thirty.

The younger man on the floor was trying to crawl. She stepped on his hand without looking and he stopped.

“Where are they taking her?”

“I don’t know, I swear—”

Rita drove the staple gun into the broken wrist.

Denny screamed so hard his voice gave out halfway through. He folded over his lap, breath sawing.

“Where.”

“The pump station!” he choked. “Old retention pump off County Nine, before the bridge. They use it for transfers because nobody goes there at night.”

Rita stepped back. The inside of her chest felt airless and enormous at once.

“You should’ve gone farther,” Denny whispered, crying now from pure body, not sorrow. “You should’ve taken the kid and run.”

“Maybe,” Rita said.

She hit the younger man once behind the ear on her way out and left them both alive because the night had changed shape.

The road to County Nine was all black water and intermittent sodium light. Rita drove too fast with both windows cracked, rain smell and marsh smell coming in hard. She called the prepaid once. Eunice picked up on the first ring, breathing like she had come from violence.

“They came,” Eunice said.

Rita gripped the wheel until her hand ached. “Ava?”

“Took her. Deputy and two others. Broke my office door and hit me with my own phone. Bastards tracked mud on the parish rugs.”

“Are you hurt bad?”

“Head wound. Pride worse. Go get the child.”

“I am.”

Eunice’s voice sharpened. “Rita.”

“What.”

“Don’t die stupid.”

The line went dead.

County Nine cut through a run of low marsh and new infrastructure no one had fully inhabited yet. The retention pump station sat off the road behind a locked chain-link gate and a concrete shed painted county beige. Beyond it, black water spread under reeds and construction runoff. The whole place smelled like algae, wet cement, and machine oil.

Rita killed her headlights half a mile out and rolled the rest by dark.

Two vehicles at the gate. One county Tahoe. One black F-150.

Kearse and Doran, then. Good.

She parked behind a mound of fill dirt and went the rest on foot through the runoff channel, water to mid-calf, flashlight off, gun heavy in the back of her jeans. The pump station generator hummed low, masking smaller sounds. Men’s voices carried in pieces. A child’s voice did not.

At the edge of the concrete apron Rita saw them.

Kearse stood near the open shed door, jacket off, shirtsleeves rolled. Doran leaned against the truck in a pale golf shirt gone dark at the chest with rain. Another man smoked under the eave. Inside the shed, light spilled over pipes, control panels, and Ava sitting zip-tied to a metal chair, the orange weather radio on the floor by her sneaker.

Ava’s face was blotched from crying or rage. Hard to tell from there.

Doran said, “The thing about children is they always tell the truth eventually.”

Kearse looked toward the dark marsh. “Depends who asks.”

Rita moved.

The smoking man died first because he was easiest. She came up behind him through the generator noise, hooked his chin, and cut deep under the ear with the boot knife before he understood the scene had changed. He collapsed against the wall making a surprised animal sound.

Kearse spun. “Hey—”

Rita fired from the dark and took him high in the shoulder. He slammed into the shed doorframe, swearing.

Doran dove behind the truck with far less dignity than his polo implied.

Ava screamed, “Rita!”

“Down!” Rita shouted.

The yard exploded into noise. Kearse was reaching left-handed for his weapon. Rita advanced through the rain, firing once more. The truck’s windshield crazed. Doran shouted for somebody who was already leaking out under the eave.

Kearse got his gun up and fired blind. Concrete chipped near Rita’s head. She dropped behind a bollard, breath coming hard and cold.

“Rita,” Doran called from behind the truck, trying for command and landing on panic, “you are making this much worse than it needs to be.”

“Too late,” she said.

Ava was crying now in furious little gasps. “He took my radio.”

“I see that.”

Kearse moved wrong for a wounded man—disciplined enough to flank. Rita caught the motion in the pump-house window reflection and pivoted just as he came around the shed corner. They hit each other hard, close enough for guns to become bad tools. His forearm crushed her throat. Her bad knee almost buckled.

“You insane bitch,” he hissed, hot breath and blood.

She drove her thumb into the bullet wound in his shoulder.

He made a sound she would think about later and lost the arm for half a second. Enough. Rita head-butted him in the nose and took him down on the slick concrete. The gun skidded away.

He was stronger, bigger. She was lower and angrier. She got on top long enough to smash his face against the apron once, twice, then had to roll as Doran fired from under the truck. The shot punched sparks from the pump casing.

Rita crawled to the shed, kicked the fallen gun inside, and slashed Ava’s zip ties with the knife.

“You okay?”

Ava nodded too fast. “He said my mom left town.”

“She probably did.”

Ava absorbed that with one terrible blink.

Outside, Kearse was groaning and Doran’s truck engine turned over.

Rita looked at Ava, at the wet radio on the floor, at the open road beyond the gate.

“He’s running,” Ava said.

“Yes.”

Ava picked up the radio and held it out like a relic. “Then go.”

Rita took it, set it in Ava’s lap, and went back into the rain.
step_outputs.12:
Doran’s truck fishtailed through the open gate and threw muddy water in a fan behind it.

Rita got Kearse’s Tahoe started on the second turn, blood slicking the steering wheel where somebody else had already bled on it. Ava was in the passenger seat with the weather radio clutched to her chest, too shocked to argue and too angry to stay quiet for long.

“You’re shot,” Ava said.

“Scraped.”

“Your neck is bleeding.”

“Also true.”

The county road unspooled black ahead of them. Doran’s taillights bobbed in the rain, then vanished around a bend lined with half-installed streetlamps and mounds of shell fill. Kearse groaned somewhere in the dark behind them, still alive if not especially useful.

“Shouldn’t we call someone?” Ava asked.

“With what confidence?”

She had no answer for that.

Rita drove one-handed and checked the prepaid with the other at the next straightaway. Three missed calls from Eunice, one voicemail she didn’t listen to, and a text from an unknown number. Just an address and a time.

Harbor View Estates Sales Event
10 PM
He’ll go where the lights are.

No name. Didn’t need one. Somebody inside Doran’s orbit had decided the night was moving badly and self-preservation beat loyalty.

Rita laughed once through her nose.

“What?” Ava said.

“Your Mr. Doran’s got friends who can smell smoke.”

Harbor View sat on a stretch of dredged waterfront where the marsh had been bullied into pretending to be a neighborhood. Doran’s pride project. Model homes on raised pads, decorative gas lamps, banners snapping in the weather: LIVE ELEVATED. The kind of development sold with renderings of kayaks no one in it would ever own.

Of course he’d run there. Men like Doran fled toward witness, not away from it. They believed enough people seeing them intact made them so.

Rita turned off County Nine and onto the boulevard leading to Harbor View. Even in the rain she could see event lighting ahead, white tents trembling under the weather, catering vans, a row of polished trucks and Mercedes at the curb. Music drifted thin and absurd through wet air. Somebody was still holding the party.

“Stay here,” she said as they rolled dark into the service lot behind the model homes.

Ava stared at her. “No.”

“Yes.”

“You said he doesn’t get another night.”

“I also said survival is stupid and mostly following orders.”

“He’ll see me.”

“Exactly.”

Ava’s jaw set. Eleven years old and all blade. “What do I do then?”

Rita looked at her. Really looked. The child was shaking and holding still over it with professional effort. There were red marks on her wrists from the ties. Mud on her bare shins. Somebody else’s blood drying on the church sweatshirt.

“Can you use that radio’s alert tone?”

Ava blinked. “What?”

“To make noise.”

“Yes.”

“Good. When you hear shouting inside, you hit the alert and you run to the sales office with this.” Rita handed her the prepaid phone. “There are files on it. Find the oldest woman in nice shoes and give it to her. Or a reporter if you see one. Anybody who likes scandal more than fear.”

Ava took the phone. “That’s your whole plan?”

“It’s the child-sized part.”

Ava thought that over and, astonishingly, nodded.

Harbor View’s main model home was lit like a shipwrecked wedding. Through the broad windows Rita saw couples in linen, county men with drinks, women balancing canapés and disapproval. A string quartet recording leaked from hidden speakers. On the far wall, a giant rendering showed smiling families on elevated porches above impossible blue water.

Rita went in through the kitchen service entrance carrying a tray she lifted off a startled caterer in the hall.

No one looked at her twice.

That was the useful thing about a lifetime spent being infrastructure. In a rich room, a woman over forty in dark clothes carrying something was translated instantly into harmless labor. Eyes slid off her. Conversations continued around her. It would have insulted her if it weren’t so practical.

She ditched the tray in a butler’s pantry and moved through the model home’s staged perfection: throw pillows no child had ever leaned on, bowls of decorative lemons, candles no one lit. Kearse’s blood was drying tacky at the edge of her sleeve. She wiped it with a monogrammed dish towel and kept walking.

Doran stood in the great room near the fake gas fireplace, one hand bandaged badly with a cocktail napkin, smiling at a bank manager and a blonde woman in white. He had changed shirts. Of course he had. The man believed in costuming.

His smile slipped when he saw Rita.

Only a little. Enough.

He excused himself with admirable smoothness and moved toward the hallway as if he’d merely remembered another obligation. Rita let him think she’d follow and took a left instead.

Deputy Kearse was in the downstairs study with the door half shut, sitting in a leather chair under a painting of a sailboat, pale around the mouth and trying to tape gauze over his shoulder one-handed. His badge sat on the desk beside a tumbler of amber liquor.

When he looked up and saw her, his face emptied in a way she liked.

“You do not know when to stop,” he said.

“Funny. I was thinking that about county payroll.”

He reached for the desk drawer.

Rita shot the drawer front. Wood splintered into his hand. He shouted and half rose, then sat back hard, breathing through his teeth.

Out in the great room someone laughed too loudly at nothing.

Kearse swallowed. “There are people here.”

“I know. Must be comforting.”

“You kill me in a room full of donors and board members, that doesn’t end clean.”

Rita closed the door behind her with her foot. “Leon, nothing in your life has ever ended clean. You just had a badge to drag over it.”

His eyes went small and hateful. “You think you’re different?”

“No. I think I’m honest.”

He lunged anyway, because men like him always did one last stupid thing to preserve the story they told about themselves. He came over the desk with a letter opener in his left hand, shoulder failing mid-motion.

Rita sidestepped, caught the wrist, and drove him face-first into the desk edge. His teeth hit wood with a crack she felt in her own jaw. He sagged. She kept his hand, twisted, and pinned the letter opener through the soft web between thumb and finger into the desktop.

He screamed.

She leaned close enough for him to smell rain on her. “That deputy voice you do? Hate that.”

Then she took the heavy crystal paperweight from the desk and hit him once in the temple.

He dropped and stayed down.

Outside the study, the music stuttered. Then, from somewhere near the foyer, a piercing electronic squall rose over the chatter—the shrill NOAA alert tone, impossible and urgent and wrong in that polished room.

Ava.

Conversations broke. Somebody said, “What is that?” Somebody else said, “Oh my God, is that blood?”

Good girl.

Rita stepped back into the hall as panic began to ripple through Harbor View in little embarrassed circles. Phones came out. Voices lifted. The oldest woman in nice shoes was already looking for a story to own.

At the far end of the corridor, through the kitchen and out the open rear sliders, Rita saw Doran moving fast across the rain-dark yard toward the unfinished showcase home on the next lot—the one still all framing and concrete and promise.

He glanced back once.

She followed.
step_outputs.13:
The unfinished house next door had no windows yet, just black cutouts where windows would promise safety to future buyers. Rain blew through the frame and slapped the plywood floors. Temporary work lights glared on extension cords, making the place look less haunted than interrogated.

Doran had gone in through the rear opening, shoes slipping in the mud. Rita followed at a slower pace because she knew better than to chase a panicked rich man into a dark structure as if panic made him stupid. Panic just made people honest.

The first floor was all studs and shadow, plumbing lines and stacked drywall. Somewhere above, a board creaked. Doran breathing hard. Good.

Rita moved through the shell with one hand on a damp two-by-four and the other low on the gun. Her neck throbbed where Kearse had forearmed it. Her knee had become a separate weather system. Somewhere behind her, muffled through rain and distance, Harbor View was coming apart in tasteful voices.

“Rita,” Doran called from the dark above. “Listen to me.”

“No.”

His laugh came back raw. “You don’t understand what happens after this.”

Rita started up the temporary staircase. “I understand enough.”

He was on the second floor near what would one day be a primary bedroom overlooking expensive water. For now it was open framing, a blue tarp flapping in one wall cutout, coils of electrical wire, and a drop cloth over a bathtub waiting to be installed. Doran stood by the far opening with a nail gun in one hand and his expensive shoes white with drywall dust.

It might have been funny if he weren’t pointing a compressor-fed weapon at her chest.

He looked worse than she’d expected. Hair plastered. Polo ruined. One side of his face muddy. The broad civic confidence had leaked out of him. Underneath was just a county boy with money and a terror of losing it.

“Jesus,” he said, seeing her fully under the work light. “Look at you.”

Rita kept moving until the nail gun twitched. Then she stopped.

“Was that the line?” she asked. “You rehearse that?”

“Don’t,” he snapped, and then breathed himself back down. “Don’t make me do this.”

She looked at the nail gun. “Mick. You paid men to break into a house with a child in it.”

He had the decency not to deny it. “I paid men to retrieve property. This spiraled because everyone around me got sentimental or greedy.”

“Mm.”

“Mercer stole from me. Kearse got sloppy. Your little church stunt turned everything theatrical.”

“Did I?”

“You think you’re avenging innocence here?” He barked a laugh. “That girl’s father was in it up to his neck. Her mother knew enough to run. These people are all dirty.”

“Probably.”

Something in her face unsettled him. Good.

“You don’t get it,” he said. “This county runs on handshakes and omissions. Half the people in that room next door know exactly what I am. They still came for the wine and the river view. That’s how the world works.”

Rita shifted her weight off the bad knee. “That speech usually work on people?”

“It’s not a speech. It’s reality.”

“No. It’s how you excuse yourself to yourself.”

He smiled then, desperate and ugly. “And what are you, Rita? Babysitter by night, saint by weather emergency, knife in the dark when your feelings get hurt?”

There it was. The class note. The reduction. Not enemy, not witness, not avenger. Help with an attitude.

Rita felt something settle cleanly inside her.

“Wrong twice in one sentence,” she said.

Doran fired.

The nail hit the stud inches from her shoulder with a vicious metallic thunk. Faster than a man deserved from a tool like that. Rita dropped left behind a stack of drywall as two more nails punched white dust into the air where her head had been.

Compressor whine. Doran moving.

She came low through the framing while he was still aiming at where she’d been. He swung the nail gun toward her. She caught his wrist with both hands and slammed it against a stud. The gun discharged with a snapping bark. A nail buried in the floor between them.

He was stronger than she wanted him to be. Dead weight and panic. He drove his shoulder into her ribs and they crashed sideways through hanging plastic into the bathroom area, feet skidding on the drop cloth over the tub. Rita’s gun flew from her hand and vanished under a sheet of plastic insulation.

Doran got an arm around her neck and dragged her backward against his chest.

“I built this place,” he hissed into her ear, as if that explained the right to kill in it.

Rita drove her heel down on his instep. Expensive shoes were always softer than boots. He grunted but held on.

The compressor hose snaked across the floor under their feet. The tarp at the wall opening snapped in and out with rain gusts. Below them, beyond the open joists, the first floor dropped dark and unfinished to the concrete slab.

Rita took his thumb in her hand and bent it backward until she felt the joint peel wrong.

He screamed and let go.

She turned and hit him, not pretty. Palm heel to nose. Elbow to jaw. Her body remembered ugly work better than careful work. He stumbled back into the tub alcove and grabbed for the nail gun again with his left hand.

“Stay down,” she said.

He answered by firing.

The nail caught her upper arm and glanced, hot and shocking, more punch than puncture. She swore and charged him before he could place another. They went together into the half-set bathtub under the drop cloth, porcelain and plastic and limbs. The nail gun clattered out. Doran got both hands on her throat this time.

His face above her was red and wet and unbelieving. “You should have taken the money,” he panted.

Rita clawed blindly, found the loose compressor hose coupling by touch, and ripped it free from the gun line.

Air exploded in the enclosed space with a violent whip and scream. The hose lashed across Doran’s face. He recoiled instinctively, hands lifting to protect his eyes.

Enough.

Rita surged up, grabbed the back of his belt and collar, and heaved with everything her knee and rage had left. His feet hit the plastic-covered edge of the tub, slid, and kept going.

For one absurd second he windmilled there in the work light, framed by studs and rain, a man who had spent years believing gravity was for other people.

Then he fell backward through the open joists.

He hit the first-floor framing once, hard enough to change shape, then the concrete slab below with a sound Rita felt in her teeth.

Silence after was never total. Rain. Compressor. The flapping tarp. Far off, someone shouting at Harbor View. But Doran made no sound at all.

Rita stayed where she was for a second, kneeling in torn plastic, breathing through a throat full of copper. Then she got up and looked over the edge.

He lay twisted on the slab under a beam of temporary light, one arm under him, one out, face turned away. Blood ran into construction water and made pink tributaries through gray dust.

Ava called from somewhere outside the house, small and carrying. “Rita?”

“Here,” Rita shouted back.

She found her gun under the insulation, checked it, and made her way downstairs. At the bottom she paused by Doran’s body only long enough to be certain.

No breath. No argument.

Outside, dawn was beginning to think about the horizon. Not sunrise yet. Just the sky loosening from black over the marsh and the rows of half-finished houses.

Ava stood under the porch overhang in the church sweatshirt, soaked hair drying wild, the prepaid phone still in her hand. Behind her, up at the sales office, sirens finally bloomed red and blue across wet pavement. Real cops, late enough to count as weather.

“What happened?” Ava asked.

Rita looked back once at the skeleton house swallowing its shadows.

“He’s not getting another night,” she said.

Ava nodded. Not relieved. Not happy. Just understanding.

They walked to the Tahoe through mud and shell fill. Rita opened the passenger door for her. Ava climbed in, set the weather radio carefully in her lap, and after a moment said, “You really don’t talk like babysitters.”

Rita shut the door and went around to the driver’s side.

“No,” she said.

The tires rolled through runoff pinked by somebody else’s blood as the first clean light touched Harbor View Estates, and the beautiful houses looked, for half a second, exactly like what they were: frames, lies, and wet concrete.

The class critique embedded in the setting (Harbor View Estates, decorative lemons, bowls of limes no one was eating) is consistent and pointed without being heavy-handed.

"A face that looked unimpressed before she'd even knocked," "thin as a question mark," "the brittle shine of somebody holding a scream by the throat"—these are individually fine but the accumulation in Chapter 1 creates a slightly strained quality. Some metaphors don't fully land: "the sky loosening from black" is vague, and "a separate weather system" for the knee is a bit cute.

Doran's final confrontation is the weakest chapter. His villain speech ("This county runs on handshakes and omissions") is the most on-the-nose writing in the piece, and his death—falling through open joists—is somewhat anticlimactic given the buildup. Celia Mercer is underdeveloped. She's established as brittle and complicit, then disappears. The text acknowledges this ("your mother finally got brave enough to be useful by text") but it still feels like an unresolved thread.

My dad lies like he wants credit for being bad at it" is excellent—it's the kind of thing a sharp, lonely child would actually say, and it tells us everything about the Mercer household without a word of exposition. Her weather radio obsession, the label-peeling, the dead-phone question—all of this is consistent with the profile and feels organic rather than planted.

Celia Mercer is efficiently sketched in her brief appearance. The detail of her kissing the air near Ava's temple, the wine through the pores, the too-fast departure—these are good. She's not overwritten.

**Plot and Structure**

The chapter follows the plan closely and hits all the required beats: Rita's arrival, house inventory, Ava introduction, Celia's departure with the "don't answer the door" warning, the disabled camera, the torn jacket, the dead-phone question, and the arrival of the men. The pacing is well-judged—the chapter doesn't rush to the knock but doesn't dawdle either. The unease builds naturally through accumulation of small details rather than telegraphed dread.

The chapter plan called for seeding unease through specific details (mud on tile, torn jacket, disabled camera), and the model executes this well. The mud is there, the jacket is there, the camera is there. These feel like clues a careful reader will register without the narrative underlining them.

**Dialogue**

The dialogue is one of the chapter's genuine strengths. It's spare, character-specific, and does real work. The watch/warning exchange establishes Ava's personality and her relationship to systems. The "you don't talk like babysitters" exchange is efficient and warm without being saccharine. The dead-phone question lands with genuine unease. Celia's dialogue is appropriately brittle and evasive.

**Weaknesses**

The chapter is almost too controlled—there's very little that surprises. The beats are well-executed but somewhat predictable in their arrangement. A reader familiar with the genre will see the shape of everything coming. This is partly inherent to the setup, but the plan promised something "jagged" and this chapter is quite smooth.

The ending is effective but slightly conventional—the three hard raps is a well-worn thriller beat. The reflection-in-glass reveal is good, but the final line ("Not tentative. Not neighborly.") is the kind of thing that tells us what we've already understood.

The class texture is present but could be sharper. The "almost nothing in the kitchen you could eat without assembly" observation is good; some of the other wealth-signaling (brass fixtures, bowl of limes) is competent but not distinctive.

**Faithfulness to Plan**

The chapter follows the plan very closely—perhaps too closely in places, as it reads like a careful execution of a checklist rather than a story that discovered itself in the writing. But all the required elements are present and handled with skill.

Overall, this is a confident, well-crafted opening chapter that establishes character, atmosphere, and threat efficiently. Its weaknesses are mostly of degree rather than kind: slightly too smooth, occasionally reaching for a metaphor that doesn't quite earn its place, and ending on a beat that's effective but familiar. It's professional-quality pulp fiction with genuine literary ambition in the characterization.

Chapter 5 is a strong piece of pulp fiction writing that largely delivers on its plan and character profiles. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions.

STRENGTHS:

The chapter opens with a confident, specific sense of place. "Saint Bartholomew's annex hall sat two blocks from the bayou behind a chain-link fence and a row of crape myrtles that had survived more storms than most marriages" is a good line—the comparison earns its weight because it's grounded in the setting's logic (storms, endurance, Southern rot) rather than being decorative. It doesn't feel forced.

Eunice Bell is immediately vivid and consistent with her profile. The T-shirt gag ("JESUS LOVES YOU, EVERYBODY ELSE THINKS YOU'RE A PROBLEM") is exactly the kind of mean, earned humor the plan called for. Her dialogue throughout—"Baby, if you brought trouble in here, at least wipe its feet," "I have opinions and a Louisville Slugger. Same effect up close"—is sharp and character-specific without tipping into quippiness. She feels like a person, not a device.

The Rita-Ava dynamic is handled well. The exchange about Ava's father is the chapter's emotional core, and it works because it's delivered obliquely. "Children in rich houses always heard through vents" is a clean, specific observation that earns its place. Ava's revelation about taking the card—"I thought maybe if I had something, somebody would tell me what was happening"—is psychologically precise and consistent with her profile: the child who steals information to feel agency in a world that withholds it.

Rita's investigation of the card is handled efficiently. The chapter doesn't linger on exposition; it gives us enough to understand the stakes (a covered-up death, Doran's voice on audio, Kearse's complicity) without becoming a data dump. The decision to transfer files to multiple locations rather than print them is a small but smart practical detail that feels true to Rita's character.

The farewell scene between Rita and Ava is the chapter's best moment. "Will you come back? Not please. Not promise. Just the one question she could stand to ask." This is genuinely moving without being sentimental. Rita's plain "Yes" lands because the narration has established that she doesn't make promises she can't cash. The emotional restraint is earned.

The ending is appropriately lean and ominous. "A shadow moved past the frosted window. Good. Somebody was home." The chapter closes on forward momentum without over-dramatizing.

WEAKNESSES:

The chapter is competent and consistent, but it occasionally settles for the expected beat rather than the surprising one. The structure—arrive at shelter, exposition dump about the card, emotional farewell, drive to confrontation—is clean but somewhat predictable. The plan called for Rita to "corner the surviving intruder from the house attack, now getting patched up in a trailer behind Doran's construction lot" and conduct an interrogation that reveals key information. The chapter ends before this happens, meaning the chapter's promised dramatic content (the interrogation, the message-sending, Doran's realization) is deferred. This is a significant deviation from the chapter plan, which specified that Chapter 5 would include the interrogation and the wrecking of Doran's operation. Instead, Chapter 5 ends at the trailer door. This means the chapter is essentially a transitional chapter rather than the action chapter the plan promised.

Some lines are slightly over-written. "The water in the basin ran pink and then clear" is fine, but "the same old cold room opening inside her" at the end is a bit vague and abstract for a writer who otherwise deals in concrete sensation. "Childhood looked worst when it returned at the wrong time" is a decent observation but slightly on-the-nose for this voice.

The Doran audio transcript is functional but the dialogue there ("You think because it was an accident that makes him less dead?") is a little on-the-nose as villain exposition. It tells us exactly what we need to know but doesn't surprise us.

The chapter's pacing is slightly uneven—the shelter section is rich and well-developed, but the transition to the construction yard feels rushed, as if the chapter ran out of space for what it promised.

OVERALL: This is confident, well-crafted pulp fiction with strong character work, good dialogue, and a clear sense of place and voice. Its main weakness is that it doesn't fully deliver on its own chapter plan—the promised interrogation and escalation are deferred to the next chapter. The prose is clean and mostly avoids purple excess. The characters are consistent with their profiles. The emotional beats are earned rather than manufactured.

Chapter 7 is a strong piece of pulp fiction writing that largely delivers on its plan and maintains the voice established in the character profiles. Let me assess it carefully across the relevant dimensions.

STRENGTHS:

The chapter's greatest achievement is its tonal consistency. The prose is lean and muscular without tipping into self-parody. Lines like "Men like Doran fled toward witness, not away from it. They believed enough people seeing them intact made them so" are genuinely insightful character observations that feel earned rather than decorative. The class commentary is woven into action rather than announced—Rita's invisibility as a middle-aged woman in dark clothes carrying a tray is dramatized, not explained.

Rita's voice is consistent with her profile throughout. Her exchange with Ava in the car ("With what confidence?") is exactly the kind of dry, non-performative response the character profile calls for. The Kearse confrontation is well-executed: his lunge "because men like him always did one last stupid thing to preserve the story they told about themselves" is a sharp psychological observation that fits both characters. The letter opener through the web of the hand is specific and ugly in the right way—not action-hero flourish, but practical, bodily, and memorable.

Ava's role is appropriately child-sized. She's given the NOAA alert task, which fits her obsession with weather systems and emergency tones perfectly. Her "That's your whole plan?" / "It's the child-sized part" exchange is one of the chapter's best moments—economical, character-revealing, and genuinely funny in the earned, sparse way the plan calls for.

The Harbor View setting is well-realized. "Decorative gas lamps, banners snapping in the weather: LIVE ELEVATED" and "throw pillows no child had ever leaned on, bowls of decorative lemons" are specific class signals that do real work. The model home as a stage for violence is thematically resonant—staged perfection as backdrop for ugly truth.

The anonymous tip device (the text with just an address) is handled efficiently. It doesn't overstay its welcome and moves the plot without requiring elaborate explanation.

WEAKNESSES:

The chapter has some moments where the prose reaches slightly beyond what it earns. "Harbor View's main model home was lit like a shipwrecked wedding" is a striking image but "shipwrecked wedding" is a slightly strained compound—it gestures at something evocative without quite landing the specific image. Similarly, "Ava's jaw set. Eleven years old and all blade" is effective but the "all blade" construction is the kind of compressed metaphor that works better in some contexts than others; here it's fine but not exceptional.

The Kearse confrontation, while satisfying, moves somewhat quickly. The plan called for settling that account "brutally in a domestic/showroom space—something ugly amid staged perfection." The execution delivers on ugliness but the "something ugly amid staged perfection" irony isn't fully exploited—we're in a study with a sailboat painting, which is fine but not as richly textured as the rest of the model home. The confrontation also resolves a bit too cleanly for a chapter that's supposed to be building toward the final act.

The anonymous tip is a slight convenience—the plan didn't specify this device, and while it works, it's a mild shortcut. The chapter plan mentioned Doran fleeing to Harbor View because "men like Doran fled toward witness," which Rita herself articulates, but the tip makes it feel slightly less like Rita's deduction and more like plot assistance.

The string quartet detail ("a string quartet recording leaked from hidden speakers") is good, but "leaked" is a slightly odd verb choice—it implies something more sinister than a recording playing at a party.

Kearse's final moments are satisfying but the line "That deputy voice you do? Hate that" is the closest the chapter comes to a quippy action beat—it's not Marvel-level, but it's slightly more self-conscious than Rita's usual register.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is a well-executed chapter that follows its plan closely, maintains character consistency, and delivers on the pulp promise without becoming generic. The class texture is present and functional. The violence is specific and bodily. The child's role is appropriately scaled. The prose is controlled and mostly earns its moments. It's not a masterpiece—some images strain slightly, the Kearse confrontation could be more textured, and there are minor convenience shortcuts—but it's genuinely good pulp fiction writing with a distinctive voice.

Rita behaves exactly as profiled: checking the phone files with clinical efficiency, refusing to perform emotion, feeding Ava chips with a terse command, noticing the bleeding only when pointed out. Her laugh at Celia's text is perfectly calibrated—contemptuous but not cartoonish. The line "Rich people saved panic for when it might cost them" is Rita's voice precisely.

Ava is well-rendered. Her lie about not looking down, her tiny furious bites of chips, her flat "No" to the religious question—these feel like the specific, difficult child described in the profile rather than a generic precocious kid. "Adults always say calm down like it's a button somewhere" isn't in this chapter but the spirit of it is: "You keep saying that. Because I don't know. That seemed to offend her more than a lie would have." That's a sharp, specific observation about this particular child.

**Following the Chapter Plan**

The plan called for: emergency room parking lot, police station drive-by, a call to an old nurse friend, establishing no safe institutions, Kearse's false narrative, Ava confirming her father's fear, Rita deciding not to hand Ava to anyone local, and ending at the church with Eunice. The final line about the card's contents and Rita deciding to go after Doran is absent—the chapter ends on arrival at the church rather than with Rita's decision to hunt. **Dialogue**

The Celia text exchange is well-handled. The chapter avoids over-explaining through dialogue. **Overall Assessment**

This is accomplished genre writing with a distinctive voice, consistent characters, and controlled prose. [Analysis]

This is a confident, accomplished piece of pulp noir fiction that largely delivers on its premise. Let me assess it carefully across multiple dimensions.

STRENGTHS:

The prose voice is the story's greatest asset. The writer has a genuine, consistent noir sensibility that doesn't feel imitated—it feels inhabited. Lines like "the kind of place developers named after birds they'd run off" and "men like Doran fled toward witness, not away from it" are genuinely sharp observations that earn their place. The voice is economical and specific without being showy.

Rita Vale is a well-constructed protagonist. Her competence is shown rather than told—she inventories the house, notices the dead camera, clocks the ripped jacket, reads the child's attachment to the radio. Her backstory is implied rather than explained, which is the right choice. The "old cold room inside herself" is a recurring motif that works because it's used sparingly.

Ava is the story's second-best element. The dialogue between Rita and Ava is genuinely good—the weather watch/warning correction, the slime comment, the "I'm eleven" exchange. Ava feels like a real child who has been overexposed to adult dysfunction rather than a precocious plot device. Her arc from suspicion to trust is earned through small, specific moments.

The action sequences are competent and grounded. The kitchen fight in Chapter 2 is particularly well-executed—the pantry door on the wrist, the skillet grease, the marble corner. These feel like real improvised violence rather than choreographed movie fights.

The world-building is efficient and atmospheric. The Florida development landscape—retention ponds, Tyvek skin, ornamental palms browning at the tips—is rendered with genuine specificity. The class critique embedded in the setting (Harbor View Estates, decorative lemons, bowls of limes no one was eating) is consistent and pointed without being heavy-handed.

WEAKNESSES:

The metaphor density occasionally tips into excess. "A face that looked unimpressed before she'd even knocked," "thin as a question mark," "the brittle shine of somebody holding a scream by the throat"—these are individually fine but the accumulation in Chapter 1 creates a slightly strained quality. Some metaphors don't fully land: "the sky loosening from black" is vague, and "a separate weather system" for the knee is a bit cute.

The plot mechanics are somewhat conventional. Corrupt deputy, construction site body, memory card MacGuffin, corrupt developer—these are familiar noir furniture. The story doesn't subvert or complicate these elements much. The "what's on the card" reveal (construction site body, shell invoices, recorded conversation) is exactly what a reader would predict.

Doran's final confrontation is the weakest chapter. His villain speech ("This county runs on handshakes and omissions") is the most on-the-nose writing in the piece, and his death—falling through open joists—is somewhat anticlimactic given the buildup. The nail gun as weapon is clever but the fight itself is messier and less precise than the earlier action.

The Eunice character, while charming, is slightly too convenient—the wise church lady with the perfect T-shirt and the Louisville Slugger. She exists primarily as a plot mechanism and her T-shirt slogan is a bit too cute.

Celia Mercer is underdeveloped. She's established as brittle and complicit, then disappears. The text acknowledges this ("your mother finally got brave enough to be useful by text") but it still feels like an unresolved thread.

The pacing in the middle chapters (3-5) is slightly rushed. The transition from the Mercer house to the church to the construction yard happens quickly, and some of the procedural logic (how Kearse tracks them to the church so quickly) is glossed over.

The "unearned transformation" question: Ava's trust in Rita develops naturally and is well-paced. Rita's character doesn't transform—she's consistent throughout, which is appropriate for this genre. No significant unearned transformations.

The ending is appropriately restrained—no false uplift, no tidy resolution for Ava's family situation. "Not relieved. Not happy. Just understanding" is the right note.

Overall, this is a genuinely skilled piece of genre fiction. It's not a masterpiece—the plot is conventional, some metaphors strain, and the final confrontation underdelivers—but it demonstrates real craft, a consistent voice, and genuine character work within the pulp revenge framework.
