# Eli Mercer

Eli Mercer is thirty-five, old enough to have disappointed himself several times and young enough to keep pretending there’s still time to become somebody cleaner. He grew up in a rented apartment over a laundromat on the south side of the city, raised mostly by a mother who worked double shifts in elder care and a grandfather who believed in polished shoes, shut mouths, and men not making spectacles of themselves. Eli was the first in his family to get a stable city job, which is one reason becoming a cop felt less like ideology than gravity. It paid on time. It came with respect, or at least the costume of it.

He was not a noble cop and should not think of himself as one. He looked away from plenty before he quit. He learned quickly how paperwork can erase a bruise, how a report can become fiction by changing three verbs, how some neighborhoods got called “high-risk” so often the phrase stopped meaning anything. What finally pushed him out was not pure conscience but proximity: a fire in a building the city should have condemned years earlier, a dead teenage witness, and pressure to bury evidence that would have embarrassed men with better watches than him. He refused, badly and too late. He resigned before they could fire him, and nobody from the department misses him except one retired dispatcher who still leaves him voicemails on holidays and never says why.

Now he works as a private investigator out of an office with warped blinds and a radiator that only knows two settings, dead and infernal. Most of his cases are not romantic noir material. They are fathers looking for sons who don’t want to be found, women checking whether a husband really stays late at work, landlords wanting leverage, debtors running thin. He is good at finding people because he notices what they spend money on and what they avoid looking at. He is less good at invoicing, sleeping regularly, or admitting when loneliness has curdled him.

Personality-wise, Eli is observant, dry, and slower to speak than most people expect. He does not enjoy small talk, but he is very good at the fake kind that gets information. He is not naturally charming; when he tries to charm, it comes out as deadpan or faintly rude, which occasionally works better. He can be patient in interviews and impatient in intimacy. He likes things lined up: receipts in stacks, keys in the same bowl, notes in one specific notebook with a torn blue cover. He tells himself he hates nostalgia, but he keeps an old matchbook from a bar that closed ten years ago in his desk drawer and has never thrown it away.

His idiosyncrasies should feel unglamorous and lived-in:
- He peels labels off beer bottles absentmindedly when thinking.
- He still says “perp” in his head sometimes and hates himself for it.
- He remembers expensive shoes and cheap cologne better than faces.
- He eats badly when stressed: vending machine peanuts, stale pretzels, coffee with too much sugar.
- He knows the names of old bars and demolished buildings the way other people know baseball stats.
- He does not smoke anymore, quit six years ago, but still notices the brand if someone lights up near him.
- He has a habit of checking exits the second he enters any room, then pretending he didn’t.
- He doesn’t like being touched unexpectedly and hides that by stepping away like he simply had somewhere else to be.

His flaws matter. He is suspicious in ways that can harden into smugness. He tends to mistake emotional restraint for strength, which means he can be quietly cruel when someone asks something of him he cannot bear to give. He is vulnerable to men who seem self-possessed, partly because he isn’t. He can turn moral disgust into performance; sometimes “I know what kind of man you are” really means “I’m scared I know exactly why I want you.” He also likes being right too much. If a clue confirms his worst reading of someone, there is relief in that. It lets him avoid hope.

He has a history with queer life in the city, but not a neatly sentimental one. In his twenties he spent years in bars where everyone knew which cops were safe to flirt with and which ones to avoid. He dated a public-school art teacher for three years and never quite admitted to himself that the relationship ended because he was already learning how to leave parts of himself in locked drawers. He still knows bartenders, old drag queens, one former activist now in real estate, a locksmith who does side work for him and refuses to stop calling him “Officer.” He’s close with no one in an uncomplicated way.

Physically, Eli is lean to the point of looking underfed in bad light. He has dark hair he cuts himself with inconsistent results, a nose slightly off from having been broken once and never properly reset, and the kind of face that becomes handsome only when he’s paying attention. His eyes make people think he’s colder than he is; they are watchful and set deep, with permanent shadows from bad sleep. He dresses like a man trying not to be noticed: dark jackets, serviceable boots, shirts that survive wrinkling. He carries himself with residual cop economy—standing where he can see the room, not wasting movement—but there’s more fatigue in him now, and more care taken to appear unthreatening when he interviews frightened people. He often looks like he’s bracing for weather even indoors.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- He takes Ana’s case partly for the money, partly because Marta’s contempt stings him, and partly because the pattern of fires touches an old nerve from the case that made him leave the police.
- He wants to think he is on Ana’s side, but he has to earn that.
- His allegiance is mostly to whatever remains of his own code: find the missing, don’t hand vulnerable people back to the people who hurt them, don’t trust institutions to become decent just because you ask.
- He distrusts the police department as a body, but he still has old habits of thinking through systems and leverage.
- He is drawn to Rafe immediately and resents this on sight.
- Marta sees him as useful but suspect.
- Ana, if alive long enough to interact directly, would likely regard him as one more ex-cop trying to repurpose himself and would not be wrong.

Flavor voice:

- “The city liked to call the waterfront up-and-coming, which was one way to describe a place after you’d set fire to the people who could still afford it.”
- “He looked expensive in the way trouble always does when it knows somebody else is paying.”
- “I’d quit smoking six years ago. Didn’t matter. Some men still made the whole room smell like relapse.”
- “I wasn’t a good man. I was a man with a filing system and a low tolerance for liars, which sounds noble right up until you meet me.”

# Rafael “Rafe” Navarro

Rafe Navarro is thirty-eight and has spent most of his adult life becoming useful to men he does not respect. He was raised in a narrow apartment above a travel agency in a neighborhood that no longer exists in any affordable form. His mother worked reception at a dental office and his father drifted between jobs, charm, and debt. Rafe learned early that there are people who move through every room expecting to be forgiven, and people who survive by making themselves necessary to the first group. He was bright, attractive, and impossible to intimidate for long, which is a lucrative combination if attached to enough self-preservation and not too much conscience.

He did not begin as a fixer in any cinematic sense. In his twenties he worked nightlife: door lists, private events, party promotion, introductions, smoothing over scandals before spouses or tabloids got hold of them. He learned who cheated, who paid, who scared easily, who thought being discreet meant outsourcing their shame to better-dressed men. Over time, he became the person who could solve messes—quietly moving someone out of a hotel, getting footage deleted, paying off the right cousin, finding a witness before a lawyer did. Eventually he moved into bigger rooms with richer men. Developers and deputy mayors are not that different from closeted financiers at 2 a.m.; they just call their sins strategy.

Rafe has always told himself he is not ideological. He is practical. He solves the problem in front of him. But practicality has put him in service of increasingly ugly machinery, and he knows that. He has watched neighborhoods disappear under the smooth language of renewal. He has delivered envelopes and made calls he no longer knows how to justify except with a shrug and “somebody would have done it anyway.” The shrug is wearing thin.

He is charismatic, but not in a broad, extroverted way. He is socially exact. He knows how to make one person at a time feel singled out, conspired with, correctly read. He is often funny, though he uses humor mostly to redirect attention or keep people from asking a second question. He dislikes earnestness unless it comes from someone he finds impossible to dismiss. He is generous in oddly specific ways and selfish in others that matter more. He remembers birthdays if remembering them gives him leverage, but he also once spent half a night driving a junior bartender to urgent care and never mentioned it again. He steals little things from expensive places when he’s bored—hotel pens, monogrammed matchbooks, a silver spoon from city hall catering—and leaves them in coat pockets for weeks.

Important idiosyncrasies:
- He smokes when he’s thinking or waiting, not constantly. Eli’s first impression catches him in one of those suspended moments, which is why it lands so hard.
- He uses expensive cologne too sparingly, like he doesn’t trust abundance.
- He tips beautifully in diners and terribly at luxury bars.
- He hates driving and does it aggressively.
- He has a weakness for old boleros and terrible gossip.
- He straightens crooked picture frames in hotel rooms.
- He speaks excellent bureaucrat when he needs to: “regrettable,” “containment,” “optics,” “exposure.”
- He almost never raises his voice. The rarer it is, the more unsettling.
- He has an ugly scar under one shoulder blade from a knife incident he tells three different lies about depending on company.
- He does not like being photographed without warning and will turn his face slightly before most people notice.

His flaws are substantial. Rafe compartmentalizes so aggressively that he often mistakes dissociation for control. He can be genuinely kind in one breath and utterly mercenary in the next. He is vain, though not only about appearance—he is vain about competence, about being the calmest man in the room. He resents people who still believe they can stay clean. He has a tendency to mock what he envies, especially conviction. He is also capable of disappearing emotionally the second he senses dependence, because needing people has historically gone badly for him. If Eli gets under his skin, Rafe’s first instinct will be to turn that fact into irony.

He has known queer life in the city from the angle of access and performance. He has been loved by men who wanted danger at a discount and by men who wanted him hidden. He had one long affair in his early thirties with a married council aide who cried after sex and eventually got promoted into public respectability. He has old friends in nightlife, enemies in private security, and a tailor who knows more city secrets than most elected officials. He is not a community pillar. He is the man some people call when they need a problem to become less visible by morning.

His relationship to Ana should have some grit. Perhaps she approached him once because she knew he could identify shell companies or tell her which private security firms were being hired. He gave her one answer too many, maybe because he admired her nerve, maybe because he was bored, maybe because some part of him wanted the machine jammed. That makes him partly responsible for her getting further than she should have and more entangled in the consequences than Eli first realizes.

Physically, Rafe is built with deceptive softness: not bulky, but broad enough through the shoulders to fill a doorway. He dresses too well for most rooms he enters, though never in a flashy way—good wool, good shoes, dark coats, shirts that look effortless and are not. He has black hair cut with money, olive skin gone a little sallow at the edges from too many late nights, and a face made more interesting by tiredness than youth. His mouth often looks amused before he actually is. He uses stillness as power. Where Eli scans, Rafe settles. He leans instead of fidgets. He offers cigarettes, lighters, half-smiles, and very little he hasn’t chosen. When he’s truly angry, the biggest tell is that he gets more precise, not less.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- His official allegiance is to the developer’s operation and the political men attached to it, because they pay him and because he is too deeply in to walk away clean.
- His real allegiance is to his own continued survival and to a shrinking private line he no longer wants to cross.
- He does not think of himself as a good person, which can become an excuse.
- He wants Ana found before his employers find her, partly because she has evidence, partly because he knows what will happen if the wrong people reach her first.
- He is attracted to Eli because Eli is sharper than most men, less easy to charm than most men, and still carrying around a conscience like a cracked rib.
- He also finds Eli irritatingly earnest in exactly the places Eli would deny being earnest.
- He has complicated loyalties to a handful of people in nightlife and city backrooms, and those loyalties may matter in small practical ways during the story.
- He mistrusts institutions less morally than aesthetically: he thinks they are ugly, hungry, and banal.

Flavor voice:

- “You say corruption like it’s an exotic animal. It’s paperwork with a decent tailor.”
- “I’m not asking you to trust me, Eli. I’m asking you to develop better priorities.”
- “Everybody in this city wants clean hands. Funny thing is, they keep hiring men like me to do the washing.”
- “You look at me like you’ve already decided which part is the lie. I haven’t decided whether to be offended or flattered.”

# Ana Valez

Ana Valez is thirty, queer, Puerto Rican, and too disciplined to be mistaken for reckless by anyone paying real attention. The city would call her an activist; she would call herself an organizer if she was feeling patient and “a person trying to keep my neighbors from being turned into an investment brochure” if she was not. She grew up in the waterfront district before anyone thought of it as desirable, in a rent-stabilized apartment her grandmother fought for and nearly lost twice. She knows the block histories, who owned which storefront, which landlord let mold spread for years before selling, which church basement can be borrowed for meetings if you ask the secretary and not the priest.

Ana works part-time in housing advocacy and part-time wherever she can patch income together: grant-funded nonprofit work, translation gigs, training volunteers, helping elderly tenants document harassment. She is very good at making systems legible to frightened people. She can explain code violations, notice periods, insurance games, and public comment procedures in plain language without sounding patronizing. That makes her dangerous to the people who benefit from confusion.

She should not be sanctified. Ana is intelligent, relentless, and often difficult. She can be impatient with people who are slower, more frightened, or less politically developed than she is. She has scorched promising alliances by refusing to soften an argument. She sometimes mistakes being right for being persuasive. She keeps too much in her own head because she does not trust institutions and only half-trusts movements. She has broken up with people for asking her to stop working so much and then complained they lacked commitment. She is capable of using people strategically while disliking herself for it later.

Her idiosyncrasies:
- She color-codes files obsessively but loses chargers constantly.
- She wears men’s watches bought secondhand because she likes things that can take a hit.
- She annotates flyers and city memos in pen so aggressively they become new documents.
- She drinks terrible coffee without complaint and excellent coffee with suspicion.
- When angry, she gets quieter, which people mistake for calm right before she ruins their week.
- She hates the word “revitalization” on principle.
- She has a voice memo habit: half notes, half arguments with herself while walking.
- She once taught a room full of tenants how to document mold using rulers and timestamps and made it funny.

If she appears in person, she should have immediate friction with Eli. His ex-cop status is not a quirk to her; it is a material fact. She may hire or use him because Marta insisted or because she needed someone deniable, but she does not hand out trust because a man looks regretful in low light. Her relationship to Rafe is also not simple. She may have approached him because she knew he floated near the edge of money and scandal. He may have helped her identify names or fronts. She may think he likes to imagine himself more conflicted than he really is. She may not be wrong.

Physically, Ana is compact, quick-moving, and harder to read than either Eli or Rafe at first glance. She has curly dark hair she keeps tied back when working and forgets to fix when it escapes. Her clothes are practical: layered jackets, old boots, tote bag full of paper and cables and snacks she forgets to eat. She has strong hands, bitten nails, and a look of concentration that can seem hostile if you don’t know her. When she’s tired, she rubs the bridge of her nose with ink-stained fingers and keeps going. She occupies space like someone accustomed to needing to justify it and having decided to stop.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- Her allegiance is to tenants first, not to nonprofits, media, or heroic narratives.
- She wants evidence released in a way that protects people on the ground, not just in a way that produces headlines.
- She loves her sister Marta and lies to her for tactical reasons.
- She distrusts Eli because he once belonged to an institution that made people like her easier to evict, arrest, and ignore.
- She distrusts Rafe because he profits from proximity to men who burn neighborhoods down in installments.
- She may still work with both if necessary, which does not equal forgiveness.
- Her motive is not abstract justice; it is preventing the final fire and forcing enough truth into public view that the machine stutters.

Flavor voice:

- “If they say revitalization, check your wallet. If they say community partnership, check the exits.”
- “I don’t need either of you to be good men. I need you to be useful for the next six hours.”
- “Fear is administrative in this city. That’s the trick. Nobody has to point a gun at you if they can shut off the heat in January.”
- “You don’t get points for growing a conscience after the paperwork’s filed.”

# Marta Valez

Marta is Ana’s older sister by four years and the person who actually gets the plot moving by refusing to wait politely for institutions to fail in predictable ways. She works as a respiratory therapist at a public hospital and has the bearing of someone who spends twelve-hour shifts managing panic in fluorescent light. She is not political in Ana’s way, but she is practical, observant, and deeply unimpressed by men whose job titles require euphemism.

Marta and Ana love each other hard and badly. Marta thinks Ana takes impossible risks and confuses martyrdom with effectiveness. Ana thinks Marta underestimates how quickly caution becomes surrender. They fight in the shorthand of siblings who know exactly where to press and how much not to say. Marta is the one who notices when Ana’s routines change, when her messages get too careful, when fear enters by subtraction rather than declaration. Hiring Eli is not a leap of faith; it is triage. She hires him because formal channels are already closing and because she can see, with the instincts of someone who reads distress for a living, that he carries some old wound this case might hook into.

She has very little patience for self-dramatizing men. This makes her useful as a grounding force around both Eli and Rafe. She should not become a “tough sister” cliché; her specificity matters:
- She keeps protein bars in every bag she owns.
- She sends texts with no punctuation when calm and full punctuation when furious.
- She names neighborhood feral cats after doctors she hates.
- She can cry from exhaustion and then ask for your insurance card in the same minute.
- She notices nicotine stains, hand tremors, and whether someone is lying about having slept.

Physically, Marta has Ana’s eyes but steadier posture. She wears scrubs under weatherproof coats, keeps her hair braided or clipped up, and moves quickly even when standing still somehow. She smells faintly of hospital soap and peppermint gum. Her face is open until it closes; once closed, it takes work to get back in.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- Her allegiance is to Ana first, then to whatever gets Ana home alive.
- She does not care about exposing corruption as an abstract civic triumph unless it materially protects people.
- She sees Eli as potentially useful and potentially weak in the ways men with guilt often are.
- She sees through Rafe almost instantly and dislikes the fact that he knows she does.
- If Ana survives, Marta will still be furious with her.

Flavor voice:

- “I’m not paying you to feel bad about the city, Mr. Mercer. I’m paying you to find my sister.”
- “You can both stop doing that thing where men decide which one of them has the sadder eyes. It’s embarrassing.”
- “Hospitals, cops, city hall—it’s all the same building when you’re the one waiting for news.”
- “If Ana says she’s fine, that means she’s either bleeding or planning something illegal.”

# Deputy Mayor Simon Coyle

Simon Coyle is in his fifties, expensively maintained, and has the smooth, health-conscious sheen of a man who has spent years outsourcing consequences. He came up through planning commissions and “public-private partnerships,” which means he learned to describe extraction as stewardship long before he reached elected office. He is not a snarling villain. He is worse: articulate, patient, and genuinely convinced that history belongs to those capable of monetizing it before anyone else can sentimentalize it.

Coyle sees neighborhoods as assets, constituencies as obstacles or opportunities, and moral language as a tool for television. He likely believes some version of his own rhetoric. He can speak sincerely about affordability while engineering the conditions that erase it. He does not consider himself corrupt so much as adult. Fires, pressure campaigns, strategic neglect—these are regrettable excesses in a necessary transition, and he has learned not to look too closely at the men he hires to make necessity happen.

He may have known Eli in a former life as just another departmental nuisance. He certainly knows Rafe as a useful instrument, though one he does not mistake for loyal. His relationship to Ana is the purest expression of his politics: she is not a person to him but a friction point, someone making noise where process should be allowed to function.

Idiosyncrasies:
- Drinks green juice and bourbon with equal ritual.
- Calls everyone by their first name to imply intimacy he has not earned.
- Never carries his own umbrella.
- Uses “we” when discussing decisions made entirely for private gain.
- Has the eerie calm of a man accustomed to staff absorbing his anger before it becomes visible.

Physically, Coyle is silver-haired, fit in a careful indoor way, and always looks recently pressed. He smiles with his teeth and listens as if granting a favor. He touches people lightly on the arm when making threats sound collaborative. His office and clothes should suggest expensive taste just shy of flamboyance.

Motives, allegiances, relationships:
- Allegiance to power, legacy, and the donor class.
- He wants the waterfront project completed because it secures money, influence, and a lasting physical monument to his tenure.
- He regards Rafe as useful but disposable.
- He would underestimate Eli until it became inconvenient.
- He would never think of Ana as an equal adversary, which is part of his blindness.

Flavor voice:

- “Progress always feels violent to the people invested in standing still.”
- “Let’s not romanticize disorder because it has sentimental architecture.”
- “My concern, Eli, is that men like you confuse proximity to mess with understanding it.”
- “Containment is not the same thing as cruelty, whatever the newspapers prefer to imply.”

Ana Valez’s sister came into my office at four in the afternoon carrying hospital coffee and the kind of anger that made the room look smaller.

My office was on the second floor above a locksmith and below a tax preparer who believed in the healing power of stomping. The blinds were bent, the radiator hissed like it had opinions, and the name on the frosted glass still belonged to the man who’d had the place before me because replacing it cost money. Most days I handled work that fit the room: husbands with lipstick on collars, sons late on debts, landlords who wanted a tenant found before the paperwork caught up to them. Nothing with ideals in it. Ideals paid badly and got blood in places hard to clean.

She stood just inside the door and looked me over like she was triaging me.

“Eli Mercer?”

“Depends who’s asking.”

“Someone in a hurry.”

That was my first clue she wasn’t there to cry. People who came to cry sat down before I told them to.

She wore navy scrubs under a dark coat shiny from rain, and there was a hospital badge clipped to her pocket with the photo turned inward. Her hair was braided tight, her face all sharp planes and sleeplessness. She had the same eyes as the woman in the picture she set on my desk a second later. Same mouth, too, though the one in the photo was smiling with less restraint.

“My sister,” she said. “Ana Valez. She’s been gone two days.”

I looked at the picture. Thirty, maybe. Dark curls tied back, denim jacket, a tote bag slung over one shoulder heavy enough to pull her sideways. There was a flyer in her hand. In the background, a folding table, bad coffee urn, church basement cinderblock.

“Police report?” I asked.

She gave me a look usually reserved for contagious diseases. “Of course there’s a police report.”

“And?”

“And they took it.”

I waited.

“They also told me she’s an adult, adults leave, and maybe I should consider whether she needed space.” Her voice stayed level in a way that took effort. “My sister does not take space without telling me who gets her cat and where she hid the rent money.”

I picked up the photo again. There was a phone number scrawled on the back in blue ink and one line: **If something happens, ask about Mariner.**

“Mariner what?”

“That’s the problem,” she said. “I don’t know.”

Rain tapped at the window. Downstairs, a key machine screamed into metal. I leaned back in my chair and let the silence stretch enough to see if she’d fill it with something useful.

She did.

“She organizes tenants on the waterfront,” she said. “Mostly in the old warehouse district, the row houses behind it, buildings the city forgot until developers remembered them. She said she found something. She wouldn’t tell me what. Just that if anything happened, I shouldn’t let it disappear with her.”

“You and your sister close?”

“We fight beautifully,” she said. “Does that count?”

“Sometimes.”

“She tells me too little when she’s scared. She gets efficient.”

That, more than the report, I believed. Fear had a housekeeping quality in some people. They started labeling jars and making lists.

“You know what kind of work I do?” I asked.

“Yes. Men who cheat. Kids who run. Missing people when their families can’t get the right doors opened.” Her gaze flicked to the old brass shield in my drawer, visible where it had stuck half-open. “And before this, you did other work.”

There it was.

“You hired me anyway.”

“I’m not hiring a conscience,” she said. “I’m hiring a skill set.”

I almost smiled. “What’s your name?”

“Marta.”

She put the hospital coffee on my desk like an offering she resented making. “She mentioned you once,” she added.

That surprised me. “Did she.”

“She said if she ever went missing on purpose, you’d probably still find her, and if she went missing by accident, you’d hate everyone involved enough to keep going.”

“Not exactly a recommendation.”

“No,” Marta said. “More a warning.”

I took Ana’s photo, the number, and the envelope Marta slid across the desk with half the fee in cash and the other half promised if I found her before a detective remembered how phones worked. There was one more thing in the envelope: a matchbook from the Lantern, a bar on Harbor Street I hadn’t been inside in three years.

“Why this?”

“She was there the night before she disappeared,” Marta said. “Met someone. She didn’t tell me who. She texted me a photo by accident after midnight. Just a doorway and somebody’s coat. Then she unsent it.”

“Still got it?”

Marta already had her phone out. She handed it over.

The picture was blurred by rain and motion. Doorway lit pink by neon. Wet pavement. The edge of a man in a dark coat, one hand lifted near his face, ember lit at the tip of a cigarette. Nothing useful and somehow too much. You could build a whole mistake around a silhouette like that.

“I’ll start there,” I said.

Marta stood. “I don’t care if she’s angry when you find her,” she said. “I’d actually prefer it. Angry means breathing.”

Then she hesitated, just once, and in that second she looked less like a woman holding herself together and more like a tired sister in a hallway outside bad news.

“They’re burning people out down there,” she said quietly. “Everybody knows it. Buildings fail inspection, pipes burst, fires start in places the wiring somehow passed last month. If she found proof...” Her jaw tightened. “Don’t take this to people with city badges unless you like your evidence disappearing.”

When she left, the room smelled faintly of peppermint gum and rain.

I waited ten minutes, mostly out of habit, then put on my coat and headed for Harbor Street.

The Lantern sat between a shuttered print shop and a boutique wine bar with polished brass handles no one from the block used. The old sign still buzzed red over the door. Inside, it was early enough for the place to feel caught between shifts: two men playing pool badly, one bartender polishing glasses she had no intention of making shine, a jukebox humming something old enough to remember cigarettes indoors.

The bartender recognized me, which I pretended not to notice.

“Thought you quit this neighborhood,” she said.

“Didn’t take.”

“Nothing ever does.”

I showed her Ana’s photo. She took one glance and nodded.

“Organizer,” she said. “Mean little tote bag. Yeah, she was here. Met a man.”

“Description.”

The bartender snorted. “Handsome in a way that made me tired. Coat cost more than my rent. Smoked outside because men like that always think they’re being considerate while making themselves look interesting.”

That narrowed the city to half its worst ideas.

“He got a name?”

“He got several, I’d bet.”

I thanked her and stepped back into the rain.

He was leaning against the brick across the alley like he’d been there all along, one shoulder to the wall, cigarette glowing between his fingers. Dark coat, dark hair, face half-shadowed under the awning of the closed print shop. He didn’t startle when he saw me. Men who startle are amateurs or decent.

For a second all I registered was the smoke curling white in the damp and the stillness under it. Then the rest came into focus: expensive shoes gone wet at the edges, a mouth that looked amused before it had earned the right, a gaze too direct to be accidental.

He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.

“You’re Mercer,” he said.

His voice was low and neat, like he filed the corners off words before letting them out.

“Depends who’s asking.”

He smiled at that, not warmly. “Cute. Don’t do too much with it.”

I stayed under the Lantern’s red spill, far enough not to share the awning. “You met Ana Valez.”

“Did I.”

“You know she’s missing.”

He flicked ash into the gutter and looked past me at the bar’s door as if measuring whether this conversation was worth getting rained on for. “I know she was curious,” he said. “In this city that’s a bad survival trait.”

“Funny. I was just thinking the same thing about expensive coats.”

That got me a fuller look. Not offended. Interested.

“Here’s some free advice,” he said. “Whatever she was chasing, let the police mishandle it in peace.”

“I don’t take advice from men who lurk professionally.”

“No?” He dropped the cigarette, ground it under his heel. “Then take a fact. Harbor Street’s going to be very busy this week. If you’re smart, you won’t be standing in the middle when it happens.”

He started to walk past me, then paused close enough for me to catch the cologne under the smoke, something expensive and sparing and not quite enough to cover the night on him.

“Tell Marta,” he said, “that if her sister wants to come home, she should do it before somebody else decides home’s worth more vacant.”

Then he was gone into the rain.

I stood there a moment longer than I liked, watching the alley hold the shape he’d left in it.

When I finally moved, I saw the thing he’d dropped near the gutter wasn’t just ash and filter. It was a folded scrap of damp paper, small enough to miss unless you were looking for what men left behind.

On it, in block letters smudged by rain, were two words:

**MARINER WAREHOUSE**
