By nine the next morning Harbor Street had put on its daytime face, which was less flattering and more honest. The neon was dead, the puddles were just puddles, and the luxury banners zip-tied to construction fencing looked cheaper in sunlight. **LIVING SHORELINE. REIMAGINE WATERFRONT LIFE.** That was one way to describe evicting half a neighborhood and charging the survivors for a view.

I started with coffee from a place that called itself artisanal and tasted like resentment. Then I went to Mariner Warehouse.

It sat three blocks inland from the piers, a brick hulk with boarded lower windows and a fresh city notice stapled crooked to the chain-link: **UNSAFE FOR OCCUPANCY. ENTRY PROHIBITED.** Someone had spray-painted **FOR WHO** across the bottom.

The padlock looked official. The fence did not. It had been cut and twisted back at one corner recently, then bent into place again by someone who cared more about gesture than security. I crouched by the opening and found muddy shoe prints, a cigarette butt gone soft in the night, and one tiny pink scrap of paper caught in the wire.

Flyer stock. Church-basement weight.

I pocketed it and circled the building instead of going in first. Old habits. Check exits, windows, neighboring sightlines, who could watch you without getting wet. Mariner backed onto an alley full of dumpsters and soggy cardboard, and from there I could see the rear loading doors, one chained, one hanging a little crooked. Somebody had been using the place after condemnation.

Inside smelled like river damp, old timber, and something sharper underneath—electrical burn, maybe, or memory of it. My flashlight found dust, pallets, graffiti, rat shit, and recent footprints overlaying older ones. A camp stove sat in one corner beside a milk crate and an empty gallon jug. Not homeless occupation, not exactly. Temporary. Intentional. On a far wall, under a broken window, someone had taped plastic sheeting over a section of brick. Behind it, hidden in a shallow gap, was a waterproof document pouch.

Ana had not been casual.

The pouch held copies, not originals. Inspection reports, permit applications, property transfers through shell companies with names like Bay Civic Renewal and Anchor Development Partners. Three addresses on Harbor and one on Leland Street. Every building had had a fire, burst pipe, gas leak, or sudden structural emergency in the last fourteen months. Every building had changed hands within eight weeks. Every inspection signature came from one of two city officials I recognized from my old life—not famous names, just exactly the kind of men who stayed unremarkable long enough to do damage.

At the bottom was a sticky note in aggressive blue ink:

**Ask who benefits from vacant. Ask who signs after midnight.**

There was also a key taped inside the pouch and a receipt from a self-storage place on the edge of downtown.

I was halfway through photographing the lot when I heard tires in the alley.

Not a panic stop. Slow. Deliberate. I killed the flashlight and moved toward the loading door, pausing behind a stack of warped pallets with a good view of the rear entrance.

A black SUV idled outside. Municipal plates in front, which meant either someone very stupid or someone counting on nobody wanting to make the call. A man got out in city work boots too clean for city work, checked his phone, and nodded to somebody still inside. Then a second man emerged from the passenger side carrying coffee and wearing a windbreaker with the developer’s logo small over one breast: a silver wave swallowing a line of skyline.

I took two pictures through the gap in the door and sent them to myself before my signal started choking.

The men didn’t come in. They looked at the warehouse, looked up and down the alley, talked too quietly to hear. The one in boots laughed at something. Then they got back in the SUV and drove off.

I stayed where I was another full minute because patience had once been the difference between a clean report and a bottle to the temple. Then I slipped out the front and headed for city records.

The clerk on duty at Municipal Services had a shaved head, green nail polish bitten to the quick, and the expression of a woman who would rather be diagnosed with something serious than help me before lunch.

I gave her the addresses. She gave me the rules.

“Public request form, five business days.”

“I don’t have five business days.”

“Then I guess this is going to be a short friendship.”

I slid one of the inspection reports across the counter. She looked at the signature, then at me.

“Where’d you get this?”

“Found it in church.”

“That’s not funny.”

“It wasn’t a joke.”

She tapped the paper once. “Caldwell signs like that when he’s tired. Usually after six. Not after midnight.”

“Midnight?”

Her face changed the way a door changes when somebody realizes they’ve left it open.

“Didn’t say that.”

“You kind of did.”

She sighed, glanced over her shoulder, then leaned in just enough to make us co-conspirators against her will. “Files have been getting amended after hours,” she said. “Not by me. You hear things. Systems log changes. Sometimes inspections appear that nobody remembers doing. Sometimes condemnation moves fast when a council office starts leaning.”

“Which council office?”

She gave me a look dry enough to preserve flowers. “The one with donor events on rooftops and opinions about revitalization.”

“Deputy Mayor Coyle.”

“I didn’t say that either.”

“Do you want to?”

“No.” She shoved the paper back at me. “I want to keep my pension. Fill out your form like everybody else, and if I were you, I’d stop carrying original documents in a coat pocket that cheap.”

It took me half a second to realize she was looking past me.

I turned. Rafe Navarro was by the entrance security gate, one hand resting on the metal bar like he’d wandered in to admire municipal architecture. Daylight made him look less spectral and more expensive. Charcoal coat, open at the throat, no tie. He had sunglasses tucked into one breast pocket and a paper cup in his hand from the coffee place downstairs everyone pretended not to hate. He lifted the cup slightly when he saw me, as if greeting an acquaintance at a gallery instead of a records office.

“Mercer.”

“Navarro.”

The clerk muttered, “Absolutely not,” and stood up. “I’m on break.”

She left us there with all the dignity available under fluorescent lighting.

Rafe walked over, glanced at the public request forms, then at the report in my hand. “You really do enjoy making things harder than necessary.”

“That line work often for you?”

“Often enough.”

I looked at the coffee. “Municipal Services seems beneath your pay grade.”

“Nothing involving city paperwork is beneath my pay grade. That’s why I have one.”

He smelled less of smoke today and more of starch and whatever he’d put on his skin in place of sleep. Up close, there was a faint bruise-yellow exhaustion under his eyes. It made him look more human and therefore less trustworthy.

“You left me a note,” I said.

He took a sip. “Did I.”

“At Mariner.”

He smiled over the cup. “And here you are. So I suppose literacy survives.”

“What’s in the warehouse?”

“Dust. Liability. City history no one can monetize unless they knock it down first.”

“Try again.”

He considered me, head tipped slightly. “A woman with your phone number would have chosen someone less obvious.”

“A woman with my phone number knew exactly what she was doing.”

That, finally, got the smallest real reaction—a narrowing at the eyes, the recalculation of a man who’d hoped Ana had been improvising and now knew better.

“She was here after midnight,” I said. “Looking at amended inspections. Somebody with city access met with somebody from Shoreline Civic Development this morning at a condemned building your people are interested in. You can tell me to let the police mishandle it again, but at least vary the wording.”

“Those aren’t my people.”

“You cash their checks.”

“Sometimes,” he said. “Which is not the same thing.”

“It usually is.”

He set the coffee down on the counter between us, took a folded public form from the stack, and wrote something on the back with a pen from his coat. Then he slid it toward me.

“Storage unit,” he said. “Downtown. Same facility your organizer likes. If you go, don’t go alone.”

I looked at the unit number. It matched the receipt from the pouch.

“Why help?”

He shrugged. “Maybe I’m sentimental about women who ask impolite questions.”

“Maybe you’re trying to get there first.”

“That too.”

Two uniformed officers came through the front doors laughing about a lunch order. Rafe saw them before I did, his gaze flicking once toward the lobby cameras.

“Time to go,” he murmured.

“I’m not done.”

“No,” he said. “You’re standing in a public building with stolen records in your pocket and two men from your old profession thirty feet away. What you are is about to become inconvenient.”

He took my elbow—not hard, but like a man used to moving people without making a scene—and steered me toward a side corridor lined with vending machines and city recycling posters.

I could have shrugged him off. I didn’t.

At the far exit he let go. “There’s a diner on Polk,” he said. “Blue awning, bad pie. If you’re still free in an hour, don’t come.”

“Threat?”

“Advice.” His mouth twitched. “You hate it when I’m considerate.”

He walked away before I could answer, disappearing into the wet brightness of the street.

I looked down at the paper in my hand. Beneath the unit number, he’d written one more line.

**If she stored it, they know. Hurry.**
step_outputs.8:
The storage place sat under the freeway in a row of practical businesses no one visited unless they were hiding, moving, or lying to one ex about the other. **SAFEHOLD SELF STORAGE**, blue letters faded to resignation. A bail bonds office on one side, a discount flooring warehouse on the other, and above all of it the steady throat-noise of traffic heading somewhere richer.

I parked half a block down and watched the entrance through rain stippled across the windshield. People came and went carrying the usual archaeology of failure: plastic bins, a mattress rolled and cinched with rope, two framed prints nobody had wanted enough to hang but not little enough to throw away. Nobody in a charcoal coat. Nobody who looked like municipal trouble. That didn’t mean much. Trouble dressed down when it had to.

Rafe had said don’t go alone. He’d also said don’t come to the diner. I had ignored one instruction and intended to ignore the other on principle if nothing else.

Unit 418 was on the second floor, climate-controlled, narrow hallway that smelled like cardboard and carpet cleaner. The lock was cheap but new. Ana’s key turned smoothly.

Inside: banker’s boxes, one duffel, a folding chair, and a battery lantern on the floor. A temporary archive. Not panic storage—working storage. Someone had been here recently enough that the air still held stale coffee and wool.

I closed the unit behind me and got to work.

The first box held tenant files: names, contact sheets, complaint logs, photographs of mold, burst pipes, exposed wiring, dead heaters. The second held printouts from city procurement databases and corporate registries, all highlighted in Ana’s furious blue pen. The shell companies tied back, through enough layers to insult a weaker woman, to Shoreline Civic and two subsidiaries with donor overlap in Simon Coyle’s campaign reports. There were invoices to private security firms, cleanup contractors, emergency board-up crews. Everyone got paid. That was the city’s purest language.

The duffel had a hard drive, three burner phones wrapped in socks, and a manila envelope marked **IF I PANIC / IF I DISAPPEAR**.

Inside the envelope was a handwritten timeline, two memory cards, and a photo printed at the kind of pharmacy kiosk that still made everything look faintly ashamed. In the photo, taken from a distance through rain, Deputy Mayor Simon Coyle stood in profile under a warehouse awning beside a man I recognized from old internal briefings as Lieutenant Caldwell from Fire Investigations. They were speaking to a third man with his back to the camera, expensive coat, one hand lifted in a shape I already knew too well.

Rafe.

I stared at the picture long enough for my own pulse to become annoying.

The angle was bad. It could have been anyone with good posture and a costly overcoat. It was not anyone else.

One of the burners still had charge. I powered it on. Ana had used it like a field notebook: photos of permit notices, voice memos, snapshots of envelopes and license plates. On the oldest memo, her voice came through distorted by traffic and distance but unmistakable—quick, low, irritated with the world and herself.

“Okay. If this is me overreacting, fantastic. If not: Shoreline’s using code enforcement as a pressure tool, and the fire reports are being amended after incident. Caldwell signs after midnight. Coyle’s office pushes emergency declarations, buildings clear, property transfers inside sixty days. The man with Coyle tonight is called Navarro by one of the security guys. Fixer. Not payroll exactly. He knows who everybody really works for.”

The memo clicked off. I played it again, then the next. More notes. Addresses. Names. One half-captured argument with someone male, voice too distant to identify, Ana saying, “You don’t get to talk to me about regret like it’s a tax deduction.”

I smiled despite myself. Then I heard footsteps in the hallway.

Not passing. Stopping.

The storage latch twitched.

I killed the lantern and the phone screen went black in my hand.

A voice outside, male and irritated. “You sure?”

“Unit was accessed. He’s in there.”

He. Good to know.

The latch rattled harder. Then a metallic scrape as someone tried a second key or a shim.

I moved fast, stuffing the phones and memory cards into my coat, the envelope into the inside pocket, hard drive under my belt at the back. There was no rear exit. Just cinderblock, metal roll door, one narrow ceiling vent too small for optimism.

The roll door jumped up three inches with a shriek.

A flashlight beam sliced under.

“Mercer,” somebody called. “Open it up. We just want the files.”

I knew that voice—not from anywhere personal, just the broad civic slurry of men who had done contract security around city events and learned to sound friendly while crowding people backward.

I kicked the folding chair into the door. It wouldn’t hold long. Bought me seconds.

The flashlight beam jerked away. “Cut it.”

I looked around for a weapon and found only the banker’s boxes, the lantern, and a rusting floor bracket bolted half-loose near the wall. I got the bracket up on the third wrench, skinning two knuckles. Better than nothing.

The first slice of a saw screamed against the bottom lock.

Then the hallway lights snapped off.

Total dark beyond the door. A voice outside: “What the hell?”

Another, closer now and very calm: “Gentlemen. You’re making a lot of noise for men who don’t want witnesses.”

Silence.

Then one of them said, “This doesn’t concern you.”

“I’m flattered,” Rafe said. “But you did just break into my afternoon.”

A scuffle. Hard shoes on concrete. A grunt, another, the flat ugly sound of somebody hitting the cinderblock wall. The saw clattered away. The roll door dropped an inch.

I didn’t wait for a formal invitation. I hauled the door upward just enough to duck under and came out low with the metal bracket in both hands.

One of the men was on the floor clutching his wrist. The other had Rafe shoved against the opposite wall with a forearm to his throat. Rafe looked more annoyed than distressed, which was either impressive or very stupid.

I swung the bracket into the standing man’s kidney. He folded with a noise like a couch giving up.

For a second all three of us just breathed in the dark corridor, fluorescent emergency lights turning everyone hospital green.

Rafe straightened his coat cuffs.

“Well,” he said, voice rougher than before, “that was almost collaborative.”

I still had the bracket up. “You brought them.”

“If I had brought them, they’d be better dressed.”

The man on the floor with the ruined wrist was trying to crawl toward the saw. Rafe stepped on his hand—not hard enough to break, just enough to stop him.

“Who sent you?” I asked.

The man spat something creative and useless.

Rafe crouched smoothly, took the guy’s phone from his pocket, and checked the screen. “Contract boys,” he said. “Shoreline adjacent. No names worth the trouble.” He slipped the phone into his own coat. “You can hit him again if it helps your mood, but we should leave.”

I was still looking at the photo in my mind. Coyle. Caldwell. Rafe under the awning like a man discussing catering.

“You were there,” I said.

He glanced up. “I’m in a lot of places.”

“With Coyle.”

“That narrows it less than you’d think.”

“Was Ana talking to you?”

He stood. For the first time since I’d met him, some of the polish dropped off his face. Not enough to show me the whole truth. Enough to prove there was one.

“Yes,” he said. “And if you want to keep being angry about that, get in line somewhere warmer.”

Sirens wailed distantly under the freeway. Not close yet, but not decorative.

I grabbed the most critical box and left the rest. We moved fast down the hallway, Rafe a step behind me, then alongside, then somehow ahead by the time we hit the stairwell.

Outside, the rain had turned mean.

My car was at the curb. So was a black sedan I hadn’t noticed before, engine running, parking lights on.

Rafe saw it and said, “Not your car.”

“No.”

“Then don’t—”

The rear passenger door of the sedan opened.

A man inside raised a gun with the blank professionalism of someone clocking in.

Rafe hit me in the chest and we both went down hard onto wet concrete as the first shot took out the storage office window behind us in a scream of glass.
step_outputs.9:
The second shot hit my car door with a crack that sounded expensive. I was already on the ground, rain in my mouth, Rafe’s shoulder jammed into my ribs hard enough to bruise. Somebody in the storage office started screaming. The gunman fired once more into the glass and then the sedan peeled away from the curb, tires spitting water.

Rafe lifted his head first.

“Still alive?” he asked.

“Annoyingly.”

“Good.”

He got to his feet in one economical motion and hauled me up by the arm before I could decide whether to be insulted. My coat was soaked through on one side, my palms gritty with pavement. The storage office alarm had finally found the energy to become a real alarm. Under the freeway, sirens echoed strangely, close and not close.

“My car,” I said.

Rafe looked at the fresh hole in the driver-side door. “I’d call that aspirational.”

“Very funny.”

“I’m not joking. If they know the make and plate, they’ll wait to see where you take it.” He put his hand out. “Keys.”

I stared at him.

“Mercer.”

“You’ve got your own.”

“I do. They know that one too.”

That tracked, which annoyed me more.

I handed him the keys. He popped the trunk, moved with quick precision, and took out my go-bag, the extra phone charger, and the cheap camera I kept in a shoebox with three old case files. Then he locked the car again and pocketed the keys like theft was an administrative step.

“We’re walking,” he said.

“Where?”

“Somewhere with fewer sight lines and worse linens.”

I should have ditched him there. Should have taken the evidence and the rain and made my own bad decisions in private. Instead I followed him three blocks through underpasses and alleys because the city had just tried to shoot me and he was the only person in sight acting as if he’d expected that level of discourtesy all along.

The motel was on Polk above a discount pharmacy and beside a Vietnamese bakery that still managed to smell good in weather like this. Blue awning. Bad pie, just as promised. The clerk behind the plastic window didn’t ask for ID after he saw Rafe. That told me more than I wanted.

In the room, the bedspread was floral in a way that felt punitive. The air conditioner dripped into a bucket. The TV had been mounted crooked and left to live with itself. Rafe locked the door, drew the curtains, and put my box of documents on the small table under the mirror.

Then he took off his coat and rolled up one shirtsleeve. The cuff had a dark stain.

“You’re bleeding,” I said.

He looked down as if this were mildly interesting. “Occupational hazard.”

“From what?”

“One of your new friends had a key in his fist.” He crossed to the bathroom and came back with a washcloth gone pink at one edge. “You should sit down before your next heroic impulse.”

I stayed standing.

He sighed. “Fine. Bleed with dignity.”

I watched him wrap his forearm with the kind of competence that comes from either practice or habit, neither of them comforting. Up close in motel light he looked less expensive and more tired. His shirt was damp through at the shoulders. There was a faint bruise darkening along one side of his throat where the security man had pinned him. His hair, careful this morning, had given up.

“You knew they’d come for the unit,” I said.

“I knew it was likely.”

“You sent me there anyway.”

He finished tying the cloth one-handed. “I sent you there because you were going regardless, and because I preferred you know what she’d found before someone set fire to the whole floor.”

“She was talking to you.”

“Yes.”

“About what?”

“Exactly what you saw. Inspections, shell companies, men who bill violence as civic improvement.”

“And you helped her?”

“Intermittently.”

“Which means?”

“It means I answered a question once, then another one, then regretted being useful to a woman with no instinct for self-preservation.”

I let that sit a second. “That sounds like admiration.”

“That sounds like a problem.”

Rain needled the window. Down on the street, a siren passed and then another. The motel room had that peculiar stale stillness of places used for sleeping and lying in roughly equal measure.

I opened the banker’s box and laid out what mattered: the permit amendments, corporate filings, the photo of Coyle with Caldwell and Rafe, the handwritten timeline, one burner phone. I put the photo in the center.

“Explain this.”

Rafe glanced at it, then at me. “I won’t insult you by pretending it isn’t me.”

“That’s generous.”

“Isn’t it.”

“Why were you with Coyle?”

He sat on the edge of the ugly chair and leaned forward, elbows on knees, hands hanging loose. It was the first posture I’d seen from him that looked like effort instead of style.

“Because Coyle uses men like me,” he said. “Because men like me get used if we’re too useful to replace and too compromised to sanctify. Because the city runs on private arrangements with polished shoes.” He lifted one shoulder. “Pick your favorite.”

“I’m in no mood for philosophy.”

“You think that’s philosophy?” His mouth bent. “That’s bookkeeping.”

I held up the burner. “Ana says you know who everybody really works for.”

“She overestimated me.”

“She overestimated nobody. That’s why she’s missing.”

That landed. He looked away first.

“She came to me six weeks ago,” he said. “Not because she trusted me. Because she knew I’d recognize certain names buried in donor paperwork and security contracts. She had enough to be dangerous and not enough to survive being right. I told her to stop. She called me a coward with tailoring.”

“That all?”

“I gave her two names and one address.”

“Out of kindness?”

He laughed once, without humor. “Out of vanity, probably. I liked that she hated me accurately.”

I thought of Ana’s voice memo: **Fixer. Not payroll exactly.** Thought of the photo. Thought of him appearing outside the Lantern at exactly the right time to warn me off and leave me a clue. Too helpful to trust, too compromised to dismiss.

“Did you sell her out?”

“No.”

“You hesitate like a guilty man.”

“I hesitate like a man deciding how much truth you can tolerate without becoming theatrical.”

I took one step toward him. “Try me.”

For a moment I thought he’d deflect again. Instead he said, flatly, “I told her where not to go. She went anyway. Then Coyle’s people started asking about a tenant organizer with a storage unit and a martyr complex. I realized my advice had become traceable. Does that answer your question, or would you like me on my knees for the full effect?”

There it was—shame, but sharpened into cruelty before anyone else could touch it.

I should have hit him. Instead I said, “You think making it ugly first saves you trouble.”

“No,” he said. “I think it saves time.”

We looked at each other across the table, the photo between us like evidence at confession.

Finally I sat down on the bed because my left knee had started throbbing and because staying upright had become more about pride than strategy.

“I left the police over a fire case,” I said.

His eyes shifted to me, alert but unreadable.

“Not immediately,” I added. “That’d be the version I’d tell if I wanted to sound decent. I left after. After reports got changed. After people started using words like unforeseeable and procedural oversight. After a kid died in a place everybody had ignored on purpose.” I rubbed a hand over my mouth. “So if you’re waiting for me to be shocked by how the city works, don’t.”

Rafe was quiet long enough that I regretted speaking.

Then he said, “I’m not shocked by your guilt either.”

“Good.”

“I didn’t say I was bored by it.”

That almost made me smile. Almost.

He stood, crossed to the room’s little sink, and came back with two wrapped plastic cups. He filled them from the tap, tasted his, made a face, and drank anyway.

“You cannot go to the police with this,” he said.

“I know.”

“You cannot sit on it either. If Ana’s still moving, they’ll smoke her out by nightfall.”

“You think she’s alive.”

“I think if she were dead, someone would have arranged for the body to make a point.”

A hard thing to say. A useful one.

I looked back at the timeline. There were three locations circled in Ana’s hand. One I knew. One was crossed out. The third was an old mutual aid office above a bodega on Leland, shuttered after an electrical fire last winter.

“Leland,” I said.

Rafe nodded once. “That’s where I’d put a woman who thinks hiding counts more if it smells like mildew and principle.”

I stood. “Then we go.”

He didn’t move right away. “Mercer.”

“What.”

He held my gaze for a beat too long. “If we find her, let her decide whether she wants to throw the first punch. I’ve earned it more directly.”

“Generous.”

“I’m trying something new.”

At the door, as I reached for my coat, his hand closed around my wrist. Not hard. Warmer than it had any business being.

I turned.

For one stupid second it looked like one of us might kiss the other just to shut him up.

Instead Rafe let go and said, “If anyone asks, you’ve been making worse choices than me for years.”

“Don’t flatter yourself,” I said.

But my pulse was not where I’d left it when we walked into the room.
step_outputs.10:
The old mutual aid office above the bodega on Leland had once been a legal clinic, then a food pantry, then three things at once depending on who had keys and whether the church next door was feuding with the landlord that month. Now the downstairs awning still advertised **CHECK CASHING / MONEY TRANSFER / COLD BEER**, but the second-floor windows were papered over from the inside and the fire escape had been chained halfway up in a gesture of civic concern.

Rafe parked two blocks away in a car I didn’t ask about.

“You steal this?” I said as we got out.

He locked it with a small chirp. “Borrowed. The owner’s a cousin in the cultural sense.”

“Comforting.”

“I thought so.”

Leland in daylight looked like a place people still used because they hadn’t yet been priced out of memory. Beauty supply store with bars on the windows. Botanica with saints fading in blue paint. Bakery smell under cut metal and bus exhaust. One building newly skinned in pale luxury brick, like a dental implant in a bad mouth.

The bodega owner downstairs didn’t know me and knew Rafe too well, which made me dislike them both on instinct.

“She upstairs?” Rafe asked.

The owner, a man in his sixties with a Yankees cap and one milky eye, kept stacking plantain chips. “Depends who’s asking.”

“That line worked on me yesterday,” I said.

He ignored me. “She’s not upstairs,” he told Rafe. “She was. She left at six. Said if the ex-cop came, he should try the church basement on Garrison.”

“She says why?” I asked.

Now he looked at me, not kindly. “She said if you wanted trust, you should’ve picked a less stupid career.”

Rafe’s mouth moved at the edge. I gave him a look that made him stop.

On Garrison, the church basement smelled like wet coats, old coffee, and bleach trying to convince everyone this was still a clean world. Folding chairs stacked against one wall. Hand-painted posters in English and Spanish curling at the corners. A box of donated canned goods under a table no one had moved since the Clinton administration. Someone had once tried to make the room cheerful with yellow paint and lost nerve halfway through.

Ana Valez was standing at the far end in a red knit cap and a green rain jacket, arguing quietly with a woman old enough to dismiss both me and Rafe on sight. When Ana saw us, she did not look relieved. She looked offended by inevitability.

“Absolutely not,” she said.

“That’s twice this week,” I said. “I’m starting to think people don’t like me.”

“They don’t.” Her eyes slid to Rafe. “And you. Great. Exactly the two men I would not call in a flood.”

“Good to see you too,” Rafe said.

The older woman took one look at all three of us and left with a muttered prayer or curse. In that room they were often the same thing.

Ana folded her arms. Up close she was smaller than the photo suggested and harder in the face, all concentration and sleepless energy. She had ink on the side of one hand and a split thumbnail taped over. Her tote bag sat on the table behind her, overstuffed enough to count as a weapon.

“You found the storage unit,” she said.

“You left enough breadcrumbs to franchise a bakery,” I said.

“I left insurance.” Her gaze sharpened. “Marta hired you.”

“She did.”

“And he found you,” she said to Rafe, not pleased.

“Apparently I’m slipping,” he said.

Ana pinched the bridge of her nose, then dropped her hand. “Okay. Fine. We’re all here. That’s unfortunate but usable.” She pointed at me. “You don’t get to take this to the cops.”

“I know.”

“You don’t get to grandstand to a reporter who’ll write one elegant feature and go home.”

“Also know.”

She pointed at Rafe. “You don’t get to talk like regret is a moral position.”

“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

That earned him a bare half-second of contemptuous amusement. It was the warmest she’d looked.

On the table she spread out maps, copies, a thumb drive, and a packet of insurance records so heavily marked they looked like she’d been trying to stab them through paper. This was Ana in her native habitat—not inspiring, not saintly, just ferociously competent.

“It’s not just the fires,” she said. “The fires are the blunt instrument. The real machine is code enforcement, insurance pressure, emergency orders, and shell buyers. They create conditions where tenants either take insult money or get pushed out by fear. Then if a building still won’t clear...” She tapped one report. “Something accidental happens.”

“Mariner?” I asked.

“Mariner, Harbor House, the old clinic on Voss. Three others I can’t prove all the way yet.” She looked at me. “Your friends in Fire Investigations amend reports after the fact. Caldwell signs. Coyle’s office leans on inspections and permitting. Shoreline’s cleanup contractors and private security move in before anyone can get a lawyer.”

“And the final act?” Rafe said quietly.

Ana looked at him for a moment, then reached into her tote and pulled out a glossy brochure for a future luxury development. Renderings, rooftop garden, happy women with impossible dogs. Across one page she had circled a low brick building near the water.

“The Seafarer Records Annex,” she said. “Public archives on paper. Tenant ledgers, land transfer documents, old lease records. Basement still has municipal overflow nobody digitized because the city only believes in history once it can charge admission.”

I knew the place. Everybody in the district did. A damp little records building no one loved until someone threatened it.

“Why burn that?” I asked.

“Because half the ownership trail for the waterfront runs through paper older than digital indexing and sloppier than modern fraud,” Ana said. “You torch the basement during a ‘wiring failure,’ then grief does the rest. No records, no delays, no tenants proving what used to belong to whom.”

“When?” Rafe asked.

“Tonight or tomorrow. They moved up one inspection already.” She looked at him sharply. “You know that, don’t you?”

He didn’t answer fast enough.

Ana laughed once without pleasure. “Of course you do.”

“I know Coyle’s impatient,” he said. “I know he’s had calls with Shoreline’s board and a contractor they use when they want plausible deniability with accelerants. I don’t know the exact hour.”

“You always know enough to survive,” Ana said. “That’s your whole thing.”

The room went still around that. It wasn’t just accusation. It was familiarity with his type, maybe with him. He let it land. That told me more than any defense would have.

I asked, “Why not go public now?”

Ana turned to me. “Because public with the wrong timing gets tenants hurt and evidence buried. Because if they know exactly what I have before copies are in enough hands, they pivot. Because fear is administrative and so is damage control.” She slid the thumb drive toward me. “This is one dump. The rest is split.”

“Where?”

She smiled without humor. “You don’t trust me. Why would I trust your filing system?”

Rafe, unexpectedly, laughed softly. Ana looked disgusted to have entertained him.

Then, because human beings are obscene that way, the tension broke not with revelation but with hunger. Ana’s stomach growled loud enough to bounce off cinderblock. She glared at it as though betrayed.

I dug two crushed peanut packs out of my coat pocket and put them on the table. Rafe produced, from nowhere I could see, a sleeve of crackers. Ana stared at us both.

“This is the worst team-up in the city,” she said.

“Probably,” I said.

She ate the crackers anyway.

For ten minutes we worked like people who had no business sharing a room and less business wanting to keep each other alive. We built a plan in fragments: copies to a journalist Ana trusted only marginally, one packet to a legal aid attorney, one to a tenant network off-site. I wrote names and times. Rafe made two calls from a number he snapped in half after using. Ana corrected both of us whenever ego got in the way of logistics.

At some point the rain eased. The quiet that followed felt temporary.

When the plan was set, Ana slung her tote back over her shoulder. “I’m moving,” she said. “You two go nowhere together obvious. The annex gets watched before dark.”

“You shouldn’t be alone,” I said.

She gave me a look. “I’m least safe with men currently under active consideration for betrayal.”

That was fair enough to sting.

At the church door she paused, looked back at us, and said, “If one of you screws this up because you’re in love with your own damage, I’ll come back and haunt only the stupid one.”

She left before I could ask which one that was.

Rafe watched the door swing shut. “I’m almost afraid to guess.”

“Don’t strain yourself.”

We stood there in the stale church-basement quiet, no Ana to absorb the room’s voltage. Rafe was the first to look away. His hand came to the bruise at his throat, then dropped.

“You hungry?” he asked.

It was such an ordinary question I almost laughed.

We ended up eating terrible soup from paper cups in a back pew upstairs while rain guttered against stained glass. He sat one pew ahead of me, sideways, jacket off, sleeves rolled. The church was empty except for us and a saint with a chipped face.

“You could still walk,” I said.

“So could you.”

“Not what I meant.”

“I know.” He looked down into the soup like it had failed him personally. “No, Eli. I could still disappear. Walking is for men with fewer records.”

That was as close to honesty as he’d come all day.

I set my cup down. “Why didn’t you?”

He turned then, one arm draped over the pew back. “Because once in a while,” he said, “someone asks me a question like they expect an answer worth hearing.”

I didn’t move. Neither did he.

The church made our breathing sound borrowed.

When I kissed him it was not graceful. Too sudden, too much anger still in it, my hand in his damp collar, his mouth opening in surprise a split second before he kissed me back hard enough to make the pew creak. It lasted longer than it should have and ended worse than it began—both of us pulling away as if the other had started a fire.

Rafe’s forehead touched mine once, briefly.

“This,” he said, voice low and wrecked around the edges, “is an exceptionally bad idea.”

“Yeah,” I said.

Then his phone buzzed in his coat on the pew beside us, and the look on his face when he checked it took every trace of warmth out of the room.

“What?” I asked.

He stood.

“We’ve been found,” he said.
step_outputs.11:
“We’ve been found” is the kind of line that sounds melodramatic until you hear it in an empty church from a man who isn’t prone to wasting syllables.

I stood too fast and sloshed cold soup down my wrist. “Who?”

Rafe was already pulling his coat on. “Depends how poetic you’re feeling. Practically? Private security with city cooperation.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

From downstairs came the bang of the church basement door opening and a woman’s startled voice cutting off mid-sentence. Then men. Not shouting yet. Controlled. Men who expected the room to belong to them in thirty seconds.

Rafe moved into the aisle and looked up toward the side transept windows. “Back sacristy,” he said. “There’s usually a service exit.”

“You know a lot about churches for a sinner.”

“My mother enjoyed guilt architecture.”

We went fast. Through a side door, past a rack of moth-eaten vestments and a folding table stacked with funeral programs. The service exit was there, chained from the outside.

Rafe swore in Spanish, softly and beautifully.

The voices from the nave were getting closer. I could hear the sound of shoes on old tile, the cough of a cheap radio. I shoved the crash bar anyway. Useless.

“Windows?” I said.

“Leaded glass and bad odds.”

A flashlight beam swept under the sacristy door.

“Mercer,” someone called. “Open up.”

I knew that voice. Officer Denny Walsh, six years on patrol when I left, the kind of man who treated every encounter like paperwork inconveniencing his lunch. He’d gotten broader since then and no wiser.

“You’ve improved your timing, Denny,” I said.

“Don’t do this.”

“Strong opening.”

Rafe’s hand was in his coat. When it came out, he had a slim lock knife and the kind of expression men wear when they’ve accepted bad options and started ranking them for speed. He crouched by the chain outside the crash bar and worked the blade through the gap.

“That won’t hold long,” I murmured.

“Then be inspiring.”

The door latch hit once. Hard. Then again.

“Mercer,” Walsh said, louder now. “You’re in possession of stolen city documents and material evidence in an active investigation. You come out now, maybe I can help.”

I laughed before I meant to. “You were never that ambitious.”

Rafe’s knife slipped. He muttered something obscene, adjusted, and sawed harder. The chain shifted with a metal whine.

Then came a second voice from beyond the door, one I didn’t know but recognized on sight anyway—the polished tone of a private man paid to stand near public violence.

“You’re done, Mr. Mercer. Open the door.”

Rafe looked up at me. “Window.”

I understood in pieces. The sacristy window was small and high, old latch half-painted shut. I dragged over a wooden chair, climbed, shouldered the pane. It cracked but held. Behind me the door frame splintered.

I hit the glass with the chair leg. This time it gave, showering cold fragments over my coat. The opening was mean and narrow, but men have escaped worse things through less dignity.

“Go,” Rafe said.

“I’m not—”

The chain dropped from the crash bar.

Too late for argument. I shoved the box of documents through the window, then the hard drive from inside my coat. As I started to climb, the sacristy door burst inward and Walsh came through with two uniforms and one private security bastard in a dark jacket.

There are moments in life where your body decides before your principles do. Mine decided to turn, not jump.

The private guard moved for Rafe first. Rafe stepped aside and hit him once in the throat with the heel of his hand, then took Walsh’s baton strike across the shoulder because there were too many bodies and not enough room. I swung the broken chair leg into the nearest uniform’s wrist. He yelped, more offended than injured.

Then Walsh drove me into the wall hard enough to bounce my head against a shelf of hymnals. Light flashed white and stupid behind my eyes.

“Jesus, Mercer,” he hissed in my ear. “You always did know how to pick losers.”

I kneed him badly and got one arm free. It would not have ended well. It didn’t need to.

Because over Walsh’s shoulder I saw Rafe stop fighting.

Not lose. Stop.

He put both hands up slightly, just enough to signal terms.

“Enough,” he said, breathless but composed. To the private guard, not to me. “You want the files, not a church full of blood. I can get you Mercer’s copies.”

I went still in the middle of the struggle. Walsh didn’t. He slammed me facedown onto the table, twisted my arm up my back, and cuffed me with cheap satisfaction.

“You son of a bitch,” I said, not to Walsh.

Rafe did not look at me immediately. He was holding one sleeve over the cut on his forearm now, blood spotting through fresh. When he finally turned, his face had gone back into its polished blankness, every human fracture neatly filed away.

“Take him,” he told the guard.

The room rang. Partly from my head, partly from something else.

“Eli,” he said then, and using my first name made it worse, not better. “Don’t be dramatic. It doesn’t suit you.”

That was the last thing he said to me before Walsh marched me through the church basement, past two overturned folding chairs and a volunteer with both hands over her mouth.

By the time we hit the sidewalk, the rain had started again.

At the precinct they booked me for possession of stolen municipal records, obstruction, and a handgun found in the trunk of my car that had definitely not been there yesterday. The desk sergeant kept his eyes on the forms while he lied. That was almost respectful.

They put me in an interview room for an hour and a half before anybody came in. No lawyer because nobody had officially decided whether this was theater or leverage yet. The fluorescent light hummed like a petty grudge. My head ached where it had hit the hymnal shelf. My right wrist had gone numb under the cuffs.

Walsh came first with coffee and a face I might have remembered fondly if I’d suffered a stroke.

“Bad week,” he said.

“Bad haircut.”

He sat opposite me. “You don’t have to make this ugly.”

I looked at him. “Denny, ugly was when you all started doing donor protection with squad cars.”

He smiled with just one side of his mouth. “Still talk too much.”

“What do they want?”

He didn’t answer directly. That’s how you know someone finally made lieutenant in his imagination.

“Coyle’s office is very concerned about documents circulating that could create public confusion.”

“Public confusion,” I repeated. “That what arson is this week?”

His gaze flicked to the observation mirror and back. “Tell me where the copies are.”

“I don’t know.”

That was almost true. Ana had split things. I had what I had. The rest was moving by now if she’d had any luck.

Walsh sipped his coffee. “Your friend Navarro’s being helpful.”

I stared at him.

“Funny thing,” he said. “Man like that, I always figure he’ll save his own skin first.”

He wanted a reaction. He got none I’d admit to.

After he left, they kept me another two hours. No beating, nothing dramatic. Just enough waiting to make time feel handled by someone else. Then the cuffs came off, and a different officer I’d never met handed me a release form with visible irritation.

“Charges pending,” he said. “Don’t leave the city.”

Outside, dusk had started dropping over the precinct in dirty blue sheets. My phone, wallet, and keys came back in a plastic tray. The hard drive was gone. So was the envelope marked **IF I PANIC / IF I DISAPPEAR**.

At the bottom of the tray sat one thing that hadn’t been there when they booked me: a folded napkin from the Blue Lantern diner.

Inside, in Rafe’s sharp, slanted hand, were six words and an address.

**Annex tonight. Midnight. Don’t be late.**

No apology. No explanation. Just the location of the Seafarer Records Annex and the kind of instruction that could mean trap, warning, or both.

I stood under the precinct awning while rain misted the street and read it three times.

Then I laughed once, because humiliation and hope can look a lot alike from far enough away.

Whatever Rafe had done in that church, it had cost him something. Maybe me. Maybe only the luxury of being despised cleanly.

Across the street, a local news van rolled past toward the waterfront.

Midnight, then. At least the city still knew how to keep time.
step_outputs.12:
By eleven-thirty the waterfront had that deadened feeling cities get when they’ve decided to let something happen.

The Seafarer Records Annex sat three streets off the harbor behind temporary fencing and a banner promising **PUBLIC ACCESS IMPROVEMENTS COMING SOON**. The building itself was a squat brick box with narrow windows, municipal ugly in the way old records buildings often are—built to last, then neglected because lasting isn’t profitable. A security floodlight had been set up near the side entrance, washing the wet pavement in pale glare. Beyond it, harbor fog moved low between the piers, softening cranes and chain-link and making every shadow look rented.

I came on foot from the north side, cutting behind a shuttered bait shop and an empty lot where someone had spray-painted **NOT YOUR VISION BOARD** across the plywood. My head still hurt. My shoulder had tightened up in the cold. I had no gun, no backup, and one folding knife in my boot I’d probably only use badly. Which was to say I was optimally prepared.

Ana had not answered either of the two numbers she’d given me. That worried me. So did the fact I was there at all.

There were three vehicles near the annex: one city SUV, one black sedan I recognized too late from the storage lot, and a white contractor van with no markings. Men in dark rain jackets moved between them carrying metal cases and rolled sheeting. Not movers. Cleaners.

At the side entrance, under a jut of concrete that pretended to be weather protection, stood Simon Coyle in a dark overcoat with no umbrella and the expression of a man personally inconvenienced by moisture. Beside him, Lieutenant Caldwell from Fire Investigations, thick through the middle now and holding a clipboard like it was a moral principle. And a step behind them, coat collar up, one hand in his pocket, Rafe.

Even from across the lot I could read the set of him. Too still. Too polished. The look of a man balancing on something narrow.

I stayed in the dark and took photos until my phone buzzed against my palm. Unknown number.

I answered without speaking.

“She’s clear,” Ana said. Wind shredded her voice. “Tell me you’re not already in line of sight.”

“Depends who’s sighting.”

A breath that might have been a curse. “Journalist has the first packet. Legal aid has the second. Tenant network’s sitting on the third till they see smoke or news. You do not get noble on me now.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

“Good. There’s accelerant in the contractor van. They’re not just burning records. Basement stacks go up, they’ll call it electrical because Caldwell already signed the pre-failure inspection.” A pause. “Rafe there?”

I looked across the lot. Rafe had shifted slightly, enough to put himself nearer the annex door and farther from the men unloading cases.

“Yeah.”

Another pause, smaller this time. “Then either he’s buying you time or selling everybody out. I hate men who make those look similar.”

“You and me both.”

“Mercer.” Her voice flattened, all business. “If you can get visual proof of Caldwell and Coyle on site before ignition, do it. If you can’t, live.”

The line died.

I moved along the fence until I found a cut panel folded inward behind a stack of wet plywood. Somebody had made himself a service entrance. I slipped through and kept low along the annex wall, boots soundless in the soaked gravel. Through a basement window I could see rows of shelving and two men laying a line of something along the floor that caught the light too oily. One of them laughed.

A hand closed around my collar and yanked me backward into the shadow of the loading alcove before I could make the worst move available.

I elbowed on instinct. Rafe caught the blow on his forearm and hissed.

“Still charming,” he muttered.

I shoved him off and hit the wall hard enough to jar my teeth. “You left me in cuffs.”

“Yes.”

“Good explanation.”

“Working on one.”

We stood inches apart in the cold dark. Up close he looked terrible. Not dramatic terrible—human terrible. Bruise deep at his throat, shirt collar frayed, fatigue graining his skin under the floodlight spill. Rain had darkened his hair at the temples. There was ash already on one sleeve.

“You gave me the address,” I said.

“I know.”

“That doesn’t balance the church.”

“No,” he said. “It doesn’t.”

A shout came from the far side of the lot. Caldwell asking for the timing. Coyle saying, “Do it clean.”

Rafe looked toward the sound, then back at me. “I told them you’d hidden one copy in your office and handed the rest to a tenant who panicked and ran. Bought a few hours. Not enough.” His mouth tightened. “When Walsh put you in cuffs, if I objected, we both stayed in that room and Ana lost tonight.”

“You could’ve said something.”

“I’m saying it now.”

It was not enough. It was also all there was.

“What’s the move?” I asked.

“Basement first. They’ve wired the stacks and the electrical panel. Once ignition starts, Caldwell signs failure, city seals the site, contractors ‘stabilize,’ and half the paper trail disappears by dawn.” He reached into his coat and handed me a phone. “Video’s already running. Get Coyle on it if you can. Better if he says something stupid. He enjoys hearing himself.”

I took the phone because my anger had no better use.

“What about you?”

Rafe gave me a look almost amused. “I’m going to continue making regrettable life choices.”

Then he stepped out into the floodlight before I could stop him.

“Simon,” he called.

Coyle turned, irritated first, then attentive. “What now?”

Rafe walked toward him with the easy, unhurried confidence of a man carrying ordinary news. I stayed in shadow at the alcove edge, phone aimed through the gap. My pulse had become a separate weather system.

“We have a problem,” Rafe said. “Mercer’s out. The first packet hit a journalist.”

Coyle went very still. “Who?”

“I’m narrowing it down.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

Caldwell swore under his breath. One of the contractor men started toward the van, likely for a radio.

“Relax,” Coyle said, though his voice had sharpened. “Nothing’s live yet.”

Rafe tilted his head. “No? Then what exactly are we doing with accelerant in a public records building, Simon?”

There it was. On camera. Not enough by itself, but a start.

Coyle saw the turn a second too late. “Careful.”

“With what?” Rafe asked softly. “Optics?”

Caldwell moved first, hand dropping toward the inside of his jacket, where sensible public servants always keep their panic. I stepped out and hit him low with all the bad grace I had left. The two of us went down in wet gravel, his clipboard spinning off into the dark. The contractor by the van shouted. Somebody else yelled, “Gun—”

Then everything happened at once.

Coyle lunged backward toward the annex door. Rafe caught his coat and slammed him into the concrete jamb hard enough to crack the expensive calm right off his face. Caldwell got an elbow into my ribs and half-drew his pistol before I smashed his wrist against the ground. The shot went off into the basement window. Glass exploded inward.

Inside, something caught.

A bloom of orange rolled low along the floor, sudden and hungry.

“Shit,” someone screamed.

The contractor men bolted for the side entrance, one of them dropping a metal case that burst open in tools and rags. Fire belched through the broken basement pane, sucking air. The harbor wind took one curious breath and turned the annex into intention.

“Eli!” Rafe shouted.

I had the phone still recording in one hand and Caldwell’s gun skidding away into darkness with the other. Smoke punched out through the basement window, black and immediate. Through it all Coyle was still struggling, not for life exactly, but for escape with deniability intact. I saw him wrench free of Rafe and go for the contractor van.

I ran after him on instinct and stupidity. He got the driver’s door half-open before I hit him between the shoulders. We went into the side panel together. He was stronger than he looked in a gym-funded way, all resentment and leg press. He drove an elbow back, caught my jaw, and hissed, “You have no idea what this city costs.”

“More than you,” I said, and shoved his face into the van window.

It cracked. Not enough.

Then Rafe was there, dragging me back as the annex windows burst behind us with a roar and a sheet of heat like the opening of an oven door in hell.

“Leave him,” he snapped.

Coyle stumbled free and ran coughing toward the lot, one hand over his face, looking for all the world like a man who had just discovered consequences had smoke in them.

We ran the other way.

Halfway to the fence a beam gave out inside the annex with a sound like a ship splitting. Something slammed into my back—not debris, Rafe’s body turning me down and away just before another basement window blew. We hit the ground hard. Fire rolled overhead and rain hissed against it uselessly.

When I got enough air back to think, I realized his hand was still locked around mine.

For one ridiculous second in all that smoke and sirens and heat, that was the thing my body noticed most.

Then the first fire engines hit the street and the whole night filled with red light.
step_outputs.13:
The city got to the fire in time to save the shell of the annex and late enough to lose what mattered, which felt about right.

By dawn every local outlet had the same aerial footage: black water in the harbor, steam lifting off the roof, firefighters moving through smoke like figures cut from wet paper. By eight, somebody had leaked a clip of Simon Coyle on-site, overcoat open, voice sharp with annoyance and proximity. By nine, the first article was up naming Shoreline Civic, a string of shell companies, amended fire reports, and “unanswered questions” regarding accelerated redevelopment in the waterfront district.

The journalist Ana trusted only marginally turned out to trust a headline plenty. Legal aid got their documents online before noon. Tenant organizers started posting building histories and permit irregularities faster than the city could describe them as isolated discrepancies. Caldwell was put on administrative leave by lunchtime, which in municipal language means they’d found a room where he could do less damage while they decided what parts of him to deny.

Coyle appeared on television at three, unburnt except for one angry scrape along his cheekbone, and called the footage “selectively edited,” the allegations “deeply misleading,” and the fire “a tragic consequence of long-term structural neglect.” It takes talent to stand beside a crater you ordered and blame gravity. He had talent.

There would be hearings. There would be reports. There would be three men in expensive offices arguing over whether this could be survived with a consultant and a temporary resignation. The city would go on wanting what it wanted. But for one ugly, useful day, the machine stuttered.

I watched most of it from an urgent care waiting room with an ice pack melting down my collar and a paper bracelet around my wrist.

Nothing in me was broken badly enough to require dignity. Bruised ribs, mild concussion, smoke inhalation they wanted to sound more dramatic than it was, one shoulder strained where I’d gone down under Rafe’s weight and the fire’s. They cleaned the cut on my scalp where the church shelf had kissed me and sent me out with instructions to rest as if rest were a civic option.

Rafe was three curtains down and refused, on principle or instinct, to be where I could see him for most of an hour. I knew he was there because I heard a nurse say, in the tone nurses reserve for difficult handsome men, “Sir, you still need the stitches.”

Ana texted at 4:12 a.m. and 11:47 a.m.

**Alive. Marta furious. Good.**

Then:

**If anyone says we won because of one fire and one article I will set them on fire too.**

That felt like her.

Marta came by urgent care just before noon in scrubs and rain boots, looked at me for a long time without smiling, and handed me a protein bar.

“She’s at my place,” she said. “She won’t stay.”

“Figures.”

“She says thank you in the abstract and distrust in the specific.”

“Also figures.”

Marta’s eyes flicked toward the curtain where Rafe was not being visible. “And him?”

I unwrapped the bar. “Complicated.”

She snorted softly. “You think too much like a man who still believes words should improve things.” Then, after a beat: “You found her.”

“Yeah.”

“You also got half the precinct and city hall mad enough to invent charges. So congratulations on your growth.”

I took the hit. She’d earned a few.

Before she left she squeezed my shoulder once—careful of the bruise—and said, “For what it’s worth, Ana was wrong about one thing.”

“What thing?”

Marta glanced toward the curtain again. “You’re not the stupid one. Just the slower one.”

Then she was gone, smelling faintly of hospital soap and peppermint.

By evening the rain had finally exhausted itself. The streets were still wet enough to hold the city’s reflections but not enough to wash it clean. I got my coat back from urgent care, found my wallet damp in one pocket and a folded discharge summary in the other, and stepped outside into the wan kind of post-storm light that makes everything look briefly forgivable.

Rafe was sitting on the low concrete wall by the parking lot smoking half a cigarette he didn’t seem to want.

He saw me and put it out at once, which was more intimate than apology would have been.

“Doctor say you’re unfit for melodrama?” he asked.

“Only light melodrama for forty-eight hours.”

“Tragic.”

There were stitches hidden under his hairline and a bandage peeking from under his shirt collar where the contractor’s elbow or the annex or God had gotten in a good one. He looked worse than yesterday and more himself than he had in the church.

I stood in front of him a moment without speaking.

“You left me in cuffs,” I said.

“Yes.”

There was no point pretending otherwise.

He turned the dead cigarette between his fingers. “If I’d fought it, Walsh would’ve searched you properly. He’d have found the phone, the cards, everything. Ana would’ve been spending tonight naming bodies instead of shell companies.”

“I know.”

“I still left you in cuffs.”

“Yeah.”

He nodded once, accepting that the knowledge didn’t erase the fact. Human of him, which was inconvenient.

A bus sighed at the curb out front and took nobody useful away.

“You gave me the note,” I said.

“I did.”

“Why?”

He looked out toward the street, not at me. “Because by then there were only two options left. Save myself in a way that doesn’t actually work, or stop pretending I’m the kind of man built for surviving this neatly.”

“Which are you?”

His mouth bent. “Ask me next week.”

I sat beside him on the wall because standing there accusingly had started to feel theatrical. For a while we watched traffic push dirty light through puddles. A woman in hospital scrubs argued with a parking meter. Two teenagers walked past sharing fries and not noticing us at all. Across the street, a pharmacy sign blinked **OPEN** like a threat.

“I don’t trust you,” I said finally.

“That seems healthy.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.” He rubbed at the bandage under his collar with two fingers, then stopped. “I’m not asking for trust, Eli. I’m asking whether you’re done using distrust as a place to hide.”

That was irritatingly close to the bone. I looked at him. “You rehearse these?”

“Only the ones I regret.”

I laughed then, once, because painkillers or exhaustion or simple defeat had made honesty cheaper than usual.

He looked relieved enough not to hide it quickly enough. That did something complicated to my chest.

“My office window still sticks,” I said.

He blinked. “What?”

“I’m not making declarations in an urgent care parking lot. I have standards.” I stood carefully, ribs objecting. “But my office window still sticks. The radiator sounds possessed. There’s coffee if you hate yourself, and a bottle of bourbon if you don’t.” I shoved my hands in my coat pockets. “If you want to come upstairs and be a problem where I can keep an eye on you.”

Rafe stared at me like I’d switched languages.

“That,” he said after a second, “is a terrible invitation.”

“Yeah.”

His smile this time was real and tired and not nearly as controlled as the others had been. “All right.”

We started walking toward the bus stop because my car was still evidence and his borrowed one had become someone else’s cultural problem. Halfway there he touched my wrist lightly, asking rather than taking.

I stopped.

He kissed me once, brief and careful around the bruise on my jaw, like he understood exactly how much hurt a body could carry before tenderness started to feel arrogant.

When he pulled back, he said, “For the record, I’m still mostly bad ideas.”

“Good,” I said. “I’d worry if you got optimistic.”

The bus came in a shudder of brakes and tired fluorescent light. We got on with the rest of the evening crowd—nurses, kitchen staff, one man carrying lilies nobody deserved—and took the back seats where the city looked longest through scratched glass.

Outside, the waterfront kept burning in headlines and committee statements and the private panic of men with too many donors. Inside, beside me, Rafe sat with one hand loose on his knee and his shoulder warm through both our coats.

The city was still for sale. The files were still ash. Morning would not arrive cured.

But the smoke, for once, was not the only thing between us.

chapter_raw_judge_text.1:
[Analysis]

This is a strong opening chapter that demonstrates considerable craft. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically.

**Voice and Characterization**

Eli's first-person voice is well-calibrated. The prose has the dry, observational quality the plan calls for without constantly performing. Lines like "Ideals paid badly and got blood in places hard to clean" and "She put the hospital coffee on my desk like an offering she resented making" feel earned rather than strained. The voice is specific to someone who used to be a cop and now survives in the city's margins—he notices the badge turned inward, the cost of the coat, the brand of cigarette. This is showing character through perception rather than declaration.

Marta is rendered efficiently and with real texture. The detail about Ana not leaving without telling her "who gets her cat and where she hid the rent money" is excellent—it's specific, it reveals character, and it's funny without being cute. Her line "We fight beautifully" is one of the chapter's best. She doesn't become a cliché tough sister; she has the bearing of someone who reads distress professionally and is applying that skill here.

Rafe's entrance is handled well. The plan called for the prompt line to land with weight—"He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas"—and it does. It arrives at the right moment, after enough setup that it feels like a conclusion rather than a decoration. The subsequent dialogue is appropriately evasive and charged without being melodramatic. His parting gift of the note is a nice structural move.

**Dialogue**

The dialogue is generally strong. The exchange "You're Mercer." / "Depends who's asking." / "Cute. Don't do too much with it." is sharp and establishes their dynamic efficiently. Marta's dialogue is particularly good—she speaks with the economy of someone who doesn't have time for performance. The bartender's description of Rafe ("Handsome in a way that made me tired") is a standout line that does double duty: characterizes Rafe and characterizes the bartender as someone who's seen too many men like him.

One weakness: "Depends who's asking" appears twice in the chapter—once with Marta and once with Rafe. This is either a deliberate character tic (Eli's default deflection) or an oversight. If deliberate, it's too subtle to read clearly as intentional mirroring; if accidental, it's a notable repetition in a short chapter.

**Plot and Structure**

The chapter follows its plan faithfully. We get Eli's world established, Marta's hiring, the case setup, the bar visit, Rafe's introduction, and the clue (Mariner Warehouse). The pacing is good—the chapter moves without rushing. The matchbook as a connector to the bar is a clean noir device. The blurred photo Marta shows Eli is nicely handled: "You could build a whole mistake around a silhouette like that" is one of the chapter's better lines.

The ending with the dropped note is slightly convenient—a fixer of Rafe's caliber leaving a paper trail feels a bit too tidy for the character as described. It's a functional plot device but slightly undermines Rafe's established competence. The plan called for "a note, key, or recorded message" from Ana, but what we get is Rafe leaving a clue, which is a different thing. This is a minor deviation but worth noting.

**Metaphor and Prose Quality**

Most of the metaphorical work lands. "Fear had a housekeeping quality in some people. They started labeling jars and making lists" is precise and original. "The jukebox humming something old enough to remember cigarettes indoors" is evocative without being overwrought. The radiator that "hissed like it had opinions" is a small, good touch.

A few moments strain slightly. "The alley hold the shape he'd left in it" is reaching—alleys don't hold shapes, and the image is more atmospheric gesture than concrete observation. "Wet at the edges" for the shoes is good; the overall description of Rafe's entrance is controlled.

The prose avoids purple excess. It's stylized but disciplined. The chapter doesn't mistake every sentence for an opportunity to perform.

**Consistency with Profiles**

Eli matches his profile closely: the cop habits (checking exits, reading shoes and cologne), the dry humor, the vulnerability to self-possessed men, the residual shame about his past. Marta is exactly as described—practical, unimpressed, specific. Rafe's entrance matches his profile: socially exact, using stillness as power, the expensive-but-not-flashy coat, the sparing cologne. The "amused before he's earned it" quality of his mouth is captured.

**Weaknesses**

The chapter's main weakness is that it's doing what good noir does competently rather than doing something unexpected with the form. The beats are well-executed but recognizable: the client who doesn't quite trust the PI, the bar with the knowing bartender, the mysterious man in the alley. The plan called for pushing away from "a merely polished genre exercise," and this chapter is, at its core, a polished genre exercise—a very good one, but not one that consistently surprises. The queer dimension is present but not yet doing much work beyond the setting.

The "Depends who's asking" repetition is a real flaw. The dropped note is slightly too convenient. These are craft-level issues, not fundamental problems.

Overall, this is a confident, well-controlled opening chapter that establishes voice, character, and plot efficiently. It's better than most genre fiction and occasionally rises to something more. It doesn't yet fully deliver on the plan's more ambitious goals, but as a first chapter, it does its job with real skill.

chapter_raw_judge_text.2:
[Analysis]

Chapter 2 of this queer neo-noir romance is a confident, well-executed piece of genre fiction that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me examine it across the relevant dimensions.

VOICE AND PROSE QUALITY

The first-person voice is consistently strong and specific. Lines like "coffee from a place that called itself artisanal and tasted like resentment" and "the expression of a woman who would rather be diagnosed with something serious than help me before lunch" are genuinely funny and character-revealing without straining. The prose is controlled and readable, mixing procedural observation with dry wit. The narrator's cop habits (checking exits, patience as survival skill) are shown through behavior rather than announced. This is the chapter's greatest strength: the voice feels inhabited rather than performed.

There are occasional moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard. "Dust. Liability. City history no one can monetize unless they knock it down first" is a good line, but it's Rafe speaking, and it works because it fits his character's mode of speech. The chapter mostly avoids the trap of making every sentence perform.

DIALOGUE

The dialogue between Eli and Rafe is the chapter's centerpiece and it largely succeeds. The exchange is evasive, flirtatious, and irritated as planned. Lines like "I didn't say that either" / "Do you want to?" and the final note "If she stored it, they know. Hurry." create genuine tension and forward momentum. The clerk's dialogue is particularly well-handled—she's a minor character who feels specific and real, with her own agenda and self-interest. The "Absolutely not" exit is a small comic gem.

The dialogue occasionally tips toward being too clever in a way that slightly undermines naturalism. Both Eli and Rafe speak in very polished, aphoristic rhythms throughout, which is consistent with the noir register but occasionally makes the exchange feel like a tennis match of witticisms rather than two people actually circling each other with real stakes. The line "Maybe I'm sentimental about women who ask impolite questions" is a touch too smooth, too ready.

PLOT AND STRUCTURE

The chapter follows its plan closely and effectively. Eli investigates the warehouse, finds Ana's evidence cache, encounters the suspicious SUV, visits city records, gets the clerk to slip information, and has the key encounter with Rafe. The pacing is good—each scene has a clear purpose and moves the investigation forward. CHARACTER: Eli Mercer is well-drawn—a former cop with a specific backstory that's revealed economically and earns its emotional weight. Rafe Navarro is the more interesting creation: morally compromised, genuinely ambiguous, and his arc from antagonist to reluctant ally to romantic interest is handled with more care than these stories usually manage. The key scene where he leaves Eli in cuffs and then explains why is the piece's best character moment—it refuses easy redemption while still making the relationship believable. Ana Valez is vivid despite limited page time; her voice in the memos and her direct confrontation scenes feel authentic. Marta is functional but thin.

THE ROMANCE: The queer element is handled naturally—there's no announcement of it, no explanation, it simply is. The kiss in the church is earned by the tension built across four chapters. The ending is appropriately restrained rather than triumphant. The "bad ideas" motif from the prompt is woven through effectively.

PLOT AND COHERENCE: The conspiracy plot is competent but somewhat generic—shell companies, corrupt officials, arson for development. This chapter is a strong piece of neo-noir writing that largely succeeds on its own terms. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically.

STRENGTHS:

The dialogue is the chapter's most impressive achievement. Lines like "I hesitate like a man deciding how much truth you can tolerate without becoming theatrical" and "I think it saves time" feel genuinely earned rather than performed. The exchange about Ana—"She called me a coward with tailoring"—is economical and characterizes both absent Ana and present Rafe simultaneously. The banter has the right texture: evasive, slightly cruel, with attraction running underneath like a current neither man wants to name. This is difficult to execute and the chapter does it well.

The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The plan called for: uneasy alliance, Rafe admitting he was sent to retrieve Ana's files while insisting he didn't want her harmed, Rafe revealing himself selectively, Eli revealing his police past without heroic monologue, an almost-kiss that ends awkwardly, and ending with a decision to find Ana. All of these are present and handled with appropriate messiness rather than clean resolution.

Character consistency is high. Eli checks exits, notices expensive shoes, peels back his own self-flattery ("Not immediately. That'd be the version I'd tell if I wanted to sound decent"), and maintains the dry observational voice established in his profile. Rafe uses humor to deflect, gets precise when cornered, and his shame-sharpened-into-cruelty moment ("Does that answer your question, or would you like me on my knees for the full effect?") is exactly the kind of self-protective cruelty his profile describes. The line "I liked that she hated me accurately" is a small gem that reveals character efficiently.

The pacing is controlled. The chapter moves from action (aftermath of shooting) to interrogation to confession to tentative alliance without feeling rushed or padded. The motel setting is appropriately unglamorous—"floral in a way that felt punitive," the dripping air conditioner, the crooked TV—without overdoing the squalor.

The emotional arc is handled with restraint. The almost-kiss is genuinely almost: "For one stupid second it looked like one of us might kiss the other just to shut him up." This is the right level of indirection. The final beat—pulse not where he left it—is understated enough to work.

WEAKNESSES:

The opening action sequence (the shooting, the escape) is competent but slightly rushed. "The second shot hit my car door with a crack that sounded expensive" is a good line, but the transition from gunfire to motel happens very quickly, and the physical danger doesn't quite register as visceral. The plan called for the attack to be "quick, ugly, and practical," which is achieved, but there's a slight sense that the chapter is eager to get to the dialogue and moves through the action perfunctorily.

Some lines strain slightly. "Blue awning. Bad pie, just as promised" references something not established in this chapter (presumably from an earlier chapter), which creates a minor coherence issue for a reader encountering this chapter in isolation. "The motel room had that peculiar stale stillness of places used for sleeping and lying in roughly equal measure" is a bit too neat—the parallel construction draws attention to itself as a constructed line rather than observed detail.

The Eli confession about the fire case is handled well but is the chapter's most "on the nose" moment. The plan specifically warned against "heroic monologue" and this isn't quite that, but it does feel slightly more expository than the surrounding material. The line "So if you're waiting for me to be shocked by how the city works, don't" is a touch defensive in a way that reads as the author managing the reader rather than Eli managing Rafe.

The ending wrist-grab is the chapter's weakest beat. "Not hard. Warmer than it had any business being" is the kind of line that works in romance but feels slightly generic here—"warmer than it had any business being" is a familiar formulation. The chapter has been doing something more specific and interesting than this phrase delivers.

The "Leland" exchange at the end moves quickly and efficiently, but Rafe's line "That's where I'd put a woman who thinks hiding counts more if it smells like mildew and principle" is slightly too clever—it's the kind of line that sounds good but doesn't quite mean anything precise.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is accomplished genre writing with genuine literary ambition that mostly pays off. The dialogue is the standout element. The characters are consistent and specific. The chapter follows its plan faithfully and advances both plot and romance arcs with appropriate messiness. The weaknesses are real but minor: occasional over-construction, one slightly generic romantic beat, and action that's functional rather than vivid. This is not a masterpiece but it's well above average work.
