# Chapter 2 – The Library Window

The west library window was a more idiotic prospect than the schoolroom’s.

Ada stood beneath the terrace wall shortly before midnight and examined it with a dislike so profound it was almost respect. The library occupied the older central block of Foxglove Court, above the stone-flagged terrace and below a line of narrow bedchambers. Its lower windows were too exposed to the south front; its upper casements looked over a jut of balustrade and a shallow leaded roof that any rational architect ought to have made inaccessible. Instead, some dead Vale with a taste for ornament had contrived exactly enough projection to tempt a desperate woman into folly.

She gathered her skirts higher, tied them off clumsily with the cord she had brought, and set one foot on the lip of a rainwater barrel left under the wall. Her shoulder still ached from the schoolroom descent. Her left palm had a shallow cut where the ivy had slipped. She was tired, underfed, and conscious in a practical way of what a broken ankle would cost. None of this altered the fact that the scrap in her glove had given her a direction, and directions were dangerous things to possess if one meant to sleep.

“Up, then,” she told herself.

The climb was uglier than the first. There was no ivy here, only decorative stone and cold iron. Twice her boot slid before finding purchase. Once she had to flatten herself absurdly against the wall while some shutter banged above her and nearly dislodged her entirely. By the time she pulled herself onto the leaded roof, she was breathing hard enough to be angry at it.

The casement stood unlatched.

Ada froze.

It was possible, of course, that country houses simply allowed their windows to drift into criminal convenience. It was also possible that she was expected.

She eased the casement inward. Warmth met her first: banked coals, leather, the dry smell of books. The west library lay in low amber light from a shaded lamp left burning on the great desk near the center of the room. Rows of shelves climbed into shadow. The curtains were half drawn. A dispatch box sat on the desk.

And Nathaniel Vale, one shoulder against the mantel, looked up from where he had evidently been waiting.

“I confess,” he said, “I had not thought you would choose the most difficult route available.”

Ada remained on the sill. “Then your imagination wants exercise.”

She was absurdly conscious of herself: hair loosened by the climb, cloak damp, hem tied up in a manner no woman raised to decency would willingly display before a stranger. His glance touched the cord at her skirts and moved away so quickly it was almost courtesy.

“You might come in,” he said.

“I might also go away.”

“Yes. You are particularly devoted to that portion of every conversation.”

She came inside because the dispatch box was there, because she had not frozen her fingers on wet stone for the pleasure of retreat, and because a house was always easier to understand from within than without. She let the casement settle behind her and untied her skirts with more impatience than grace.

Nathaniel watched, then looked at the box. “If that is what brought you, I have saved you time. It contains estate accounts, some correspondence, and a very dull argument over tenant drainage from twelve years ago.”

“You opened it.”

“It was in my library.”

“Your family’s library,” Ada said before she could stop herself.

Something sharpened in his face. “That distinction requires explanation.”

“So does lying in wait for women in upper windows, but here we are.”

He almost smiled; the expression vanished before it had fully formed. “You did not answer my question the other night.”

“No.”

“Then permit me to ask a better one. What precisely are you seeking?”

Ada crossed to the nearest shelves, more to give herself occupation than from any hope that answers hid among calf bindings. The room was not as she remembered. Smaller, somehow. Or perhaps she had once imagined it larger because as a child it had seemed forbidden, and forbidden rooms always acquired dimensions. Over the mantel hung a portrait of a pale woman she did not know. Below it, on the side table, lay a family register in tooled red leather.

She knew she should not touch it. She touched it at once.

“Miss—?” Nathaniel prompted.

Ada opened the register.

Births. Marriages. Deaths. Vale after Vale entered in a clerk’s neat hand and later in several less disciplined domestic ones. She turned pages too fast, then slower. Nathaniel had moved from the mantel but not yet close enough to prevent it. On one page a line had clearly been cut out. Not torn. Removed with a blade so fine that only the rougher edge of the paper and the disturbance in the ruling gave it away.

Ada stared.

He was beside her now. “What is it?”

She laid a finger just below the missing strip. “Someone has taken a name.”

Nathaniel’s eyes narrowed. “That could have happened at any time.”

“Yes,” she said. “That is generally the convenience of destruction.”

He looked at her, really looked this time, and she saw him trying to place not just her face but the species of her certainty. People who invent tales were often eager in the wrong places. She was not eager. She was furious.

“Who are you?” he said again, more quietly.

Ada shut the register. “A woman who is tired of hearing that memory is a form of poor breeding.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is what I have instead of one.”

He drew a breath, and when he spoke his tone had cooled. “I can call the housekeeper this instant and ask whether any woman matching your description has sought employment here before. Or I can ring for the butler and let him decide what to do with a trespasser. I have done neither. You may take that as generosity and cooperate with it, or as stupidity and misuse it. I should prefer the first.”

The words were measured; their effect was not. Ada felt the old hot flush of being managed rise from collar to cheek. He had all the weapons of his sex and station and still wanted gratitude for not deploying them fully.

“Generosity,” she repeated. “How liberal.”

His mouth tightened. “You make demands on a house not yours and speak as though aggrieved that anyone should ask your purpose.”

“Not ask. Doubt.”

“I doubt because this is absurd. You appear out of the dark, scale walls like a poacher, hint at family scandal, and expect belief as your due.”

Belief as your due. There it was. The easy male contempt, polished to reason. Ada turned from him before she said something unforgivable. Her gaze fell on the side table again, on the portrait above it, on the tiny brass label fixed to the frame. She stepped closer.

The painted woman was identified as Mrs. Adrian Vale, 1848.

Adrian Vale. Her mother had used the name Adrian only once, in fever, and afterward denied it utterly.

Ada’s throat went tight.

“You know the name,” Nathaniel said.

She should have denied it. Instead she heard herself say, “My mother did.”

Silence opened between them.

He did not move. “Your mother.”

“Yes.”

“And who was your mother?”

The room seemed suddenly too warm. Ada kept her eyes on the painted stranger’s placid face. “Marianne Wren.”

Nathaniel said nothing at first. Then, with maddening carefulness: “I have never heard the name.”

“Of course not.”

“Miss Wren—if that is your name—do you claim some connection to this family?”

The words claim and connection made her want to strike him. How quickly men made blood sound legal.

“I claim nothing from you,” she said. “Not money, not welcome, not even intelligence, though I begin to miss it. I seek papers. If they are gone, say so, and I shall save myself the climb.”

He looked at her long enough that she wondered whether he could hear the hammering of her heart. “If your object were honest,” he said at last, “you would have come by day.”

She gave a short laugh, all edge. “If your household were honest, Mr. Vale, I should not have needed windows.”

His face changed—less with offense than with some involuntary recognition that there, at least, was no rehearsed speech.

Ada moved to the casement.

“Miss Wren.”

She put one hand on the latch.

“Come tomorrow,” he said. “By the door.”

Now she did turn. “Would you admit me?”

He hesitated. It was slight, perhaps even unconscious. It was enough.

“I thought not,” she said.

She climbed onto the sill before he could answer. This time when she lowered herself to the roof, she felt the cut in her palm reopen. The pain steadied her. Behind her she heard him step quickly toward the window.

“I have not accused you,” he said.

“No,” Ada answered into the dark. “You merely arranged the room for it.”

She found the terrace edge with her foot and dropped the last dangerous stretch badly enough to jar her teeth. By the time she reached the shelter of the clipped laurel walk, she was shaking with anger more than exertion.

Marianne Wren. Adrian Vale. A cut line in the register.

Not enough. Never enough.

But Nathaniel Vale had heard the name now, and the house, which had once denied even the fact of her, could no longer pretend she had not spoken inside it.

# Chapter 3 – The South Gallery

For three days Ada did not go near Foxglove Court.

This was partly prudence and partly temper. Prudence said a house newly put on alert should be left to settle. Temper said she would not scramble over another wall to be measured, doubted, and offered civility in place of sense. She occupied herself by practical means: mending the tear in her cloak, selling a pair of silver-backed brushes that had belonged to her mother, and walking one morning as far as the churchyard to read, for the fourth time, the weather-softened Vale names on family stones.

Adrian Vale was there. Died in Italy. 1853.

No wife mentioned. No scandal engraved. Stone, like paper, kept only what it was instructed to keep.

On the fourth afternoon, she returned to her lodging in the village to find a folded note laid beneath the cracked china shepherdess on the mantel. Mrs. Biddle, her landlady, claimed ignorance in the manner of those paid to know very little. The note was brief, unsigned, and written in an economical hand she recognized at once.

If you are still intent on searching, the south gallery window is often left unsecured in warm weather. Ten o’clock. Come if you wish to be told what I have found.

No apology. No flourish. No confidence that she would come.

Ada sat with the note open in her lap until the fire shrank and the room turned violet with evening. It would be like him to expect punctuality after insult. It would be like her to refuse and lose some crucial chance out of pride. In the end she despised pride in others more than she valued it in herself.

At ten o’clock she was on the narrow lawn below the south wing, looking up at a line of tall windows set over a lower passage roof. The gallery route was easier than the library’s, though that said little. She had chosen darker clothing and left her skirts less voluminous, which improved matters at the cost of looking almost like a woman with sense. The air was softer tonight, carrying damp earth and the faint sharp sweetness of box hedges newly clipped.

The gallery casement yielded under her hand.

Inside, the long room held the afterglow of a day’s trapped light. Portraits stood rank on rank in gilt and shadow, Vales of every persuasion regarding posterity with confidence, boredom, and expensive neckcloths. The moon, riding clear now, silvered the polished floor and drew a pale line the length of the room.

Nathaniel stood near the middle, a lamp turned low on a side table. He had not dressed for effect. Dark coat, no gloves, hair insufficiently obedient at the temples as though he had run a hand through it too often. The detail irritated Ada because she noticed it at all.

“You came,” he said.

“You left a note as though summoning a tradesman. I thought I ought to hear the terms.”

To his credit, he accepted that. “I found no mention of your mother in the household books under that name.”

“No.”

“But there are omissions.” He gestured toward a table where several ledgers and an open portfolio lay. “Portrait inventories revised at least twice in ten years. A miniature listed in one hand and absent in another. Several private expenses entered to my father’s account without description.”

Ada moved nearer despite herself. “How private?”

He turned one ledger toward her and put his finger below a line of close entries. “Cash disbursed by instruction. Repeated over six months. Then again, a year later.”

She read the figures. Not large enough to signify open acknowledgment. Too regular to be charity.

“And?” she said.

“And Mr. Pritchard’s hand appears in the margin of one page.” Nathaniel looked at her, not defensively now but with an expression she did not yet trust. “You were right that something has been managed.”

It was not triumph she felt but a queer lightness under the ribs, almost nausea. So much of one’s life could be built on what others called impossible. To have impossibility shift, even a little, was physically unsettling.

“You sound surprised.”

“I am surprised,” he said. “Not by family concealment in the abstract. By the form of it.”

Ada glanced up at the portraits. “You expected vice to be more decorative.”

One corner of his mouth moved. “That was unkind.”

“Yes.”

“And not inaccurate.”

She looked back to the ledgers. “What changed your mind?”

He was quiet long enough that she wondered whether he would answer. “The register,” he said at last. “The cut line. And the fact that you were angrier than frightened.”

“That does not seem a reliable system of inquiry.”

“No,” he said. “But it is human.”

The word, in his mouth, should have sounded condescending. Instead it landed oddly between them, less as praise than admission.

Ada set both hands on the table and studied the pages. “If Pritchard touched the accounts, then any paper worth having may have passed through him first.”

“Or through Mrs. Vale.”

At that Ada looked sharply at him. “You say that easily.”

“Not easily.” His gaze had gone to a portrait at the far end of the room. “Merely more easily than before.”

Foxglove Court was full of rooms in which one was expected to understand more than was said. Ada disliked that language and spoke it fluently.

“My mother,” she said, “came here as companion to old Mrs. Vale’s sister. Before your time, I think. She never explained much. Only that she had once believed herself secure and later learned the difference between being sheltered and being protected.”

Nathaniel listened without interruption.

“She had a blue prayer book,” Ada went on, her eyes on the ledger because looking at him would make the words feel theatrical. “Inside it was written M. from A. on the day of—something. I never saw the rest. She kept it wrapped in linen and moved lodgings with it as though it were plate.”

“Where is it now?”

“Gone. Or hidden. Or sold when she grew desperate enough to believe God would forgive receipts.”

A faint sound in the corridor beyond made them both go still.

Steps.

Not near yet, but nearer than comfort allowed.

Nathaniel moved at once, not toward the door but toward the lamp, turning the wick lower. “Behind the east screen,” he said quietly.

There was no time to argue. Ada gathered her skirts and slipped behind a folding screen set between two ancestral ladies. The space smelled of varnish and stale fabric. A second later Nathaniel stepped in after her and drew the panel a fraction more closed.

The footsteps entered the gallery.

Ada could not see much through the narrow angle, only the sweep of moonlit floor and the hem of a servant’s coat moving down the room. House patrol, perhaps, sent because someone had remembered old draughts and unsecured windows. The man paused once, coughed, then moved on.

Ada became acutely aware of Nathaniel’s sleeve against hers. Not touching, exactly. Near enough that any small shift would become contact. He held himself very still, but not with the complacent stillness of a man at ease. This was effort. She could hear his breathing, kept deliberately quiet. The absurdity of hiding behind portraits in his own house might have amused her in other circumstances. As it was, she found herself noticing that he smelled faintly of starch, lamp smoke, and the colder night air he must have crossed to reach the gallery before her.

The servant’s steps receded.

Neither of them moved at once.

Then Nathaniel said, low enough that the words brushed rather than carried, “There is a locked cabinet in Mrs. Vale’s morning room.”

Ada turned her head. In the dimness behind the screen his face was nearer than she had expected, all the lines reserve usually flattened made suddenly sharper by shadow.

“How do you know?”

“I saw Pritchard there yesterday afternoon. He had no business in that room.” A pause. “I also asked, indirectly, whether any old family papers were kept elsewhere. Mrs. Vale answered too quickly.”

Ada might have laughed if she had not been so conscious of his breath. “And now you propose burglary.”

“I propose inquiry.”

“From the roof?”

His mouth altered again, almost despite him. “I begin to understand your preference for upper windows.”

“That would be a first.”

He drew back then, the moment breaking not because it had resolved but because both had recognized it. Nathaniel stepped out from behind the screen and offered her space to follow.

Ada did so more slowly than she ought.

At the far end of the gallery a portrait label glinted in the moonlight where one screw had been recently disturbed. Nathaniel saw her see it.

“Another omission?” he asked.

“Or a rearrangement.” Ada crossed to it and touched the empty mark beneath a woman’s painted hand. “Your house is forever tidying itself.”

He looked at her for a long moment. “Then let us stop it.”

Not *I*. Not yet. But *let us* was nearer than she had expected him capable of coming.

Outside, the night pressed dark and mild against the window through which she had entered. Ada knew she should leave at once. She also knew, with the uncomfortable certainty of a shifting world, that she would come back.

# Chapter 4 – The Morning Room Roof

It was one thing to climb into a house alone.

It was another to do it while the master of that house stood below on the terrace in shirtsleeves, looking up with the expression of a man who had agreed to an operation and only now seen the knife.

Ada, crouched on the low balustrade above him, could not help herself. “You may still retreat,” she whispered down. “No one has yet forced you into crime.”

Nathaniel glanced toward the dark run of windows behind the clipped yews. “You are very free with that word for someone halfway across my mother’s—my stepmother’s—roof.”

“Only because ‘inquiry’ does not improve the footing.”

The plan, if such a thing deserved the dignity of the term, had been hers. Mrs. Vale’s morning room lay on the east side, accessible by a narrow lead roof above the conservatory and a small upper casement often opened in warm weather to release heat from the glasshouse below. Going through the corridor would mean passing under too many lamps and too many eyes. Going over the conservatory meant trusting Victorian ironwork and Providence.

Neither had yet failed her entirely.

The night was close and damp, the sky low with cloud that reflected the house’s own faint light. Beneath the glass roof of the conservatory, moon-pale leaves pressed against the panes. Ada had tied up her skirts again and borrowed from necessity the old sensation of moving in a body made mostly of angles and intent. Nathaniel had come out without his coat, perhaps from haste, perhaps because coats were impediments where walls were concerned. His sleeves were rolled once above the wrist, exposing the pale line of an old scar.

She noticed too much about him lately. It was becoming inconvenient.

“Step where I step,” she said. “Not where it appears reasonable.”

“That is an ominous instruction.”

“It is an accurate one.”

She crossed the first stretch of lead with care, testing each join with the side of her foot. The conservatory roof dipped almost imperceptibly toward the guttering. Water had left the metal slick. Behind her, Nathaniel followed with the controlled caution of someone who hated this but refused to perform the hatred aloud. Ada reached the stone lip beneath the morning room casement and put out a hand for balance. His hand closed around her forearm at once.

Not graceful. Not romantic. Simply immediate.

“Loose seam,” he murmured, indicating with his chin the edge of the lead near her boot.

She looked down. A narrow split showed black beneath.

“Well,” she said, after a beat, “you are teachable.”

He let go, though not before she had felt the warmth of his palm through the damp wool of her sleeve. “You may note it in your ledger.”

The casement was shut but not latched. Ada eased it upward inch by inch. The hinges gave a tiny whine that sounded to her as loud as a shriek. They both froze. No one came.

Inside, Mrs. Vale’s morning room was all arranged mildness: pale walls, a writing table, a sofa with its cushions not merely plumped but aligned, little tables set precisely where a woman of taste might let a book fall from her hand and expect it to be found there again. Everything smelled faintly of lavender and coal smoke. The room looked as though no human discomfort had ever been admitted into it.

Ada swung herself in and turned to help Nathaniel, who required none but accepted the steadiness of her hand anyway. Once inside, he closed the casement softly behind them.

“You are smiling,” he said under his breath.

“I was reflecting that this must be dreadful for you.”

“It is.”

“Good.”

That brought the nearest thing to a laugh she had heard from him, quickly suppressed.

The cabinet stood against the inner wall, walnut with brass escutcheons and doors paneled in dark burr. It was locked, naturally. Ada had expected no less. She knelt at once before it, taking out her knife and the slender strip of tempered wire she had once persuaded a tinsmith’s son to shape for a purpose he had not asked to know.

Nathaniel looked down at the implements. “Should I inquire how—”

“No.”

“I thought not.”

He moved instead to the writing table, opening drawers with methodical care. Ada listened to wood and metal, to his measured handling of papers, to the soft tick of a little gilt clock on the mantel. Her own breathing seemed too loud. The lock resisted. Mrs. Vale, who likely had no illusions about the world’s benevolence, had chosen good brass.

“Tell me,” Nathaniel said quietly from the desk, “did you truly climb here before deciding the route was possible, or did you simply resent the wall until it yielded?”

Ada felt the edge of a smile despite herself. “Do not distract me.”

“I ask for practical reasons. If I am to continue assisting, I should like to know whether lunacy is method with you or merely atmosphere.”

She worked the wire, listening for the tiny shift in tumblers. “My first attempt was on a rectory pear tree when I was twelve. I fell. The second was at a lodging-house attic because the landlady locked us in after eleven. The third—”

The lock clicked.

Ada looked up. “—was successful.”

Nathaniel had found something too. He held up a folded paper browned along one edge as if snatched from fire. “Pritchard’s hand,” he said.

She crossed quickly to him. The note was brief and infuriatingly oblique.

Certain informal papers should not remain among the household effects. Quiet disposition recommended. The family’s interests are best served by discretion.

No names. No dates beyond a smudged year. Enough to suggest. Not enough to settle.

“Coward,” Ada muttered.

Nathaniel’s brow rose. “Pritchard?”

“Everyone.”

She turned back to the cabinet and opened it fully. Inside were bundles of correspondence tied with ribbon, account books, household memoranda, a locked dispatch case too heavy to remove quietly, and at the back, beneath a folio of estate maps, a packet wrapped in faded blue paper.

Ada’s hand shook as she drew it out.

The paper was not linen, not a prayer book cover. Yet blue enough to strike somewhere raw and childish in her. She untied the string. Inside were household vouchers, nothing more intimate than wax and arithmetic—except for one small enclosure slipped among them, as though hidden in plain dreariness. She opened it.

A bill. Physician’s visits. Paid in cash. Patient unnamed. Address omitted.

“Anything?” Nathaniel asked.

“Only proof that concealment is expensive.”

His own search had yielded more: a page torn from a private account book showing repeated payments to “M.W.” entered under household contingencies, and another note in Mrs. Vale’s hand instructing that a miniature be removed from the gallery before Easter guests arrived. Ada read the initials twice, then pressed the paper flat against the desk.

“M.W.,” she said. “How pious of them to reduce a woman to letters.”

Footsteps sounded in the corridor.

This time there was no long approach, no warning drift. They were near at once and accompanied by the soft unmistakable jangle of keys.

Nathaniel moved first, gathering the loose papers. “Behind the curtain.”

“No,” Ada hissed. “The casement.”

“Too late.”

The handle turned.

He caught her by the wrist and drew her into the narrow space between the cabinet and wall just as the door opened. It was scarcely a recess at all, more accident than hiding place, and far too close for safety or dignity. Ada was pressed against the paneling; Nathaniel, angled before her to block the view from the room, had one hand braced above her shoulder. Through the gap between cabinet edge and wall she could see only a slice of carpet and the hem of Mrs. Vale’s dress entering the room.

A lamp was raised.

“I was certain I left this drawer closed,” Mrs. Vale said.

Her voice was low, even pleasant, and all the more terrible for it.

Another voice answered—Mr. Pritchard’s dry murmur. “You may be overtired.”

“No,” said Mrs. Vale. “I am seldom overtired where disturbance is concerned.”

Ada became acutely aware of everything at once: the rough grain of cabinet wood against her back, Nathaniel’s sleeve brushing her bodice as he shifted his weight, the humiliating speed of her own pulse. He smelled of cool night air and metal and the starch of laundered linen beginning to yield to heat. One dark lock of his hair had fallen forward. She wanted, absurdly, to push it back. She wanted, more sensibly, not to be found in a widow’s morning room at midnight with her stepson arranged around her like impropriety itself.

Mrs. Vale moved nearer. A drawer slid. Papers turned.

Pritchard said, “If something was handled, it was likely by a maid.”

“Yes,” Mrs. Vale replied. “Maidservants are forever developing legal curiosity.”

Nathaniel’s mouth tightened. Ada saw it from inches away.

After a moment too long, the footsteps receded. The door closed. The key turned.

For several seconds neither of them moved.

Then Nathaniel let out one careful breath. “I begin,” he said very softly, “to hate this room.”

Ada looked up at him. “You are improving with astonishing speed.”

His eyes met hers in the dark slit of space between cabinet and wall. There was no room in that narrow place for politeness, and none for pretending they had not crossed some threshold less visible than a roofline.

“We have enough?” he asked.

“Enough to be dangerous,” she said.

“Not enough to be safe.”

“No.”

Somewhere under the fear and the anger, something else had begun to take shape—worse than either, because it made return inevitable.

When at last they moved, it was with the care of conspirators and with the knowledge that Mrs. Vale had smelled disturbance in the air. Foxglove Court, so long arranged to deny the past, had begun to feel the furniture shifting under it.

# Chapter 5 – The Nursery Stair / Tower Room

Ada had not meant to trust memory again.

Memory had already cost her too much. It gilded what had been merely tolerable, sharpened what had been cruel, and omitted all the dull connective tissue in between. Yet for two days after the morning-room search she could think of little else but a particular image from childhood: her mother on the old nursery stair, one hand on the rail, a small blue book pressed flat beneath her shawl. Not descending from the front rooms, as Ada had always half-assumed, but from higher up—from the tower end of the house, where the oldest rooms stood under the eaves and no one went unless there was storage to be bullied into order.

She told Nathaniel in the shadow of the stable wall at dusk, where he had come to meet her with a lantern shuttered and his coat thrown over one arm as though he were merely an owner examining drains.

“The nursery stair?” he repeated. “That wing is half shut.”

“So much the better.”

“That is becoming your solution to everything.”

“It is usually your household’s,” Ada said.

He accepted that with the weary look of a man too deep in his own house to protest its habits. “If we are seen there—”

“We shall be seen there anyway, eventually. Better while looking than waiting.”

The route this time required less climbing and more stealth. Mrs. Haskell, who had once been nursery maid and now seemed to belong to the upper regions of the house by right older than ownership, had not exactly helped. She had only intercepted Ada by the church lychgate that afternoon, thrust a stale biscuit into her hand as if feeding an animal, and muttered, “If you mean to go creeping where you shouldn’t, miss, the nursery stair sticks at the third turn. Lift the latch before you put your weight to it. And mind the tower room chest. Bad hinge.”

Then she had gone on toward the village as though discussing weather.

Now, by her instruction and Nathaniel’s key, they entered through a disused side passage and took the back stairs up. The upper house smelled different from the rooms below: colder, dustier, with that faint trapped sweetness old linens acquired in sealed presses. The nursery stair was narrow and turned sharply, the treads worn hollow in the center by feet long gone. At the third turn Ada lifted the latch before leaning; the stair gave only a dull complaint instead of a shout.

Nathaniel, behind her with the shuttered lantern, said quietly, “You have allies.”

Ada did not turn. “I have people who dislike lies.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“No,” she said. “It is often better.”

The tower room stood at the top beneath a sloped ceiling and a small round window rattling in its frame. It had once perhaps been a day nursery or school annex. Now it was a repository for defeated things: a cracked rocking horse, rolled carpets, a trunk with one handle missing, boxes of moth-eaten drapery, and a tall press with one door hanging slightly awry.

Ada stood very still.

“I know,” Nathaniel said.

“No, you do not.”

Because what she knew, or thought she knew, was not legal or practical but bodily—that once, long ago, she had been here. Not often. Once. The room had smelled then of starch and apples. There had been sunlight on the floorboards. Her mother had laughed at something just outside the door and then gone abruptly silent. Memory gave her no more than that. It was infuriatingly insufficient and all she had.

They began to search.

Not heroically. Not elegantly. Search was mostly lifting, shifting, coughing into sleeves, and discovering that every old house stored ten times as much rubbish as revelation. Ada knelt to open a chest of nursery copybooks swollen with damp. Nathaniel dragged aside a stand of broken screens. Dust furred his dark hair at the temples and streaked his cuff where he had put a hand on the floor. The sight was absurdly endearing and therefore annoying.

“Nothing,” he said after ten minutes at the press. “Unless your mother concealed her marriage among obsolete wall brackets.”

“She may have had a sense of comedy.”

“She did not pass it on.”

Ada shot him a look over the rim of an old trunk. “You improve, and then you destroy the effect.”

He almost answered, then stopped and bent to lift the rocking horse away from the wall. Behind it the plaster was cracked in a clean square line too regular for damage.

Ada was beside him at once. “There.”

The panel had been painted over years before and the seam disguised badly by dust. Nathaniel set down the lantern and pressed at one corner. It did not move. Ada took out her knife, slid the blade gently under the edge, and worked at the old paint until the panel loosened with a soft dry sigh.

Inside was a shallow recess.

A blue prayer book lay on top.

Ada stared at it without touching it. For a moment all sound in the room seemed to rush away from her—the rattle of the tower window, the distant soft booming of doors below, even the blood in her own ears. The book was wrapped in the same linen she remembered, yellowed now, one corner gone through with age.

Nathaniel said nothing. It was the kindest thing he had done all evening.

Ada lifted it carefully. Beneath it lay a packet of letters tied with faded ribbon, a folded paper sealed once and now broken, and what looked like the torn lower half of some legal draft. No cache of perfect justice, no miraculous complete confession. Just paper that had survived because someone had hidden it where only memory, luck, and obstinacy would combine to find it.

Her fingers trembled as she opened the prayer book. On the flyleaf, in a firm masculine hand grown faint with time:

_Marianne, from Adrian, on the day of our marriage. St. Jude keep what the world will not._

Ada shut her eyes.

Not because she had doubted entirely. Because certainty hurt.

Nathaniel took up the folded paper and read by lantern light. “It references a settlement,” he said after a moment, his voice altered. “And provision for ‘my wife Marianne Wren and any issue of that marriage’—the end is gone.”

“The end is enough,” Ada said, though it was not enough and both of them knew it.

The letters proved more and less than she hoped. Adrian’s hand, unmistakably intimate and not solely romantic: practical arrangements, fears of his father’s temper, mention of speaking with Pritchard, one reckless line about being tired of hiding her “like a shame.” There was no formal certificate among them. But there was a letter from a clergyman acknowledging receipt of an urgent request and a date that aligned too neatly to dismiss.

“It is enough to expose them,” Nathaniel said. “Perhaps not enough to settle every legal—”

The tower-room door opened.

Mrs. Vale stood on the threshold, lamp in hand, Mr. Pritchard just behind her shoulder. Neither looked surprised. Only exhausted, as if at the final proof of a bad opinion.

For one second no one moved.

Then Mrs. Vale’s gaze dropped to the prayer book in Ada’s hands.

“Oh,” she said, with dreadful softness. “So that is where she put it.”

Ada had no recollection afterward of deciding to hide the letters in her bodice and pass the torn settlement page to Nathaniel. She only knew that movement erupted all at once. Pritchard came forward, sharp and brisk. Nathaniel stepped between him and Ada. The lantern was knocked sideways and rolled, throwing crazed shadows over the walls.

“Stand aside,” Pritchard snapped. “This woman is stealing family papers.”

“She is recovering them,” Nathaniel said.

Mrs. Vale’s composure thinned. “Nathaniel, do not be absurd.”

Ada tried to edge for the stair, prayer book under her arm, but Pritchard seized at the packet. The ribbon snapped. Letters spilled over the floorboards like startled birds. One page slid toward the lantern flame and blackened at the edge before Nathaniel stamped it out.

For one heartbeat he looked down—only to save the paper, only by instinct—but the hesitation was there.

Pritchard caught Ada’s sleeve.

She tore free with a violence that ripped the seam from wrist to elbow. “Do not touch me.”

“Miss Wren,” Nathaniel said, but whether to stop her or clear the way she could not tell, and the uncertainty went through her like cold iron.

She fled.

Down the nursery stair, one hand on the rail, the prayer book wedged hard against her ribs, the surviving letters burning against her skin. Behind her voices broke into shouts at last—too late, too public. By the time she gained the side passage and the dark beyond the service yard, her breath was tearing at her throat and her eyes stung with rage.

Not because they had been found. Because for one second he had paused.

It might have been nothing. It was enough.

In the shelter of the beech walk she bent over, shaking, and pulled the rescued pages into her hands. Damp, torn, incomplete.

Enough to expose them. Not enough to trust anyone with. Not him. Not yet.

Above the trees the tower window showed a small yellow light where the old room had given up its dead. Foxglove Court had opened at last, and as ever, opening had meant violence.

# Chapter 6 – Shut Out

For the next week, every upper window at Foxglove Court seemed to have grown eyes.

Ada knew this was not literally true. Windows did not become sentient merely because one had once trusted them. Yet each time she crossed the lane beyond the park wall or took the long footpath above the orchard, she found herself glancing up at the house and seeing vigilance everywhere: fresh-polished panes catching late light, shutters fastened earlier than before, servants moving in rooms once left dim and private. The house had closed itself.

It was a foolish thing to feel personally betrayed by glass. Ada felt it all the same.

She kept to her lodging, went out only when necessity required, and slept badly. The rescued papers lived wrapped in linen under the mattress, where each night she dragged them out and each night they remained stubbornly the same: the prayer book with its inscription; three letters in Adrian Vale’s hand; the torn draft of a provision too incomplete to compel any court on earth by itself; one note from a clergyman whose parish, when she investigated, had been dissolved and merged years before. Not fantasy. Not enough.

Not enough was the history of her life.

She replayed the tower-room scene far more than was useful. Pritchard’s hand on her sleeve. Mrs. Vale’s appalling calm. Nathaniel saying _She is recovering them._ Nathaniel looking down. It was that she returned to, despite herself. The glance, the pause, the tiny surrender to training that had come at precisely the instant she needed certainty. Perhaps he had meant only to save the letter from the lantern. Perhaps any decent man would have done the same. Ada did not care for explanations in the small hours. She cared that she had seen in him, at the crisis, the whole weight of blood, upbringing, and male hesitation settle before action.

You arranged the room for it, she had told him in the library.

He had arranged the moment no better.

Mrs. Biddle, who had the generous incuriosity of a woman paid regularly and warned rarely, brought up weak tea one grey morning and said, “A note come for you yesterday, miss, but the boy with it wouldn’t leave his name. I sent him off. I thought perhaps you were resting.”

Ada looked up sharply. “What note?”

Mrs. Biddle blinked. “Oh. Burned it with the cinders, did I not? It looked gentlemen’s business.”

Ada shut her eyes.

By noon she was out despite the rain, walking hard toward the village church because there was nowhere else to put the anger. The churchyard grass soaked her hems. Yews dripped blackly. Beside the lichened south wall, bent over some resolute labour among graves, stood Mrs. Haskell in an old bonnet and a shawl that had long since ceased to correspond to fashion.

The old woman straightened slowly when she heard Ada approach. “You look peevish,” she observed.

“A note was burned.”

“That does happen to paper.”

Ada made an impatient sound. Mrs. Haskell watched her with the expression of someone allowing weather to pass.

After a moment she said, “He’s a fool, if that’s the shape of it.”

“Which one?”

“The gentleman kind. They are all fools where decision is wanted quickly.” She plucked a dead sprig from the yew with capable fingers. “Still. Some are fools only once.”

Ada wanted not to ask. “Has he sent again?”

Mrs. Haskell reached into the basket on her arm, beneath cuttings and twine, and produced a folded sheet sealed badly enough to show haste. “This was to be left where it might be found. I found it first.”

Ada took it.

The note was in Nathaniel’s hand.

_I was wrong to hesitate. There is more. Pritchard’s copies, household cash books, and the old parish ledger survive if one knows where to look. Mrs. Vale means to settle the matter publicly by denying you before the county at Thursday’s musicale. If you can bear one more encounter with this house, come to the east lodge at nine tomorrow evening. If you cannot, send word by Haskell and I will place what proof I have in safer hands than mine._

No plea. No explanation beyond the first sentence. No demand that she forgive him because his motives had been mixed and therefore noble. The economy of it should not have moved her. It did.

Mrs. Haskell, busied now with a bunch of rosemary no one had asked for, said, “I told him if he wrote anything elegant I’d refuse to carry it.”

Ada let out a sound not unlike a laugh. It hurt.

“Do you trust him?” the old woman asked.

“No.”

“Good. Trust’s expensive.” Mrs. Haskell tucked the rosemary under her arm. “Question is whether you trust him enough.”

That was, infuriatingly, the right distinction.

The next evening the east lodge stood empty except for damp air, a cracked settle, and Nathaniel Vale, who looked as though he had not slept much and had no expectation that he deserved more. Rain had passed in the afternoon; the ground still smelled of wet leaves and shaken earth. He took off his hat when she entered, then seemed to think better of the formality and set it down awkwardly on the settle instead.

“Miss Wren.”

“Mr. Vale.”

It was almost funny, after roofs and hidden rooms, to arrive at a meeting by opening an ordinary door and finding politeness the most uncomfortable part of it.

He did not begin with defense. “I failed you.”

Ada folded her hands to keep from doing something unhelpful with them. “Yes.”

“I thought”—he stopped, evidently deciding that whatever thought had governed him did not improve in the telling. “No. It does not matter what I thought. It mattered that I moved too slowly.”

The simplicity of that disarmed her more than argument would have done.

Nathaniel drew several folded papers from inside his coat and laid them on the settle between them. “Pritchard keeps copies. Not of everything. Enough. I took these this morning from the old muniment room while he was in the lower offices.” His mouth altered very slightly. “By means less acrobatic than yours.”

Ada looked down. Two account pages. A copy of a letter from the clergyman whose original lay under her mattress. A household memorandum in Mrs. Vale’s hand directing that “Miss Wren’s matter” be removed from the family register and all references adjusted. The date made Ada’s stomach go cold. It was two weeks after Adrian Vale’s death.

“She wrote it plainly enough,” Ada said.

“Because she did not suppose anyone but Pritchard would read it.”

“And now?”

“Now she intends to make an end of uncertainty.” Nathaniel’s gaze met hers directly. “Thursday’s gathering was meant to restore confidence in the house after mourning. She means to use it to reduce you to a trespasser and me to a foolish son misled by one.”

Ada’s first response was not fear but fury at the elegance of the move. Public rooms had always been where women like Mrs. Vale did their cleanest work.

“Then why warn me? Why not let her?”

“Because I know what she is. Because I know what I nearly was.” He looked away briefly, then back. “And because I would rather break the house than let it close over you again.”

That was too much to answer at once. Ada moved to the window and stood looking out at the dark dripping branches. The east lodge glass was thick and bubbled; beyond it the lights of Foxglove Court glimmered through trees, distant as if belonging to another life entirely.

“There is still not enough,” she said.

“Not enough to settle every question beyond appeal, perhaps. Enough to expose bad faith. Enough that denial becomes ridiculous if spoken before witnesses.” He joined her at the window, not close, not touching. “Mrs. Haskell believes the old curate’s widow is alive in Bath. A servant in the house remembers your mother. I can compel Pritchard’s presence if need be.”

Ada thought of entering again. Not for papers this time, but for exposure. Not to search in hidden rooms, but to stand where the house would have to see her.

“They will still call me an adventuress,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You may lose half your county to disgust.”

“That may be cheap at the price.”

Something in her chest gave way—not softened, exactly, but shifted enough to make breathing different.

“When?” she asked.

Nathaniel’s face, which had held itself in check as if expecting refusal, changed almost imperceptibly. “Thursday. The balcony over the ballroom opens from the old music room. The outer casement is warped. If you insist on your preferred methods, it is the surest way.”

Ada looked at him sidelong. “You have thought about this.”

“I have spent several days considering windows with more respect than I once thought decent.”

That, from another man, might have been flirtation. From him it was apology in the only language he trusted: precision, observation, altered practice.

Ada turned from the glass. “Very well.”

“Very well?”

“You may stop looking as though I hold your sentence in my pocket, Mr. Vale. I said very well.”

A breath—not quite relief, not quite laughter—left him.

Thursday, then.

One final entrance. Not to steal. To refuse erasure in the only way Foxglove Court seemed capable of understanding: by finding, once again, that its upper windows were not secure against the wrong kind of woman.

# Chapter 7 – The Ballroom Balcony

On Thursday evening Foxglove Court shone as if no one had ever wept, lied, or hidden a woman in it.

The south front blazed with candlelight. Carriages rolled over the gravel in a steady glittering procession. Music drifted thinly through opened lower windows where servants passed in swift dark intervals with trays and folded napkins and all the ordinary devices by which great houses persuaded themselves of permanence. Ada, standing in the trees above the east lawn, thought there was something almost obscene in the brightness.

She had dressed carefully because contempt was easier to arrange when one looked as though one belonged nowhere. Her plain dove-grey gown had been brushed, let out at the sleeves, and mended at the hem so cunningly that only the mender could see where necessity had bitten. She wore her mother’s small jet brooch at the throat. Over all this she had a dark cloak suitable for climbing, because dignity and absurdity were old acquaintances by now.

The route to the old music-room balcony was one she would once have called impossible and now merely called Thursday. Nathaniel had described it well: up the espaliered wall by the orangery, across a narrow run of guttering, onto the shallow slate beneath the balcony rail. The outer casement was indeed warped. It yielded after two careful pushes and one muttered insult.

Inside, the old music room stood unlit except for the spill of brightness through the open inner doors to the balcony gallery. Dust veiled the pianoforte. A pile of sheet music slumped on a chair. From beyond came the rise and turn of conversation, the scrape of dancing shoes, a soprano laugh too practiced to be joyful.

Ada untied her cloak, folded it over the back of the chair, and listened.

This was not courage. Courage was too clean a word for the condition of wanting to be sick and proceeding anyway.

She moved toward the inner doors. Through the carved gallery rail she could see the ballroom below: ladies in pale silk and diamonds, gentlemen in black and white, candlelight multiplying in mirrors, Foxglove Court transformed into a machine for admiration. Mrs. Vale stood near the far hearth in deep plum satin, one hand resting on a fan closed like a weapon. Pritchard lingered at the edge of a knot of local gentlemen, his professional face arranged into attentive neutrality. Nathaniel was nowhere in sight.

For one awful moment Ada thought he had failed her again.

Then a stir moved through the room—not loud, not dramatic, simply that subtle shift by which company acknowledges the entrance of someone it already belongs to. Nathaniel had come in by the principal door from the corridor beyond, not hastily but with a composure so exact Ada recognized effort in every line of it. He crossed to Mrs. Vale and spoke. Ada could not hear the words, only see the change in his stepmother’s expression: not surprise, not yet, but alertness sharpened to danger.

Guests drew a little closer without appearing to.

Nathaniel turned. His gaze lifted—once, briefly—to the gallery.

He knew exactly where she stood in the dark.

That was all the signal she got.

Ada set one hand on the rail and came forward into the candlelight.

The effect below was not instant uproar but a curious break in conversation, as if some note had gone wrong in a familiar tune. Faces tilted upward. A woman near the musicians’ dais half-raised her opera glass before remembering the impropriety. The musicians, uncertain whether they had ceased to be required, wavered into silence.

Mrs. Vale looked up fully then, and if Ada lived to be eighty she would remember that one moment of naked loathing in a well-bred face.

Nathaniel spoke first. “Before the evening proceeds,” he said, his voice carrying cleanly through the room, “there is a matter concerning my family which will not bear further private management.”

No one coughed. No one moved. The county loved nothing so much as decorum under visible strain.

Mrs. Vale’s smile appeared exactly where one would expect. “Nathaniel,” she said, with just enough amusement to imply filial overexcitement, “this is scarcely the time.”

“It is precisely the time,” he replied.

Pritchard stepped forward. “Mr. Vale, perhaps if there is some household concern—”

“There is,” said Ada from above, and heard the room take her in.

She had not intended to speak so soon. The words had simply come because hearing herself discussed as if absent was older to her than fear.

Every face turned upward now. Ada was aware of the absurdity of her position—woman on a gallery, no announced name, no invitation visible, as if she had dropped from the rafters in search of scandal. Let them think it. She had entered through upper windows before; she could survive a staircase of eyes.

Mrs. Vale’s voice remained gentle. “Miss Wren, I believe. If indeed that is your name. You have already caused distress enough in this house. Must you turn even mourning into display?”

The cruelty of that was expert. Not open accusation, but the smooth recasting of injury as vulgarity.

Ada rested both hands on the rail because they wanted badly to shake. “Display,” she said, “is what houses like this call truth when truth arrives uninvited.”

A few faces flickered—not sympathy exactly, but interest becoming thought.

Pritchard cleared his throat. “This young woman has trespassed repeatedly and removed private family effects. I must advise—”

Nathaniel cut across him. “You may advise yourself, Mr. Pritchard. The papers in question concern the deliberate suppression of a lawful connection between the late Adrian Vale and Marianne Wren.”

The room did not gasp. Good breeding rarely gasped. It breathed in as one body.

Mrs. Vale’s fan snapped open. “This is monstrous.”

“Yes,” Nathaniel said. “It is.”

Ada saw then that he was afraid. Not of her. Not even chiefly of scandal. Afraid in the plain human way one is when crossing from what can still be managed into what cannot be recalled. The sight steadied her more than confidence would have.

She drew the prayer book from beneath her cloak and held it up. “This belonged to my mother. The inscription is in Adrian Vale’s hand.”

Pritchard was already moving. “A sentimental object proves nothing.”

“No,” Ada said. “That is why there are also account copies in your keeping, and a memorandum in Mrs. Vale’s hand directing that references to my mother be removed from the family register. Mr. Vale has seen them.”

Mrs. Vale turned on Nathaniel with something close to fury at last. “You would expose your father’s household on the word of a woman who climbs in windows?”

At that there was a murmur—not at the substance, but at the nakedness of the phrasing. She had meant to degrade Ada and instead had made vivid the lengths to which denial had forced her.

Ada answered before Nathaniel could. “One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows when one has been denied the door.”

This time the murmur changed. It moved through the room not as scandal alone but as recognition that some forms of impropriety belonged first to the house, not to the woman compelled by it.

From the back, a voice spoke unexpectedly. Mrs. Haskell, planted by the service entrance in black silk too old to flatter anyone, said, “That child’s mother was married, and any soul in this house old enough to remember knows why no one said so after Mr. Adrian died.”

Pritchard’s face tightened. “You are a servant.”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Haskell. “That is why I know where things are put when gentlefolk mean never to see them again.”

The room, so carefully arranged for music and rank, had become impossible to govern. One gentleman muttered to another. A lady lowered herself abruptly to a chair as if scandal might better be heard seated. The curate’s sister—Ada recognized her vaguely from the village—said in a clear carrying tone, “My brother mentioned a hasty ceremony years ago and was told to forget it. I had thought it one of his fancies.”

Mrs. Vale looked suddenly older, not because pity had entered the scene but because control had begun to leave it.

“This is vile,” she said. “To drag private grief before strangers—”

“You made it a household policy,” Nathaniel said. “I make it public because private decency failed.”

The house had been forced to see her. That was all. It was enough.

# Chapter 8 – After Entry

In the week after the musicale, Foxglove Court became a house devoted to lowered voices.

The county did not explode. It adjusted itself, as counties do, by degrees and with malice distributed unevenly. Some declared Nathaniel Vale noble and unfortunate. Some thought him weak. Some regarded Ada as a victim, which annoyed her more than being called an adventuress had done. Others continued to regard her exactly as that. Mrs. Vale left the house two days later “for the sake of her nerves,” which was the sort of phrase society used when no one wished to say exile and no one could quite say victory. Mr. Pritchard remained just long enough to submit a resignation full of legal caution and moral vacancy.

Nothing miraculous occurred. The papers did not suddenly produce a title, a fortune, or universal apology. The surviving evidence was enough to force acknowledgment of wrongdoing, enough to restore Marianne Wren’s name to places from which it had been cut, enough to make further denial look like panic. It was not enough to tidy the whole matter into righteousness, and Ada found, to her own surprise, that this prevented bitterness less than success might have done. A neat ending would have felt false. Lives such as her mother’s were not repaired by clerks.

She spent those days in the village, receiving more callers than she had ever wanted and answering fewer than decency advised. Mrs. Biddle became almost proprietary in her administration of tea. Mrs. Haskell appeared once with a jar of gooseberry preserve and once without explanation at all. On the fifth day Nathaniel sent a note asking if he might call. Ada allowed it because refusing forever was childish and because she had already discovered that refusing him did not prevent thinking of him.

He arrived in the afternoon on foot and alone.

The weather had turned mild after rain. The little parlour looked smaller than usual with him in it, too low-ceilinged for reserve. He stood by the window for a moment after Mrs. Biddle left them, hat in hand, as though uncertain whether ordinary furniture could bear what extraordinary roofs had.

“I have come,” he said, “to ask whether you would walk with me.”

Ada, seated by the fire with mending she had no intention of completing, looked up. “That is a remarkably modest proposal from a man who has lately overturned his household in public.”

“I am trying not to presume upon momentum.”

“That would be a first.”

His mouth moved. “Yes.”

She set the mending aside.

They walked not through the village proper, where observation had grown exhausting, but along the edge of the park where new nettles were up under the wall and the rooks had begun their annual arguments in the high elms. For some minutes they said nothing. It was less uncomfortable than it had once been, which was its own disturbance.

At length Nathaniel spoke. “The old register has been repaired as far as possible. Not invisibly. I did not want it invisible.”

Ada kept her eyes on the path. “Good.”

“Mrs. Haskell oversaw the copying of the surviving letters before they were placed with the family papers.”

Ada gave him a sidelong glance. “You entrusted the family archive to Mrs. Haskell?”

“I have learned to respect practical authority.”

“Again, astonishing progress.”

He accepted the rebuke and the compliment in one. “There may still be legal questions. The settlement draft is incomplete. Pritchard has left matters in a condition designed to be tiresome.”

“He has a gift.”

Nathaniel stopped walking.

Ada, after another step, stopped too. Beyond him, through a thinning stand of beeches, Foxglove Court showed pale in the afternoon light, less theatrical now than on the night of the ball. A house, merely. Stone, windows, roof. Not innocent. Not alive either, however often she had imagined it breathing against her.

“I asked you here,” he said, “not for documents.”

“That would have been efficient. I see the objection.”

He looked briefly exasperated, which pleased her unfairly. “Miss Wren—Ada—”

It was the first time he had used her Christian name. The effect was disproportionate.

“I owe you an apology that no useful action can entirely replace. I also owe you more than apology, though I am aware that saying so may sound suspiciously like self-importance.” His gaze held hers now with the same difficult directness he had shown in the ballroom. “I do not ask you to forget what I failed to do. I ask whether you can imagine a future in which that failure is not the whole account between us.”

Ada had prepared, she realized, for eloquence or restraint. This plainness was worse.

“The whole account,” she repeated, because buying time had become one of her finer arts. “You speak like a ledger, Mr. Vale.”

“I speak like a man who knows he cannot improve on honesty.”

“Can you not?” she said softly. “How disappointing.”

He laughed then, properly this time, low and brief and helplessly surprised into it. The sound went through her with embarrassing ease.

Ada looked away toward the house. “Do you know what is most irritating?” she said. “Not that Foxglove Court denied us. Houses do what people teach them. It is that I spent years imagining that if I could only force my way back in, something in me would settle.” She folded her hands into the opposite sleeves, feeling the old habit of self-possession rise and loosen together. “It has not. Not exactly.”

“No,” Nathaniel said. “I thought something similar. About inheriting it, perhaps. That if I returned and understood the accounts and the roofs and the tenants and all the practical machinery, the house would become mine in some final sense.” He glanced toward the pale front. “It has not. Not exactly.”

That, more than apology, was companionable.

They had reached the side drive without either of them deciding to. It curved toward the less ceremonial entrance near the library wing, where tradesmen once came and children probably had and women without proper standing certainly did. The front steps were visible beyond the sweep of gravel, grand and useless in the afternoon light.

Nathaniel followed her gaze. “I might ask you to come to the house,” he said, “and I realize the symbolism would be insufferable whichever door I chose.”

Ada’s mouth twitched. “You improve enough to recognize your own symbolism. This is becoming dangerous.”

“I mean only this: there are papers in the library copied for you, and the room is warmer than this lane. If you come, I should prefer that you come because you wish to.”

She considered the house, the side entrance, the long history of thresholds. The old childish part of her, the one that had wanted front doors and acknowledgment and rooms that matched stories, stirred faintly and then quieted. What she wanted now was stranger and smaller and perhaps better.

“The library,” she said. “Not the front door. I have always thought the library a room improved by truth.”

He inclined his head, not as to a victor but to an equal making terms. “As you wish.”

They walked the rest of the way together. No servants announced her. No audience assembled. The side door opened on a passage smelling faintly of beeswax and spring damp. From there the turn into the west library was only a few steps. Ada paused on the threshold.

This was the room she had entered through a warped casement with mud on her hem and anger enough to hold her upright. The same shelves, the same desk, the same portrait over the mantel. But the family register now lay open on the side table, and beneath the repaired cut line a new hand had entered, carefully and without flourish, Marianne Wren.

Ada stood looking at it until the blur in her vision cleared.

Behind her, Nathaniel said nothing.

At last she crossed the room.

Not by the window. Not by permission in the old sense either. By choice, which was rarer.

When she turned, he was still by the door as if unwilling to presume even now. Ada thought of roofs, hidden cabinets, damp stone, his hand on her arm, his hesitation, his return, the ballroom lit like accusation, the ridiculous persistence of both of them. Hope, she had learned, was not a grand opening of doors. It was smaller and more stubborn than that.

“You may come in farther,” she said.

And when he did, Foxglove Court, which had taught her so thoroughly the uses of exclusion, seemed at last to make room.

This is an ambitious, sustained piece of Victorian-inflected literary fiction that demonstrates considerable craft. Let me assess it carefully across all dimensions.

STRENGTHS:

The prose style is genuinely accomplished. The author has internalized a Victorian register without merely imitating it—sentences have period-appropriate weight and rhythm while remaining readable. Lines like "A dispatch box might hold deeds or sermons or receipts for coal. It might be long emptied. It might already be ash. But it was movement, and movement was often guilt in livery" show real control: the final clause earns its metaphorical turn. The voice is consistent across eight chapters, which is a significant achievement.

Ada Wren is a well-constructed protagonist. Her anger is specific rather than generic, her competence is demonstrated rather than asserted, and her emotional arc—from pure instrumentality toward something more vulnerable—is handled with restraint. The author wisely avoids making her either a victim or a superhero. Her rudeness as a fear response ("fear always made her rude") is a nice character note that pays off repeatedly.

The dialogue is generally strong. Exchanges like "You may note it in your ledger" / "You speak like a ledger, Mr. Vale" / "I speak like a man who knows he cannot improve on honesty" feel genuinely witty without being anachronistically sharp. The banter has period-appropriate indirection. Mrs. Haskell's voice is particularly well-differentiated.

The plot mechanics are solid. The mystery unfolds logically—inventory scrap to dispatch box to register to morning room to tower room—and each discovery is appropriately incomplete, which is realistic and avoids the trap of tidy revelation. The decision to make the evidence perpetually "not quite enough" is thematically resonant and structurally honest.

The prompt integration is excellent. "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows" is woven throughout as both literal action and thematic statement, culminating in Ada's public declaration of it in Chapter 7. This is exactly the kind of prompt-faithful execution that elevates the piece.

WEAKNESSES:

The piece occasionally tips into what might be called "aphorism density"—too many sentences that want to be quotable. "Memory had already cost her too much. It gilded what had been merely tolerable, sharpened what had been cruel, and omitted all the dull connective tissue in between." This is good. But when such formulations appear every few paragraphs, the cumulative effect is slightly exhausting, and some land less well than others. "Movement was often guilt in livery" is excellent; "hope was not a grand opening of doors. It was smaller and more stubborn than that" is a bit too neat, too self-consciously conclusive.

Nathaniel Vale is somewhat underdeveloped compared to Ada. We understand his position and his arc intellectually, but his interiority is largely filtered through Ada's perception. His hesitation in the tower room—the central moment of his failure—is described but not fully inhabited. We're told he was afraid in the ballroom, but the fear doesn't quite land with the same specificity as Ada's emotions. He risks becoming a function of her story rather than a full character.

The "unearned transformation" concern is moderate. Nathaniel's shift from suspicious householder to active co-conspirator happens fairly quickly across chapters 2-3, and while the author provides some justification (the cut register line, Ada's anger), the speed of his conversion to her cause feels slightly accelerated. A Victorian gentleman of his station would likely have more institutional resistance.

Some metaphors are strained. "Letters spilled over the floorboards like startled birds" is a cliché. "The county loved nothing so much as decorum under visible strain" is a generalization that sounds clever but is actually vague. "The house had closed itself" is fine but the personification of the house is used so frequently it becomes a tic rather than a technique.

The climactic ballroom scene (Chapter 7) is well-constructed but slightly too neat in its social mechanics. The curate's sister appearing to corroborate at exactly the right moment, Mrs. Haskell's perfectly timed intervention—these feel slightly stage-managed. Real social confrontations are messier.

Chapter 8 is the weakest chapter. The resolution is handled with appropriate restraint, but the final scene—walking into the library, seeing the name in the register, the closing exchange—is somewhat predictable in its emotional beats. "And when he did, Foxglove Court, which had taught her so thoroughly the uses of exclusion, seemed at last to make room" is a fine closing sentence but perhaps too tidy for a story that has otherwise resisted tidiness.

The pacing is generally good but Chapter 6 (the week of exclusion) is slightly slow—it functions as necessary breathing room but the Mrs. Biddle/burned note subplot feels like padding.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is a genuinely accomplished piece of literary fiction that demonstrates sustained craft, a consistent and well-realized voice, and genuine thematic coherence. It is not a masterpiece—Nathaniel's characterization is thinner than Ada's, some metaphors misfire, and the resolution is slightly too comfortable—but it is well above average work. The prompt is honored throughout, the mystery plot is competent, and the central character is memorable.

The prose style is genuinely accomplished. The author has internalized a Victorian register without merely imitating it—sentences have period-appropriate weight and rhythm while remaining readable. Lines like "A dispatch box might hold deeds or sermons or receipts for coal. It might be long emptied. It might already be ash. But it was movement, and movement was often guilt in livery" show real control: the final clause earns its metaphorical turn. The voice is consistent across eight chapters, which is a significant achievement.

Ada Wren is a well-constructed protagonist. Her anger is specific rather than generic, her competence is demonstrated rather than asserted, and her emotional arc—from pure instrumentality toward something more vulnerable—is handled with restraint. The author wisely avoids making her either a victim or a superhero. Her rudeness as a fear response ("fear always made her rude") is a nice character note that pays off repeatedly.

The dialogue is generally strong. Exchanges like "You may note it in your ledger" / "You speak like a ledger, Mr. Vale" / "I speak like a man who knows he cannot improve on honesty" feel genuinely witty without being anachronistically sharp. The banter has period-appropriate indirection. Mrs. Haskell's voice is particularly well-differentiated.

The plot mechanics are solid. The mystery unfolds logically—inventory scrap to dispatch box to register to morning room to tower room—and each discovery is appropriately incomplete, which is realistic and avoids the trap of tidy revelation. The decision to make the evidence perpetually "not quite enough" is thematically resonant and structurally honest.

The prompt integration is excellent. "One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows" is woven throughout as both literal action and thematic statement, culminating in Ada's public declaration of it in Chapter 7. This is exactly the kind of prompt-faithful execution that elevates the piece.

WEAKNESSES:

The piece occasionally tips into what might be called "aphorism density"—too many sentences that want to be quotable. "Memory had already cost her too much. It gilded what had been merely tolerable, sharpened what had been cruel, and omitted all the dull connective tissue in between." This is good. But when such formulations appear every few paragraphs, the cumulative effect is slightly exhausting, and some land less well than others. "Movement was often guilt in livery" is excellent; "hope was not a grand opening of doors. It was smaller and more stubborn than that" is a bit too neat, too self-consciously conclusive.

Nathaniel Vale is somewhat underdeveloped compared to Ada. We understand his position and his arc intellectually, but his interiority is largely filtered through Ada's perception. His hesitation in the tower room—the central moment of his failure—is described but not fully inhabited. We're told he was afraid in the ballroom, but the fear doesn't quite land with the same specificity as Ada's emotions. He risks becoming a function of her story rather than a full character.

The "unearned transformation" concern is moderate. Nathaniel's shift from suspicious householder to active co-conspirator happens fairly quickly across chapters 2-3, and while the author provides some justification (the cut register line, Ada's anger), the speed of his conversion to her cause feels slightly accelerated. A Victorian gentleman of his station would likely have more institutional resistance.

Some metaphors are strained. "Letters spilled over the floorboards like startled birds" is a cliché. "The county loved nothing so much as decorum under visible strain" is a generalization that sounds clever but is actually vague. "The house had closed itself" is fine but the personification of the house is used so frequently it becomes a tic rather than a technique.

The climactic ballroom scene (Chapter 7) is well-constructed but slightly too neat in its social mechanics. The curate's sister appearing to corroborate at exactly the right moment, Mrs. Haskell's perfectly timed intervention—these feel slightly stage-managed. Real social confrontations are messier.

Chapter 8 is the weakest chapter. The resolution is handled with appropriate restraint, but the final scene—walking into the library, seeing the name in the register, the closing exchange—is somewhat predictable in its emotional beats. "And when he did, Foxglove Court, which had taught her so thoroughly the uses of exclusion, seemed at last to make room" is a fine closing sentence but perhaps too tidy for a story that has otherwise resisted tidiness.

The pacing is generally good but Chapter 6 (the week of exclusion) is slightly slow—it functions as necessary breathing room but the Mrs. Biddle/burned note subplot feels like padding.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT:

This is a genuinely accomplished piece of literary fiction that demonstrates sustained craft, a consistent and well-realized voice, and genuine thematic coherence. It is not a masterpiece—Nathaniel's characterization is thinner than Ada's, some metaphors misfire, and the resolution is slightly too comfortable—but it is well above average work. The prompt is honored throughout, the mystery plot is competent, and the central character is memorable.
