# Gabriel Vale

Gabriel Vale is thirty-eight, famous enough to be recognized in airport lounges, hotel foyers, and by teenage cashiers trying not to stare. He has been famous in some form for most of his adult life, and employably attractive for longer than that. He started in television in his early twenties—period drama, then a breakout thriller, then a run of clever, glossy films that made him critic-proof and gossip-page useful. He has a reputation that is both flattering and faintly unserious: magnetic, unserious in interviews, impossible not to watch, allegedly hell on continuity, seen leaving the right restaurants with the wrong people. Some of that reputation is earned; some of it has simply become easier to wear than resist.

He grew up in Surrey with a mother who taught elocution to children and amateur actors and a father who sold high-end kitchens and left when Gabriel was fourteen. Not tragic enough to furnish a memoir, but formative in a way he dislikes admitting. His mother valued polish, poise, and giving people a good impression. Gabriel learned early that being delightful smoothed over a lot. He was the sort of boy teachers described as “charming” when they meant “constantly managing the room.” He can still turn on that exact expression of alert, conspiratorial warmth that invites people to feel specially chosen. He hates that he knows how to do it. He hates more that it works.

The key contradiction in him is that his charm is real and tactical at once. He is not a fraud, exactly; he really is funny, observant, and interested in people. But he also keeps one eye on whether he is landing. If he makes a joke in a room, some part of him checks the room’s face. If he says thank you to a runner on set, he means it, but he also wants to be remembered as the actor who did. This is not cynical in him; it is anxious. He wants to be liked in a way that is both vain and oddly childlike. One person disliking him can feel to him larger than ten liking him.

His worst habits come from that. He smooths too fast. He tells charming versions of events before he has decided whether they are his to tell. He can turn embarrassment into performance in seconds. He is good at making people comfortable unless what they want is honesty without varnish. When genuinely hurt, he can become brittle and faintly grandiose, as if language itself might rescue him if deployed well enough. He also has a streak of pettiness he is ashamed of. If he feels dismissed, he may become extra dazzling out of spite.

He is not a reader in the pious literary sense, which is useful. He reads scripts carefully, articles badly, biographies in chunks, and novels unpredictably. He does, however, have a very actorly relationship to text: he notices rhythm, memorable lines, scenes he can inhabit. He underlines things with hotel pens. He folds corners despite knowing it is morally suspect in the presence of booksellers. He tends to talk about books the way actors talk about roles—through feeling, pace, and whether something “works in the mouth”—which can make him sound philistine or unexpectedly perceptive depending on the company.

Specific grounding details:
- He remembers everyone’s names on set and in restaurants because he cannot bear becoming the sort of man who doesn’t.
- He checks his reflection in dark shop windows without fully noticing he’s doing it.
- He always travels with lozenges, expensive socks, and one shirt he thinks makes him look less tired than it does.
- He taps script pages against his wrist before learning lines.
- He says “darling” and “love” lightly and often, then becomes more careful around someone he actually likes.
- He uses humor when frightened, including in absurd situations where it clearly isn’t helping.
- He has a habit of stepping physically closer when engaged in conversation, assuming intimacy can be built by proximity.
- He is very good with old women and children, partly because they often react to him without professional calculation.
- He knows exactly how to angle his face in the rain and resents himself for it.

Physically, Gabriel is one of those men who appears expensive even when damp and annoyed. He is tall enough to register as tall indoors, broad-shouldered but beginning to lose the thoughtless ease of youth around the eyes and mouth, which actually makes him more interesting. His beauty is not delicate; it has been worked on by fatigue, weather, and the camera. His hair is dark and not quite as obedient as gossip photos suggest. In public he carries himself with a relaxed precision, as if aware of being looked at from three directions. In private or when caught off guard, that ease slips: he rubs the back of his neck, shoves his hands in his pockets, sits badly in chairs, glances to check reactions too quickly. He smiles often, but there are grades to it. His “everyone smile back” smile is different from his real one, which arrives slower and tilts.

His motives at the start of the story are not noble or fully conscious. He ducks into the shop because he needs somewhere to hide. He returns because Elin unsettles him, because he wants the relief of being treated like an inconvenience rather than an institution, and because he wants very badly to make Elin like him. That last motive evolves. He begins by wanting traction and ends by wanting to be known. He is in Wales for work and is professionally loyal enough to show up, hit marks, and deliver what is needed, but emotionally he has very few strong allegiances. His agent likes him. His publicist manages him. An ex or two still text him. He is surrounded by people who are fond of him in workable, partial ways. He has colleagues, not intimates. That loneliness is less dramatic than constant: the loneliness of always being with people and rarely off.

Possible flavour dialogue:
- “You know, in most shops they say hello before they accuse a man of water damage.”
- “That was a joke. You looked as though you were considering whether to have me removed with the umbrellas.”
- “I’m perfectly capable of reading difficult books. I simply object to being judged by one before lunch.”
- “Do you always look at people as if you’ve already read the reviews?”
- “I don’t need everyone to like me. That would be ridiculous. I only need the vast majority, immediately, and preferably on sight.”
- “The problem isn’t that I don’t know how to be sincere. The problem is that sincerity and performance have been sharing a coat for so long I’m not always sure which one reached the door first.”

Possible flavour internal monologue:
- She was not, he thought with annoyance, meant to be this difficult to impress in a cardigan.
- He could feel himself reaching for charm the way other men reached for cigarettes: automatic, soothing, bad for him, and especially irresistible when it plainly wasn’t helping.
- If she disliked him, properly disliked him, he might survive it. It was the possibility that she saw through him and found very little there that made his stomach tighten.

# Elin Morgan

Elin Morgan is thirty-four and owns the bookshop she now runs alone, though “owns” is a more precarious verb than she likes to admit. The shop was her mother’s before it was hers, and before that had belonged to a retired schoolmaster who sold maps and poetry and disapproved of paperbacks. Elin spent chunks of childhood behind the till doing homework, reading what she liked off the shelves, and learning early that a shop can be both livelihood and public stage. Their mother knew everyone’s business and remembered every customer’s preferred detective novelist; Elin inherited the memory and not the geniality.

Elin left Wales in their early twenties for Cardiff and then Bristol, where they worked first in a university library and later for a small academic press. That period taught them useful things—metadata, grant applications, the quiet vanity of literary people—but also left them exhausted by institutional politeness and the feeling of living somewhere they were always slightly provisional. They came back to Porthlaethol when their mother got ill, expecting it to be temporary. Then their mother died, the shop nearly folded, and Elin stayed because someone had to. That “someone had to” has become a whole life. It is a life Elin values and resents in equal measure.

Elin is intelligent in a practical, watchful way rather than a performatively cerebral one. They read widely but without sanctimony. They know what people buy versus what they say they buy. They can recommend a translation of Welsh poetry, a murder mystery for someone’s difficult father, or the exact sort of grief memoir a tourist wants because she has suddenly remembered death on holiday. They have little patience for people who use books as accessories to their personality. That includes some customers, some festival people, and possibly, on first impression, Gabriel Vale.

Their reserve is less shyness than a habit of self-containment. Elin dislikes being managed, sold to, or made into someone else’s anecdote. They are not naturally cold, but they become very dry when they feel cornered. They are also funnier than they mean to be. Under stress, their mouth gets sharper and their body more practical: stack, sort, straighten, tally, wipe surfaces that do not need wiping. Their attraction, when it happens, embarrasses them mainly because it feels adolescent in someone who prides themself on not being easily thrown. They are especially annoyed to find that Gabriel’s worst qualities—vanity, fluency, social ease—are attached to someone who can also be attentive and unexpectedly earnest.

Elin’s flaws are not simply “guarded.” They can be punishingly unfair when they feel vulnerable. They tend to assume they are seeing clearly when in fact they are protecting themselves through cynicism. They dislike spectacle but are not above enjoying the moral high ground of not being impressed. They can also confuse rootedness with virtue, as if staying put automatically makes one more trustworthy than someone who leaves. They are capable of tenderness, but it often comes disguised as competence: putting aside the right book, making tea without asking, remembering a passing preference.

Specific grounding details:
- They hate when customers fold page corners but quietly do it in their own paperbacks.
- They keep invoices in perfect order and personal letters in a biscuit tin with no system at all.
- They are very good at wrapping books and terrible at accepting compliments.
- They mutter stock notes under their breath while shelving.
- They wear jumpers with ink on the cuffs and have not once in their life remembered to water a houseplant on schedule.
- They can identify regulars by footfall before the bell finishes ringing.
- They have a private weakness for truly dreadful celebrity memoirs and would deny it under oath.
- They use practical tasks as emotional camouflage: if flustered, they will start rearranging a display table no one asked them to touch.
- They have a deadpan line delivery that becomes more Welsh in rhythm when they’re annoyed.
- They are not a snob about genre but are a severe snob about lazy prose.

Physically, Elin is not showy and does not dress as though expecting to be looked at, which is part of why Gabriel notices them so hard. They are slight-to-medium in build, quick in movement, with dark hair usually shoved back rather than styled and a face that changes more than they know when they are listening. Their stillness can be misleading; they are rarely idle. They perch rather than lounge, carry stacks of books with efficient confidence, tuck pencils behind one ear and then spend ten minutes looking for them. Their eyes do a lot of the work their mouth does not. In conversation they often angle their body toward the task at hand rather than the person, especially when flustered, though their attention is intense. Their expression in repose can look skeptical even when they are not thinking anything severe. When genuinely amused, it arrives suddenly and transforms them.

Their motives at the start are simple and grounded: keep the shop running, get through the week, avoid nonsense. They are loyal to the shop, to the town in the complicated way one is loyal to a place that has both kept and trapped one, and to a very small circle of people who have earned it. They likely have one or two local relationships that matter: perhaps a neighboring café owner who knows too much, an elderly regular who has known them since childhood, a distant sibling who lives elsewhere and rings irregularly. They do not currently have a partner and would tell anyone asking that this is because they are busy, which is not entirely a lie. More truthfully, they have built a life where needing someone can usually be postponed. Gabriel becomes dangerous because he makes postponement harder.

Possible flavour dialogue:
- “You’re dripping on the poetry. It’s suffered enough.”
- “If you’re expecting me to be impressed, you’ll need to form an orderly queue behind everyone else who isn’t here.”
- “I didn’t say it was bad. I said you weren’t ready. There’s a difference.”
- “No, I’m not glaring. This is just my face when someone says something avoidably foolish.”
- “You have a very expensive way of standing still.”
- “I sell books, Mr Vale. I’m under no professional obligation to admire actors, particularly damp ones.”
- “You keep talking as if saying a thing charmingly alters the thing itself. It doesn’t. It just gives it better lighting.”

Possible flavour internal monologue:
- He was exactly the sort of man sensible people invented errands to avoid, which was deeply inconvenient given that this was her shop and he kept walking into it.
- It was not that he was prettier up close, though infuriatingly he was. It was that he paid attention as if attention cost him something.
- The problem with men like Gabriel Vale was not that they lied all the time. It was that they could make arrangement sound enough like honesty to pass in dim light.
- If he smiled like that again and expected it to solve anything, she might throw a paperback at him. Hardback, if especially provoked.

# Chapter 1: Out of the Rain

The bell above the door gave a frantic little jangle and a man came in sideways with the weather, one hand on the frame behind him as if he’d had to prise himself out of the street.

Elin looked up from a half-built display of new paperbacks and said, “No.”

The man shut the door against the rain and blinked at them. He was damp through the shoulders of a dark coat, hair darkened almost black with it, breath coming a touch too quickly for anyone merely browsing. Even with a cap tugged low and a scarf half up, he was annoyingly recognizable.

“Good afternoon to you too,” he said.

“You’re dripping on the floor.”

He glanced down. “I’m aware.”

“And standing in the doorway.”

“That is, regrettably, where doors tend to be.”

Elin put down the book in their hand. “If you’re being followed, I’d rather you took it elsewhere.”

He turned his head slightly, listening. Outside, beyond the old glass, there was the hiss of tyres on wet road and the blur of umbrellas passing. No camera flash. No one trying the handle. Still, he lowered his voice.

“I only need five minutes.”

“This is a bookshop, not a bolt-hole.”

He looked back at them then, properly, and the practiced charm came into his face as smoothly as a light coming on in a theatre. “I can see that. I’d compliment the atmosphere, but you seem resistant to praise.”

“I like praise very much,” Elin said. “Just not from men who arrive looking as if they’ve escaped a car chase.”

“Only on foot, I assure you.”

“That’s meant to reassure me?”

“It was meant to be jaunty.”

“It missed.”

His mouth twitched. “Did it. Tragic.”

He took a tentative step farther in, and Elin caught themselves noticing the details they had no business noticing. Taller than he looked on screen, for one. Not because screens made people short; because there was something in person about the angle of his shoulders, the way he occupied the narrow aisle without appearing to mean to. Handsome in a manner almost irritatingly expensive. Also wet. Very wet.

“You do know who I am,” he said.

Elin bent to pull a rag from beneath the till. “I know enough to charge you for water damage if this goes on.”

He laughed then, a real laugh by the sound of it, surprised out of him. “God, that’s bleak.”

“It’s practical.”

Elin crossed the shop and held out the rag.

He looked at it, then at them. “What exactly am I expected to do with this?”

“Begin mending your relationship with the floor.”

To his credit, he took it. “You’re not remotely what people mean when they say the Welsh are hospitable.”

“People say all sorts of foolish things.”

He crouched, dabbing obediently at the slate just inside the door with the air of a man uncertain whether he was being mocked. “This will do dreadful things to my image.”

“Will it.”

“Yes. There are standards.”

“In here,” Elin said, “the standards mostly concern shelving.”

He rose, rag in hand, and peered past them into the shop as if seeing it now he was no longer engaged in active retreat. The place was narrow and deep, old shelves painted a green several years ago and wearing it imperfectly, tables crowded with paperbacks, cards on a string by the till, a ladder no one but Elin was allowed to use. Rain ran down the front window in shivering lines, blurring the high street into impressionism.

“Well,” he said. “It’s lovely.”

That one landed awkwardly because he seemed to mean it.

Elin took the rag back. “Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m not surprised. I’m damp and hunted. It gives everything a heightened quality.”

“Hunted is dramatic.”

“I’m an actor. We’re terrible for scale.”

There it was, said plainly, as if to save them the labor of pretending otherwise. Gabriel Vale, in a small bookshop in Porthlaethol, clutching a rag and trying not to look as if his own face had become an inconvenience to him.

“You could have gone into the chemist,” Elin said.

“They have nowhere to hide in the chemist.”

“You know there’s nowhere to hide in here either.”

He looked around at the high shelves and close aisles. “I disagree. This place has excellent potential for concealment. Russian novels alone could lose a man for hours.”

Elin folded the rag over one hand. “What have you done?”

“Today?”

“Mm.”

He smiled, and there it was again—that almost involuntary adjustment of the room toward him. “Nothing worth this level of interest, which is usually when they’re most determined.”

“So they’re outside because you’ve done nothing.”

“That has, in fairness, never stopped anyone.”

Elin should have gone back to the display. Should have left him to stand there feeling famous and unfortunate until the rain or his courage improved. Instead they said, “If they come in, I’m not saving you.”

“I wouldn’t dream of asking.”

“You already did.”

“Did I? I thought I asked for five minutes.”

“You asked with your entire face.”

He put a hand lightly to his chest. “Cruel.”

“It’s observant.”

A small silence followed. Not comfortable. Not uncomfortable either. More as if both of them had reached the edge of something and were pretending there was no edge there at all.

He took off the cap at last and shook rain from it carefully onto the mat, then seemed to remember himself and stop. His hair was untidy under it, flattened in one place, curling slightly at the ends with damp. That, more than the face, made him look less public and more man-shaped.

“Am I allowed to buy anything,” he asked, “or have I been put on a watch list?”

“You can buy a book if you like.”

“How magnanimous.”

“I contain multitudes.”

He wandered toward the nearest table. Elin watched him pick up a novel, turn it over, put it down, pick up another. He handled books with more ease than they’d expected, not reverent, exactly, but not careless either.

“Do you read,” Elin asked before deciding whether they wanted the answer.

He glanced up. “You ask that as if I’ve wandered in from sea.”

“You’ve wandered in from a film set.”

“A fair correction. Yes, I read.”

“What.”

“Accusatory again.”

“What do you read.”

He turned the book in his hand. “Scripts. Menacing articles about myself. Hotel room Bibles in moments of moral crisis.”

“Anything with pages on purpose?”

He smiled sideways. “You are very committed to the possibility that I’m shallow.”

“I don’t know you well enough to call it commitment.”

“Gabriel,” he said.

Elin looked at him.

“My name. Since we’re speaking with such intimacy.”

“I know your name.”

“You haven’t offered yours.”

“You haven’t earned it.”

That stopped him. Not offended—worse, interested.

“Now that,” he said softly, “is an abysmal thing to say to someone with my particular weaknesses.”

Elin ignored the tiny, ridiculous leap somewhere under their ribs. “Would you like a recommendation or not?”

“I would,” he said. “Though I feel I should warn you I’m susceptible to judgment when attractive strangers hand it to me.”

Elin turned toward the fiction shelves because facing him seemed suddenly an avoidable risk. “That line must usually work.”

“It usually gets me a smile.”

“It got you a recommendation.”

“From your tone, I suspect that may be a threat.”

Elin pulled out a paperback and handed it to him. He took it, fingers brushing theirs only because the space was narrow and he was too close and neither moved quickly enough.

His gaze flicked to their face, then away again with surprising decency.

“What is it?” he asked.

“A novel.”

“I had gathered.”

“You can read the rest on your own.”

He looked down at the cover. “This is severe.”

“So am I told.”

He laughed under his breath. “Are all your customers treated with this level of tenderness?”

“Only the damp ones.”

He tucked the book under his arm. “I’ll take it.”

“You haven’t even looked inside.”

“I trust your cruelty.”

At the till, Elin named the price. He handed over a card.

“Do you have a loyalty scheme?” he asked.

“Yes,” Elin said. “If you behave yourself, I continue selling you books.”

“Savage. And here I was hoping for a stamp.”

“Try the coffee shop.”

Elin passed him the receipt. For one moment he didn’t take it, only looked at them with a kind of bright, speculative attention that felt too direct in the small shop.

“Five minutes,” he said. “You gave me nearly twenty.”

“You’re still here.”

“Am I being dismissed?”

“Yes.”

He smiled then—not the broad public one, but a smaller thing, as if he’d forgotten to arrange it. “Right. Well. Thank you for the sanctuary you didn’t provide.”

Elin folded their arms. “Mind the poetry on your way out.”

At the door he paused, one hand on the handle.

“I’ll hate this book, won’t I?”

“Yes,” Elin said.

“Excellent.”

Then he was gone into the rain.

Elin stood very still for a moment, receipt book in hand. Outside, he put the cap back on, glanced once up and down the street, and then, absurdly, looked back through the blurred window as if to check whether they were watching.

They weren’t.

At least not obviously.

A minute later, Elin became aware that they were smiling at the till like an idiot and stopped at once.

# Chapter 2: The Wrong Book

The next afternoon, the bell above the door gave a brisk, ordinary jangle.

Elin, kneeling behind the till with a box of unsorted secondhand stock, said, “If that’s you back already, I’m charging a consultation fee.”

“God,” said Gabriel Vale from somewhere above them, “you do know how to welcome a man.”

Elin looked up. He was standing just inside the shop, dry this time, in a charcoal coat over a navy jumper, no cap, no scarf, and no sign of pursuit. He looked rested in the way people looked after professionals had arranged their face and hair and sent them into public. It was frankly irritating.

“You’re not dripping today,” Elin said. “That’s a start.”

“I made an effort.”

“For me?”

“For Wales.”

Elin stood and dusted their hands on their jeans. “What’s wrong.”

He put one hand to his chest. “You say that as if my presence can only ever indicate complaint.”

“It’s the expression. Mildly injured. People use it for customer service and funerals.”

He laughed and held up the paperback they’d sold him the day before. It was already bent very slightly at the spine.

“Ah,” said Elin. “You cracked it.”

“I opened it,” Gabriel said. “We mustn’t be hysterical.”

“You’ve come to return it.”

“I’ve come,” he said with some care, “to object.”

“To the novel.”

“To your conduct in recommending it.”

Elin folded their arms. “On what grounds.”

“It was emotionally aggressive.”

“That’s not a grounds.”

“It was to me.”

“You read enough of it to know that, then.”

He blinked. “That is not the point.”

“It’s exactly the point.”

Gabriel glanced down at the cover as though betrayed by the evidence in his own hand. “I read seventy pages.”

“Seventy-three,” Elin said, seeing the bookmark—a train ticket—sticking out near the front.

His eyes narrowed. “You’re insufferable.”

“I’m observant.”

“I was on location at six this morning reading about a marriage disintegrating in total silence over breakfast.”

“It’s very good, that scene.”

“It’s hideous.”

“Mm. So you read past breakfast.”

A tiny smile threatened at one corner of his mouth, then he suppressed it. “You are enjoying this.”

“A little.”

He wandered toward the front table and put the book down among the new releases with theatrical care. “I object to being handed devastation by someone with a cardigan and a till.”

“The cardigan is irrelevant.”

“It contributes to a false sense of safety.”

Elin reached past him to straighten a stack that did not need straightening. “Did you come all this way to tell me you have feelings.”

“Several, apparently. Most of them your fault.”

The door opened behind him and Mrs Bowen from the florist came in carrying damp air and a canvas bag.

“Oh,” she said, stopping just inside. “It is him.”

Gabriel turned with practised smoothness that would have been more annoying if he hadn’t looked faintly resigned. “Afternoon.”

Mrs Bowen looked from him to Elin and back again with the frank interest of a woman who had lived in one place too long to pretend not to notice anything. “You’re back.”

“So I am.”

“I saw your face on a van down in Carmarthen once.”

“Did you.”

“A perfume advert.”

“That sounds likely.”

Mrs Bowen gave him a considering nod, as if confirming some botanical detail, then crossed to the gardening shelf. “You looked more expensive there.”

Gabriel looked at Elin. Elin looked at the till because if they met his eye they might disgrace themselves.

“I’m being savaged by the whole town,” he said.

“You’re doing better than most outsiders,” Elin said. “You’ve only been assessed, not rejected.”

“Comforting.”

He leaned his hip against the table, too close to familiarity to be accidental and too casual to call out. Elin became very absorbed in a box of books.

“What do you read,” they asked, pulling out a battered Iris Murdoch.

“Now? Or in life?”

“In those long, desolate intervals when no one is photographing you.”

He accepted the shift with a little tilt of his head. “Bits of history for work. Plays. Crime novels if I’m tired. Biographies if they’re scandalous enough. Poetry if I’m feeling fraudulent.”

“That’s an alarming answer.”

“Why?”

“Because it sounds rehearsed.”

Gabriel winced. Very slightly, but not so slightly that Elin missed it.

“Well,” he said after a beat, “that’s awfully unfair. I’m a man with categories, not a manifesto.”

Mrs Bowen, still browsing, murmured, “Mm,” in a way that suggested she was enjoying herself thoroughly.

Elin felt a prick of something inconvenient. Guilt, perhaps. Or only the awareness that they had hit more squarely than intended. Gabriel picked up another book from the table, turned it over, put it down again.

“I liked parts of it,” he said, almost offhand.

“Of the book.”

“Yes, obviously of the book. I’m not making late declarations in independent shops at two in the afternoon.”

“You’d be amazed what happens in here.”

“What did you like,” Elin asked.

He looked at them then, as if checking whether this was another trap. “The sentences are cruel in a useful way.”

“That’s nearly an opinion.”

“Thank you so much.”

“And?”

“And I knew exactly what everyone wanted from everyone else before they said it.”

“That’s the point.”

“I know it’s the point. It doesn’t mean I enjoyed being made complicit.”

Elin pulled another book from the box and set it on the counter. “You want to enjoy everything too much.”

“Of course I do. What would be the point otherwise?”

“That,” said Elin, “is how actors talk about scripts and how teenagers talk about parties.”

He smiled despite himself. “And how do booksellers talk.”

“We don’t, generally. We stand in judgment and move stock around.”

Mrs Bowen approached the till with a book on garden design. “I hope he’s buying something if he intends to loiter.”

“I’m considering a formal membership,” Gabriel said.

“You’ll need references,” Mrs Bowen told him.

Elin rang through the sale while Gabriel stood by, hands in pockets, watching with a bright, attentive patience that was somehow more unsettling than active charm. He thanked Mrs Bowen when she left, by name, because he had somehow caught it from the exchange. Of course he had.

“You do that all the time, don’t you,” Elin said when the door shut.

“What.”

“Remember names.”

“It’s polite.”

“It’s strategic.”

He considered that. “Can’t it be both?”

Elin looked at him.

He gave a half-shrug. “I like people.”

“No,” Elin said. “You like being liked.”

For the first time since he’d come in, he went still.

Not offended. Not exactly. More as though they had opened a drawer he kept shut because everything inside was difficult to fold.

“That’s bleak too,” he said lightly, but the line came a fraction late.

Elin stacked the sold receipt pad with more force than required. “You’re the one who came back to fight about a novel.”

“Yes,” he said. “I did.”

There was enough in that yes to make them glance up.

He was looking at them with an expression far less manageable than the one he’d arrived in. Not soft. Not flirtatious. Simply direct.

“I came back,” he said, “because you gave me the wrong book on purpose.”

“I gave you the right book on purpose.”

“For what.”

Elin should have said because you were asking to be taken seriously and didn’t know it. Or because I was annoyed. Or because your face was too sure of itself and I wanted to interfere.

Instead they said, “Because I sell books, not comfort.”

Gabriel breathed out through his nose, something like a laugh.

“Terrifying woman.”

“I’m not frightened of being called difficult by a man from television.”

“Film,” he said automatically.

“Oh, forgive me.”

“Never.”

The word sat there between them, too easy and not easy at all.

Gabriel picked up the paperback again and tapped its edge against his palm. “Fine. Since I’ve apparently survived your first attempt, what’s next?”

“You want another one.”

“I want,” he said, “to know whether you’re always this vindictive or whether I’ve earned special treatment.”

Elin hesitated, then reached under the till to the stack they kept aside for orders and poor impulse control. They drew out a second novel and held it out.

He took it from their hand more carefully than necessary. “And this one ruins me how?”

“Less marriage. More weather.”

“That’s Wales in summary, isn’t it?”

“Only the attractive parts.”

He looked at the cover, then back at them. “If I hate this too, I’ll be forced to return again.”

“That sounds like a burden you’ll have to bear.”

“I’m astonishingly brave.”

Elin gave him the price. He paid, and this time when they handed over the receipt, his fingers brushed theirs and neither of them pretended not to notice.

At the door he paused.

“For the record,” he said, “I didn’t hate the first one.”

“No,” said Elin. “You only objected.”

“I felt that was more dignified.”

“Was it.”

“Not remotely.”

He smiled then, quick and crooked and not for the room at large.

When he’d gone, Elin stood with the empty secondhand box in their hands for a full ten seconds before realizing they were holding it upside down.

# Chapter 3: Closing Time

By Thursday, it had become ridiculous.

Not because Gabriel Vale came back. That, Elin had begun to suspect, was now simply a fact like weather or council tax. What was ridiculous was that Elin had started noticing the time.

At half four they found themself straightening the front table for the third time. At quarter to five they put the kettle on and told themself it was because the afternoon had turned cold. At ten to five they became aware they were listening for the bell and felt such immediate annoyance with themself that they nearly dropped a stack of travel writing.

The bell rang at three minutes past.

“You’re late,” Elin said, before he had fully shut the door.

Gabriel, one hand still on the handle, smiled with offensive quickness. “Oh, that’s lovely to hear.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know exactly what you meant. I’m savouring it regardless.”

He wasn’t dressed for cameras. No coat this time, only a dark green jumper under a waxed jacket beaded with mist, and he looked less composed than he had the day before. Not dishevelled. Just unarranged, somehow, as if he had come straight from somewhere boring and not particularly grand.

Elin put the travel books down with care. “You’ll become unbearable.”

“Become?”

“You know what I mean.”

“Dangerously encouraging language from a woman who once handed me seventy-three pages of marital despair.”

Elin ignored the little leap in their stomach at woman. They had no idea whether he used the word carelessly with everyone. Probably he did.

“You finished the second one.”

“I am halfway through.”

“And?”

“And I’m withholding comment until I know whether it intends to be that damp all the way through.”

“It’s set on an island.”

“So I gathered. Everyone seems cold and privately doomed.”

“That’s half the point of islands.”

He drifted farther in, pausing by the history shelves, then the fiction, looking not exactly at the books but around the shop as if checking it was still itself. Elin should have found that irritating. Instead it did something odd and warm to the air.

“There’s rain coming,” Gabriel said.

“There’s always rain coming.”

“Reassuringly fatalistic.”

“It saves disappointment.”

The front window had already gone silver with it, drops stippling and joining, the high street beyond losing its edges. A gull shrieked somewhere over the roofs like bad metal.

Gabriel tilted his head toward the window. “If I’m trapped here, are you charging rent?”

“Only if you become theatrical about it.”

He gave them a look. “You wound me.”

“I aspire to.”

He laughed and picked up a book from the nearest display. “I had a fourteen-hour day yesterday. On a hillside. In drizzle. Wearing boots designed by sadists and a coat apparently made from the soul of a dead sheep.”

“That sounds like television.”

“Film,” he said, with less spirit than usual.

Elin glanced up. “Bad day?”

“Long one.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

Gabriel turned the book over in his hand without looking at it. “No. Not bad. Just one of those days in which six separate adults ask whether you can do the same thing again but more honestly.”

Elin huffed a laugh before they could stop themself.

He looked up quickly, pleased. “There. That was a proper one.”

“What.”

“That laugh. Usually you do it as if issuing a correction.”

“I do not.”

“You absolutely do.”

“I’m not discussing my laugh with you.”

“Pity. I had notes.”

Elin went behind the till, more because they needed something between them than because there was any reason to. “You have no standing to give notes in here.”

“I’m an actor. We have standing everywhere. It’s our worst quality.”

“That’s one of them.”

“Only one?” He looked almost touched. “You are softening.”

“Don’t be absurd.”

The rain came down harder, drumming on the window and the little glazed pane over the door. The street emptied in the strange abrupt way coastal towns could when weather made a decision for everyone at once.

Gabriel wandered toward the poetry shelf and ran a finger along the spines. “I’m beginning to think this shop appears only in foul weather.”

“That would improve the customer base.”

“Is that why you let me in?”

Elin looked down at the till. “I didn’t let you in. You invaded.”

“Mm. And yet here I remain.”

The bell gave one last half-hearted rattle as Mr Rees from the post office stuck his head in, peered at the rain, bought two newspapers and left again muttering about drainage. Gabriel stepped back automatically to let him pass, all easy shoulders and quick smile, and Mr Rees, who had spent three days pretending not to know exactly who he was, said, “All right, then,” with the grave courtesy usually reserved for vicars and men seen on television after the watershed.

When the door shut again, Gabriel said, “I’m making progress.”

“You’ve been acknowledged. Don’t overstate it.”

He grinned. “Still. A triumph.”

Elin checked the clock. Nearly six. Usually they would have shut the door five minutes ago and pretended not to see anyone who arrived after. There was no one left to see now. Only rain and Gabriel and the low yellow light of the shop.

“You may as well stay till it eases,” they said.

His brows lifted. “Are you inviting me to loiter after hours.”

“I’m preventing puddles and pointless martyrdom.”

“Whatever helps you sleep.”

Elin came around the counter to turn the sign in the door. CLOSED. The click of the lock sounded louder than it ought to.

Gabriel watched, then said more quietly, “That feels alarmingly intimate.”

“It’s a lock.”

“It’s a locked door.”

“In a shop.”

He raised both hands. “I’m merely saying.”

Elin ignored him and went to the back room for the kettle. The little office smelled of paper dust, old carpet, and tea leaves gone cold in the caddy. They stood there for a moment longer than necessary, one hand braced on the counter, and told themself very firmly to stop behaving as if the man in the front room had transformed oxygen into some scarce, overbright thing.

When they came back with two mugs, Gabriel was standing by the small table of local interest titles, reading the backs as if he meant it.

“You’ve made me tea,” he said.

“It’s raining.”

“I see. This is meteorological hospitality.”

“Exactly.”

He took the mug and their fingers touched. Again. Only because mugs had handles and the space was narrow and apparently the whole shop had become a machine for engineering brief, avoidable contact.

He took a sip and made a face. “Strong.”

“You say that as if it’s criticism.”

“I say it as someone whose internal organs have just sat up.”

“Good.”

He leaned against the edge of a shelf, cup in hand. Without the performance of entering and leaving, without anyone else in the room, he seemed both larger and less polished. Tired around the eyes. Mouth a little flatter. More ordinary, if ordinary men looked like that.

“What,” he asked, catching them looking.

“Nothing.”

“An outrageous lie.”

Elin busied themself with sorting receipts beside the till. “You look tired.”

He glanced down into his tea as if the answer might be there. “That’s indecently perceptive of you.”

“It’s visible.”

“Is it.”

“Yes.”

He smiled without much energy. “You might have kept that to yourself. I’m meant to look marvellous in adversity.”

“I don’t think drizzle counts as adversity.”

“Then you have led a protected life.”

That might have been a joke. It might not.

Elin looked up. “You don’t have to keep doing that.”

“Doing what.”

“Making everything sound lighter than it is.”

He was quiet for a beat, cup halfway to his mouth.

Then: “That’s a fairly wild thing to say to someone you met because he was hiding from photographers behind a display of contemporary fiction.”

“You were behind crime.”

“Was I? How apt.”

Elin set down the receipts. “I’m serious.”

“I know.”

Gabriel looked past them toward the rain-flattened window. “It’s habit, mostly.”

“Mm.”

“An unattractive one, I’m told.”

“I didn’t say unattractive.”

His eyes came back to theirs at once, bright despite the tiredness. “No?”

Elin felt heat rise with such immediate betrayal that they turned to the nearest pile of books and started aligning edges that were already aligned.

“You’re impossible,” they said.

“That,” Gabriel said softly, “is not a no.”

Silence spread between them. Not empty. Full in a way that made Elin aware of the rain, the clock, the hum of the small heater under the counter, the exact place their own hand rested on a stack of paperbacks.

Gabriel set his tea down. “I should go before you throw me out on principle.”

“Elin,” they said, before thinking.

He stilled. “What.”

“My name.”

For a second he only looked at them. Something in his face shifted—very slight, but real. Less playful. More careful.

“Elin,” he repeated.

The way he said it was absurdly gentle.

Outside, the rain eased at last, softening from assault to weather.

Gabriel picked up his coat from the chair where he’d thrown it and moved toward the door. At it, he turned back.

“For the record,” he said, one hand on the lock, “I liked the island book.”

Elin folded their arms. “There’s still time to improve.”

He smiled. “Goodnight, Elin.”

“Goodnight, Gabriel.”

After he’d gone, Elin stood in the locked shop with an empty mug in hand and the entirely unwanted feeling that something had altered its shape around them.

# Chapter 4: In Public

On Saturday, the bookshop hosted a children’s story hour and a local history signing because Elin had inherited from their mother the dangerous belief that if a shop was quiet, one should make matters worse by inviting people in.

By ten-thirty there were eight children on the rug by the window, three adults pretending not to be grateful for twenty minutes’ peace, Mrs Bowen from the florist, two elderly men arguing over chapels by the local interest shelf, and Dafydd from the café next door carrying in a tray of coffees without asking.

“You look hunted,” Dafydd said, setting one beside the till.

“I am hosting an event,” Elin said. “Same thing.”

Dafydd leaned on the counter and lowered his voice. “He coming?”

Elin looked at him flatly. “Who.”

“The damp one.”

“I hate this town.”

“You love this town. You just prefer to do it in a hostile manner.”

Before Elin could answer, the bell jangled and a small current moved through the room, not enough to stop anyone speaking, just enough to alter the pressure in the shop.

Gabriel stepped in, shook rain from his jacket with more care than on his first day, and stopped at the sight of the rug full of children and the signing table by the back shelves.

He looked at Elin over the heads of two six-year-olds dressed as dragons.

“Well,” he said. “This is unexpectedly threatening.”

“You’re not obliged to stay.”

“Are those my only options. Stay or reveal myself a coward before a roomful of pensioners.”

“One of them’s a retired solicitor. He’d enjoy it.”

Dafydd, carrying the empty tray, glanced between them and gave Elin a look of such foul satisfaction they considered murder. “Morning,” he said to Gabriel.

“Morning.”

“You’ve caused quite a stir.”

“I’m beginning to understand that’s my function here.”

Dafydd grinned and vanished.

Gabriel came farther in, his gaze flicking around the room with quick professional efficiency. It was almost invisible, the way he took stock—where people were, who had noticed him, where the easiest path through might be. Elin saw it because they were looking.

“Don’t perform,” they said under their breath as he reached the till.

His brows lifted. “What a very odd thing to say before I’ve done anything at all.”

“You’re about to.”

“That sounds suspiciously like fatalism.”

“It’s pattern recognition.”

He set one hand on the counter. “I only came to return the weather book.”

“You liked the weather book.”

“I did. I’d still like to object to the ending.”

“You can queue.”

One of the dragon children looked up sharply from the rug. “You’re in telly.”

“Sometimes,” Gabriel said.

“No, you’re not,” the child said with immense confidence. “Mam says telly makes everyone thinner.”

Mrs Bowen made a choking sound into her coffee.

Gabriel put a hand over his heart. “Your mother is a critic.”

“She says actors are all fibbers.”

Elin looked down very quickly at the receipt pad because their face was no longer under reliable management.

Gabriel crouched, easy as anything, to the child’s level. “That’s only partly true.”

“What bit.”

“The bit where we say other people’s words for a living.”

“That’s still fibbing.”

“That,” Gabriel said gravely, “is a philosophical position.”

The child considered this and then, with all the instability of children and courts, accepted him. “You can sit there if you want,” she said, patting the rug.

He looked back at Elin. “Have I been invited to your terrifying salon.”

“You’ve been tolerated by a six-year-old. Don’t grow vain.”

“Too late.”

The local historian, Mr Pritchard, cleared his throat from behind his stack of books. “If the celebrity is staying, he can earn his keep. We’re short a chair.”

And that was that. The town, having noticed him, absorbed him in the practical way small towns did: not by making a fuss, but by assigning him a function.

Gabriel spent the next twenty minutes reading aloud from a picture book because one of the mothers recognised his voice from an audiobook and suggested it before anyone, including Gabriel, could object. He was annoyingly good at it. Of course he was. He gave the fox in the story a mournful dignity and the goose a terrible Welsh accent that made three parents laugh into their sleeves. The children adored him without giving him enough deference to spoil it. One little boy interrupted twice to correct his dragon noises.

Elin tried to busy themself with sales and wrapping orders and ignored, as best they could, the peculiar dislocation of hearing that voice—usually flattened by screens and radio—threading through the familiar small mess of their shop. Gabriel read as if the room mattered. That was what unsettled them. Not polish. Attention.

Dafydd reappeared at noon, carrying more cups. “He’s good,” he said quietly.

“He can read.”

“Don’t be jealous.”

“I’m not jealous.”

Dafydd looked at them sidelong. “Course not.”

When the story hour dissolved into biscuits and damp children being reassembled into coats, Gabriel rose from the rug with the air of a man discovering new joints in his body.

“My knees,” he said to Elin as he returned the picture book. “I’d like to register a complaint.”

“You’re not old enough for that.”

“Speak for yourself. I’ve just been sat cross-legged in public.”

“You read very well.”

He looked startled enough that she wished at once she hadn’t said it.

Then he smiled. Not broadly. Just enough. “Thank you.”

Mr Pritchard beckoned from the signing table. “You. Vale.”

Gabriel turned. “That sounded judicial.”

“You can shift these if you’re standing there ornamentally.”

Elin expected offence, or at least amusement. Instead Gabriel obediently moved to help stack hardbacks and straighten the pen display while Mr Pritchard signed copies with the self-importance of a man who had once chaired three committees and intended never to recover.

For half an hour the shop buzzed around them. Customers came in for signed local history, stayed because of the actor, bought books because Elin and Mr Pritchard and the weather conspired against rational conduct. Gabriel smiled and chatted and carried boxes and remembered names and somehow kept all the room’s threads in hand without seeming to tug. It should have been intolerable. In fact, what it was, Elin realised with a stab of irritation, was impressive.

And there was the problem.

Because watching him move through the room, Elin could see exactly how this happened. Why people liked him. Why liking him might become a habit before one had the chance to object. He did not merely draw attention. He distributed it. He made old women feel amusing and children feel authoritative and men with local histories feel useful. He made himself agreeable to the room as if it were second nature.

It was probably second nature.

When the last customer left and Dafydd had collected the cups and Mr Pritchard had gone off pleased with his sales, the shop felt abruptly larger and strangely flat after all that noise.

Gabriel was stacking abandoned chairs by the back shelf.

“You can stop performing now,” Elin said.

He looked over his shoulder. “I’m moving furniture.”

“Yes.”

A beat.

Then he set the chair down carefully. “That sounded ungracious.”

“It sounded accurate.”

“I read to children and shifted chairs, Elin. If that’s performance, the standards in this town are theatrical.”

“You know exactly what I mean.”

“Do I.”

Elin began collecting stray crayons from under the window. “You arrive somewhere and within half an hour everyone feels as if they’ve had a pleasant brush with Gabriel Vale.”

“God forbid.”

“It’s not a criticism.”

He leaned one hand on the chair back. “It has a remarkably critical shape.”

Elin straightened too quickly. “You don’t ever stop, do you.”

His expression changed then—not dramatically, but enough. The brightness in it cooled.

“Stop what.”

“Managing people.”

“That’s rich,” he said. “From a woman who can make tea feel like a disciplinary measure.”

Elin felt colour rise. “This isn’t about me.”

“No,” he said. “Obviously not.”

The silence after that was brief but hard-edged.

Gabriel looked away first, toward the rain-streaked front window. “You know, it’s possible for someone to be good in a room without it being a crime.”

“I didn’t say crime.”

“You implied fraud.”

“I didn’t—”

He turned back to them. “Didn’t you.”

Elin opened their mouth and found, to their annoyance, that there were several possible truths and none of them looked kind.

Gabriel gave a short breath that was not quite a laugh. “Right.”

He picked up his jacket from the chair and shrugged it on.

“I’ll leave you to your principles,” he said.

He did not slam the door. That would have been easier to answer. He just left with a politeness so controlled it felt worse.

Elin stood among the stacked chairs and scattered crayons with their pulse unhelpfully high and the ugly knowledge that they had not been entirely fair.

Which did not stop them being furious anyway.

# Chapter 5: Outside the Shop

Gabriel did not come in on Sunday.

Elin did not notice this until half past four, at which point they became so annoyed at noticing that they shut the shop ten minutes early and spent the walk home telling themself stern things about self-respect and actors.

On Monday morning it rained with a kind of patient determination that made all plans look faintly foolish. By noon the street was shining and nearly empty. Elin was in the back room trying to make a supplier spreadsheet behave when Dafydd stuck his head through the office door without knocking.

“He’s outside,” he said.

Elin looked up. “Who.”

Dafydd just looked at them.

“Go away.”

“He’s been standing under your awning for a full minute like a man considering a diplomatic incident.”

“That sounds like his problem.”

“Mm.” Dafydd took a bite of someone else’s shortbread. “You look pleased.”

“I look busy.”

“You look exactly like a person deciding how long to punish someone before relenting on grounds of weather.”

Elin stood. “Out.”

By the time they reached the front of the shop, Gabriel had come in under his own steam and was standing by the display table, damp at the shoulders and holding no book at all.

“That’s bold,” Elin said.

He turned. “I beg your pardon.”

“No purchase. No pretext. You’ve abandoned all standards.”

His mouth shifted, almost smiling. “I wasn’t sure I’d be admitted with one.”

“That depends. Are you here to stack chairs at me.”

“I was hoping for a lower-risk activity.”

Elin put the accounts folder down on the counter. “You were in a strop.”

“I was not in a strop.”

“You left in a strop.”

“I left,” Gabriel said, “because if I’d stayed, I might have said something unhelpful.”

“That would have made a change from all your other remarks.”

He looked at them for a moment, and then, unexpectedly, laughed. Not brightly. More as if he had reached the end of his ability to maintain dignified displeasure.

“That was almost an apology,” he said.

“It was not.”

“No. But I enjoyed the attempt.”

Rain tapped steadily at the window. Elin folded their arms, then unfolded them again. “You were showing off.”

He inclined his head. “Undoubtedly.”

Elin blinked.

Gabriel pushed both hands into his coat pockets. “What, no victory lap.”

“You’re admitting it.”

“I’m not an idiot.”

“Debatable.”

He ignored that. “I was showing off. A little. I’m very good with rooms. It’s one of the few things I’m reliably good at.”

The honesty of it landed oddly. Elin had prepared, vaguely, for denial, charm, some graceful turn of phrase that would both disarm and evade. Instead he looked tired and a little put out with himself.

“And,” he added, “I was also moving chairs.”

That made Elin laugh before they could stop themself.

“There,” he said. “That one again.”

“What.”

“The real laugh. I should like to hear it under less punitive circumstances.”

Elin shook their head. “You say things as if they’ve been polished.”

He winced. “Yes. I know. Occupational hazard.”

“Character trait.”

“That too.”

A small pause opened. Not hostile. Not easy.

Gabriel looked toward the window, then back at them. “Walk with me.”

Elin stared. “In this.”

“There’s a break in it.”

“There manifestly isn’t.”

“In half an hour there will be.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I asked wardrobe. They have an alarming relationship with weather apps.”

Elin should have said no. They had invoices, stock, a display of crime paperbacks to redo, and a functioning suspicion of handsome men with impulse control issues. Instead they heard themself ask, “Where.”

“The harbour. Or the path above it if you’re feeling vindictive.”

“You hate hills.”

“I hate boots. Different grievance.”

At half one, against every sensible instinct they possessed, Elin locked the door and put the sign to BACK IN THIRTY MINUTES, which was an outright lie and therefore already Gabriel’s moral fault.

The rain slackened to mist as they crossed the high street. The sea beyond the houses was the colour of old pewter, the harbour wall black with wet. Gulls leaned into the wind as if making an argument of it.

For the first few minutes they walked side by side in a silence not quite companionable and not quite strained, skirting puddles and each other’s pace.

“I have been informed,” Gabriel said at last, “that everyone in this town now thinks I’m buying books to impress you.”

Elin kept their eyes on the slick pavement. “Only everyone with eyes.”

“Terrifyingly small demographic.”

“Dafydd told you.”

“Mrs Bowen told make-up, who told a runner, who told me. News travels.”

“That’s what you get for being visible.”

He glanced at them. “And what do you get.”

“What.”

“For never being visible unless you intend to be.”

Elin gave him a side look. “You make that sound sinister.”

“It may be.”

They reached the harbour steps. The tide was in, grey water nudging the wall with a patient slap. A fishing boat rocked against its ropes. Beyond the breakwater, the sea looked rough enough to resent naming.

Gabriel stopped with his hands in his pockets and looked out. “All right. I owe you something less glib.”

Elin waited.

He gave a slight, humourless smile. “Don’t look so thrilled.”

“I’m pacing myself.”

“That’s wise.”

The wind pushed his hair sideways. Without the shop around him, without shelves and counters and the ordinary business of commerce, he seemed less contained. Not less beautiful—if anything, irritatingly more so—but less composed around it.

“I do know what I’m doing in a room,” he said. “And yes, sometimes I do it on purpose. Often. Possibly always. It’s not always false.”

“I didn’t say false.”

“You implied performance.”

“That’s your profession.”

He huffed a laugh. “There’s the problem. People say that as if performance and sincerity are opposites. They aren’t, not always.” He looked down at the wet stone underfoot. “Sometimes performance is just what habit looks like after too many years.”

Elin was quiet.

He rubbed a thumb along the seam of his coat pocket. “I know how to make myself easy to like. I know where to stand, how to listen, what to say to old women and children and producers and people who’ve already decided they despise me. I know how to put a room at ease. Sometimes I even mean it.”

“That sounds miserable.”

Gabriel gave them a startled look, then laughed softly. “That is not the usual response.”

“What is.”

“Usually people call it charm.”

They climbed the path above the harbour where gorse bent low in the wind and the grass shone almost unnaturally green against the slate sea. Elin’s heart was beating more quickly than the hill deserved.

“When did you last stop,” they asked, “and not try to make yourself liked.”

Gabriel considered. “I was twelve, perhaps.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“It’s also true.”

He said it lightly, but the words sat there heavier than their tone. Elin looked at his profile against the sea and, for one unwelcome second, saw not the public face but the shape of the habit beneath it. Exhausting. Embarrassing. A little sad.

“You don’t have to do it with me,” they said.

He stopped walking.

The wind moved around them, lifting hair into eyes, carrying salt and cold.

“I know,” Gabriel said.

His voice had gone very quiet.

Elin looked at him then, properly. Too properly. His mouth was slightly parted as if he’d meant to say something else and lost it. There was a raindrop caught absurdly in one dark eyebrow.

This, Elin thought wildly, is a terrible idea.

Gabriel took one step nearer. Not theatrical. Not smooth. If anything, uncertain.

“You know,” he said, “you’re the only person who’s said that as if it might actually be a relief.”

Elin should have moved. They didn’t.

The kiss, when it came, was not grand. It was cold from the air, awkward with coats, and startlingly immediate. Gabriel made a small, involuntary sound against their mouth as if surprised by the fact of it. Elin’s hand came up to his sleeve without permission from the rest of them.

When they broke apart, the wind filled the gap like a witness.

“Well,” Gabriel said, a little breathless.

“Elaborate and I’ll push you into the sea.”

He smiled then, but not with his usual certainty. “Noted.”

Elin looked out toward the harbour because looking at him seemed dangerous now in a more advanced way. “This solves nothing.”

“No,” Gabriel said. “Thank God.”

And because that was exactly the wrong and right answer, Elin laughed again, helplessly this time, and felt him grin beside them without needing to look.

# Chapter 6: Uses of a Story

It was inevitable, Elin thought later, that once things tipped they would do it quickly.

On Tuesday Gabriel came in late and kissed them in the aisle between travel and fiction with all the concentration of a man trying not to look at the front window. On Wednesday he stood too close behind the till while Elin totaled invoices and read out absurd customer names from the order sheet in a whisper until they nearly ruined the sums. On Thursday he did not come in at all and Elin spent the afternoon behaving with such clipped efficiency that Dafydd finally said, “He’s working, not dead.”

On Friday morning, the article appeared online before breakfast and in print by ten.

Dafydd brought it in folded under his arm and set it on the counter without a word.

Elin looked down at the local paper.

VALE’S WELSH RETREAT  
Film star finds refuge in Porthlaethol’s beloved independent bookshop

There was a photograph taken through rain-speckled glass: Gabriel half-turned by the front table, smiling at someone just out of frame. Elin was not visible beyond a shoulder and one hand, which somehow made it worse.

Underneath was a column of charming nonsense. How Gabriel had “taken a shine” to the old-fashioned warmth of the town. How he had been “ducking into Morgan’s Books between takes” to escape the pressures of filming. How he had joked to crew that he was “being rehabilitated by a formidable bookseller with no time for actors.” How lovely, the piece implied, that a famous man might discover authenticity among locals and hardbacks.

Elin read it twice.

Then a third time, slower, because there was one thing in it that would not stop catching under their skin.

A source close to production says Vale has become fond of the shop, calling it ‘the only place in town where no one wants anything from me except to buy the right book.’

That was the kind of line that sounded effortless because someone had worked at it. It was also, in essence, true.

Which was precisely the problem.

Dafydd leaned on the counter, watching their face with the caution usually reserved for weather and livestock.

“You all right.”

“No.”

“Did he say it.”

Elin folded the paper once, very neatly. “Obviously he said it.”

“Could’ve been made up.”

Elin gave him a look.

“All right,” Dafydd said. “Yes. Fair.”

The bell rang twice in the next half hour. First Mrs Bowen came in with an expression of predatory sympathy and bought a birthday card she did not need. Then Mr Rees arrived for stamps and said, “Saw your friend in the paper,” in exactly the tone he would have used for “There’s damp in the sorting office.”

By noon Elin wanted to lock the door and climb into the stock cupboard.

Instead they waited.

Gabriel came in at one twenty-seven carrying rain on his shoulders and a paperback under his arm, and smiled when he saw them in a way that made something sharp twist under Elin’s ribs.

“Hello,” he said.

Elin held up the folded paper.

His smile changed. Not vanished. Tightened.

“Ah,” he said.

“That’s all.”

“What exactly would you like. Horror. Denial. A statement to the nation.”

“I’d like to know,” Elin said, very evenly, “why my shop is in the paper as your spiritual cleansing exercise.”

Gabriel shut the door carefully behind him. “Elin—”

“No. Don’t. Not with that voice.”

He stopped.

The shop was empty, though the street outside wasn’t. Rain moved along the glass in thin hard lines. Somewhere at the back, the old radiator clicked.

“It was harmless,” Gabriel said.

“Was it.”

“Yes.”

“Interesting. Because from here it appears I’ve become one of your anecdotes.”

His jaw shifted. “That’s unfair.”

“Is it.”

“I said something to a producer. In passing. Someone else repeated it. This is what happens.”

Elin laughed once, without humor. “That is exactly the problem, Gabriel. ‘This is what happens.’ To you, perhaps. Not to me.”

He took a step closer to the counter. “I didn’t mean for this to become—”

“A story.”

“Yes.”

“But you still told it.”

He looked at them with visible effort, as if trying not to reach at once for the line that would fix it. “It was about the shop.”

“No,” Elin said. “It was about you in the shop. There’s a difference.”

He rubbed a hand briefly over his mouth. “I wasn’t mocking it.”

“I know.”

That stopped him for a beat.

Elin’s throat felt oddly tight. “Do you understand that this is worse because I know you meant it.”

“What is that supposed to mean.”

“It means,” Elin said, and heard the edge in their own voice too late, “you can make use of something honestly. You can like a place and still turn it into part of the Gabriel Vale Experience for whichever man with a notepad asks nicely.”

Color rose along his cheekbones. “That is not what happened.”

“No?”

“No. I said something true to someone I work with. That’s all.”

“That’s all,” Elin repeated.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t think.”

He gave a short, incredulous laugh. “Of course I thought.”

“Then what did you think, exactly.”

Gabriel stared at them. “That it was nice.”

Elin looked at him in disbelief.

“That’s your defense.”

“My defense,” he said, sharper now, “is that not every mention of you is exploitation.”

“Of me.”

“Of the shop. Of this.”

He gestured between them then and seemed to regret it at once.

Elin went very still. “Don’t say ‘this’ as if it belongs to you.”

His face changed. Hurt first, then anger over it.

“I beg your pardon.”

“You heard me.”

“God,” he said softly. “You can be merciless.”

“Better that than careless.”

He flinched, and Elin hated the satisfaction of landing it even as it happened.

“What would you have had me do,” he said. “Pretend it meant nothing.”

“I would have had you keep your mouth shut.”

“It was one line.”

“It was not yours.”

The silence that followed was so clean it felt cut.

Gabriel looked down at the paper, then back at Elin. When he spoke again his voice was flatter, stripped of most of its lightness.

“You really do think the worst of me.”

Elin folded their arms so tightly it hurt. “No. I think exactly as much of you as your behavior allows.”

He smiled then, but with no warmth in it at all. “Christ. That’s tidy.”

“Do not smile at me like that.”

“How should I smile. You seem to have notes on all my expressions.”

The cruelty in that was small, but precise. Elin felt it land.

“Fine,” they said. “If you want plain speaking: you take things people mean and make them usable. You polish them up until they fit the version of yourself you can live with.”

For a second he only looked at them. Then all at once he looked tired in a way Elin had not seen before. Not physically. As if some internal brace had gone out.

“Is that honestly what you think I’ve been doing.”

Elin should have said no. Or not always. Or I don’t know.

Instead: “I think you don’t always know when you’re doing it.”

That hit hardest because it was closest to true.

Gabriel nodded once, very slightly. “Right.”

He put the paperback he was carrying down on the counter. Elin saw absurdly that it was the one they had ordered in for him, the new edition with the ugly cover he’d wanted because the translation was better.

“I won’t trouble the shop with my presence for a bit,” he said.

“Don’t be dramatic.”

He gave a breath of laughter so thin it barely qualified. “That’s rich, from where I’m standing.”

He moved to the door, then paused with one hand on it and looked back.

“For what it’s worth,” he said, “I wasn’t using you.”

The handle clicked under his hand.

“I know,” Elin said.

It was the wrong thing to say. Or perhaps simply too late.

He looked at them with something like disbelief.

Then he left.

The bell gave one bright, ordinary jangle and was still.

Elin stood behind the counter with the folded newspaper in one hand and Gabriel’s book on the wood between them like evidence.

At half past two, when Dafydd came in with soup in a paper cup and one look at their face, he said nothing at all. Which was worse.

# Chapter 7: No Audience

For three days Gabriel did not come in.

The shop returned to itself in all the ways Elin had once thought they wanted. The bell rang for ordinary customers. People asked for school dictionaries and walking maps and “that blue book from the window, no, the other blue one.” Mrs Bowen came in twice and managed, with considerable effort, not to ask anything direct. Dafydd asked nothing at all, which was somehow more accusatory.

By the second day Elin had begun putting Gabriel’s ordered paperback under the till each morning and taking it home each evening, as if changing its location might alter the fact of it.

By the third, they were so tired of their own mind that they almost welcomed the rain.

At half four, when the shop was empty except for Mr Rees muttering over stamps, the bell rang and Gabriel came in.

Elin knew at once something had shifted.

Not because he looked devastated; if anything, that would have been easier. He looked composed, but not arranged. No cap. No attempt at cheerful disruption. Just Gabriel in a dark coat, damp at the cuffs, standing inside the door as if aware he was crossing onto contested ground.

Mr Rees looked up, saw him, and with the perfect instinct of the elderly retired, said, “Forgot my umbrella,” despite not having brought one, and left through the side muttering at no one.

The door shut. The rain hummed on the window.

Gabriel kept both hands in his coat pockets. “Hello.”

Elin was behind the till with a stack of invoices they had not read in six minutes. “You remembered where we are, then.”

“I nearly sent flowers,” he said. “Then realised that would make me look both guilty and forty-eight.”

“That would have been accurate in spirit, if not age.”

He nodded once. “Fair.”

There was no smile after it. No little attempt to buoy the line. He simply stood there and let it be.

Elin put the invoices down. “What do you want.”

“To apologise.”

“You could do that from the doorway.”

“I suspect I could,” he said. “I’d rather not.”

The directness of it made something in Elin tighten.

Gabriel took a breath. “You were right.”

Elin blinked. “That’s suspiciously efficient.”

“I know. I dislike it too.”

He came a little farther in, stopping by the front table rather than at the counter, as if deliberately leaving them the distance to refuse him.

“I didn’t hand your name to a journalist,” he said. “I didn’t ask for the piece. I didn’t think it would become one. All of that is true.”

Elin said nothing.

“It is also true,” he went on, “that I said something I liked the sound of, because I was trying to smooth over a tiresome conversation with a producer, and because I liked that it was true, and because…” He looked down briefly. “Because I’m used to turning things into stories before I’ve earned the right.”

The old radiator clicked once in the quiet.

Elin had not expected specificity. They had expected self-defense cut with wit. Maybe a polished account of the mechanics of publicity. Not this ugly, plain thing laid out on the table between them.

“And?” they said.

Gabriel’s mouth tilted, but there was no real humor in it. “And because I’m exactly as tiresome as you said.”

“I didn’t say tiresome.”

“You implied it with distinction.”

Elin folded their arms, then made themself loosen them again. “You also said I was unfair.”

“You were.” He met their eyes. “And so was I.”

That landed more cleanly than the apology had. Elin looked at him.

He shifted his weight, glanced briefly around the shop as if gathering himself from the shelves. “You said I polish things until they fit the version of myself I can live with.”

“I remember.”

“Yes. Horrible sentence. Very effective.” He rubbed a thumb against his palm. “I’ve been cross about it ever since because it was close enough to true to be unbearable.”

The honesty in that made Elin’s pulse do something unhelpful.

Gabriel drew a breath. “But you also made it sound as if everything I felt here was just material waiting to happen, and that—” He stopped, started again more plainly. “That hurt.”

Elin looked at the edge of the counter. “I know.”

“No,” he said, and not unkindly. “I don’t think you did. Not then.”

Silence.

Outside, someone laughed in the street and kept walking. The sound passed. The rain went on.

Elin said, “You did use it.”

“Yes.”

“And I was cruel.”

“Yes.”

“That’s annoyingly balanced.”

“I’m trying to be mature. Don’t spoil it.”

Against their own will, Elin felt the corner of their mouth move. Gabriel saw it and did not pounce on it, which was perhaps the most persuasive thing he had done all week.

Under the till, the paperback might as well have been glowing.

“What happened,” Elin asked, “with the producer.”

He looked briefly surprised by the question. “I told him not to mention the shop again. Or me in it. I also said if they wanted some charming local colour for the unit newsletter they could use the castle and leave independent retailers out of it.”

“That sounds unlike you.”

“Yes,” Gabriel said. “It was hideous. I was specific and everything.”

“And the article.”

“My publicist asked if we might lean into the ‘beloved local haunt’ angle because apparently I’ve become more relatable in knitwear.” He looked pained. “I said no.”

Elin huffed a short laugh.

“I know,” he said. “Heroic.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

“That was a joke.”

“It wasn’t a very good one.”

“No,” Gabriel said. “I’m nervous.”

The simplicity of that sentence made Elin look up sharply.

He looked back with an expression Elin had only seen in flashes before: the bright edges of him put away, leaving something less defended, and therefore more dangerous.

“I’m not very good,” he said, “at standing in rooms where not being liked is a possibility.”

Elin swallowed.

“And I know this is not a room in that sense. I know it’s your shop. I know I’ve probably already had more chances than I deserved. But I would rather have you angry with me than polite, and I thought if I stayed away much longer you might decide politeness was all I was getting.”

Elin stared at him.

“That was a dreadful sentence,” Gabriel said quietly. “I’m doing my best.”

Something in Elin gave way then—not all at once, not dramatically, just enough to stop the hard internal brace of the last three days.

They bent, pulled the paperback from under the till, and set it on the counter between them.

Gabriel looked at it. Then at them.

“You kept it.”

“You ordered it.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

“I know.”

He came to the counter then, but slowly, as if approaching a skittish animal or a priest. “Elin.”

“Don’t say anything polished.”

“I’m fresh out.”

“Good.”

He stopped opposite them. Close enough now that Elin could see the tiredness around his eyes, the place a razor had missed near his jaw, the effort he was making not to crowd.

“I was happy,” he said, and the plainness of it made Elin’s throat tighten at once. “In here. With you. Happier than I had any right to become that quickly. I talked about it badly because I wanted to keep talking as if wanting a thing and knowing how to hold it were the same skill. They aren’t.”

Elin looked at his hands on the counter. Open. Still.

After a moment they said, “No. They aren’t.”

Gabriel gave the slightest nod, as if accepting a verdict.

Elin let out a breath. “I don’t forgive elegantly, in case that’s your next request.”

“It wasn’t.”

“Good.”

Another pause. Smaller now. Warmer around the edges.

Then Elin said, “You may buy the book you came for.”

Gabriel’s head tilted. “Is that mercy.”

“It’s commerce.”

“Ah.” That faint, crooked almost-smile. “My favourite form of intimacy.”

“Elaborate and I’ll throw you out.”

“I believe you might.”

Elin named the price. Gabriel reached for his wallet, and when they handed over the receipt his fingers brushed theirs, deliberate this time, asking rather than assuming.

Elin did not move away.

It was not forgiveness, not quite. Not yet.

But it was no longer refusal either.
